# Canva Browser Mastery

Use this skill when you design in Canva in a browser for Kind, including BLACK BOX social posts, MOTORLIST demo tiles and any other graphic. It covers the Canva web editor only. Kind forbids every Canva AI feature, so this playbook teaches manual design only, built from templates, elements, shapes, text and uploads.

## Design without Canva AI

- Never open Magic Write, Magic Design, Magic Media, Dream Lab, Magic Edit, Magic Eraser, Magic Expand, Magic Grab, Magic Switch, Magic Resize, Magic Animate, Background Remover, Upscale or the Canva AI chat for Kind. Kind forbids all Canva AI generation.

- Build every design by hand from templates, elements, shapes, text and uploads. If a task seems to need an AI tool, stop and ask Kind instead of working around the ban.

- Do not use the Canva connector image generation tools for Kind either. The connector is fine for creating designs, uploading files and exporting, but its image generation and background removal tools stay off limits.

- Remove a background without AI by using a source image that already has a transparent background, or crop the image tightly and place it inside a frame.

- Resize a design without Magic Resize by creating a new canvas at the new size and copying the elements across, then fixing the layout by hand.

- Write copy yourself or reuse copy Kind approved. Do not ask Magic Write for headlines or captions.

- Generate images outside Canva only if Kind asks for that route. Never present an AI image as a manual design.

## Start a design

- Sign in at canva.com with Google and choose <YOUR_GOOGLE_ACCOUNT>. If Google shows a password screen, stop and let Kind enter it himself.

- Dismiss the Canva passkey prompt with Skip for now when it appears. It is a Canva account checkup page, not a required step.

- Click Create a design at the top right of the home page, then pick a preset or Custom size.

- Use presets when they match the destination. Instagram Post square is 1080 by 1080 px. Instagram Story and Reel are 1080 by 1920 px. Presentation is 16 by 9. A4 is 210 by 297 mm.

- Pick Custom size when no preset matches. Type the width and height and choose px, in, mm or cm. Canva accepts 40 to 8000 px per side and the total area must stay under 25,000,000 square px, so an 8000 px wide design can be at most 3125 px tall.

- Name the design at the top of the editor so it is findable later under Projects. Canva autosaves every change to the cloud.

## Read the editor

- Learn the three zones. The canvas sits in the centre. The left side panel holds the tools. The top toolbar changes with the selected element.

- Open Templates from the left panel to browse ready made layouts. Open Elements for shapes, lines, icons, stickers, charts, frames, photos and videos. Open Uploads for your own files. Open Text to add headings, subheadings and body text. Open Brand for brand colours, fonts and logos. Open Apps for extras such as Bulk Create.

- Read the top toolbar from left to right. File holds save, settings and print bleed. Undo and redo sit near the top left. Resize sits in the top bar and needs Pro. Share sits at the top right.

- Find finished and in progress designs under Projects in the left menu of the home page. Use folders once you have more than about 20 designs.

## Build from a template

- Choose the design type first so templates are filtered to the right dimensions. Then search the Templates tab with two or three keywords such as minimal product launch.

- Scan the first row of results before scrolling further. Canva relevance ranking usually puts a good match in the first five.

- Treat a small crown on a thumbnail as a Pro only template or element. You can load it on a free plan to preview, but the export carries a Canva Pro watermark unless you replace every Pro element.

- Change one element at a time and keep the template layout intact. Replace the text, swap the photo, then adjust colours to the brand. The spacing and font pairing in the template are what make the result look professional.

- Double click any text to edit it. Drag a new photo over an old one to swap it while keeping its position, size and crop.

- Save a finished layout as your own template with File then Save as template when you need the same format again. This needs Pro.

## Add and style text

- Press T to add a text box anywhere on the canvas. Or open Text in the left panel and pick Add a heading, Add a subheading or Add a little body text.

- Keep three levels at most. One headline, one subheading and one body style. Give the headline the biggest size and the boldest weight.

- Change font, size, colour, alignment, line spacing and letter spacing from the top toolbar with the text selected.

- Pair at most two fonts in one design. Use one display font for headlines and one readable font for body text. Keep the template fonts on a first pass because beginners usually pick worse pairings.

- Open Effects in the top toolbar with text selected to reach Drop, Hollow, Splice, Echo, Glitch, Neon and Curve. The current editor labels the shadow effect 'Drop', not 'Shadow', and there is no 'Lift' effect in the list (verified in the first browser build, 2026-11-06).

- Use Drop for depth and set its offset, direction, blur and transparency with the sliders — on the full desktop layout only. In the narrow layout the Effects panel offers the effect choice but no sliders.

- Use Hollow for an outline only look and set its thickness. Hollow works best with chunky fonts. Use Splice for an outline plus shadow cut out look.

- Use Echo for repeated shadow layers on short bold text. Use Glitch for a digital distortion look and pick one of its two colour pairs. Use Neon for a glow that works best on dark backgrounds.

- Use Curve at the bottom of the Effects panel under Shape to bend text into an arch or a circle. Drag the slider right for a downward arch and left for an upward smile shape. Curved text suits badges, seals and circular logos.

- Apply one effect per text box to solve one visual problem. Stacking effects muddies the text. For layered looks, duplicate the text box and style each copy separately.

- Keep body text readable over photos by adding a semi transparent rectangle behind it or by applying Lift or Shadow. Never place small text over a busy photo without a backing shape.

## Shapes, elements, frames and grids

- Press R for a rectangle, C for a circle and L for a line. Or open Elements and search for the shape, icon or graphic you need.

- Drag a corner handle to resize an element and keep its proportions. Drag the centre to move it. Press Delete to remove it.

- Recolour a shape from the top toolbar with it selected. Use the eyedropper in the colour picker to match a colour already in an uploaded image.

- Search Elements for frame to find shapes that crop photos. Drag a frame onto the canvas, then drag a photo onto it. Canva snaps the photo into the frame shape.

- Double click a photo inside a frame to reposition it or change its zoom without breaking the frame outline. This is the fastest way to make circular profile photos and shaped image crops.

- Use grids from Elements to build multi photo layouts. Drag one photo into each cell of the grid.

- Use charts from Elements for simple data graphics. Edit the values in the chart panel after placing one.

## Photos and uploads

- Open Uploads in the left panel and click Upload files, or drag a file from the computer straight onto the editor. Uploaded files stay in the account and are reusable in every later design.

- Search Photos in the left panel for free stock photos. Filter results to Free under Price to avoid Pro assets.

- Replace a photo by dragging the new one over the old one. Canva keeps the old position, size and crop.

- Keep uploads under the plan storage limit. Free plans include 5 GB. Check the file size before uploading large videos.

## Edit photos without AI

- Select a photo and click Edit in the top toolbar. The panel offers Adjust, Filters, Crop and Effects.

- Work in this order. Crop first, then fix light, then fix colour, then add detail.

- Start Adjust with Auto adjust for a quick fix, then fine tune brightness, contrast, saturation, warmth, highlights, shadows and clarity with the sliders.

- Open Select area under Adjust to limit changes to All, Foreground, Background or a brushed area.

- Pick a filter and drag its Intensity slider down. Most filters look best at half strength or less.

- Use Effects for Duotone, Glitch, Pixelate, Vignette and similar treatments. Each has an intensity slider.

- Crop with the Crop button in the top toolbar and drag the handles, then click Done. Double click a photo inside a frame to adjust its crop instead.

- Do not use Upscale, Magic Eraser, Magic Edit or Background Remover for Kind. All four are AI tools and stay off limits even though they sit in the same Edit panel.

## Layers, position and alignment

- Treat every object as a layer in a stack. The top layer in the list is the frontmost object on the canvas.

- Open the Layers panel with Position in the top toolbar, then the Layers tab in the left panel. Click any row to select that exact element, which beats hunting for overlapping items on the canvas.

- Drag rows up or down in the Layers panel to reorder the stack. Or right click an element and pick Bring to Front, Bring Forward, Send Backward or Send to Back.

- Select several elements by holding Shift and clicking each one, or by dragging a selection box around them.

- Group a selection with Ctrl G so the pieces move and resize as one unit. Ungroup with Ctrl Shift G.

- Align a selection with Position then Arrange. Pick Left, Centre, Right, Top, Middle or Bottom. Select three or more objects and click Tidy Up to space them evenly.

- Watch for purple smart guides while dragging. They appear when an element lines up with another element or with the page centre.

- Lock a finished background or logo with Alt Shift L so later edits cannot move it by accident. Unlock it from the Layers panel.

- Change an element opacity with the Transparency button in the top toolbar. A semi transparent rectangle over a photo makes a clean backing for text.

- Type exact X and Y values under Position then Advanced when a drag is not precise enough.

## Colour and brand

- Open Brand in the left menu of the home page to set up a Brand Kit. Add logos, colours, fonts and templates there once and reuse them in every design.

- Paste HEX codes for brand colours instead of picking by eye. Keep the palette to 5 to 10 colours with 2 to 3 primary, 2 to 3 secondary and 2 to 3 neutrals.

- Upload logos as transparent PNG or SVG. Keep at least a full colour version, a white version for dark backgrounds and an icon only version.

- Set font roles in the Brand Kit for heading, subheading and body text. Pick from the Canva library or upload a licensed custom font on Pro.

- Know the free plan limit. A free Brand Kit stores 3 brand colours only. Logos, extra fonts and multiple kits need Pro, so on a free plan keep a written list of brand HEX codes and font names beside the skill and reapply them by hand.

- Do not invent brand colours. Use only the HEX codes Kind approved for that brand.

## Video and animation

- Start video from a video preset such as Video, Instagram Reel or YouTube Short. Reel and Story are 1080 by 1920 px.

- Add clips from Elements then Videos or from Uploads. Drag clips onto pages in order. Each page is one scene.

- Trim a clip by dragging its handles at the bottom of the editor. Split a clip at the playhead with Split in the top toolbar.

- Reorder clips by dragging them along the timeline at the bottom of the editor.

- Add a transition by clicking the plus icon between two clips and picking Add transition. Choose a style such as Fade or Slide and set its direction and duration. Use Apply between all pages for one consistent transition.

- Animate an element by selecting it and clicking Animate in the top toolbar. Pick Rise, Pan, Block, Pop, Breathe, Tumble or Drift and set speed, direction and easing.

- Animate a whole page by clicking empty canvas and picking a Page Animation. Do not use Magic Animate for Kind because it is an AI tool.

- Add music from Elements then Audio. Drag a track onto the page and trim it like a clip. Set volume and fade in or out from the audio toolbar.

- Set each photo page to 3 to 5 seconds for social clips. Export finished video as MP4.

## Download, share, publish and print

- Click Share at the top right, then Download. Pick the file type first, then the pages, size and quality.

- Export PNG for social posts and anything that needs a transparent background. Export JPG for photos and smaller files. Export PDF Standard for documents and online sharing. Export PDF Print for professional printing. Export MP4 for video and GIF for short looping animations. SVG needs Pro.

- Turn on Transparent background only for PNG, SVG or GIF. The checkbox appears after you pick one of those types. It needs Pro, Teams, Business or Education. Delete the page background first or set it to white.

- Use PNG at the highest size for Instagram posts and carousels. For a multi page carousel, export all pages as PNG in one download.

- Share a design with Share then Copy link. Choose View only, Can edit or Template link. A template link lets others copy the design without touching your original.

- Publish a design as a live website from Share then Publish as website. The page updates live when you edit the design. Canva gives it a Canva URL.

- Schedule social posts from Share with the Content Planner. It posts to Instagram, Facebook, Pinterest, LinkedIn, X and TikTok at a set date and time.

- Order prints from Share then Print with Canva Print, or export PDF Print and take it to a print shop.

- Prepare print files with File then Settings then Show print bleed and add 3 mm of bleed. Keep important content inside the safe zone. Export PDF Print with the CMYK colour profile and Flatten PDF ticked for offset printing. Home or office printing can use PDF Standard with RGB.

## Collaborate

- Invite people from Share by email or link and set Can edit, Can view or Can comment. Owners control the design, editors can change it and viewers can only see it.

- Leave feedback with a comment. Select the element, press Ctrl Alt M and type the comment. Comments are visible to collaborators.

- Open Version history from File to restore an earlier version of a design.

- Organise shared work in folders under Projects. Set folder permissions separately from design permissions.

- Request approval before publishing on Teams plans. Approvers get an email link to approve or reject with feedback.

## Keyboard shortcuts

- Undo with Ctrl Z and redo with Ctrl Shift Z. Save on demand with Ctrl S even though Canva autosaves.

- Copy with Ctrl C, paste with Ctrl V and duplicate with Ctrl D. Cut with Ctrl X.

- Select all elements on a page with Ctrl A. Deselect with Esc.

- Add a text box with T, a rectangle with R, a circle with C, a line with L and a sticky note with S.

- Group with Ctrl G and ungroup with Ctrl Shift G. Bring forward with Ctrl right bracket and send backward with Ctrl left bracket.

- Copy a text style with Ctrl Alt C and paste it onto another element with Ctrl Alt V.

- Bold with Ctrl B, add a link with Ctrl K and make text uppercase with Ctrl Shift K.

- Grow the font with Ctrl Shift full stop and shrink it with Ctrl Shift comma.

- Lock an element with Alt Shift L. Tidy up spacing with Alt Shift T. Show rulers and guides with Shift R.

- Add a page with Ctrl Enter. Open Quick Actions with forward slash and search for any command by name.

- Zoom in with Ctrl plus, zoom out with Ctrl minus and return to 100 percent with Ctrl zero.

- Start a presentation full screen with Ctrl Alt P. On a Mac use Cmd in place of Ctrl and Option in place of Alt.

## Free versus Pro

- Stay on the free plan until a Pro feature earns its keep. Free covers templates, elements, photos, text, uploads, filters, basic video and 5 GB of storage.

- Treat the crown icon as the Pro marker. It appears on templates, elements, photos, fonts and features that need Pro.

- Pro adds Background Remover, Magic Resize, premium templates and stock, full Brand Kits, custom font upload, transparent background export, SVG export, Bulk Create, Save as template and higher AI limits. The AI items on that list stay off limits for Kind even on Pro.

- Pro costs about 13 to 15 US dollars a month, or about 120 to 144 US dollars a year. Check canva.com/pricing before quoting a price because Canva changes it.

- Education and Nonprofit plans include Pro features free for eligible users. Check eligibility with a school or work email.

## Browser driving notes

- Drive Canva in the live browser with browser.browse. Pass <YOUR_GOOGLE_ACCOUNT> as the account hint and sign in with Google. If Google shows a password screen, stop and let Kind enter it himself.

- Expect the Canva passkey prompt after sign in. Click Skip for now to reach the home page. The signed in account shows in the More menu.

- Use Custom size for exact dimensions. The Create a design dialog lists Instagram Post as 4 by 5, which is not the square 1080 by 1080 post. Type 1080 by 1080 in Custom size instead.

- Wait for side panels to load before clicking inside them. Templates, Elements and Photos load thumbnails over the network and a fast click can land on the wrong item while the list is still shifting.

- The editor can render in a narrow, mobile-style layout (bottom-sheet panels, bottom tab bar) and switch back to the full desktop layout on its own. Do not fight it — keep working; the same tools are there, just arranged differently.

- The Share dialog shows only the invite field and the owner, with no visible 'Copy link' row. Clicking the purple Share button copies the design link (toast 'Link copied to clipboard'), but the copied text cannot be read back — report the editor's edit URL as the verifiable link, and do not create a public view link unless Kind asks.

- Confirm every click by reading the new state. After picking a template, check the canvas changed. After typing text, check the words appear. Never assume a click worked.

- Prefer keyboard shortcuts for repeat actions because they are deterministic. Clicking small toolbar icons and drag handles is the least reliable part of driving Canva in a browser.

- Avoid drag operations that need pixel precision when a panel field exists instead. Use Position then Advanced to type exact X and Y values for placement.

- Uploads use the browser file picker. The browser task must be able to reach the file path. Keep source files under the workspace so the path is stable.

- Downloads land in the browser default download folder. Check the file exists and open it to confirm it exported as expected. Never trust a success message alone.

- Canva autosaves, so there is no save button to press. Confirm the save state in the top bar before closing a design.

- Some dialogs cannot be driven by clicking. The resize dialog on a free plan shows an upgrade prompt instead of resizing. Use the manual new canvas workaround from the resize bullet instead.

## What is verified and what is not

- Verified first hand in the paused browser task on 2026-11-06. Google sign in as <YOUR_GOOGLE_ACCOUNT> completed with no password screen. The Canva passkey prompt appeared with a Skip for now button. The Create a design menu opened, and the dialog lists Instagram Post as 4 by 5 rather than square 1080 by 1080.

- First full build verified 2026-11-06 ('BLACK BOX test card', 1080x1080): Custom size, hex background, Montserrat ExtraBold 100 pt headline with letter spacing 8 and Drop shadow, Position > Advanced X/Y, rename and autosave all worked. Montserrat weight 800 shows as 'ExtraBold' on screen (live region says 'Ultra Bold'). Background used standard charcoal #232323 because no approved BLACK BOX hex was on file — if Kind supplies one, swap it in.

- First full design built in the browser with this playbook on 2026-11-06 (see above). The playbook corrections from that build are folded in.

- Everything else in this skill comes from web research, not hands on use. Treat UI labels as current as of November 2026 and recheck them live because Canva renames panels.

- Pro pricing and the number of Brand Kits on Pro vary across sources. Check canva.com/pricing before quoting either.

- Canva rebuilt the video editor in 2025 around a multi layer timeline. Older video tutorials may show the old editor layout.

- No full design has been built in the browser yet with this playbook. The first build is the test that proves it.

## Available connectors

- [Canva](/opt/hatch/connectors/canva/CONNECTOR.md) for creating designs, uploading files, exporting and resizing through the Canva API instead of the browser. Do not use its image generation or background removal tools for Kind.

- Use `muse.connector_search` to find other connectors and `muse.skill_search` to find related skills.

- If nothing here fits, look on the web for a maintained API or MCP server and set it up with [Custom Connectors and MCPs](/opt/muse/skills/custom-connector-setup/SKILL.md), or build a custom connector.

## Websites

- [Canva](https://www.canva.com/) for the editor. Carry <YOUR_GOOGLE_ACCOUNT> as the account hint, sign in with Google, and verify each step in the browser task.

- [Canva YouTube channel](https://www.youtube.com/@canva) for official tutorials. Use it to check a feature that changed since this skill was written.

## Alternatives for better results

- Start from a template and change one element at a time when speed matters more than originality.

- Build a Brand Kit before a batch of posts so colours and fonts stay consistent without retyping HEX codes.

- Design social carousels as one multi page file so the pages share one style and export together.

- Ask Kind for the exact wording and the brand HEX codes before designing, because guessing copy or colours creates rework.

- Use the Canva connector to create a design from a brief when the browser is busy, and finish fine details in the editor.

## CanvaLoop (Kind's process, set 2026-11-06; learning step added 2026-11-07)

- Kind rated the first BLACK BOX card 'not even 1/10'. A canvaloop is the fix process, and 6 canvaloops were ordered for that card.
- One canvaloop = (0) LEARN FIRST (see below), (1) study award-winning and viral designs in the browser and analyse them, (2) harshly critique the current design against what was learned, (3) rebuild or improve it in Canva applying the lesson plus every lesson from earlier loops.
- Across the 6 loops, study at least 100 designs in total (about 17 per loop). Sources: Awwwards, Behance, Dribbble, Canva template gallery, and other top design showcases.
- Each loop extracts exactly ONE key technique, names it, and applies it in the rebuild. The lesson goes into this playbook under 'CanvaLoop lessons' with the loop number, the technique, and what changed in the design.
- Never skip the inspiration step and never rebuild from the same ideas that produced the weak version. If a loop's rebuild still scores low with Kind, the next loop studies harder, not faster.

### Learning step (Kind's rule, set 2026-11-07 ~21:44 — applies to EVERY canvaloop from loop 103 on)

- BEFORE the study, learn from a teaching source, rotating by loop: **YouTube video → Instagram Reel → website article → YouTube video → Instagram Reel → website article → …** (loop 103 = YouTube, 104 = Instagram Reel, 105 = website article, 106 = YouTube, and so on).
- The worker decides what to search for — what the card needs most right now (e.g. how to make a minimal poster look premium, how to make a design unskippable, how to make black posters feel loud). Pick the single most relevant teaching source, not a random one.
- WATCHING means watching AND listening, in full: watch the video/Reel frame by frame, read the subtitles so you know what is being said, and if there are no subtitles, listen to the audio properly. Capture everything, listen to everything, understand everything — every detail, until you think you have mastered it. For an article: read the whole thing, every section, not just the headline and pictures.
- The learning goes into this playbook FIRST (before the study, before the critique, before the rebuild) under 'CanvaLoop lessons', with the loop number, the source (title, author/channel, URL), and what was learned.
- The rebuild/improvement MUST apply what was learned from that source — every canvaloop applies its learning step, not just the study's technique.
- NEVER re-watch, re-learn or re-read a source already used in a previous canvaloop. Keep the watched list below and check it before picking a source. If the best-looking source is already on the list, pick the next best one.

### Watched / learned sources (never reuse — check before picking)

- Loop 103 (YouTube): "5 Poster Design Tips to Make Your Work Stand Out" — Collect & Contrast (Austin Dingess), https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WZsawVesxY0, 8:15, published 24 Feb 2025.
- Loop 104 (Instagram Reel): "Graphic Design Tip — Master Visual Hierarchy" — thecampuscreative / The Campus Creative, https://www.instagram.com/reels/DfOIXbXOZDO/.
- Loop 105 (website article): "Typography Hierarchy Poster: A Practical Reading Path" — Linh Nguyen, inkydesignworks.com, https://www.inkydesignworks.com/posts/typography-hierarchy-poster, 28 Sep 2026.
- Loop 106 (YouTube): "Graphic Design Principles Master-Class! (Ep 1 White Space)" — Satori Graphics, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FDFD2-poyGw, 10:14, published 15 Jul 2025.

## CanvaLoop lessons

- Loop 1 (2026-11-06): studied 24 designs (Awwwards 10, Behance 4 in detail, Dribbble 2 in detail, Canva templates). Technique: MAKE THE WORDS THE IMAGE — one enormous tightly-tracked wordmark as the single hero at near-full width, tiny microcopy only. Top 5 recurring techniques: (1) extreme palette restraint, (2) oversized wordmark as hero, (3) one focal object in vast space, (4) tactile material/glow on dark, (5) strict grid with small-caps microcopy and hairline rules. Applied to v2: BLACK BOX enlarged to ~90% width, spacing tightened, tagline shrunk to microcopy, hairline rule added, background deepened to #040404.
- Loop 1 build notes (v2, 2026-11-06): size wordmarks by width %, not pt — 116 pt spans 90% of a 1080 canvas (200 pt would be ~1690 px wide, off-canvas). A rectangle cannot be a 1–2 px hairline (5 px minimum height) — use a Line element with stroke weight 2. The R shortcut fails when focus is not on the canvas — add shapes from the Elements panel. In the narrow layout a font-size sheet can stick open — dismiss it by tapping the canvas. If a PNG download reports an unknown outcome, use Canva's 'download here' fallback link in its dialog.
- Loop 2 (2026-11-06): studied 24 NEW designs (Behance black branding, Dribbble chrome search, Awwwards winners, Pinterest chrome pins). Technique: ONE CHROME FOCAL DEVICE — a single small centred reflective object (the box itself, chrome/glass with a twist) at ~1/5 poster height, wordmark untouched. Top 5: (1) one chrome/reflective object centred small, (2) vast empty black as subject, (3) tone-on-tone depth (emboss, grey-on-black), (4) light as only accent, (5) living/modular focal device. Applied to v3: chrome box centred in the lower empty field below the tagline; sourced from Canva stock Photos/Elements only, never AI-generated.
- Loop 2 BLOCK (2026-11-06): no usable chrome box in Canva free stock — every reflective chrome/glass cube is Pro (would watermark the export), and the photo candidates sit on white backgrounds (white rectangle on a black poster). Closest: Elements 'Metallic, textured cube floating against a stark black background' (Pro). Design left unchanged as v2 per the fallback. Way forward: a free-licence chrome-cube photo from outside Canva stock (Unsplash/Pexels, black background), uploaded via Uploads — or a Pro upgrade, which is Kind's call.
- Loop 2 hunt result (2026-11-06): no clean solid chrome cube exists free on Unsplash or Pexels after extensive search (groups of cubes, liquid chrome, patterned cubes, non-black backgrounds). Closest found: a GLASS cube on pure black by Veli Batuhan Aytaç, Unsplash Licence, https://unsplash.com/photos/a-glass-cube-refracts-light-on-a-black-background-SsAOhMZ60Ao — single cube, reflective/glowing faces, thin rainbow dispersion edges. It is a 3D render, not a photo of metal. Saved locally as ~/workspace/canva-assets/glass-cube-black.png (converted from the WebP download). Using it for v3: glass counts under the loop-2 technique ('chrome or glass'); the rainbow fringes are thin edge-light, close to the 'light as only accent' technique.
- Loop 2 build notes (v3, 2026-11-06): the Position panel's ratio lock defaults UNLOCKED — lock it before resizing; a height-only resize squishes the image and can corrupt the frame (if it goes wrong, delete the image and re-add it, then resize proportionally). An object can sit off-centre inside its own image — centre the OBJECT, not the frame: measure the object's offset inside the frame and shift the frame to compensate. SEAM LESSON: a photo's pure black (#000000) against a #040404 background shows a faint rectangle edge around the image — the worker claimed 'no visible rectangle' but the seam is visible on the export. Fix: match the background to the photo's black (#000000) or crop the image tight to the object. Uploads file picker opened first time, no retry needed.
- Loop 3 (2026-11-06): studied 24 NEW designs (Behance minimal black poster grain, Dribbble black poster, Awwwards winners, Pinterest dark typography). Technique: THE THUMBNAIL-FIRST SUBTRACTION TEST, applied to the one junction. Top 5: (1) two-colour discipline — every Awwwards winner lists exactly 2 colours (ViV and Grids black + white; Grail near-black + off-white; Agrumea deep red + #E94E1B — the same red as BLACK BOX); winners do not add a third colour for emphasis — the single accent does all the work; BLACK BOX already obeys this (guardrail, not a change), (2) one giant wordmark as the whole top of the composition (ViV, AGRUMEA FARM, GRAIL, GRIDS, MECHA, DEEPBOOK, FERM LIVING, Swiss posters — name at maximum scale, centred, the top half; nothing competes with it above the fold; the wordmark must stay at full scale and stay readable at a glance — it is the poster's first and last fact), (3) one hero object, whole, in empty space (Marcus one circle/beam, Solune one shape, Thmanyah one symbol, Lucifer Sans one poster, Clover one portrait — never cropped, never doubled, never overlapped by type; validates the settled cube: whole, 676×380, 40 px clear of the right edge, 15 px above the footer, pale face untouched; cropping it or adding a second object would be the single fastest way to break the poster), (4) hairline rules + microcopy on one strict grid, with the grid made visible (Ferm Living's hairline rows, Treatise's corner microcopy and converging diagonals, Juliett's grid-system posters, Arc'teryx's '//001' labels, Solune's published dashed grid, Grids as a whole project — the rule is never decorative: it ends exactly on an inset, and the microcopy sits on its baseline; for BLACK BOX this is the Y 560 hairline, the Y 575 tagline and the Y 1020 footer baseline — they must share the same inset, or the eye reads three different systems), (5) the thumbnail-first, subtractive finish (at thumbnail size only three things remain — the wordmark silhouette, the one accent, the hero silhouette; everything else becomes texture; winners finish by deleting one element at a time at small size and keeping only what changes what the piece IS — if removing it changes nothing at 10%, it is either texture that earns its place at close range, or clutter). FINAL POLISH PASS ORDER: (1) thumbnail/squint first, before any pixel work, (2) distance: 3 m / 10% — what survives, (3) guides on: every edge, rule end and baseline — hairline's ends against the wordmark inset, tagline's right edge against the same inset, cube's edges against its 40 px / 15 px clearances, footer's single Y 1020 baseline, (4) optical gaps, not measured gaps: the star's down-right point against the cube's corner, the slash's entry at the left edge at the hairline's height, the spine's vertical text against the wordmark's left edge, (5) microcopy tracking last — the smallest, most tempting thing to over-tighten, the least load-bearing, (6) fresh eyes / overnight — the only test no grid can replace. THUMBNAIL READING: at 10% this poster should read as three things only — 'BLACK BOX', one red diagonal gesture, one pale cube; the tagline, spine, top microcopy and footer all vanish, and that is correct (credibility at close range, not recognition). THE ONE REMAINING RISK: the star — at 38 px it is about 4 px at 10%, where it cannot read as a 4-point star and risks reading as a printing speck or a thickening of the slash tip on the cube's corner; at full size it is a deliberate mark, at thumbnail it is ambiguous. DONE-NESS TEST: thumbnail test + subtraction test (removing anything else removes meaning, not decoration) + repeatability test (the system could make a second poster without a new idea). On that test the poster is done EXCEPT for one conditional subtraction: the star. The spine, tagline, top microcopy and three-part footer all pass the subtraction test at close range (spine = genre, tagline = premise, microcopy = provenance, footer = system), and none competes with the wordmark at distance because they vanish there. The star is the only element whose job duplicates another element's job at the same place: the slash already says 'diagonal red gesture ending at the cube'. DECISION RULE: run the poster at 10% before touching any pixel, delete one element at a time at that size, keep only what changes what the poster is — 10% with everything, 10% without the star, 10% without the top microcopy, 10% without the centre footer item. If the star reads as a star at 10%, keep it and stop touching the poster. If it reads as a blob on the slash tip, it is the one more subtraction — remove the star and let the slash end cleanly at the cube's corner. Nothing else should be removed, nothing should be added. A near-touch reads as a mistake, while a clean bite or a clean gap reads as intention — the junction at (631,783) is the only contact point, so it carries the whole audit.

NEW QUESTION (Kind rated v22 3/10, same as v12, and ordered 40 more loops): what makes a minimal black poster feel LOUD and electric instead of quiet and empty? Technique: GO BIGGER — make BLACK BOX the poster. Top 5: (1) poster-scale type — the name/hero word at 80–100% of the width, often cropped or bleeding; type is the image, not a label on it (STUDIOGUSTO, War in Ukraine, Rose Island, Cannabis Europa, Bold Typography, Ego Itaewon, Dream Bigger), (2) one accent colour as a FIELD, not a line — red/orange as a full panel, footer strip or large shape (War in Ukraine's red field; Rose Island's #EA5600 block; IronPulse's orange blocks; Swiss red disc); the current red is all thin — spine, 8 px slash, 38 px star, (3) collision and breakout — hero breaking out of type, type masking a photograph, objects overlapping and cropping, a diagonal that actually cuts something, tilted/fanned layers, (4) light made physical — specular highlights, gloss, hard shadows, bloom and spill: the light lands on neighbouring elements and proves the object is really there (LED billboard lights the floor, wall and a silhouette; Black Paper's specular streaks cross the whole surface; Null's bloom fills the lower half; JUNNI's gloss models the whole object; the cappuccino splash bursts through the type) — a glow that only outlines its own object reads as a sticker, (5) a charged void — grain, blur, repetition, a dense microcopy band, or a second huge element in the top third; never flat empty black with two small lines of microcopy. FINDINGS: (a) LOUD vs QUIET — the source of the energy is tension: scale, collision and density; loud posters have one thing that is too big, too close, cropped, or breaking out of something else; quiet is everything with room — aligned, inset, hairlines, small type, polite margins; the current BLACK BOX is audit-clean and therefore polite — wordmark centred with air around it, a hairline rule, a 20 pt tagline, a cube neatly inset 40 px clear and 15 px above the footer; nothing collides, nothing is too big, nothing is at risk — that, honestly, is why it can be 'finished' and still read 3/10, (b) SCALE — the wordmark and hero are too small and too contained; the loud ones go to 80–100% of the width and crop or bleed; the cube at 676×380, tucked low-right with clear space on three sides, reads as an object placed on the poster — in the loud examples the hero fills, crowds or breaks the frame; Solune is the one quiet exception, and it works because its hero is photographic, real and huge, not a contained render, (c) THE EMPTY TOP THIRD — dead space as it stands, because nothing charges it; a prestige void only works when the void is charged (Dream Bigger: tracked microcopy, a rule and a star/orbit; Swiss: a saturated shape; Null: blurred bloom and grain; Thmanyah: hard sunlight and shadow stripes; Black Paper: wet specular light); 'N° 01' / 'EST. 2026' microcopy alone does not charge black — microcopy needs to be a dense band, or the top third needs a giant element intruding into it (enlarged wordmark, glow spill, red field, diagonal), (d) GLOW AND LIGHT — the cube's glow is too contained: it rims the object and stops; glow must spill onto something — the rule, the wordmark, the footer — or be big enough to touch another element; pure black also needs texture (grain, blur, gloss or hard shadow) or it reads as flat empty, (e) INSTANT ATTRACTION — in the first half-second the eye hits the biggest, highest-contrast thing, then it sticks because there is a collision to resolve (solid vs outline, photo inside type, black block vs red field, lion's eyes, the lifter); in the current poster the biggest thing is the wordmark, but it is white-on-black like everything else, with no collision and no anomaly, so the eye slides off; the 8 px slash and 38 px star are the right idea — a diagonal and a point of impact — but at ~5% of the cube's width they are too small to be the second hit. SINGLE TECHNIQUE: GO BIGGER — enlarge the wordmark to near-full width (and the cube with it, so the two are in scale tension rather than one floating above the other), and let them touch, overlap or crop: break the settled 'everything inset with polite clear space' rule. It can be done inside the hard constraints — the wordmark stays readable and stays the name, the cube stays whole with its pale face untouched, the red column stays, one red only (#E94E1B), no Canva AI — but it does mean breaking the inset/margin rule and the hairline's quietness, and using the red as a larger field rather than only as thin lines. If only one thing changes, change the scale; a brighter glow on a small, polite composition will still read quiet. NOTE FOR A LATER LOOP (not this one): the red-as-a-field idea — a red block the slash/star sit on, or the glow spilling across the rule.

FINDINGS: (a) no winner lets an image cross its footer baseline — they shrink and lift the hero, contain it in a frame/band, or give the footer its own band; the clear zone was typically several times the footer type height (~5–10% of the poster's height) and read as breathing room, not waste, whenever it was flat, the same colour as the ground, and aligned with the side margins; it read as waste only where a small hero was centred with equal void on all sides and anchored to nothing; on a pure-black poster the gap merges with the ground, so the eye registers a finished hero, not an empty strip, (b) winners keep a shrunken hero dominant by pushing it hard to an edge or cropping it at a side/top edge, isolating it in a vast flat field, making it the brightest or only photographic object, overlapping it with another element, or letting the giant wordmark carry the scale (the BLACK BOX wordmark already does this), (c) a diagonal that ends in mid-air reads as a mistake; one that bites a corner reads as a pointer. Technique: LET THE CUBE'S GLOW SPILL — give the existing glowing cube a soft #E94E1B light falloff that extends from the cube up-left along the slash into the lower-left void and faintly upward into the top zone, fading out well before the footer baseline and before the top microcopy — so the black is graded, not flat, in exactly the two empty zones, with no new element added. Top 5: (1) glow / light spill from the hero — the commonest charge on black (DeepBook's halo, denormalized's spotlight, UNIWAY's blurred red orb bleeding over the type, SHOW's acid-yellow glow on textured black, Crypto wallet's gradient circles, Sonnet's gradients); the hero does not sit ON black, it lights it; the glow is strongest at the hero and falls off, so the void is graded, never flat, and no new object is added, (2) a faint structural system in the void — grid, hairlines, repeated microcopy (Paul Rand's dotted grid, Grids' visible grid, Crypto wallet's 'COINS' repeated around the frame, ABConvert's diagram lines, 50 Swiss's tiny corner copy); at low contrast this reads as engineering, not decoration, and makes empty black look measured and deliberate — the most BLACK BOX-native technique after glow (the poster already has a hairline rule and a spine), (3) one vertical or diagonal element bleeding off an edge to anchor a tall void (Helvethic's two white bars dropping from the top edge above a low-set giant title — the closest direct precedent to BLACK BOX's top zone; Paul Rand's black diagonal block; tubik's yellow caution-tape diagonal); a tall void feels like tension, not a mistake, when something touches the top edge and points at the title — the eye has a route down; BLACK BOX already has this in miniature (the shortened spine at X ~20), and the winners show the anchor needs to be bolder or to connect to the hero to read at a glance, (4) type as mass — crop it, stack it, or make it the texture (50 Swiss 'BLOCK'/'BIG BANG', Pinterest 'DESIGN IS THINKING MADE VISUAL' and 'LIFE MOVES PRETTY FAST', MECHA cropped at the bottom edge, Don't Look Up stacked dead centre); a giant wordmark sitting low with a tall, flat, unanchored void above it is the one configuration that repeatedly read as a mistake rather than tension — it reads as the title having slipped down, unless (a) the top is anchored, (b) the ground is graded/textured, or (c) the title is so large it touches the edges, (5) never use flat pure black — grain, texture, or a gradient field (Student Cultural Centre grain, Sonnet gradient/grain circles, Helvethic textured dark grey, SHOW #0E0E0E textured, Typographic Posters II crumpled paper); in every case the 'black' is visibly a material; flat #000000 only appears in the winners as a presentation background around a poster, never as the poster's own ground. ON THE LOWER-LEFT VOID: winners do three things, in frequency order — (i) leave it empty but let glow, gradient or a diagonal reach into it (Poster Expo fan, denormalized spotlight, UNIWAY orb), (ii) put the smallest possible counterweight there — a date, coordinates, a tiny paragraph, a small mark — never a second hero (Make Music's bottom-right paragraph, Crypto wallet's vertical microcopy, 50 Swiss's corner copy), (iii) leave it truly empty, which only works when the opposite corner is very heavy and the ground is textured or glowing ('Fearless', 'inside'); nothing in the sample fills the opposite corner with a large second element — that always weakened the hero. WHY GLOW, ABOVE THE OTHERS: it is the only technique that charges BOTH voids at once; it uses only what the poster already owns (the cube, the slash, the star, the single red #E94E1B), so it respects every constraint; it is the most frequently recurring winner's move (technique 1, seen in at least 8 of the 26); and it directly answers 'LOUD rather than quiet' — light spilling out of the hero is what makes the black feel electric instead of empty, whereas a grid or grain alone would make it feel measured but still quiet. The glow should be strongest at the cube/star and die away with distance: that falloff is what turns the lower-left void from 'nothing' into 'the cube's light reaching across the poster', and it gives the tall top void a faint charge without touching the wordmark. The faint grid (technique 2) is the recommended SECOND step, not the first. IMPLEMENTATION NOTE (main Muse): a glow in Canva must be built manually — a native radial-gradient shape (Elements, search 'gradient') in #E94E1B fading to transparent, low opacity, placed BEHIND the cube/slash/star/wordmark/tagline/spine/footer; or a blurred red shape. Never an upload (uploads have failed silently before) and never Canva AI. Verify the glow in the exported PNG: visible but subtle, strongest at the cube, fading out before the footer baseline and before the top microcopy.

- Loop 27 (2026-11-07): studied 27 NEW designs (Behance: Swiss Style A0 Poster Grid System, Müller-Brockmann Beethoven Geometric Analysis, 50 Swiss Style Posters, Technical Aesthetics Exhibition, GRAPHIC DESIGN PORTFOLIO 2026, TFCO; Dribbble: Cyber Hygiene Poster Series, Fynex, ISOBAR, KRYK Theatre posters, Gesamtkunstwerk, Bilochornia, FRACTURE, Neon Music Festival Poster, Fieldhouse, One step at a time; Awwwards: Grids, DeepBook, denormalized/Grail; Pinterest grid 'dark minimal poster grid design': 'Fearless', 'THE MIND', 'inside', 'CURIOUS?', 'AVa. limited-connections', 'Less isn't Empty', 'Observation', 'Swiss Style' — grid-viewed around the login modal, no sign-in). Technique: MEASURE THE POSTER WITH ITS OWN RULE — extend the existing Y560 hairline into a minimal measurement system in the lower-left void only: two or three faint vertical hairlines at the same weight as the rule, dropped from the rule toward — but stopping above — the Y1020 footer, each aligned to an edge that already exists on the poster (the cube's left edge at X 393; the slash's entry at the left edge; the wordmark inset), each closed with a small tick, and one tiny grey dimension label in the manner of Swiss A0's top spec labels (a size or the 18° angle). Top 5: (1) hairline modular/column rules at near-invisible contrast, aligned to real edges (Swiss A0 pale red hairlines, Grids black hairlines, Fynex hairlines dividing labelled cards, Portfolio 2026 pale graph paper, Cyber Hygiene hairline frame) — the lines are barely visible at a glance and appear on a second look; they always sit on the layout's own edges, never as an independent pattern; on black the observed 'felt, not read' greys are #2F2F2F–#47483D on #010101–#080808 (One step at a time; Bilochornia ghost type), (2) microcopy as specification — tiny labels that give measurements (ISOBAR 7–9 pt repeated microcopy as texture, Swiss A0 dimension labels across the top, Fynex card labels, Cyber Hygiene numbered 1–5 callouts, Fieldhouse metric blocks, Bilochornia vertical microcopy on the diagonal strip) — this is what makes a void read as 'measured' rather than decorated: the text states a fact; labels that must be read sit higher, at observed #989CA1 on #040506 (Fynex) and #A8A8A1 on #080808 (Bilochornia), (3) dot fields that fade, confined to one zone (DeepBook halftone dots fading across black, Neon dotted arcs + dot field in the lower half only, denormalized/Grail sparse starfield) — dots are quieter than lines on black because they break up, but Neon proves they get loud quickly if bright or everywhere, so winners fade them and confine them, (4) registration / crop / crosshair marks at the frame only (Portfolio 2026 crop marks framing the title, Gesamtkunstwerk tiny circled-cross marks on the centre axis, Pinterest 'THE MIND' crosshair + red squares, 'Less isn't Empty' orange corner ticks, 'CURIOUS?' '+' marks) — four to eight tiny marks, at edges/corners, never in the middle of the void, (5) one diagrammatic gesture / one rule, not a system (FRACTURE one occlusion rule, Beethoven one 11.25° module generating arcs and diagonals, Cyber Hygiene one numbered diagram with leader lines, Fieldhouse flowcharts + one chevron timeline, Bilochornia one diagonal strip) — the void stays a void; a single measured gesture makes the whole poster read as engineered. WHERE IT LIVES: almost never the whole poster at even strength — winners confine structure to the frame/edges (marks, microcopy at top and footer), to one zone (Neon's lower half, DeepBook's fading dot field, Cyber Hygiene's grid behind the diagram panel only), or to a companion diagram (Swiss A0); full-bleed happens once (Portfolio 2026's graph paper) and only because it is extremely pale on white. It never competes with the hero because (i) its contrast is far below the hero and the type, (ii) it aligns with existing baselines and edges, (iii) it is smaller than the hero and never crosses it, and (iv) it uses the same one or two colours — every project keeps exactly one accent and puts all structure in white/grey. The two negative cases, KRYK and One step at a time, prove the fallback: a pure void is legitimate when the type itself is the structure, so any added structure must earn its place. BLACK BOX-NATIVE: the poster already speaks the winning language — it has a hairline rule (Y560) and a vertical spine; the native extension is more of the same hairline language, not a new vocabulary (not dots, not a full grid, not a new colour). WHY THIS TECHNIQUE: (1) it adds no new vocabulary — the poster already speaks in hairlines, (2) it answers the open question literally — 'measured' comes from dimensions and alignment to real edges, not from a pattern; a dotted grid reads as texture, a dimension reads as engineering — and the two strongest witnesses, Swiss A0 and ISOBAR, get their engineering reading from labels and alignment, not from covering the surface, (3) it is confined to the one void that needs it (the lower-left, where the loop 26 glow is strongest) and cannot compete with the hero — thinner, paler and smaller than the wordmark, slash, star and cube, and it never touches the cube, the wordmark or the footer, (4) it is the cheapest to test and to remove in one loop — and if it clutters, the KRYK / One step at a time evidence gives the honest fallback (leave the void alone), (5) it respects every constraint: white/grey only (lines in the observed 'felt' band, roughly #2F2F2F–#47483D on black; the single label, if it must be legible, in the observed 'read' band around #989CA1–#A8A8A1 — bands to test in loop 28, not proven values), no new large element, spine stays shortened, footer stays on pure black, glow and the single #E94E1B untouched, cube whole and its pale face untouched. WHAT NOT TO DO: no full dotted grid across the poster (Neon shows dots get loud; Portfolio 2026's full grid only works pale on white); no structure behind, through or across the cube or the wordmark (in every winner the faint structure stops at the hero's edge); no second accent colour; nothing on the footer band. DECISIVE DETAIL (Swiss A0): the grid is shown as a companion diagram (pale red hairlines over the same layout), NOT printed on the finished poster (the finished poster is clean) — the 'measured' reading comes from tiny spec labels across the top, not from a grid on the hero. GEOMETRY NOTE (main Muse): the verticals will cross the slash — a vertical at X 393 from Y 560 down crosses the 18° slash at ~Y 688; a vertical at X 53.7 crosses it at ~Y 577. Put the hairlines BEHIND the slash in layer order so the red slash stays clean and uninterrupted, and the hairline appears to pass under it.

Technique: ONE ANCHORED MEASUREMENT, IN ONE ZONE ONLY — DO NOT MIRROR IT IN THE TOP VOID. Top 5: (1) two grey bands, not one grey — winners use a dark band (about #43413E–#605A49: TORII #43413E, Nothing #585453, Gesamtkunstwerk #605A49) for large faint shapes, lines and shadows, and a light band (about #9F9E9E–#AEACAC / #AEA98C: TORII #9F9E9E and #D7D5D4, Nothing #AEACAC, Gesamtkunstwerk #AEA98C) for small text; small information is never set in the dark band, and large faint shapes are never set in the light band; in opacity terms roughly white at 20–25% for lines and white at 60–70% for small text — applied to loop 27: the label #989CA1 sits squarely inside the light band (correctly calibrated), the hairline #3A3A3A sits just below the dark band (darker, therefore less visible, than #43413E) — it is the risky value, at the bottom edge of 'felt'; the fix is to lift the hairline into the dark band (about #43413E–#4A4A4A), not to darken the label, (2) faint structure is anchored, never floating — every faint line ends in something the eye can find: a tick, a number, a corner mark, or the edge of the hero (ABConvert's tiny numbers sit on the curves they annotate, Gesamtkunstwerk's circled ①② sit beside the text blocks they count, Nothing's white corner crop marks, ARC's structure name and date vertically on the poster's own left edge, Paul Rand's dotted hairline following the edge of the black slab); a 2 px line at #3A3A3A is invisible if it is short, isolated and unanchored — that is the point at which faint becomes invisible; it becomes clutter when there are many such lines, when they cross the hero, or when they repeat in both zones; winners keep at most two or three faint elements per zone, each with one job: one line = one measurement, one label = one fact, (3) one zone carries structure, the opposite void stays empty — the most consistent pattern in the set (about 20 of the 24: La Filmoteca, Schaumbad, Thmanyah, INFINITE, DADA, Nothing all leave the zone opposite their structure essentially empty — the glow, gradient or tilt is the only thing there); the empty void is framed by the hero's diagonal, tilt or gradient, not by a second system; the exceptions prove the rule (Grids makes the grid the subject, so it is everywhere; ARC keeps its grid as a separate diagram at the end, never drawn over the posters); a mirrored measurement system in the top zone would turn the poster's asymmetry into a template and demote the cube from hero to one cell in a grid, (4) faint reads as texture at first, information at second — dotted or dashed lines (Paul Rand's dotted grid), gradients (Marcus's circle, Nothing's fading wordmark), grain (Gesamtkunstwerk) and thin rings (INFINITE) register as texture from a distance or at thumbnail size and only resolve into measurement up close; winners do not expect a hairline to register at a glance — it is a close-up reward; the loop 27 hairlines should be judged at full size, close up, not in a thumbnail — and at full size they need length to be traceable, which the 430 px lines (Y 560–990) have, (5) small type is grouped in corners or on one baseline, with a hierarchy inside the group (Nothing's specs are red headings plus white values, TORII's text is white body plus a red subhead, Marcus puts a white headline with tiny grey-white body directly beneath it, DADA repeats one tiny label in the margins until repetition makes it findable); Technique: THE DISTINCT SECOND-VOICE BLOCK — break the tagline at its full stop into two short, right-aligned lines, in a lighter and more tracked treatment than the wordmark, separated from the rule: 'THE SYSTEMS YOU DEPEND ON.' / 'THE FAILURES YOU NEVER SEE.' as a short block, not one long line. FINDING: the tagline reads as a caption — not because 20 pt is too small, but because it shares the wordmark's voice and sits in the caption slot; at 20 pt against a 128 pt wordmark (a ratio of about 1:6.4) it is actually louder, relative to its wordmark, than most winners' second lines, which run roughly 1:10 to 1:20; what winners never do is what BLACK BOX currently does — same family, same ExtraBold weight, same caps, same white, one long line, tight under a rule; with no change in voice and no separation, the eye reads it as the wordmark's second line, or as a caption under the rule — and because the line spans nearly the full inset width, its right-alignment is invisible (a near-full-width line looks the same right-aligned, centred or justified). Top 5: (1) contrast the second voice, never echo the first — winners change at least two of weight, case, family, colour or tracking (MECHA light serif sentence-case + grotesque bold-caps wordmark, Dream Bigger tracked-out light caps + solid display face, WE ARE HERE regular sentence-case + black display type, GOLDEN tiny yellow caps + cream display type, Delulu and LESS IS MORE small grey sentence-case + black/outline display type); BLACK BOX changes none of these, (2) give the second voice its own place in a void — never tight under the hero (Dream Bigger tagline ABOVE the wordmark in the empty upper zone, MECHA above the wordmark at the top of the page, WE ARE HERE in the white void at top-right, the Swiss 'LIKE' poster sentence in the void below the image, Diane Arbus body text in its own left column); tight under a rule is, in every example seen, the caption/microcopy slot — that is exactly where BLACK BOX has put its only tagline, (3) break a long tagline, let the break carry the meaning (Nike Mind 001 fragments distributed across the poster, Dream Bigger 4 short tracked lines, WE ARE HERE 4 short right-aligned lines, the Swiss 'LIKE' poster 2–3 short sentence-case lines); a break gains each phrase landing separately, the rag giving the block a visible shape, and the line shortening so its alignment can be seen; it costs the block needing a void to hold it and an anchor (rule, edge or tracking) so it does not look accidental; the break is worth it whenever a tagline has two clauses or more than about six words — BLACK BOX has two full sentences, so it has a natural break after the first full stop; one-liners survive only when they are short (Don't Look Up's tiny grey sentence under the giant stacked title) or when they ARE the headline (Grail's 'RECLAIM YOUR LIFE'), (4) make alignment mean something by locking it to a real edge — and keep the line short enough for the alignment to be visible (WE ARE HERE's right-aligned block locks to the poster's right inset, Dream Bigger's block locks to the right edge of 'DREAM' with a yellow vertical rule on its left, UNIWAY's 'A new way of partying.' locks to the top-right corner, the Nike fragments lock to the left and right edges); right-alignment reads as deliberate only when the left edge is visibly displaced — i.e. the block is clearly shorter than the full width — or when it is paired with a rule or tick; a line that spans almost the full width, as BLACK BOX's does, makes right-alignment unreadable (it looks accidental, or like default centring), (5) anchor microcopy with a small device — or demote it honestly to the foot (Dream Bigger yellow vertical rule beside its tagline block, GOLDEN yellow 'NEW FONT' pill and yellow microcopy at the foot, Don't Look Up tiny grey centred microcopy under the title, clearly demoted, Grids tiny top-corner microcopy as part of a measurement-like system); winners never leave a mid-size bold line floating with no anchor — it is either promoted (contrasting, anchored, in a void) or demoted (tiny, grey, tracked, at the foot with the footer system); BLACK BOX's tagline is currently in neither state. WHY THE BLOCK: it is the only change that answers all three of loop 29's questions at once, and it is the one pattern that never appeared apart in the winners — every long tagline that landed combined the break, the contrast and the separation; the break makes the right-alignment visible (the left edge finally jumps in), gives each sentence its own landing, and turns a caption-length line into a block with a shape; the lighter, tracked treatment makes it a second voice rather than the wordmark's echo; the separation from the rule takes it out of the caption slot. Merely enlarging it would be the wrong lesson — the evidence says loudness is difference, not size — and merely moving it, or merely breaking it while keeping ExtraBold 20 pt, would leave it reading as a caption in a new place or as a stacked caption. TENSION FLAGGED BY THE STUDY (the rebuild's work, not the study's): two lines at the current 20 pt ExtraBold would run into the cube's top edge (Y 615), so the rebuild must test a smaller/lighter two-line block and find its home within the existing voids. Technique: DESIGN THE 108 PX VERSION AS A SEPARATE THREE-ELEMENT POSTER — one name, one hero mass, one red diagonal — and let everything else dissolve into texture; judge every decision by the 108 px view first, not the full-size view. FINDINGS: (a) only three kinds of thing survive at 10% — a full-width wordmark, a single large light or dark mass (hero), and a single saturated colour field or diagonal; everything else becomes texture or vanishes; winners do not try to keep small type legible — they build the poster so the thumbnail is already a complete, simpler poster, (b) what disappears first, in order: the 7 pt '684 × 385' label and the 2 px hairlines/ticks (sub-pixel at 108 px — gone first, and no winner strengthens lines that fine; they are a full-size reward only); then footer, top microcopy and spine text; then the 13 pt two-line tagline (its two lines merge into one grey smudge); then the full-width hairline rule; then the glow's shape (only a warm tint remains); then the star's points (it becomes a ~4 px red dot — exactly what loop 22 found: it reads as the slash's endpoint); winners accept this (Arc'teryx, Ferm Living's index, Arts & Crafts' body copy and Marcus's small print all dissolve, and the designs are not weaker for it — because the big type and hero were doing the work all along; nobody in the sample tried to rescue microcopy by enlarging it — they strengthened the survivors instead), (c) THE 10% HIERARCHY FLIPS — at full size the order is 1. wordmark, 2. cube, 3. slash/star, 4. tagline, 5. spine/footer; at 108 px the predicted order is 1. cube (the largest pale mass, 68 × 39 px, and the brightest thing on a black field, so the eye lands there first), 2. wordmark (still legible as two words because it spans the full 108 px, letters ~12 px wide and ~17 px tall, if its stroke stays bold and unbroken), 3. slash/star (one red diagonal smear ending in a red dot, the only colour hit); the tagline, spine, footer, measurement system and glow drop out of the reading order entirely; that flip — cube first, name second — is the central risk: the poster's name must not lose to its own hero at the size where it will mostly be seen. Top 5: (1) one oversized wordmark, edge to edge, as the image — not a headline on a poster (FORMAT, ESR BESPOKE, AWARDS RACING, OBYS, FERM LIVING, MOTION STATE) — the name fills the frame, so at 108 px the name is still the poster, (2) two-colour discipline: one field, one accent (FORMAT and ESR are literally #000/#fff only; Incontent red/black/gold, Barakat red/gold/black, Clover red/black/white, Solune black/white) — the accent survives as a colour block, never as detail, (3) design the dissolve: let microcopy, hairlines, rules and indexes become texture (Ferm Living's ruled index, Arts & Crafts' body copy, Arc'teryx's '// 001' labels, Marcus's small print all vanish at grid size and are plainly meant to — they reward the full-size viewer and cost the thumbnail nothing), (4) one bold geometric gesture that reads as a shape at 10% (Obys's thick red bars, Motion State's green verticals and giant letter mask, Marcus's circle and diagonal light beam, Chato's orange starburst) — a thin line does not do this; a thick, high-contrast shape does; this is the slash's job on Black Box, (5) hero as a simple silhouette or pale mass, not as internal detail (Motion State's face inside giant letters, Clover's face, Barakat's sunglasses in the red box, Mirai's bonsai, Thmanyah's arrow mark) — internal detail dissolves; outline plus light/dark mass survives — which is why the cube's pale face, kept untouched, is the right hero, and why its edges must stay crisp against the black. WHY THE THREE-ELEMENT THUMBNAIL: it is the only technique that fixes the flipped hierarchy; it uses only elements already on the poster; and it is what every strongest example actually does (FORMAT and ESR are nothing but a giant name on a two-colour field, Motion State is a green field plus giant letters plus a face). APPLIED: the thumbnail must read as black field + white 'BLACK BOX' + pale cube + one red diagonal ending in a dot, in that order; the slash is the only element that can tie the first hit (cube) back to the second hit (name), so its weight and contrast at 10% — not its full-size elegance — is the thing to calibrate next, while the tagline, spine, footer, measurement lines and glow are accepted as full-size-only texture. If the slash cannot be read as a diagonal at 108 px, the poster at thumbnail size becomes two unconnected masses; if it can, the thumbnail tells the same story as the full poster in three hits. MATH (main Muse): at 10% linear scale, 13 pt becomes ~1.3 pt, 7 pt ~0.7 pt, a 2 px hairline ~0.2 px, an 8 px slash ~0.8 px, a 38 px star ~4 px — so the current 8 px slash is sub-pixel at 108 px and reads only as a faint smear; a slash of ~14–16 px becomes ~1.4–1.6 px at 108 px, which reads as a clear diagonal line; the star at 38 px is already a ~4 px red dot and needs no change. METHOD NOTE: the study did not literally render the poster at 108 px — its 108 px claims are scaled inference; the rebuild's verification must actually downscale the export to 108×108 (PIL, LANCZOS — the loop 22 method) and look at it.

Technique: TAPER THE SLASH INTO A WEDGE — keep its full 16 px at the left-edge entry, and narrow it steadily to about 6–8 px where it meets the star and the cube's upper-left corner, so the 38 px star is the only thick thing at the endpoint. VERDICT ON THE OPEN QUESTION: at full size the 16 px uniform slash is at risk of reading as a bar, not a strike — even though loop 30 proved it at 108×108; at thumbnail scale the eye reads direction only and uniform width is invisible; at full size a long, saturated, uniform red band on black has its own weight, and it is a free-floating line (it carries no type and is not a field split). The decisive evidence is the weight ratio: the star is only 38 px against a 16 px slash — 2.4× — so the star does not clearly dominate its own endpoint; in the winners, an endpoint mark is either far smaller than the diagonal (a dot, a swoosh) or far larger (a circle/triangle many times the line), or the diagonal tapers to a point so the mark is unmistakably the terminus. The cube (385 px tall, 24× the slash) and the 128 pt wordmark are safely dominant; the slash–star pair is the weak link. Top 5: (1) taper or point the diagonal — never leave a bold diagonal uniform (Lissitzky's red wedge in Constructivist moka; the jagged red shard in Angle as Structure; the yellow point in 50 Swiss Style Posters; the navy triangle in Geometric Contrast) — a pointed end reads as direction and speed; a uniform band reads as a bar and a second hero, (2) make the diagonal a ground, not a line — or put the type in it, parallel to it (Stop Violence sets the word inside the band; Geometric Teal and Euroteam make the diagonal a striped/arced field; LIVE SESSION sets type parallel to the wedge) — a free-floating heavy line with nothing in it is the one configuration winners avoid, (3) enforce a strict size ladder: hero >> wordmark >> endpoint mark >> diagonal (Null, ViV, Grail, Don't Look Up, MECHA put the wordmark an order of magnitude above everything else; Nike and Solune put the hero/object an order of magnitude above any line or mark) — the diagonal must be the thinnest voice, or the field the others sit on — never the second-largest solid, (4) let the hero occlude or terminate the diagonal (Geometric Teal's circle, Agrumea's jars, Thmanyah's tote, the Nike shoes all sit on top of, and interrupt, the diagonal; the diagonal never runs behind or through the hero's face — BLACK BOX already does this at the cube corner, and it should be kept), (5) one saturated voice, one angle, lots of quiet (winners repeat a single angle everywhere — type, band and mark share ~18–45° — and keep the rest of that zone empty: one red only, tiny microcopy, hairlines, void; LIVE SESSION's thin red line with tiny marks, Nike's thin red curves, and the hairline rules in Angle as Structure all show the same thing: if the diagonal is bold, everything near it is thin, small or absent). WHY THE TAPER: (a) it directly answers the loop 31 question — a wedge is a strike at full size and a band is a bar, and the taper is what converts one into the other; (b) it preserves loop 30's thumbnail finding, because the thick entry end still reads at 108 px while the thinning tail is what the eye follows at full size; (c) it restores the weight ladder without touching any calibrated element — the star becomes ~5× the slash at the point of contact (38 px vs ~7 px) instead of 2.4×, the cube stays whole with its pale face untouched, and no new element, colour, type or measurement is added; (d) it is the technique the most directly relevant winners share, from Lissitzky to Angle as Structure to Geometric Contrast; (e) it keeps the star's job clear — the star, rotated to the same ~18°, is the point that bites the cube, and the slash is only the path that delivers the eye to it. NEXT TEST IF THE TAPER ALONE IS NOT ENOUGH: the ratio itself (slash to ~10–12 px, or star to ~56 px). IMPLEMENTATION NOTE (main Muse): a Canva Line has uniform weight and cannot taper natively — the taper must be a custom shape. The wedge was built as a transparent PNG at 4× supersampling (PIL, LANCZOS downscale): ~/workspace/canva-assets/slash-wedge-tapered.png — a quadrilateral on the centreline (0,560) → (663,775) at 18°, 16 px wide at the left edge tapering to 7 px at the tip, #E94E1B, full 1080×1080 canvas so it places at (0,0) full-bleed. VERIFIED BY MAIN MUSE before the rebuild: vertical thickness 15 px at x=100, 13 px at x=300, 9 px at x=600, 8 px at x=650 (perpendicular width ≈ 0.95× the vertical thickness at 18°, so ~14 px at the entry and ~7.6 px at the tip — on target); bbox x0–663, y553–777 — exactly where the slash is. The rebuild replaces the old Line with this image (same layer position: above the hairlines and the glow, below the star and wordmark) and deletes the old Line; the star stays on top. - Loop 32 (2026-11-07): studied 23 NEW designs (13 opened individually, 10 in the Pinterest search grid). Technique: RE-HUE THE ONE RED AWAY FROM ORANGE TOWARD A DEEPER, TRUE/BRICK CRIMSON. Verdict: #E94E1B is probably not the best red for BLACK BOX — it is an orange-red (hue ~16°), and the winners split sharply by intent: entertainment/sport uses pure scarlet, serious/documentary/security uses a deeper, desaturated true or brick crimson; BLACK BOX is an engineering documentary about systems and failures, with a cool blue/violet cube — so the accent should read as alarm/gravity, not as fire, warmth or sport. THE RED TO TEST: #C32D30 — the published palette of THE RED (Awwwards Honorable Mention, madethought — #C32D30 on #2D000D), a muted brick-crimson: hue ~358° (true red, not orange), darker and less saturated than #E94E1B, still warm enough to complement the cool blue/violet cube, and proven at award level for a serious, architectural subject. A close second, if #C32D30 proves too quiet, is #C90107 (Bilochornia) for more punch — but #C32D30 is the test to run first. That one change fixes three things at once: temperature (serious documentary alarm rather than warm/fire/sport), urgency (a failure warning rather than a sale or a flame), and small-size readability (the tapered wedge, the 38 px star and the 40% glow will still read as red, not orange, at a glance and at thumbnail size). Top 5: (1) choose the red by subject temperature, not by complement alone — warm-against-cool is correct in principle, but winners deepen and desaturate the red for serious subjects (THE RED #C32D30; ULTRA RED maroon; Bilochornia #C90107) and keep bright scarlet (#FD0101, #E30613) for sport, music and events; orange-reds (#E0621E, #EB6D0C) consistently read as warmth, retro, fire or punk — never as documentary gravity, (2) give the red ONE job at ONE scale — After Dark uses it as a single geometric block; Effort uses it for one emphatic word, a label bar and a slash; Bilochornia uses it as the field; winners never ask the same hue to be field, small text, glow and mark at once at the same saturation, (3) keep small type out of the red — small white/grey type lives on black (or black type on a large red block, as in After Dark); Yves Tumor's small white text on red is hard to read; DKNG's tiny red pins need a black outline and a white letter to survive; this matters directly for the 7 pt '684 × 385' label, the 13 pt tagline and the footer: none of those should sit on, or be set in, the red, (4) make the red read as RED at thumbnail size — pure and deep reds (#FD0101, #C90107, #C32D30) still read as red when shrunk; muted brick and orange-reds either vanish (Pinterest muted duotones) or shift hue — orange-red reads as orange, especially in a 40% glow over black and in a 7–16 px wedge and a 38 px star, (5) let the red echo the hero, or give it texture/shade — never leave it flat and digital (the Sneaker Drop red echoes the red shoe; Marcus's crimson disc is textured and shaded at the edges; Joaquin's orange-red is grunge-textured; August Burn Red's orange is halftoned and black-outlined) — flat #E94E1B, by contrast, risks reading as safety orange or web-UI orange; the glow is the right place for red-as-ambience (ECHO's red circle, Yves Tumor's red star/glow), provided the red is deep enough not to wash out. Keep everything else as calibrated — one red only, applied to the shortened spine, the tapered wedge, the star and the glow; white wordmark dominant; cube untouched; footer on pure black; measurement system unchanged. - Loop 33 (2026-11-07): studied 25 NEW designs (18 opened individually, 7+ in search grids). Technique: MOVE THE LIGHT FROM THE CANVAS TO THE CUBE — make the glow a small, bright, cube-anchored point source with a hard core and a fast falloff, instead of a full-canvas wash. ANSWER TO THE OPEN QUESTION: yes, the glow has gone too quiet as a wash — and no, the darker red is not the problem; #C32D30 at 40% spread over a 979×1100 radial reads as flat black in the top zone and the lower-left void, because a dark red at low opacity over black has no bright core for the eye to register as light. But the fix is not simply to turn the same wash up: across the 25 designs viewed, almost no winner charges black with a large, even, full-canvas radial wash. The darker, wine-crimson glow is actually better for gravity — provided the light is re-anchored to the hero. The top zone and the lower-left void do not need to be tinted at all: winners repeatedly leave voids flat near-black, and let the measurement system, tagline and wordmark do the work there. What must read is a light source, and it must sit at the cube. Top 5: (1) the glow lives on the hero, not on the ground (WIRES, VØID, Glow in the Dark, SREDA, Tomate, the Crimson radial photograph — the light is a bright point or a luminous object with a visible core and a steep falloff, never an even tint spread across the whole canvas; a wash with no core reads as a stain, or as nothing at all), (2) near-black, not pure black, is the ground (A24 is the exception that proves the rule — #000, deliberately flat; the dark winners sit one step up: #030303 (WIRES), #050304 (Red glows), #080808 (KATACHI), #090203 (VØID), #182124 (Grail) — the ground is alive because it is not quite black, not because it is tinted red), (3) grain, haze and texture do the 'charging' (Defeat Brutalism's grain/halftone, City after dark's photographic blur and light trails, the Pinterest red-on-black posters' heavy grain, Grail's dust/light shafts all keep black alive without any colour wash; texture reads at a glance; a 40% dark-red radial does not), (4) directional light beats radial light (Grail's shafts, RED PEOPLE FORUM's spotlights, ParaNorman's halo give the light a direction and a source; a centred radial behind everything has no direction, so the eye cannot tell what is lit or why), (5) one red, once, and bright (KATACHI states it explicitly — 'warning red appears once' per scene; VØID calls it 'a single neon red accent'; A24 and Grail win with two-colour palettes — where red works on black it is saturated and local: a word, a disc, a wire, a shape, while white and black do the rest; a dark red diluted to 40% over a huge area is the one form in which red stops reading as red). SPECIFIC TEST: a SECOND, smaller glow — keep the existing 979×1100 #C32D30 radial at 40% as the faint ambient, and add one second #C32D30 radial, roughly 420×260, centred on the cube (about X 735, Y 807), at 55–65% opacity, with a tighter falloff so its brightest core sits just behind the cube's pale face and it dies to black well before the footer baseline and before the wordmark. If only one glow may change, the equivalent single test is: shrink and re-centre the existing glow behind the cube and raise it to about 55%. Judge it at a glance and at arm's length: the cube should look lit from within, the top zone should still read as black, and the lower-left void should still read as black — with the measurement system, not the tint, giving it structure. IMPLEMENTATION ADAPTATION (main Muse — the study did not check this): the cube image (~/workspace/canva-assets/glass-cube-black.png) is RGB, OPAQUE — no alpha channel. A 420×260 glow placed BEHIND the cube would be completely hidden by the cube photo, so the study's literal size cannot work. The adaptation: a halo LARGER than the cube's frame, placed behind the cube, so only the spill around the frame's edges shows — the core is hidden (fine: the halo is the visible part). Built as a custom radial PNG (like the wedge): ~/workspace/canva-assets/cube-halo-c32d30.png — 800×450 (aspect-matched to the cube's 684×385 frame), centred on the cube (735,807) so it places at X 335, Y 582, #C32D30, core alpha 0.75, falloff alpha(r) = 0.75*max(0, 1-(r/0.92)^2) where r is the elliptical radius. VERIFIED BY MAIN MUSE before the rebuild: max alpha 0.75 at the centre, 0.528 halfway to the left edge, 0.252 at a quarter, 0.0 at the ellipse edges; ~10% at the cube's frame edge (r=0.855); 0.0 at the footer (r=0.947) and 0.0 in the top zone — so the halo rims the cube's frame at ~10%, fades to black well before the footer and the wordmark, and leaves the lower-left void black. The rebuild adds this halo BEHIND the cube (below the cube in layer order, above the ambient glow) and keeps the ambient glow as is.
