- Loop 34 (2026-11-07): studied 24 NEW designs opened individually + 6 Pinterest grid pins = 30 viewed. Technique: GIVE THE RIM A BRIGHT, NARROW CORE AT THE CUBE'S FRAME, WITH FAST FALLOFF. ANSWER TO THE OPEN QUESTION: at about 10% red at the frame, the halo will read as a stain, a smudge or nothing at all at a glance and at arm's length — none of the winners studied uses a faint, diffuse, ~10% wash as the sole rim light; every winner that reads as 'lit' at thumbnail size has a bright, narrow core at the hero's edge (near-white, orange-yellow or 100%-saturated colour) with a fast falloff back to pure black, or makes the hero itself the light source; a 10% red rim has too little luminance contrast against black to survive squinting, distance or a small thumbnail (the near-black 'Save Constantine' thumbnail effectively disappeared, while the ones that read instantly had a hard, saturated edge or a hot core). Top 5: (1) a bright, narrow core at the edge, with fast falloff (winners put the brightness in a 2–8 px line or ring hugging the hero — white-hot, orange-yellow or 100% saturated — and let it die to pure black within a short distance; WIRES, Glass Tunnel, the FOCUS ring, The Lighting Syndicate, END OF JOB — a diffuse halo with no core reads as a stain because there is no edge for the eye to lock onto), (2) the hero is the light source (the luminous thing is a solid shape — a saturated panel, a moon disc, a neon tube, a billboard, a backlit silhouette — rather than a glow painted behind a dark hero; RED PEOPLE FORUM, Halloween Night, the Subway billboard, BEYOND THE VISIBLE, denormalized — light with a visible source reads as light; light with no source reads as a smudge), (3) hard-edged saturated flat colour at 100%, no blur (Circulus's orange frame and dots, Radiant rings, NOSTAFF/SILENT — at arm's length and at thumbnail size, a hard edge survives; a 10% gradient does not), (4) one light geometry that explains the light (a ring, a disc, a beam, a strip or a tube — usually asymmetric and directional — tells the eye where the light comes from; denormalized's diagonal beams, KAELO's strips, the FOCUS ring, the moon discs — a centred radial wash with no geometry has no explanation, so it reads as fog or a printing fault), (5) pure black is protected (the glow is local and dies before the footer, the type and the edges; the ground returns to true black, so the contrast is edge-vs-black, not tint-vs-tint; Circulus, WIRES, sokolovski.pro, denormalized — when a glow spreads wide and tints the ground grey-red, it muddies the ground and competes with the hero: that is the stain threshold; the ambient glow must stay faint and separate from the rim, exactly as BLACK BOX already separates its ambient (40%, top zone / lower-left) from the cube's halo). SPECIFIC TEST: add a SECOND, tight inner halo behind the cube, hugging its frame — roughly 720 × 420 (only ~15–20 px overshoot beyond the 684 × 385 cube on each side), centred on the cube, with a core alpha of 90–100% at the frame, falling to black within about 40–60 px — lifting the rim at the frame from ~10% red to roughly 60–80% red at the exact edge, while the existing 800 × 450, 75%-core halo stays as the faint outer ambient and still dies before the Y 1020 footer. Do NOT strengthen the existing halo by raising its opacity or enlarging it — that would widen the wash, tint more ground, reach further toward the footer and the wordmark, and make the stain bigger, not the light stronger. Pass/fail test: at 350 px wide and at 2 metres, the cube's edge must still be visibly rimmed in red, and the black above and below it must still read as pure black; if the tight halo's edge still disappears at that size, the rim is still too faint; if it starts to look like a red frame or to tint the footer, the falloff is too slow or the halo is too large — shrink the falloff, not the core brightness. IMPLEMENTATION ADAPTATION (main Muse — the study did not check the poster's geometry): the cube's top edge (Y 615) is only ~8 px below the tagline glyphs (which end ~Y 607) and its bottom edge (Y 1000) is only 20 px above the footer (Y 1020), so a uniform 40–60 px falloff would tint the tagline zone and the footer. The tight halo was built with a SEPARABLE, ASYMMETRIC falloff: ~/workspace/canva-assets/cube-halo-tight-c32d30.png — 784×416, top-left at (343,602), centred on the cube (735,807), #C32D30, core alpha 0.95; horizontal falloff 50 px (1 inside the frame |dx|<=342, quadratic to 0 at |dx|=392); vertical falloff 8 px ABOVE the frame (to 0 at |dy|=200, i.e. Y 607 — exactly where the tagline glyphs end) and 18 px BELOW it (to 0 at |dy|=210, i.e. Y 1017 — before the footer at Y 1020). VERIFIED BY MAIN MUSE before the rebuild: top/bottom/left edges of the PNG are 0 alpha (no hard cut); 95% at the frame edges (left, top, bottom); 71% at 25 px left of the frame; 0% at 8 px above the frame top and 0% at 18 px below the frame bottom; colour (195,45,48) = #C32D30. BUILD CORRECTION (loop 34): the first build was 784×410 — its bottom row was at dy=204, where the falloff had not yet reached 0 (alpha 0.53), which would have shown as a hard cut 9 px above the footer; it was rebuilt at 784×416 so all four edges reach 0 alpha. LAYER ORDER: the tight halo goes BELOW the cube AND below the measurement verticals (between the ambient glow and the cube), so the measurement system stays clean on top of the bright rim. - Loop 35 study (30+ designs, running total 891): the wordmark's tracking. Answer: letter-spacing 2 is the RIGHT global tightness for BLACK BOX at 128 pt — it is already at the limit of what fits on one line — but it sits on the line between 'tight and monumental' and 'letters colliding', and the fault is NOT uniform tracking, it is PAIR KERNING. Top-5: (1) tight tracking fuses a SHORT word into one solid mass (OSPLY, FONT, GRIND, BLOCK, MACMILLAN, FORM//SYSTEM) — but every winner is 3–6 letters or stacked; BLACK BOX is 9 characters on ONE line, the longest single-line tight wordmark in the survey, so it carries more collision risk than any winner; (2) a condensed face does the tightness work, a wide ExtraBold does not — condensed grotesques keep counters open at near-zero spacing, while Montserrat ExtraBold's thick stems and small counters close first, especially B, O and A; (3) optical/pair kerning, not uniform tracking — the collisions are pair-specific (diagonal letters A, K, X need air; vertical letters B, L need none; round letters O, C need something in between; Affinity names AV/AW/VA and LT/LV/LY as the worst pairs; BLACK BOX's equivalents are A–C, C–K, O–X and K–[space]–B); uniform tracking either leaves the diagonals colliding or opens the verticals into holes; (4) contrast of voices — giant tight caps + small WIDE-tracked microcopy (Dream Bigger, November, FORM//SYSTEM) — BLACK BOX already has this (tagline letter-spacing 150, footer/microcopy), so loosening the giant would destroy a working contrast; (5) thumbnail test, and edge-to-edge OR generous margin, never in-between — BLACK BOX sits in the dangerous middle (X 3.4–1076.7, ~3 px from each edge, no bleed, no margin, reads as accidental clipping at thumbnail); at ~270 px wide the 2-unit gaps vanish, B/O/A counters fill, and 'BLACK BOX' risks reading as a black bar with notches — the line between 'tight and monumental' and 'letters colliding' is exactly this: the inter-letter white channel must still be visible as a continuous vertical line at the size the poster will actually be seen at, and every counter must stay open. SINGLE TECHNIQUE: optical pair kerning, global tracking held at 2 — loosen A–C, C–K and O–X, tighten B–L, net width change ≈ 0, so the span stays X 3.4–1076.7 and the word stays on one line at 128 pt. BUILD NOTE (main Muse): Canva has NO per-pair kerning, so the kerned wordmark was rendered as a PNG — ~/workspace/canva-assets/wordmark-blackbox-kerned.png (1080×1080 transparent, Montserrat ExtraBold at 170 px em = Canva's 128 pt, white, ink top Y409). Measured from v34's export (top-portion gaps): B–L 18, L–A 71, A–C 16, C–K 16, word space 63, B–O 12, O–X 4. Applied shifts (px): B 0, L −2, A −2, C +1, K +4, B −4, O −4, X 0 (net 0; the word space absorbs the loosening). Rendered gaps: B–L 14, L–A 70, A–C 17, C–K 17, word space 53, B–O 10, O–X 7 — every change in the right direction; the critical O–X gap nearly doubled (4→7 px, so its white channel survives at thumbnail). LESSON: a letter's ink-left at the TOP of the cap height is NOT its ink-left at the baseline — for the A they differ by ~13 px (the apex is centred, the legs spread) — so place kerned letters by their TOP-PORTION ink left, measured per letter by drawing it alone and finding the leftmost ink in the top 90 px of the glyph; placing by the full-glyph bbox puts the A ~11 px too far right. Also: PIL's getbbox and the actual renderer disagree by up to 13 px per letter (hinting) — always measure the RENDERED ink, never trust getbbox. Montserrat ExtraBold (static TTF) was fetched from Google Fonts for the render; it is NOT installed on the VM (fc-list returns nothing for Montserrat). Canva's 128 pt = 170 px em in PIL terms (128 pt at 96 dpi); PIL size-170 'BLACK BOX' is 1052 px wide vs v34's 1058 px — a faithful match.

- Loop 36 study (22 designs, running total 913): the footer's centre item. Answer: 'SYSTEMS / FAILURES' in the footer centre is a repeat that wastes the slot — in NONE of the 22 designs did the centre repeat the headline or tagline words. Top-5: (1) the footer is a data strip, not a second voice — headline/tagline = voice, footer = facts; every footer column carries a different, NEW fact, in smaller factual microcopy; putting tagline words in the footer blurs that register; (2) the centre is the when / where / action slot — the most-read footer position after the headline, spent on the fact the viewer needs next (a date, a venue/address, credits, or a URL/action); (3) three columns = who / when / where — maker-or-venue left, date centre, place-or-issue right; each column answers a different question, no column answers a question already answered above it; (4) repetition works at hero scale, not in footer microcopy — winners repeat huge, as pattern or rhythm (SOLIAFEST ×5, Swiss posters' giant words), and the footer then stays factual; a small repeat in the footer reads as filler, not rhythm, because it is too small to be a pattern and too late to be a headline; (5) if there is no new fact, leave the centre empty — a two-item footer (handle left, issue right, void centre) is a deliberate Swiss/minimal choice, not a gap; series/issue markers belong at an edge (VOL. 01 at right is correctly placed); the centre is not a second series marker, and an empty centre lets the tagline keep its monopoly on 'SYSTEMS' and 'FAILURES'. SINGLE TECHNIQUE: give every footer column a different, new fact; never spend a footer column repeating words already on the poster. Applied here: there is no verified new fact to put in the centre — 'EP. 01' would duplicate 'VOL. 01' and 'N° 01' (a third numbering); '2026' would duplicate 'EST. 2026'; a location, release date, episode subject or platform is not given, and inventing one would be fabrication; 'DOCUMENTARY SERIES' would merely repeat the spine in a different place. So the change to test is REPLACE — by deletion: delete 'SYSTEMS / FAILURES' from the footer centre, keep the Y 1020 baseline and the left/right items exactly as they are. What would earn the centre back in a later loop is a single verified new fact (a release date, an episode subject, or a watch/platform line), in that same small factual register, not as a tagline echo.

- Loop 37 study (22 designs, running total 935): the hairline. Answer: rules are inset to the content column, NEVER trim-to-trim — BLACK BOX's rule (X 3.4–1076.7) is the outlier in the sample (12 of 22 have no horizontal divider at all; all 5 that do are inset; none has a full-width white rule on a black field). Top-5: (1) rules are inset to the content column, never trim-to-trim — a rule that touches both trims reads as a page border or a crop, not as part of the grid; (2) a divider is either a true hairline or a deliberate heavy bar, never a middle weight — Null and Void use ~1 px faint/grey lines, Grids uses a thick black bar; 2 px white on black is neither (too heavy to disappear, too light to read as a bar, and white-on-black makes it shout louder than the cube's rim); (3) separation by void and scale, not by a line — App&flow, Poster Expo, Helvethic, MECHA, Sonnet and Solune all separate a wordmark from a hero by a large empty field and a jump in scale; the rule is optional, and in black-poster work its absence is the norm; (4) diagonals never enter a horizontal rule at an acute angle, and never at its endpoint — winners keep diagonals clear of rules, cross at 90°, or let the diagonal pass BEHIND a continuous rule; no sample showed an acute diagonal starting ON a rule's endpoint at the trim — which is exactly BLACK BOX's wedge at (0,560); (5) a rule needs an endpoint anchor — its ends should land on something already in the system (a text edge, a number, a footer baseline). SINGLE TECHNIQUE: make the rule an interior grid line, not a trim line — shorten it to the poster's own insets, (53.7,560)–(1026.3,560), keeping it 2 px white at Y 560 (weight deliberately NOT changed, to isolate extent). This one change answers all three open questions: its ends land on alignments the poster already owns (left on the tagline block's left edge and the X 53.7 measurement hairline, right on the tagline's right edge 1026.3); the wedge starts at (0,560) in the margin and at X 53.7 is already ~17 px below Y 560, so the acute trim-edge T-junction ceases to exist without moving the wedge, star or cube. Trade-off: the rule no longer meets the cube's right edge (1076.7) — given up in favour of the tagline/measurement alignment, shared by three elements rather than one. Follow-up tests for later loops (NOT this one): thin the rule to a true 1 px grey hairline (#989CA1, the measurement-system grey), and, as a separate loop, remove the rule entirely (the App&flow test) to see whether void alone separates the zones.

- Loop 38 study (21 designs, running total 956): the hairline's weight. Answer: demote the hairline into the measurement register — thin it to 1 px in #989CA1 (the colour of the ticks and the '684 × 385' label), keeping it inset at (53.7,560)–(1026.3,560) at Y 560. Do NOT keep the 2 px white. Top-5: (1) separation by space and scale, not by a rule — Nothing Phone (3), Null Project, Graphic, Marcus, Poster Co and INFINITE all separate wordmark, tagline and hero by size contrast and empty space alone; the gap does the work; (2) the hairline as a frame, box or short local rule, never a full-width divider — Inside Alien's 1 px white frame round 'INSIDE', TORII's short thin white rule only under 'MAMORU', Fantasy Literature's short dashes and thin gold hairline box, DADA's fine grey grid; (3) one grey register for all secondary structure, white reserved for the hero — TORII's own palette lists #43413E and #9F9E9E (BLACK BOX's measurement greys) alongside white and red; Brutalism 002 uses #9F9F9F and #5E5E5F on #010101; rules, microcopy and measurement marks live in mid-grey, white is spent only on the wordmark; (4) heavy is short, thick and singular — Swiss posters' thick black underlines, DADA's thick black bars, TORII's one red vertical bar, Grip Poster's orange disc, Halloween's orange moon; a heavy element is an accent with a job, not a line stretched across the poster; (5) the hero object's own edge does the dividing — Null Project's hard image edge, Poster Co's and INFINITE's photo edges, Brutalism's grey square, Halloween's moon, Marcus's circle; the boundary is the object itself, which is exactly what the cube's top edge at Y 615 already does in BLACK BOX. Direct answer: not one of the 21 used a full-width 2 px white horizontal divider on a dark field. A 1 px grey hairline will still register at full size and be faint — near-invisible at thumbnail — but that is acceptable, because the separation does not depend on the line (the 128 pt wordmark, the 13 pt tagline 12 px below the rule, and the cube's top edge at Y 615 already separate the zones by scale, alignment and a hard object edge). The 2 px white line is the worse option: a second white voice competing with the wordmark and the cube's rim. FALLBACK: if the 1 px grey disappears even at full size, delete the line entirely and rely on space, scale and the cube's edge — do not restore the white, and do not thicken it into a bar unless the rebuild deliberately re-briefs it as a short, thick accent.

- Loop 39 study (25 designs + 2 sightings, running total 983): does the poster need the hairline at all — the App&flow test. Answer: DELETE it as the test. In the 25 new designs, a horizontal rule between a giant wordmark and a lower hero is the exception, not the norm: separation is carried by the hero's own top edge, by an empty band, and by an extreme scale jump. BLACK BOX already has all three — a 128 pt ExtraBold wordmark against 13 pt Regular tagline, a 39 px empty band between the wordmark's base (Y 533) and the tagline (Y 572), and a luminous 684 px-wide cube whose top edge sits at Y 615. The 1 px #989CA1 rule at Y 560 is therefore, on the evidence, decoration rather than structure. Top-5 (what carries separation when a divider is removed): (1) the hero's own hard top edge as the divider — the most common device (ABConvert, Elements Unveiled, vanguard, Outpost, Black Sedan's diagonal plane, JUNNI's neon shape, Winter 2026's colour-blocked hero); a tonal or material jump reads as a line without being one; for BLACK BOX this is the cube's top edge at Y 615, reinforced by its rim and halo; (2) an extreme scale and weight jump — giant ExtraBold against tiny Regular (Student Cultural Centre, 'inside', LESS IS MORE, Make Music, Bilochornia, Vignelli); the eye cannot mistake the two voices for one block; BLACK BOX already has this at roughly 10:1; (3) a generous band of empty black as the divider — the void is the rule (Elements Unveiled, Student Cultural Centre, 'inside', Dark Typography VI, Paul Rand); CAVEAT for BLACK BOX: its void between wordmark and cube is only 82 px in total and the tagline occupies half of it, so this technique is the weakest of the five here and cannot be relied on alone; (4) anchoring the secondary text to an edge or to the hero — the small text is never left floating mid-void (Clean Minimal's 'Perspective', where the copy sits on the cube face; ABConvert's microcopy strip pinned to the top edge; vanguard's numerals drawn on the bag; Black Pig's ticket); this is what stops a small line from drifting between zones; (5) a single accent block or diagonal doing the separating — one red block (Black Pig), one diagonal plane (Black Sedan), one neon shape (JUNNI), one colour-blocked footer band (Winter 2026), one white diagonal strip (Bilochornia); BLACK BOX already owns this device in its red spine, wedge and star — it does not need a second one in the form of a grey rule. WHAT BREAKS WHEN NOTHING DOES (failure cases): (a) elements touch or overlap without a contrast jump (Bold Typography Poster, LIFE MOVES PRETTY FAST); (b) the secondary text is dense and sits on a busy hero with no clean edge (War in Ukraine); (c) repetition or texture fills the void that was supposed to separate (denser UNIWAY variants). None of the winners that removed a divider left a 13 pt line floating equidistant between two zones. SINGLE TECHNIQUE: hero-anchored secondary text — let the tagline belong to the cube by proximity, and let the empty band above it be the divider. What carries a line that starts in empty space, in order of strength: (a) a termination mark at that end; (b) a label sitting on or beside that end; (c) the object, frame or grid it touches or belongs to; (d) repetition — the same mark/system used elsewhere. Nothing in the evidence supports a lone solid line, in a precise technical system, with a tick at only one end and a measurement label, starting in empty space; the only bare ends that read as deliberate are in work that makes no measurement claim (Vlad Grama's BLUEPRINT) or are crosses, not lines (Exploring Dimensions). Across 26 new designs, a two-item top band (left + right, centre empty, no rule) is a recognised, working pattern; an empty centre is the norm, not a defect; and a horizontal rule under top microcopy appeared in 0 of 26. Top-5: (1) emptiness as the system — let the black field breathe; the most common winning choice is no top band at all (Helvethic, Sonnet, UNIWAY, LESS IS MORE), with information moved to the bottom or into the hero; black is a material, not a gap to fill; (2) two items, one invisible baseline, centre deliberately empty, no rule (Poppr, Lost in Thought, 'LOOK THROUGH' in 50 Swiss Style Posters) — it works only when the two items are different in kind (number vs. date, logo vs. action, issue vs. place) but identical in size, weight, colour and baseline, and aligned to the same left/right insets as the rest of the system; the alignment — not a line — is what makes them read as a pair; (3) centre as the only top item (JUNNI, STUDIOGUSTO, Coture Archive) — works when that centre item is the brand or the issue line itself; fails as an addition, because a centre item that is merely extra information competes with the hero wordmark below it; (4) a dense top band is a cover/index device, never a poster device (Typographical studies vol.2 is the sole 4–5-item example, and it is a cover sheet; every poster inside drops back to 0–2 items); adding a third, fourth or fifth item turns a system into a contents page; (5) no rule, ever — and information moved to an edge instead (no design used a horizontal rule to tie a top band together; systems were made by shared baseline, shared inset and shared type size; extra information went to a vertical edge or to the bottom, not to a line across the top). Pattern counts: no top band at all in about half; two-item left/right with centre empty in 4 clear cases; centre-only in 3; one-item left- or right-only in 2; a 4–5-item band in 1, and only on a cover sheet; a horizontal rule under top microcopy in 0 of 26. Answer: KEEP the star, KEEP 38 px, KEEP its centre on the wedge tip / cube corner — but its rotation does not earn its place. Top-5: (1) attach the star to a letter, a line-end or a corner — never float it; winners replace or ride a letter (*sterisk, *sigma, *Facet, *asterisk, the A in Adisrishti, the O in Onecore, the eye in Starion) or sit exactly on a junction; free-floating stars (Pinterest clip-art, Mix-and-Match's nine asterisks) read as decoration; (2) small is enough if it is isolated and the sole accent — successful small stars are ~0.25–0.5× cap height (Sigma, Facet, Bembridge), ~x-height (Awwwards Asterisk), or ~1/10 of the hero (Starion, Rise and Reason), in the brand's single accent colour, with empty space around them; BLACK BOX's 38 px against a 128 pt wordmark sits in that band — neither too big (Modern Geometric, Yudha's hero asterisk) nor too small (Four-Point Star Circle, where the star dissolves); (3) upright / grid-aligned beats tilted — almost every successful accent star is upright and aligned to the type or grid it sits with; rotation works only when rotation IS the idea (six stars rotated to make a flower, a giant asterisk as a hero glyph) or when it is 45° to make a diagonal point; a small tilt for its own sake reads as a mistake or as confetti (Mix-and-Match); (4) one star, one named job; repeat only at a very different scale (Facet = footnote/cross-reference, Sigma = guiding star, Onecore = knowledge/apex, Starion = eye/spark, Rise and Reason = the star in the sky); failures are 'sparkle / AI / pretty' with no job (Emon, CLINK & BLOOM); a system works at three scales (VOID, Glyph Pattern, Facet), repetition at the same scale does not; (5) a point must land exactly on the junction, and the star must not dissolve into another shape (Starion's star exactly at the horse's intersection, Onecore's exactly at the triangle apex, Rise and Reason's exactly in the sunburst centre); fused or repeated carelessly it becomes a flower (Aurin, Sparkle + Flower), a sun (Solune at large scale) or circles (Four-Point Star Circle). The poster is otherwise entirely orthogonal — wordmark, cube, measurement hairlines at X 393 and X 53.7, footer baseline Y 1020 — except for the thin wedge (~18°). The star's ~18° rotation inherits the wedge's angle, but the wedge is now a minor element and the cube is the hero; at 38 px the star's tilt is louder than the wedge's. every straight-sided equal-armed solid read as a plus/cross at any size (Fall of Icarus's repeated '+' field, deliberately pluses; Trato's orange mark reads as an X; BLACK BOX's star reads as a plus at 38 px); a straight-sided 4-point star with a wide waist IS a plus geometrically, so scaling it scales the plus — there is no size threshold at which the existing shape becomes a star, only a shape change (concavity/elongation) would do that; enlarging to ~76 px would also make the mark compete with the cube hero and crowd its pale face; (2) one mark, one job — never double-mark a junction (alo.ai's star above the 'i'; Match Point's dot on the rectangle edge; Poster Co's circled 'co'); a small mark is given a single clear job and is not stacked onto a corner, rule-end or hero edge that is already marked; (3) let the architecture mark the junction — corner, rule-end, grid intersection, colour-block edge or hero edge alone carries it (Grids, Swiss posters, Mark Clennon, Incite, Solune); no added symbol is needed where the construction already points at the spot; (4) small marks work in sets or fields, not alone — a trio, cluster or field of sparkles reads as stars even when each mark is tiny (Portfolio 2026 trio; Shahnur's star cluster; Pinterest fields), while a lone small mark is read literally, as a plus, a dot or a cross; (5) the technical system is the ornament — hairlines, ticks, dimension labels, grid references ('S03'), footer baselines and microcopy do the decorative work in the strongest minimal posters (Grids, Swiss posters, SL24); - Loop 44 study (24 designs, running total 1,112): the wedge — the sole diagonal, its tip is the junction. Answer: the exact vertex junction. Top-5: (1) exact vertex junction — the diagonal ends precisely on a corner or vertex, or the diagonal is the hero's own edge, so the corner is the diagonal's end (La Filmoteca, Finnair, Euroteam corner-to-corner band, ARC, Geometric Tiles, DADA, ViV's V apex); the eye is given a single, verifiable meeting point; (2) full bleed / pierce-through — the diagonal runs off the poster's edge or straight through the hero (Star Wars lightsaber, 50 Swiss, Geometric Teal, 21.co, Vancouver Design Week); there is no visible endpoint, so there is nothing to judge as a miss — the strongest option when exactness cannot be guaranteed; (3) deliberate clear undershoot, with a terminal device — the diagonal stops well short of any corner, and the stop is declared intentional by a sharp point, a dot, a tick/arrow, a rounded pinch, or a large gap (Angle as Structure's floating red point, LIVE SESSION's dotted terminus, Interrupted Lines' central break); a small gap reads as a mistake, a large finished gap reads as a decision; (4) one repeated angle, usually 45° — successful diagonals overwhelmingly use 45° (or one steep angle, as in La Filmoteca), repeated across the system so the angle reads as a rule; shallow angles near 18° are almost absent except where the diagonal is the hero's own edge, and a shallow diagonal crossing a vertical or horizontal edge creates a long, sliding intersection that magnifies any error; (5) taper to a true point, or constant width — never a blunt near-point; tapered wedges end in a sharp point (Angle as Structure shard, DADA slivers, Thmanyah arrow), bands keep a constant width and end flat at an edge or corner (Euroteam, Geometric Teal); a taper that stops at a blunt 7 px flat end is the in-between state that reads as cut off rather than aimed; one-colour discipline supports all of the above (the diagonal is in the single hero colour, never a second accent). A near-miss — ending a little before a corner, or crossing a hero's edge just below/beside its corner with a blunt end — has NO successful example in the whole sample, and a shallow ~18° angle makes that failure mode worse. CHANGE TO TEST (endpoint, not angle, not a new element): keep the ~18° angle and the 16 px base, but re-aim and extend the wedge so it tapers to a true 0 px point that lands exactly on the cube's drawn upper-left vertex — and stops there, with no overshoot into the cube and no gap before it. In practice: change the taper from 16 px → 7 px to 16 px → 0 px over the full length, and move the centreline's endpoint onto the actual drawn vertex of the glass cube (its front/top-face vertex, not the bounding box), adjusting the centreline by the minimum needed to hit that vertex. Why not the alternatives: keeping the wedge as it is leaves the junction ambiguous (a 7 px blunt tip near a corner is precisely the 'cut off' reading, and at 18° any small vertical error slides a long way along the cube's edge); overshooting/piercing the cube would contradict the constraint that the cube stays whole with its pale face untouched and would put red across the hero; falling clearly short would need a terminal device and a large gap, stranding the wedge in the void and breaking the 'line into the corner' idea. If, on rebuilding, the drawn vertex does not lie on the current 18° line, the angle — not the junction — is what gives way, by the smallest amount needed.

- Loop 45 study (24 designs, running total 1,136): the hero's scale and position. Verdict: the cube is close but not right — slightly too small, too far right, and its 3 px right margin is an accidental touch (neither a clear margin nor a deliberate bleed). Top-5: (1) width misleads; height and area decide whether a hero feels monumental — a 16:9 hero at 63% width is only 36% tall and reads as a strip or banner; low heroes that work are 40–50% of poster height (TAXI SERVICE's taxi ~55% wide, ~50% tall, cropped; Black Sedan's large car ~95% wide, ~40% tall, cropped; Goals' footballer ~50% wide, ~55% tall); below ~38% height a wide contained hero needs cropping or a second hero to avoid reading as an inset; (2) contained vs cropped is itself a scale decision — fully contained heroes need a clear margin on every side (~5% of canvas, ~55–60 px at 1080 px) to read as deliberate; cropped heroes read 10–20% larger than their box because the eye completes them; the cube is contained but touches the right edge by 3 px — the worst of both, reading as an alignment error, not a bleed; (3) ground must be balanced or occupied, not merely empty — successful asymmetric heroes put something in the ground (TAXI SERVICE's small copy bottom-left, Honda's centred car with ~15% ground each side, Lücke Dachpartner's dark wedge in the lower-right ground, La Filmoteca's silhouettes); BLACK BOX's left ground holds only the spine microcopy and the wedge — too much unoccupied black for a single-hero card; (4) low placement works only when the hero is grounded, not floating — working low heroes sit on or near the bottom edge or are anchored by a base; the cube's bottom at 1000 px (80 px gap) is a reasonable footer gap, but combined with the 3 px right touch it floats on the right and sags on the left; keep the bottom at 1000 px, do not lower it into the footer; (5) when type is already the top hero, the image must be the bottom hero — and big enough to balance the type; dual-hero examples that resolve this (TAXI SERVICE, Black Sedan, Goals, THERE HE…) make the image 55–95% wide and low, so the two heroes stack as top and bottom bands; at 63% x 36% the cube is the smallest dual-hero image in the sample relative to its wordmark. CHANGE TO TEST: enlarge proportionally by 9.1% and move up-left, keeping the bottom fixed — new cube 746 x 420 at (274,580): 69.1% wide, 38.9% tall, 26.9% area (up from 22.6%); left margin 393 -> 274 px, right margin 3 -> 60 px (deliberate, same order as the 80 px bottom margin), top 615 -> 580 px, bottom stays 1000 px, centre (735,807) -> (647,790), aspect stays 16:9. It is the smallest proportional enlargement that crosses all four thresholds — height above ~38%, area above 26%, right margin a deliberate 60 px, left ground below ~28% — without moving the bottom or touching the footer. TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE STUDY (main Muse, verified against the card's known geometry): (a) the change as specified COLLIDES with the tagline — the tagline's glyphs end ~Y607 and the new cube top is Y580, so the tagline's second line would sit on the cube; the study flagged this as its main untested risk and could not verify it, but the tagline is at Y572–612, so the risk is real. Making the change work requires moving the tagline up 35 px (to Y537–577, still 8 px above the new cube top) AND the wordmark up 35 px (ink Y409–533 -> Y374–498) to restore the ~39 px gap between wordmark base and tagline top. (b) The wedge's new endpoint is the cube's DRAWN vertex, NOT the bounding-box corner — the study's falsification test wrongly says the wedge tip should be at (274,580); the drawn vertex sits inside the cube image at source (1184,715), which maps to ~(568,758) in the new placement (scale 746/3000 = 0.2487), so the wedge's new centreline is (0,560)->(568,758) at ~19.2 deg. Consequences that must travel with the change: wedge re-anchored to the new drawn vertex; measurement system re-anchored (X393 vertical -> X274, label '684 x 385' -> '746 x 420'); both halos resize/reposition with the cube; wordmark and tagline shift up 35 px. Rejected alternatives: much bigger 864 x 486 at (156,550) (dominates, squeezes the tagline band, wedge crosses almost the whole canvas); 782 x 440 at (238,560) (overshoot, lifts the top 55 px for no decisive gain); much smaller 540 x 304 (reads as a thumbnail/sticker, left void grows to 480 px); higher top ~450–500 px (collides with the tagline, breaks the low-anchor pattern); bottom-flush at 1080 px (sits on the footer); centred horizontally (destroys the lower-right asymmetry the wedge and spine depend on); full-bleed/cropped (cuts the cube's edges and vertex, breaks the measurement label); shift-left-only 684 x 385 at (333,615) (fixes the 3 px touch but leaves height 35.6% and left void 333 px — a half-measure). Falsification: the change is wrong if the new box is not exactly 746 x 420 at (274,580), the right margin is not 60 px, the bottom is not 1000 px, the wedge tip is not exactly at the new drawn vertex ~(568,758), the label does not read '746 x 420', the tagline has less than 20 px clear above y=580 or overlaps the cube, the footer is touched, the cube still reads as a strip at a 270 px thumbnail, or the cube is visibly softer than the 684 px version (if so, re-render natively at 746 px; if impossible, revert).

- Loop 46 study (28 designs, running total 1,164): the tagline as a second voice. Verdict: keep the two lines, keep the break at the full stop, keep Montserrat Regular 13 pt with 150 tracking; change the alignment only — move the block from right-aligned to left-aligned, starting at the cube's left edge. Top-5: (1) one line vs two lines — one line is the norm for a tagline (SHADOW LINE, TYSHA, Nosferatu, RED TRACE), but BLACK BOX's copy is two opposed sentences, and collapsing them to one line would collapse the antithesis SYSTEMS / FAILURES into a single breath and read as a credit line; two lines are justified here — the one-line norm does not override this copy; (2) where the break falls — the break should fall where the meaning turns, which for BLACK BOX is the full stop between the sentences, so the current break is right; mid-sentence breaks in the sample are for display type, not for a 13 pt second voice (Swiss posters, KAGE, Darkness and Light); breaking inside 'THE SYSTEMS YOU DEPEND ON.' at 13 pt would force a re-parse and gain nothing; (3) how the break relates to the hero's edge — in the strong examples the second voice's flush edge IS a hero edge and the other edge ties to something too (SHADOW LINE centred on the title's width, KAGE left-aligned to a grid column with a hairline grid, Benzin microcopy in a top-right column under a hairline rule, DARK LIGHT's THIS HURTS DEEP left-aligned inside a right-hand column with a vertical spine); BLACK BOX's block currently ties only on the right, to the cube's right edge (X1020), and that tie ends on two full stops — the least informative characters; its left edge, where both sentences start, ties to nothing; the block needs its tie on the left, where the reader enters; (4) what weight and size the second voice takes — tiny, Regular/light, about a tenth of the wordmark (13 pt Regular against 128 pt ExtraBold, ~10:1) is the pattern (Benzin, KAGE, SHADOW LINE, RED TRACE); do not go to Medium/SemiBold or 16–18 pt — it would compete with the wordmark and the measurement label and widen the lines so the X568 tie is lost; emphasis in the sample comes from colour or position, never from weight (RED TRACE marks TRACE in red, KAGE marks FUNCTION in red, Swiss posters alternate a word in colour — a later loop, not this one); all-caps with 150 tracking is the credit/microcopy voice, a weakness, but changing case now would confound the alignment test — note it for Loop 47; (5) how it is aligned — left alignment dominates by a large margin for a dark poster with a right-weighted hero (KAGE, RED TRACE's banner variant, Darkness and Light, all 50 Swiss posters, Benzin, DARK LIGHT's THIS HURTS DEEP, Issue No. 1); right-aligned only for DARK LIGHT's four-line intro paragraph, a statement not a tagline above a hero; centred only for film posters with a centred title; a right-aligned block makes the entry point move from line to line (the reader must find THE each time) while a left-aligned block fixes it; BLACK BOX's hero is on the right, its spine and wedge enter from the left, and its tagline is the only right-aligned element — right alignment makes the composition right-heavy and leaves the left black above the cube empty. CHANGE TO TEST (alignment only): move the two-line block, unchanged in copy, case, size, weight, tracking and vertical position, to left alignment on the cube's left edge — line 1 'THE SYSTEMS YOU DEPEND ON.' left edge X274, top Y537; line 2 'THE FAILURES YOU NEVER SEE.' left edge X274, top Y557; glyphs still end ~Y572, still 8 px above the cube's top edge Y580. PREDICTION TO VERIFY: line 2's right edge lands within 15 px of X568 (the wedge point's X) — on the width estimate line 1 ends ~X560, line 2 ~X571. CORRECTION (main Muse, verified against the card's geometry): the X274 measurement hairline DOES run through the tagline band (Y560–990 vs band Y537–577, overlapping Y560–577), so the block must shift to X282 so no glyph touches the line — the alignment is to the hairline, not to the card edge. WHY: the left edge X274 is the cube's left edge and the left hairline (a hard grid line the card already has); the reading entry THE is now fixed, not floating; the block fills the empty black above the cube's left half and balances the right-heavy composition, giving a wordmark -> tagline -> cube -> wedge-point reading path; the cube's right edge does not need the tagline to reinforce it — it is already the strongest vertical on the card. Rejected alternatives: one line right-aligned (reads as a credit, loses the 40 px vertical mass, left edge ties to nothing); centred on cube centre X647 (no centred element to centre on; centred taglines pair with a centred title; would cross the wedge diagonal); a different mid-sentence break in three or four lines (forces a re-parse at 13 pt, fills the wordmark-to-cube gap and touches both); heavier weight or larger size (breaks the 10:1 ratio, competes with the wordmark and the measurement label, loses the X568 tie); keep right alignment but mark FAILURES in red (next-best alternative, rejected for this loop — does not fix the floating left edge or the right-heavy composition; test alignment first, red in Loop 47); move the tagline below the cube into the footer (reads as a footer credit, loses the 8 px relationship Loop 45 settled); no tagline at all (the cube is abstract; the tagline is the only place the subject is stated). Falsification: the change is wrong if line 1 or line 2's left is not X274 ±2 (or X282 if the hairline shift applies), glyphs do not end Y572 ±2, the gap to cube top Y580 is not 8 px ±2, any wedge pixel appears in the tagline band Y537–577, or any glyph touches the left hairline; if line 2's measured right edge is NOT within 15 px of X568, the wedge-point tie is not real and the change rests on alignment alone; if a fresh viewer reads the left-aligned version more slowly, or the two sentences blur into one paragraph, or the viewer reads tagline -> wedge/spine instead of tagline -> cube, revert; if at thumbnail size the left block looks marooned with a large empty black gap between its right edge (~X565) and the cube's right edge (X1020), and the right-aligned version looks more settled, revert. If the left version passes geometry, the X568 tie holds within 15 px, and the reading test is equal or better, keep left alignment and make Loop 47 the next-best question: does the second sentence need a red punch word (FAILURES in #C32D30), or does red belong only to the wedge?

- Loop 47 study (24+ designs, running total ~1,188): does the second sentence need a red punch word? VERDICT: No word goes red. The tagline stays all white. Top-5: (1) a red word earns its place only when it IS the headline, at display size — never as a speck inside 13 pt prose; in every successful case the red word is a whole word, a whole line, or the whole title, set large (IDENTITY. in Effort Is an Identity, CONCLAVE the entire title in red, ATTENTION, HIRING, Precision, GOOD DESIGN's DESIGN); at 13 pt Montserrat Regular, FAILURES would be a ~13 px-high red fragment, ~95 px wide, inside a two-line block — no example colours a single word inside small running text and makes it work; (2) when a word does get the red, it is the antithesis word AND the terminal word — the last word, closing the thought (IDENTITY. closes 'EFFORT IS AN IDENTITY.'; DESIGN closes 'GOOD DESIGN'; INFORMATION. closes 'DESIGN IS INFORMATION.' with only its full stop in red; the red 'to' in face to face sits between two huge black words as the pivot); FAILURES fails both halves — it is the antithesis noun, yes, but it is word 2 of 5 in 'THE FAILURES YOU NEVER SEE.', mid-sentence, not terminal; red there would start a sentence it does not finish (the eye jumps to the middle of line 2, then must return to white YOU NEVER SEE.); line 2 has no verb at all (a noun phrase), so there is no action to colour; (3) how much red is too much: one red idea per poster, and a second red only if it is the same role, same scale, or touches the first (Effort Is an Identity's three reds are one connected system on the same left edge at headline scale; DESIGN IS INFORMATION. keeps its reds in one column system); BLACK BOX already has red in three roles (the large wedge ending in a point at (568,758); the tiny red vertical spine microcopy; the measurement system) — a red FAILURES at ~X315–410, Y555–572 would be a fourth red and a second red text, in a different scale, a different role, and a different place (~180 px above and well left of the wedge point, sharing no edge, no alignment and no touch with the wedge) — exactly the disconnected-second-red pattern that splits a poster into two competing red ideas; the wedge must remain the only large red gesture; the spine is already the small red text voice; (4) small prose stays one colour even when its punch words are darker in meaning — the decisive, repeated observation (WORDS 03: red is only the header label on a red block; the prose underneath is entirely black, including SHAME, DESTRUCTION, BLACKNESS, BURN and DEATH-CLIMAX; Effort Is an Identity's small white subline reads 'SIX SLIDES ON SHOWING UP, FAILING, RISING.' — FAILING, the direct analogue of FAILURES, stays white even though the headline word above it is red; Conclave's small line stays white; ECHOES' caption stays white while red is only the disc behind the statue); designers do not colour the emotionally loaded word inside a quiet line — they colour the container, the label, or the headline, and let the sentence do its work in one colour; (5) red at small size on black is dimmer, not louder — and it reads as an error, a link, or a label, not as emphasis (white on black ~21:1 contrast; #C32D30 on black ~3.8:1, below the 4.5:1 expected for normal-size text); at 13 pt Regular with Montserrat's open letterforms and 150 tracking, FAILURES in red would be measurably harder to read than the white words around it — the punch line would become the least legible line; a single red word in otherwise white small text is the visual language of a hyperlink, a correction, or a proofing mark; the one small-scale red-in-text form that works is punctuation at headline scale (the red full stop in DESIGN IS INFORMATION.), and at 13 pt it would be a ~5 px speck. CHANGE TO TEST: a FREEZE, not a colouring — no word goes red; FAILURES stays white, Montserrat Regular 13 pt, letter-spacing 150, line 2 unchanged at X282, Y537–577, exactly as Loop 46 left it. Record explicitly: 'Tagline: all white. Red is wedge + spine only; no red word, no red full stop, no red in line 1 or line 2.' Keeping it white preserves the two-voice structure — giant white wordmark, quiet white tagline, one red wedge that points at the cube — instead of inventing a third voice for one word. Rejected alternatives: FAILURES in red (mid-sentence, 13 pt, disconnected, duplicates the red spine, dimmer than white, reads as a link/error); NEVER in red (colours the adverb, makes the line a shouted negation, still fails scale/disconnection); SEE in red (terminal, so closest to Finding 2 — but SEE is the least informative word, a verb of perception, not the failure; red on the last word turns the tagline into a punchline/command, still fails scale/contrast/disconnection); the whole of line 2 in red (semantically neat — line 1 white systems, line 2 red failures — and the only whole-line form the survey supports in principle, but a whole 13 pt line in #C32D30 on black would be the dimmest text on the card, inverting the hierarchy, and creates a second red text block with no connection to the wedge); red full stop after SEE. (works only at headline scale; at 13 pt a ~5 px speck, reads as dust or a print error, no alignment with the wedge point); FAILURES in red ExtraBold/larger (breaks the Regular voice, adds a third weight, still fails disconnection); SYSTEMS or DEPEND in red (colours the positive, inverts the antithesis, competes with the wordmark). Falsification (A/B test, five fresh viewers, 3-second glance at 100% and 25%): the no-red decision is proved wrong only if the red version passes ALL of — viewers quote line 2 unprompted and in full without hesitation; no viewer describes the red word as a mistake, link, label, or second logo; reading order stays wordmark -> tagline -> cube with the wedge still the single red idea; FAILURES is as legible as the white words at 100% and still legible at 25%; at 200% zoom the red letterforms show no loss of edge or weight. A single 'I like the red' does not overturn it — only reading behaviour does. NEXT-BEST QUESTION (named by the study): Loop 48 — if the antithesis still feels flat, does the second sentence need a weight change, not a colour change — line 2 in Montserrat Medium, still all white at 13 pt / 150 spacing, versus Regular — and does that weight shift survive at thumbnail size without breaking the quiet tagline voice?

- Loop 48 study (35 designs, running total ~1,223): does line 2 need a weight change, not a colour change? VERDICT: No. Both tagline lines stay Montserrat Regular, 13 pt, 150 tracking, all white. Top-5: (1) a 100-step is below the threshold at this size — at 13 pt on a 1080 px card the cap height is ~9 px; at a 240–270 px thumbnail it is ~2 px, and the Regular-to-Medium stem difference is well under a pixel, further washed out by 150 tracking and by white-on-black bloom; 13 pt-equivalent microcopy reads as a uniform grey block at thumbnail in every grid; a Medium line 2 would not read as emphasis — at full size it would read as uneven inking, at thumbnail as nothing at all; (2) when weight does mark a sentence, the step is at least 200 — Regular to SemiBold/Bold — and usually paired with size, and then it is no longer a quiet tagline (Incite keeps both headline lines in the same Bold with the body below in Regular — the step is between headline and body, not within the headline; Dream Bigger's two-sentence microcopy stays uniformly tiny Regular while DREAM BIGGER shouts in huge Bold; Do Something First is all the same Bold, orange/white colour does the alternation, not weight); Regular to SemiBold would create a third hierarchy level (ExtraBold wordmark, SemiBold line 2, Regular line 1/footer/spine) and turn line 2 into a sub-headline; (3) the direction is wrong — where a step exists, the heavier element is normally first, or a single key word, not the whole second sentence (YOU DIDN'T COME's first two lines share one weight and the third is smaller and Regular; Lost in Thought's title is thin/light and the body stays uniformly Regular; Blues' payoff word is lighter and more open, not heavier; Future Nostalgia's title lines share one Bold and Dua Lipa below is lighter script; the one genuine heavier-second case, MY NAME IS NOBODY, works only because NOBODY is the title itself with a very large size jump as well as weight); line 2 is a full 26-character sentence, not a title or a punch word, and making it heavier makes the failure shout while the systems line whispers — the opposite of the documentary voice, and bottom-heavy in a block that sits only ~8 px above the cube; (4) antithesis is already carried by meaning, line break and position — identical dress lets the words oppose each other; adding a second cue explains the joke (LOVE/PAIN weights only the nouns, and the second sentence actually fades; LESS IS MORE weights LESS solid vs MORE outline with the supporting sentence in uniform small italic Regular; YOU DIDN'T COME / YOU CAME OUT uses identical weight, opposition in the words alone; Motivational Typography Posters weight one word per cell, never a whole sentence); a whole-line Medium is, in effect, colour by another means, and Loop 47 closed colour for the same reason — it would re-open the red question in a quieter form; (5) at thumbnail size, what survives is (a) the giant wordmark, (b) a uniform tagline block, (c) image/wedge geometry — never a one-step weight difference inside the block (DREAM BIGGER, KAMAU&CO, Blues are all recognisable from their microcopy at grid size, but in no case could Regular be told from Medium within the small text, including in enlarged crops). CHANGE TO TEST: a FREEZE — change nothing in weight; line 1 and line 2 both stay Montserrat Regular 13 pt, 150 tracking, all white, block X282, Y537–577, unchanged. Lock both lines at Regular. Rejected alternatives: line 2 Medium (invisible at thumbnail, muddy/uneven at full size, looks like a rendering or inking fault); line 2 SemiBold (visible at full size but loud, third level, competes with the wordmark and wedge, turns the failure into a slogan, crowds the ~8 px gap to the cube); line 1 Medium/SemiBold, line 2 Regular (directionally more editorial but still invents a step inside a 40 px-high block, still fails at thumbnail, makes the systems line shout while the failure whispers); both lines Medium (uniform but heavier overall, denser block, loses distance from the wordmark, fills in at thumbnail); both lines SemiBold/Bold (tagline becomes a second headline, quiet documentary register gone); line 2 red, italic, underlined, or re-tracked (red closed in Loop 47; the others are outside this loop's weight question and would change the X282 alignment, line lengths or block geometry). Falsification (A = both Regular, B = line 2 Medium, C = line 2 SemiBold as calibration; viewed at 1080 px, 270 px and 180 px, shuffled, to at least three viewers): the Medium change is WRONG and stays rejected if at thumbnail viewers cannot name line 2 as heavier at better than chance or cannot tell A from B at all; at full size viewers describe B as 'uneven', 'bolder at the bottom', 'smudged' or 'a printing error' rather than 'emphasised'; B's line 2 looks wider, extends past line 1, or makes the block feel bottom-heavy; or viewers rank B as louder/more slogan-like than A. It could only pass if a majority name line 2 as heavier at thumbnail without prompting AND still rate B as quiet as A AND nobody calls it a rendering fault. NEXT-BEST QUESTION (named by the study): Loop 49 — if the antithesis still feels flat, is it the pause between the sentences, not their weight — with both lines locked at Regular 13 pt / 150, does widening the leading between line 1 and line 2 (lifting the whole block if needed to keep the ~8 px clearance above the cube) let line 2 land as a second, darker thought? The only weight variant left open after that is a single word — 'NEVER' in Medium, the rest Regular — to be tested only after the pause test.

- Loop 49 study: the pause between the sentences — leading, not weight or colour. Verdict: do NOT widen to 1.4, 1.5 or 1.6 — that range is a dead zone (too small to read as a pause, too large to read as a tight block). If anything is tested, test ONE decisive jump — leading 2.0, block lifted 10 px — and expect it to be hard to pass; the study's prior is that the current 1.2 is likely to survive, because the full stop after 'ON.' plus the line break already IS the pause, and the successful pauses studied are not made by uniform leading at all. Top-5: (1) a pause has a threshold; 1.4–1.6 does not cross it — two-sentence taglines that read as one statement sit at ~1.0–1.2; the ones that read as two thoughts have a gap of about one extra full line (baseline-to-baseline ~1.9–2.0x font size, white space ~1.5–2x cap height between the lines); at 13 pt that is +4 px (1.5, barely visible) vs +10 px (2.0, unmistakable); (2) the pause, where it works, is a single asymmetric break before the punchline — not uniform loosening (THE ONE YOU ARE LOOKING FOR IS -> YOU keeps its first four lines at ~1.3 then leaves a clearly larger break before the final 'IS -> YOU', reinforced by the arrow; Yes, of course it hurts breaks after 'course' and indents 'it / hurts' to the right); with only two lines, 'leading' and 'space before line 2' are the same number, so any widening is automatically a single break, but it must be big enough to be read as a break, not as loose setting; (3) long lines need tight leading; short lines can afford air — the successful wide examples all have very short lines (one to three words); this card's lines are long full sentences, 27–28 characters each, tracked-out (150), and depend on proximity to stay grouped — widening them separates them into two captions faster than it separates two short lines (the Swiss work stays at ~1.0–1.1 and lets the word break itself do the work); (4) widening thins the block; it does not darken line 2 — the same ink spread over a taller block lowers optical density (at 1.5 the block goes from 40 px to ~44 px tall with no extra ink; at 2.0 to ~50 px); line 2 looks lighter, more remote and more detached, not darker — 'darker' here is semantic (systems, then failures) and no amount of air makes the second sentence more ominous, only more alone (Muren's loose ~1.4 spec blocks dissolve into a field of data); (5) clearance is a zero-sum budget, and proximity flips at 2.0 — every extra pixel of inter-line gap must be paid for by eating the 8 px clearance to the cube top (Y580) or lifting the whole block toward the wordmark (ink ends Y498); at 2.0 the white gap between the lines is ~17 px while line 2 sits only ~8 px above the cube — by proximity, line 2 is then nearer the cube than it is to line 1, so it risks grouping with the hero as its caption, not with line 1 as the second half of the tagline; that flip, not the wordmark, is the hard limit on widening here. Rejected: 1.4 (+2.6 px, invisible, no pause); 1.5 (dead zone — white between lines ~6–7 px -> ~10–11 px, not enough to be a break, enough to thin the block and make line 2 look lighter, not darker); 1.6–1.7 (same failure, worse — taller block, line 1 nearer the wordmark, still no clear break, reads as typesetting looseness); 2.2+ / a full blank line (inter-line gap ~20 px dwarfs the 8 px cube clearance, line 2 unambiguously groups with the cube, block splits into two labels, top crowds the wordmark); widening without lifting (at 1.5 line 2 ends ~Y576, clearance ~4 px; at 2.0 it ends ~Y582, colliding with the cube top — fails the stated clearance outright); changing size or tracking to compensate (changes two variables at once, confounds the test); a rule, dot or dash between the lines, or re-centring/right-aligning line 2 (not leading, out of scope, a new mark would compete with the red wedge and the measurement hairlines, re-alignment would break the X282 left edge). Top-5: (1) deliberate versus mistake is a size threshold, and at 13 pt it is high — a step that reads as deliberate is at least a full word wide (~2–3 em, ~20–30% of the line's width) and happens at display size ('God don't / make no / junk!' — 'make no' pushed right by about a word, 'junk!' returns to the left; 'POCKET / ROCKET / FOUNDATION.' — middle line indented, third line returns left); a step of +8 px (0.6 em) or +13 px (1 em) at 13 pt is about one capital letter wide and, against hairlines measured to the pixel, reads as a typesetting slip or a ragged edge, not a decision; no grid showed a small, quiet, two-line, same-size/same-weight/same-colour tagline with only line 2 nudged right by a few pixels — that absence across 24 designs is itself evidence; (2) right is the only direction with precedent; left has none, and here it is actively harmful — every indented second line found pushes right, toward the image; a left step (outdent/hanging indent, e.g. line 2 at X258) has no precedent for a tagline and on this card would cross the X274 vertical hairline and enter the '746 × 420' label's column (label at X223, Y563; line 2 sits at Y~557–577, overlapping vertically); right, by contrast, pushes line 2 toward the cube — the very element loop 49 found line 2 grouping with; (3) the left edge is the block's only anchor, and an indent destroys it — X282 sits just 8 px right of the X274 hairline, the tagline's tie to the measurement system; indenting line 2 creates a second left edge, so the block stops being one block; that is loop 49's failure in the horizontal axis (leading 2.0 split the block vertically so line 2 grouped with the cube; an indent splits it horizontally so line 2 stops belonging to line 1 and starts belonging to the cube/wedge area on its right); in the 3-line examples a third line returns to the left edge and restores it — BLACK BOX has no third line, so there is no return; (4) the right edge cannot afford any rightward step — line 2 already ends at X618, 50 px past the wedge point X568; +26 px takes it to X644 (76 px past), the word-aligned step to ~X662 (94 px past); the indent buys punchline separation by spending the only right-edge datum the card gives, and makes line 2 — already the longer line — the widest, most protruding element in the block; (5) what actually separates a punchline in the grids is not a small indent — it is a large step, a staircase in which every line steps, a return line, a change of size/weight/colour, brackets, a dash, or a separate column; loops 47 and 48 have already closed colour (all white) and weight (both Regular), so those tools are not available here; the direct analogues for a two-line sentence whose second line is the punchline are all flush ('Insights thrive in / unlikely company' — both lines share one left edge; 'DESIGN IS NOT DECORATION / IT'S COMMUNICATION'; 'DREAM / BIGGER') — in those, the line break alone does the work. - Loop 51 study (24 designs, running total ~1,321): should the whole flush tagline block lift 12 px as one unit? VERDICT: Do NOT lift the block. The current ~8 px clearance is already right. The slot between the wordmark and the cube is only 82 px tall (wordmark ink ends Y498; cube top Y580) and the tagline block is 40 px tall — only 42 px of slack in total. Today it is split 39 px above the block and ~3 px below it (box terms), so the block is unambiguously grouped with the cube. Lifting 12 px makes it ~27 px above and 20 px below (glyph gaps ~31 px and 20 px): roughly equidistant from both neighbours, grouped with neither. A decisive 'independent statement' position does not exist in this slot: lifting ~30 px (block Y507–547) would leave only ~9 px below the wordmark ink and still only ~33 px to the cube, reading as a crowded subtitle of BLACK BOX. The geometry, not taste, forces a choice between 'caption of the cube' and 'subtitle of the wordmark' — and this tagline is the card's thesis, not a subtitle. Top-5: (1) proximity decides the reading, and there are only two stable readings — caption or independent statement; the middle is drift (small text either sits at ~half a line-height or less from the hero and is read as its caption/label, or it sits several line-heights away AND is anchored to something else; nothing strong sits at ~one line-height from both neighbours with no anchor; the proposed 20 px gap is exactly one tagline line, the unstable middle); (2) air only reads as breathing room when it is visibly deliberate — ~2–3x the tagline's line-height, or explained by a rule, grid line or edge; a 12 px move on a 1080 px canvas (1.1% of the height) is below the threshold of intentionality and reads as a nudge or a mistake, not a decision; (3) lifting the block does not just loosen the cube — it reassigns the block to the wordmark above (a 128 pt wordmark ~10x the tagline's size wins any grouping contest once the distances are comparable; small text tucked under a giant masthead reads as subtitle or credit, never as an independent thesis); (4) left-edge alignment is doing as much grouping work as vertical distance — the tagline at X282 sits 8 px from the cube's left edge X274, so it already reads as the cube's caption by alignment as well as by proximity; keeping X282 while lifting vertically would leave a text that still points at the cube but no longer belongs to it — a floating label (detachment would require breaking the alignment too, which the loop did not propose); (5) on a black field, a small white block needs a neighbour; unanchored white text reads as an error, not minimalism (black-field designs that isolate text give it an edge or frame to belong to); the measurement system reinforces this — the '746 × 420' label at X223, Y563 currently sits level with line 2, inside the tagline's vertical band, as part of the same technical-caption system; lifting the block would put the label ~3 px below the lifted line 2's glyphs (~Y560), a new near-touch that would read as an orphaned third line. CHANGE TO TEST: KEEP — lock block X282, Y537–577; both lines flush at X282; leading 1.2; glyphs end ~Y572; glyph-to-cube gap ~8 px; glyph-to-wordmark gap ~39 px. 8 px is 0.4x the ~20 px line-height, squarely inside the tight-caption band the strongest examples use, while 20 px is 1.0x the line-height, the ambiguous band no strong example uses without a second anchor. If none of those holds — both lines read as one block, the cube reads as a separate object, and a clear if narrow black channel is visible at both scales — the 8 px clearance is confirmed and the lift is dead. - Loop 52 study (30+ designs, running total ~1,351): should the tagline's left edge align exactly to the cube's left edge (X282 -> X274)? VERDICT: HOLD X282. Do not shift the tagline to X274. The 8 px is not stray air — it is the clearance to the X274 measurement hairline, and it repeats the 8 px vertical clearance from the tagline glyphs (end ~Y572) to the cube's top edge (Y580). Shifting to X274 would trade a consistent 8 px module for a collision, for a gain invisible at normal viewing size. Top-5: (1) flush earns its place only when nothing intervenes and the flush is repeated — BLACK BOX fails that test, because the X274 hairline and the '746 × 420' label sit between the tagline and the cube; flush to the cube would mean flush to the hairline as well, two anchors in one place; (2) a small offset reads as a near-miss, not a decision — unless it is a repeated module (on its own, 8 px on 1080 px = 0.74% is in the worst zone, too small to read as an intentional inset, too small to read as flush; on this card it escapes only because it is not a one-off — 8 px left of the hairline = 8 px above the cube; a repeated 8 px is a system, a single 8 px is a mistake); (3) at 13 pt, an 8 px shift is visible with guides at 100% and invisible everywhere else (0.46 em, ~two-thirds of a cap height; 4 px at a 540 px-wide view, 2 px at a 270 px thumbnail) — the shift buys nothing for a normal viewer while costing something for a close reader; the tagline's job is a caption, read at close range, so its alignment should be judged at 100%, not in the feed; (4) in technical and measurement graphics, text never sits on a dimension line (labels and numbers always sit clear of rules and leader lines, with a gap of at least ~half a cap height) — that is the card's own genre ('ENGINEERING DOCUMENTARY', a measurement system of hairlines, ticks and a dimension label); putting the tagline's first 'T' (both lines begin with 'T') on the X274 hairline would break the genre's first rule, and at Y563 the hairline is the separator between the '746 × 420' label on its left and the tagline on its right — at X274 the separator has no clearance on its right side, and the label, hairline and tagline collapse into one crowded column; (5) successful captions are anchored to their own column or container, not necessarily to the hero (masthead flush, body type inset — ImagineFX, TEASER); the giant BLACK BOX wordmark is the flush element, the 13 pt tagline is the inset body element, and its anchor is already present — the X274 hairline, with an 8 px offset — not the cube's bounding-box edge (X274 is the cube image's left edge, while the cube's drawn upper-left vertex is at (568,758); there is no straight drawn vertical edge at X274 for the eye to align the tagline to, except the hairline itself). - Loop 53 study (25 designs, running total ~1,376): should the X274 measurement hairline terminate at the cube's top edge Y580, instead of running up beside the tagline? VERDICT: Yes — shorten it, but at BOTH ends, not only at the top. THE ARITHMETIC (verified by main Muse against the card's own record): the cube is 746×420 at (274,580), bottom edge Y1000; the current X274 hairline runs Y560→990 = 430 px long — 10 px longer than the 420 it is labelled with, 20 px above the cube top and 10 px above the cube bottom. It measures a 430 px interval shifted up from the cube, not the cube. It runs beside the tagline for 17 px of block height (560–577), 12 px beside actual glyphs (560–572), only 8 px to its left. (This inconsistency has been there since loop 27: the vertical was 430 px when the cube was 684×385 — it never matched the cube's height; the label claimed the cube's dimensions while the line measured a different interval.) Top-5: (1) a dimension line is object-bound — it starts and stops at what it measures (KITCHEN SHOP DRAWING's chains terminate exactly at the object's edges; Ray Gun leaders stop at the gun outline and at the label; exploded-view leaders stop exactly at each part and never continue past the topmost platter or bottommost base into the header or footer); no example runs a dimension/leader line on past its object into an unrelated text zone; (2) a tick is the terminus, not a decoration — it must sit on the end of the dimension line, at the measured edge (a tick floating above the line end claims a different interval); the top tick at Y560 does NOT need the hairline to reach it — if the hairline moves, the tick must move with it, or the tick is orphaned; the interval [Y560, Y990] is not a sacred datum (430, not 420); (3) the only legitimate overshoot is a small, unlabelled extension line — and this is not one (in CAD, extension lines project a few px/mm beyond the dimension line, with a small gap from the object, and do not carry the label; BLACK BOX's overshoot is 20 px at the top and 10 px at the bottom, is the dimension line itself, and carries a tick and a numeric label — an order of magnitude larger than a CAD overshoot, and exactly the part of the line that invades the tagline zone); (4) a rule beside unrelated text groups with that text — unless it is visibly not a dimension (Kelman's A3 Grid System: red grid lines run the full poster height and text sits beside them, but the lines have no ticks and no numeric label, text sits inside grid cells with a clear gutter, and the lines are visibly the structure; once BLACK BOX adds a 12 px tick at each end and '746 × 420' beside the top tick, X274 stops being neutral structure and becomes a claim about a specific interval — and a line making a claim that runs 12–17 px beside a two-line caption makes the caption read as part of, or a caption to, that interval; that is the false 'near-miss' reading loop 52 named); (5) paired rules do not have to share endpoints; staggered ends signal different functions (KITCHEN SHOP DRAWING has several dimension chains, each only as long as its own segment, staggered against each other; shared Y560/Y990 is precisely what makes X274 and X53.7 read as one system measuring one (wrong) interval — staggering them is how a viewer tells a spine from a dimension). TESTABLE CHANGE: X274 hairline Y560→990 becomes Y580→Y1000 (same X274, same 2 px, same #43413E; length exactly 420 px, matching the '420' in the label); top tick Y560 → Y580; bottom tick Y990 → Y1000 (same 12 px, same #989CA1, same X274); label '746 × 420' X223 unchanged, Y563 → Y583 (same text, size 7 pt, colour #989CA1, Montserrat Regular — keeps it exactly 3 px below the new top tick, as now, but beside the cube's top-left corner instead of in the tagline zone); X53.7 hairline UNCHANGED at Y560→990, ticks at Y560/Y990 (it remains the lower-zone/page spine; X274 becomes the cube dimension; their staggered ends are the point); tagline, wordmark, cube, red wedge, left spine and footer unchanged. WHY: it makes the dimension true (420, not 430), removes the 17 px parallel run beside the tagline, and leaves a clean 3 px vertical gap (577→580) between tagline bottom and hairline top, so the 8 px horizontal inset (282−274) can finally read as a caption inset, as loop 52 hypothesised; the label stays attached to its tick, and the cube's left edge gains a true datum instead of a near-miss. Rejected: keep Y560→990 (fails on arithmetic 430 ≠ 420 and on evidence — no blueprint runs a labelled dimension line through unrelated text); shorten top only, Y580→990 (length becomes 410, 10 px short; bottom tick still floats 10 px above the cube bottom — trades a +20 error for a −10 error); shorten top only and leave the top tick at Y560 (orphaned tick 20 px above the line end; the reader cannot tell whether the interval is 560–990 or 580–990); shorten to Y577 (tagline bottom) or Y572 (glyph end) (arbitrary, still 3–8 px above the cube top, length 413/418, still wrong, creates a new near-miss just above the cube); move the hairline off the cube edge (e.g. left to X266, with extension lines, proper CAD style — a bigger redesign, breaks the established 8 px X282/X274 inset relationship, adds new elements, and still has to stop at Y580/Y1000); delete the X274 hairline entirely (removes the cube's left-edge datum and the anchor for '746 × 420'; the card's whole language is measurement, and the label would have nothing to attach to); move the tagline away/right/down (loops 47–52 closed the tagline; moving it reopens closed questions and does not fix 430 ≠ 420); keep the hairline and move the label only, or keep the label at Y563 after shortening (the label would float 17 px above the new top tick, detached in the tagline zone); keep both hairlines sharing Y560/Y990 and re-label the interval as 430 (contradicts the cube's stated 746 × 420 size and the card's own label). Falsification (export the change, inspect at 100% and at thumbnail/arm's-length; numbers first: hairline length 420 ±1 px, ticks at exactly Y580 and Y1000, label at Y583 — if any is off, the test is invalid, not the idea): PASS if the tagline reads as a caption to the cube, not to the line; the top tick touches the cube image's top-left corner and the bottom tick touches its bottom-left corner with no gap or overshoot >1 px; the label sits beside the top tick, clear of the tagline; and the staggered X274 (580–1000) vs X53.7 (560–990) reads as two different functions. PROVE IT WRONG if: (a) viewers still group the tagline with the hairline, or still report a near-miss — in particular if the 3 px gap 577→580 is too tight and the line still feels continuous with the caption; (b) the staggered tops/bottoms read as a drafting error or broken pair, with viewers asking why the two verticals do not align; (c) the bottom tick at Y1000 collides with or crowds the two-item footer (footer Y1020 — 20 px clearance, same as the cube's own bottom edge; must be checked in the export, not assumed); (d) the top tick at Y580 is lost against the cube's top edge, or is confused with the red wedge's point at (568,758); (e) the label at Y583 is read as a caption to the cube image rather than as the dimension label, or is lost against the cube edge. If (b) is what fails — the pair must stay aligned — the next-best question, loop 54, is: 'Is X274 a spine, not a dimension?' Test by stripping the ticks and the '746 × 420' label from X274, keeping Y560→990, and seeing whether it then reads as a neutral grid spine beside a clean caption.
