- Loop 54 study (27 designs, running total ~1,403): does the left spine earn its place? VERDICT: Keep the spine, keep its words, size, spacing, position and rotation — change ONLY its colour, from red to the measurement grey #989CA1. It earns its place as a genre label and a quiet left-edge marker; it does not earn its place in red. Top-5: (1) a spine earns its place only when it carries information found nowhere else — 'ENGINEERING DOCUMENTARY' passes (neither the tagline, wordmark, nor footer names the genre; delete it and the documentary claim vanishes); (2) vertical text works when it IS the title, large, or when it is neutral microcopy — tiny plus accent colour is the worst combination (BLACK BOX's spine is the opposite on all four counts: 12 pt, 313 px of ink, red, only 29% of the 1080 px height; at that size a spine can only be a filing label, like a book spine — legitimate, but it must then behave like a label: quiet, not loud); (3) one accent, one job — red must be reserved for the wedge (Lissitzky's 'Red Wedge' uses red for the diagonal alone; Müller-Brockmann's 'Musica Viva' uses diagonal arcs with horizontal microcopy; the Made Up Studio covers use one diagonal or illustration as the energy, with horizontal titles); BLACK BOX spends red twice, at opposite ends of the card — a small red label at top-left (Y42–355) and a large red wedge pointing to (568,758) at lower-right; the two never touch or cross, so the competition is not spatial, it is colour-hierarchical — the eye is given two red starting points, and the smaller, earlier one (top-left, where Western reading starts) pulls attention away from the wedge's point, the card's one deliberate focal gesture; (4) a spine must align, run, or frame something; a short, top-only, unaligned spine reads as an orphan, not an anchor (the spine ink Y42–355 ends 19 px above the wordmark, then a 205 px gap before the X53.7 hairline begins at Y560; it does not align with the tagline, the cube top, or the footer; its only structural rhyme is a broken left axis — red text above, grey hairline below, wordmark interrupting the middle — broken by colour as well as by the gap); (5) the diagonal, the measurement system and the giant wordmark already fill the three directional jobs; a spine can survive only as the quiet fourth voice, in the measurement colour — a spine in #989CA1 stops being a second red voice and becomes the top extension of the measurement system (grey text above, grey ticks and hairlines below, one left axis, interrupted — deliberately — by the white wordmark). The spine should say the genre and only the genre ('ENGINEERING DOCUMENTARY' is the right text; do not change it to 'BLACK BOX' or 'VOL. 01', which would duplicate the wordmark and footer); keep it rotated 90°, reading bottom-to-top as a left spine; keep Montserrat Regular 12 pt and letter-spacing 160 (wide tracking is what makes rotated Latin microcopy legible, and 12 pt is the correct register for a label one step below the 13 pt white tagline); keep it in the margin at X20.1; do not enlarge it (enlarging it to 'Jinxed'/Nike scale would turn a label into a second wordmark and would require longer text to fill the height). TESTABLE CHANGE: spine colour red → #989CA1 (the existing tick grey), nothing else — same words, size, spacing, rotation, position. WHY: it preserves the spine's two real contributions (the only statement of genre, and the only element in the top-left margin) while removing its one real fault, the second red voice; it uses a colour already on the card, so it introduces no new palette value; it creates a coherent grey scale (white ExtraBold wordmark 128 pt > white tagline 13 pt > grey spine 12 pt #989CA1 > grey hairlines #43413E 2 px — each step quieter, each voice distinct); it makes the broken left axis read as one system; and it leaves the wedge as the only red on the card, so the red now means one thing — the diagonal that points at the cube. Why not white: white is the wordmark/tagline voice; a white spine would be louder, not quieter. Why not #43413E: a 2 px hairline colour, too dark for 12 pt type on black and effectively illegible. Rejected: delete the spine outright (fails on content — the only place 'ENGINEERING DOCUMENTARY' appears; also leaves the entire left margin Y0–560 empty above the X53.7 hairline and removes the book-spine metaphor); keep it red (fails finding 3 — two red voices); recolour it white (joins the primary white voice, competes with the wordmark/tagline); recolour it #43413E (illegible); move it down to run alongside the cube, e.g. ink Y580–893 at X20.1 (sits 33.6 px from the X53.7 hairline, forming an unintended double vertical, crosses the wedge's entry from the left edge and crowds the tagline); enlarge it to a 'Jinxed'/Nike/'Call of the Night' scale (becomes a second wordmark; 'ENGINEERING DOCUMENTARY' cannot fill 1080 px without added words); turn it horizontal as a kicker above the wordmark (duplicates the tagline's horizontal left-aligned role, loses the vertical anchor and the book-spine idea, crowds the wordmark whose ink top Y374 is only 19 px below the spine's ink end Y355); change the text to 'BLACK BOX', 'VOL. 01' or a date (duplicates the wordmark or footer, wastes the one place the genre is named); move it to the right edge (no margin there — the cube's edge to X1020 and the footer's 'VOL. 01'; a right spine would fight the cube); shrink it or tighten its tracking (does not address the colour competition, makes an already small label less legible at thumbnail size). Falsification (A = red spine, B = #989CA1 spine, identical except spine colour; viewed at 100%, 50%, and as a 270 px thumbnail, at arm's length; 5-second glance test with at least three viewers, asking afterwards without prompting (a) what the card is about / what genre it is, and (b) where the red shape points): the grey change is WRONG, and red should be restored, if in B and not in A: (i) genre recall collapses (fewer than 3 of 5 viewers can name 'engineering documentary' after 5 seconds, or the spine is illegible at 100% on black); (ii) the left edge reads as empty and the wordmark looks unanchored at thumbnail size in B, where it looked held in A; (iii) the wedge looks stranded — viewers describe the red as isolated or unbalanced, with all the red in the lower half and nothing to answer it at the top; (iv) at thumbnail size the grey spine, grey ticks and grey hairlines merge into an unreadable smudge, while the red spine remained a distinct mark. The change is CONFIRMED if in B the first fixation order is wordmark → wedge point (568,758) → cube, the wedge is named as the only red element, and genre recall is the same as in A (or better, because the spine is no longer mistaken for a second headline). Also check on export, before judging: that the spine reads bottom-to-top (head tilts left); if it reads top-to-bottom, flip its rotation — that is a direction correction, not a second design change, and it should be recorded separately. - Loop 55 study (30+ designs, running total ~1,433): once the spine is grey, does the X53.7 hairline still earn its place? VERDICT: DELETE it entirely. Top-5: (1) a dimension earns its place only by endpoints plus a value — X274 passes, X53.7 fails (in technical drawings every dimension line touches the measured edges at both ends and carries a number; a line in the same 2 px #43413E / #989CA1-tick vocabulary as X274, but with no label and endpoints that touch nothing, is read not as a second dimension but as a failed or stray one); (2) a spine earns its place by carrying text, not by having a rule beside it (in almost every poster examined the vertical text IS the spine and no rule accompanies it; a text spine needs no hairline chaperone — adding one beside it, 33.6 px away, creates a second axis for the same job); (3) two verticals on one side earn their places only when they do visibly different jobs in visibly different languages — or when they are a whole system, not a lone pair (a solid colour band containing text, a single line at the page edge, a full faint grid; when two lines share weight, colour and tick style, as X53.7 and X274 do, the eye reads them as twins and asks which one is the real measurement — here the answer is X274, so X53.7 is the duplicate); (4) a lone line in a margin is read as a page edge, margin or crop mark — so it must sit at an edge or align to a real margin, or it reads as a near-miss (X53.7 sits 53.7 px in from the left edge and aligns to nothing — not the tagline X282, not the cube X274, not the footer, not the spine X20.1; in Swiss and technical work the genre's contract is precision, so a top 20 px off, a bottom 10 px off and a footer gap of 30 px read as alignment errors, not as intention); (5) empty black field is a legitimate, trusted choice — minimal posters do not fill a quiet quadrant with a filler rule (the lower-left field X0–274, Y580–1020 is empty except for the wedge crossing it; that emptiness is not a hole to be propped up; the one honest job X53.7 could claim — extending verticality into the lower half where the spine (ending Y355) is absent, and bracketing the empty field with X274 — is not enough, because it does that job in X274's exact visual language without X274's justification, and because the wedge already crosses and activates that field). THE ARITHMETIC: spine ink ends Y355; the X53.7 line starts Y560 — a 205 px gap, so they do not form one continuous axis; spine box at X20.1, line at X53.7 — 33.6 px apart, two parallel left axes; X53.7 is 220.3 px left of X274; the X53.7 endpoints match nothing (top Y560 is 20 px above the cube top Y580; bottom Y990 is 10 px above the cube bottom Y1000 and 30 px above the footer Y1020; it is 430 px long and nothing on the card is 430 px; it has no label); by contrast X274 matches the cube exactly at both ends (Y580 and Y1000) and carries its value '746 × 420'. Loop 54 matters: the spine and the X53.7 ticks are now the same grey #989CA1, and the line shares X274's 2 px #43413E weight — the three left elements now read as one grey system that does not align, rather than as three distinct jobs. TESTABLE CHANGE: delete the X53.7 hairline (2 px #43413E, Y560→990) AND its two 12 px #989CA1 ticks (Y560, Y990); keep X274 (Y580→1000, ticks, label '746 × 420' at X223, Y583), the grey spine, tagline, cube, wedge, wordmark and footer exactly as specified; no replacement line, label, colour or shift. WHY: it measures nothing (no label; endpoints 20 px and 10 px off the cube; 430 px matches no element); it duplicates X274 in form without X274's function; it duplicates the spine in position (33.6 px away, same grey family since loop 54) without the spine's function (it carries no text); its 205 px gap from the spine means it does not even read as the spine's continuation. After deletion the left side has exactly one spine (text) and the measurement system has exactly one dimension (X274, labelled, exact) — one job, one mark, each. The wedge also gains a cleaner entry from the left edge, with no dark hairline crossing it in the margin (the wedge crosses X53.7 at y~579). - Loop 56 study (30+ designs, running total ~1,463): does X274 alone still earn its place? VERDICT: KEEP X274 EXACTLY AS IT IS — a FREEZE, no visual change. Top-5: (1) a solitary dimension earns its place only when it is exactly anchored at both ends to the thing it measures — a stray is offset, of arbitrary length, or free at one end; X274 passes three times over (length exactly 420 px, the cube's height; ends exactly Y580 and Y1000, the cube's top and bottom; X exactly 274, the cube's left edge — it is the cube's height, traced); (2) judged by blueprint rules alone, one dimension always fails, because blueprints never isolate one dimension (orthogonal pairs, extension lines, many labels, each label mid-span and breaking its own line, each label stating only the span of that line) — but BLACK BOX is not a blueprint, it is a poster with one technical cue, and applying the full blueprint test to a poster is the wrong test; the poster test is whether one restrained cue reads as deliberate, and X274 does, because of finding 1; (3) in Swiss, minimal and editorial work, a single quiet hairline survives when it aligns to a grid or object edge and does a second job — divider, spine, or scale bar (a lone line must touch something at both ends, or be the composition's axis); X274 does a second job — it is simultaneously the cube's left edge and a vertical scale bar for its height; a line in the middle of the black field, 50 px from the cube, would be a stray, but this one is on the cube; (4) label proximity is grouping and alignment, not raw distance — and X274's label is already correctly grouped (starts X223, 51 px from the line, Y583, 3 px below the top tick, reads left-to-right beside the line it belongs to — the standard position for a vertical scale bar: beside the bar, aligned to one end; a scale bar is not required to have its label at mid-span; moving the label to mid-span, about Y786, would put it in empty black field, detached from both ticks, reading as a floating caption; moving it closer would close the small clearance it needs from the 12 px ticks and the line itself, with no gain in grouping — at 7 pt the label already sits immediately left of the line; in blueprints mid-span works only because the label breaks the line, but here the label sits beside the line, so end-alignment is the correct convention, and it is already used); (5) the ticks are what turn an edge into a dimension, and 12 px in #989CA1 at both ends is the minimum that does it (without ticks X274 would be only the cube's left edge; with a tick at Y580 and a tick at Y1000, and nowhere else, the span is closed and the line is declared a measurement; longer ticks, arrowheads, a brighter colour, or a tick at one end only would all break that declaration — longer ticks would extend into the glass cube and into the black field and become a second graphic; arrowheads would import a full drafting system that one line cannot support; brighter ticks would out-shout the 7 pt label; the existing hierarchy is also correct — the line is the quieter #43413E, the ticks the lighter #989CA1, so the closures, not the shaft, carry the signal; a stray has no closures, X274 has two, at exactly the right places). KEEP, WITH EXACT NUMBERS: line X274, 2 px, #43413E, Y580→Y1000; ticks 12 px, #989CA1, at Y580 and Y1000; label '746 × 420', Montserrat Regular 7 pt, #989CA1, at X223, Y583; no other element moves. Rejected: move the label closer to X274 (already left-adjacent, 51 px from its start to the line, top-aligned to the top tick — closing the gap risks touching the 12 px tick zone and the line, crowds a 7 pt string, and does not improve grouping; the problem, if there is one, is not distance); move the label to mid-span, about Y786 (detaches the label from both ticks, floats it in empty black, borrows the blueprint mid-span convention without the blueprint device that makes it work — the label breaking the line); change the ticks — lengthen them (12 px→20 px), make them arrowheads, brighten them to white, or keep only one (longer/brighter ticks become a second graphic and compete with the tagline and footer; arrowheads demand a full drafting system; one tick leaves the span open at one end and makes the line look unfinished); delete X274 and its label (removes the card's only measurement and leaves the 'ENGINEERING DOCUMENTARY' spine and the technical premise unsupported — the minimal posters that delete measurement do so because they have no measurement theme; BLACK BOX's spine, tagline about systems and failures, and cube-as-specimen all promise a document, so deleting the one dimension would make the card a generic black poster with a cube; if the label were kept without the line it would be orphaned; if both went, the engineering signal would be gone); restore X53.7, or add a horizontal dimension for the 746 width (loop 55 deleted X53.7, and restoring it reintroduces the pair that was judged not to earn its place; adding a width dimension would turn the poster into the blueprint system of finding 2, which the card has already moved away from). VERDICT: NO, the two-number spec does not belong on a vertical-only line — change the line label to '420' alone, and move the whole-image spec to the footer as a labelled image specification ('IMAGE 746 × 420', centre-aligned on X540, at Y1020). Top-5: (1) one line, one number — a dimension line states only its own span (the VW Logo Specification Poster labels its horizontal line 'D', its vertical line 'K', its small-square lines 'S' and 'C', its angles '24°' — one value or letter per line, with the values decoded in a key at the foot; the Ferrari F40 and Porsche 911 four-view blueprints likewise put a single number on each horizontal and vertical dimension line; floor plans do the same on their perimeter lines; a '×' on a 1-D line is a category error — '×' claims a two-dimensional area); (2) a two-number spec is honest only where two dimensions are present — inside the 2-D area it describes (floor-plan rooms labelled inside the room), as two separate labelled lines, one per axis, or in a table or legend where each number is labelled; it never belongs as the label of a single axis; (3) whole-object specs belong in a separate, labelled block, apart from the drawing (Ferrari F40 puts 'SPECIFICATIONS' in a table at top left; the Lamborghini Huracán poster puts 'Dimensions and Weight' in a labelled text block — Length/Width/Height each on its own line, never collapsed to one '×' string on a line; room-size tables put '22×28', '12 x 14 ft' in table cells under column headings; the VW poster puts its values in a legend; the Sofa instructions put their two-number part spec in a labelled parts table, not on a line); (4) a dimension is optional — so if one is kept, it must be true (the Technics SL-1200MK2 exploded poster carries no dimension line at all, only numbered leader lines to parts; the Sofa instructions carry none; Müller-Brockmann's Beethoven/Stadttheater/Strawinsky posters carry none; album and magazine covers carry none — their technical authority comes from numbering, grids and leader lines, not from a dimension; Up close it is a working technical drawing'; the Pinterest blueprints are the same — dimensions everywhere, tied to views and parts, with units, tables or a formula) — a single dimension, no unit, no second dimension, no tolerance and no part label cannot check anything; '420' alone cannot tell a reader whether the cube is correct, tall or to scale, least of all when the line sits flush on the cube's own left edge (X274), so its length is self-evident from the cube itself; it is a quotation of engineering, not engineering; (4) when a spec IS the poster, it is the content, not the footer (in Technics, Race Circuits, Retro Weapons Blueprints and Gear Ratio, the drawing and its labels are the hero, large and central) — BLACK BOX inverts this: the spec is banished to the two least-read places on the card, 7 pt at X223 in the left margin and 12 pt grey at Y1020 in the centre of the footer; placement itself tells the reader not to use it (brand identity confirms the split from the other side: grids, clearspace and dimensions appear on separate construction pages, never on the hero lock-up; album art puts any spec on the spine or back, the front is title/artist only; editorial puts a folio/page number inside, never a spec on the cover); (5) redundancy kills both items at once — the footer ('746 × 420') and the line ('420') state the same height twice, in two sizes and two places, neither with a unit, and neither adds what the other lacks in a usable way (the footer alone gives the width, 746; the line alone gives a drawn length); a reader who notices one discounts the other as decoration, and a reader who notices neither loses nothing; two measurements also imply a measurement system, but the card defines it as 'exactly ONE dimension' — a system of one is a contradiction; loop 55 already proved the card survives deleting a measurement line (X53.7), while loops 56–57 kept and moved this one without testing whether anyone uses it. This is a pure deletion test, not a redesign, and it is honest for an 'ENGINEERING DOCUMENTARY' card: a decorative dimension is a false claim to measurement, and removing it leaves the documentary claim to the spine, tagline and cube, which actually carry it. Rejected: keep both (fails findings 1, 3 and 5 — no poster in the 30+ studied repeats a file size in the footer and a single dimension beside the image; keeping both preserves a false measurement system and ignored metadata); drop the footer spec only, keep the '420' line (keeps the weaker of the two — the line gives only height, no unit, no width — and removes the only place the width 746 is stated, leaving '420' even more orphaned, and keeps a 420 px vertical whose only cross-reference has been deleted); drop the '420' line only, keep the footer spec (keeps the most ignored element of all — centre footer, 12 pt grey on black, Y1020, the last-read position, stating a file fact — and removes the only element that at least draws the eye to the cube's height); merge them, e.g. label the line '746 × 420', enlarge '420' to 12 pt, or add 'px' (a bigger or better-labelled single dimension is still a single, unactionable dimension; 'px' does not give any reader a task to perform with it, and enlarging it would compete with the tagline and wedge); add a second dimension line for 746 (top or bottom of the cube) to 'complete' the system (would change the hero, add a horizontal rule across the cube's top/bottom, and still answer no reader question — nobody needs the hero image's pixel size to read a test card; completing a measurement nobody uses is worse than deleting it); move the spec to the spine or tagline area (both are closed/locked, and a file size would contaminate them). Honest limit (stated by the study): this loop did no eye-tracking or reader testing; the conclusion is an inference from placement, repetition, completeness and genre contract across the designs above, not a measured reading — if the falsification test in (b) contradicts it, that test, not this study, should decide loop 59. VERDICT: KEEP BOTH EXACTLY AS THEY ARE (LOCK) — a FREEZE, no visual change. Top-5: (1) a blank centre holds when the two footer items are true bookends — same baseline, same size and colour, at the extreme edges (the closest direct analogue is POCKET ROCKET FOUNDATION.: its bottom row is '179.99' and '$' with the centre empty, and it reads as a designed table row, not a missing item; the same bookend logic holds in Explosion/Lines and Jacob Karlzon. the failure mode in the grids was the opposite — a weak, smaller centre item that looked orphaned) — BLACK BOX has no rule, no three-column system anywhere (wordmark centred, spine left, tagline left), so nothing implies a third footer slot; the deleted centre spec (loop 58) must not return in any form; (3) plain black in the quadrant opposite a single off-centre hero is the correct Swiss answer, and it holds at thumbnail/poster distance (ESSENCE: giant top wordmark, vast empty field, one tiny figure, one small text block bottom-left, lower-right empty — the emptiness is the design; Sonnet Posters, Arrival, BOKKA – Blood Moon, Student Cultural Centre, Jacob Karlzon — in every case the eye does not hunt for fill opposite the hero); (4) a vertical, mark or texture is needed only when the quadrant is an information zone, or when the hero is centred and symmetrical so the eye has no diagonal to follow (counter-examples: posters#002, a programme poster where density is its brief; Typographic Posters II, where type itself fills every quadrant; 50 Swiss Style Posters, dense grids; SL24, brutalist data-logistics, every cell filled; Demokratie, a black bar filling the lower quadrant) — BLACK BOX is neither: its hero is right (cube 746×420 at (274,580)), and its lower-left already has a gesture — the red #C32D30 wedge entering from the left edge and ending in a sharp point exactly on the cube's upper-left vertex at (568,758); the wedge is the lower-left's content, and a vertical would duplicate its job; (5) at poster distance there is no safe middle size for anything added in either place — anything at or below ~12–13 pt in the lower-left, or a 12 pt centre footer item, is invisible at 25% / 270 px wide and at 3 m (it would change nothing at the distance this loop is about), while anything large enough to be seen (roughly ≥24 pt, or ≥2% of the 1080 width) becomes a second hero / second headline and competes with the cube, the wedge point and the tagline; the choice is therefore binary — plain black / blank centre, or a competing element — and the evidence says the competing element is wrong here. - Loop 60 study (38 designs, running total ~1,586): footer legibility at poster distance — does a 12 pt #9a9a9a footer on black register at all at 270 px / 3 m? VERDICT: KEEP THE FOOTER EXACTLY AS IT IS — a FREEZE, no visual change. The numbers: #9a9a9a on pure black has a contrast ratio of ~7.46:1 (relative luminance ≈ 0.323), which passes WCAG AAA for normal text (7:1); white would be 21:1 (2.8× the contrast), but contrast is not what fails at distance. Size is what fails, and no offered change fixes it: 12 pt on a 1080 px canvas is a 16 px em; at 270 px wide that is a 4 px em, ~2.8 px cap height, with a Regular stroke of ~0.5 px; 13 pt is 4.3 px — an 8.3% gain, still sub-legible; white 12 pt is the same 4 px; at 3 m that is at or below normal acuity for a letter stroke, and grey's lower effective contrast at high spatial frequency pushes it under the threshold. A footer that genuinely read at 270 px / 3 m would need roughly 28–32 pt (a 9–11 px em at that scale), 2.5× larger, at which point it stops being a footer and becomes a third headline. The premise of the loop question is therefore confirmed, but it is not a defect: in every design examined, the small footer/credit does not register as words at poster distance — that is its job; it is a close-range whisper (attribution and series marker), read after the wordmark, tagline and cube, at arm's length. Top-5: (1) at 270 px / 3 m, nothing at ~12 pt registers as words, grey or white (Pinterest's 'GET BETTER EVERY DAY' at exactly 270 px wide: the giant grey wordmark registers, the small grey footer is a faint smudge — its first line only becomes readable when the crop is enlarged 2×, its second paragraph never does; the same happens to the dense small white text at the foot of 'IMPACT' and 'DEMISE', and to the top microcopy block of '"Elements Unveiled"', which reads as a grey band at tile size); (2) what registers at distance is size and isolation, not colour ('Student Cultural Centre': white text roughly 3× footer size, centred on black, is fully readable at a 355 px tile; the isolated mark 'JTM' at the foot of 'Elements Unveiled' registers while the two credit lines directly above it do not; wordmarks survive distance, their small print does not); (3) grey works close up and fails only in combination with small size, distance and dim light (the 'Poster Black Friday Sale Template' is the direct analogue: a small grey paragraph on black is a grey smudge at tile size but is plainly a paragraph at full size; 'Movie Poster – Black Earth' and 'MAGAZINE POSTER (BLACK)' show the same split — title readable, small credits not — with no loss of quality at full size); (4) the working alternatives in the wild are not 'white 12 pt' or 'grey 13 pt' — nobody does those; designers do one of three things: (a) accept distance invisibility and keep the footer as close-range credit (serial/editorial work); (b) delete the footer entirely (single-image works with nothing to credit); or (c) jump to ~24–30 pt bold white, which changes the element's job from credit to message; no sampled design used a 1 pt bump or a colour-only swap to fix distance legibility, because neither can; (5) a grey footer is a hierarchy signal, and whitening it flattens the card — the card already has two white text levels (128 pt ExtraBold wordmark; 13 pt Regular tagline); a third white level at the bottom edge would frame the card in white top and bottom, promote '@BLACKBOXSYSTEMSLAB' / 'VOL. 01' to the same visual rank as the tagline, and break the plain-black lower-left quadrant locked in loop 59; grey #9a9a9a says 'read me last, up close', which is exactly the footer's role. Rejected: white 12 pt (same 4 px at 270 px, so it still does not read at 3 m; at close range it gains nothing the footer needs — it already passes AAA — and costs hierarchy, a bright bottom band competing with the tagline and the cube, and a white frame effect with the wordmark); grey 13 pt (+8% size, 0% contrast gain, still illegible at distance, and it breaks a locked specification for a difference no viewer could detect — a noise change); delete the footer entirely (the only alternative with a real distance benefit — nothing to misread, cleaner black field — and the correct answer for a one-off image poster; it fails here because the footer carries the only attribution and the only series marker on the card — without '@BLACKBOXSYSTEMSLAB' a close viewer cannot find the maker, and without 'VOL. 01' the series framing has no on-card evidence; the sampled serial works all keep their credit line for exactly this reason; rejected, but the clear second choice, ahead of white 12 pt). Falsification (export at 1080×1080, display at 270 px wide, in normal room light, with three viewers of normal/corrected vision): (1) at 3 m, ask each to read the footer aloud — expect 0/3 to read either item word-for-word (that is the predicted, acceptable result); (2) at 0.5 m / arm's length, ask each to read it aloud — expect 3/3 to read both items within 5 seconds, first try; (3) ask whether anything at the bottom edge looks like dirt, a scratch, a rendering error or a stray mark. 'Keep' is falsified if: fewer than 3/3 read it at close range (grey is then genuinely too dim and white 12 pt, not grey 13 pt, becomes the fix); or ≥2/3 call it dirt/a defect at either distance (then delete it); or a viewer at 3 m reads it word-for-word (then the distance premise was wrong and the footer is over-prominent, so darken it). If it passes, the footer is doing its job and the question is closed. VERIFICATION BY MAIN MUSE: v60 = v58 byte-identical (sha256 cc0b949e). Contrast ratio computed independently: #9a9a9a on black = 7.46:1, passes WCAG AAA (7:1) — the study's number is correct. Footer at 270 px: the footer band shows only a faint grey smudge (a few dozen bright px, no distinguishable letterforms) — matching the prediction that 0/3 would read it word-for-word at 3 m. Footer at 100%: glyph height ~11 px (12 pt = 16 px em), clean ink, no stray pixels — readable at arm's length, nothing that looks like dirt or a defect. The fresh-viewer part of the falsification test was NOT RUN — no fresh viewers available, reported honestly to Kind. NEXT-BEST QUESTION (named by the study): Loop 61 — distance hierarchy between the two things that DO register at 3 m: does the red #C32D30 wedge's sharp point at (568,758) read as a deliberate pointer to the cube at poster distance, or does it vanish into the cube's edge, leaving only the wordmark and the cube?
- Loop 61 study (24 designs, running total ~1,610): does the red wedge's sharp point read as a deliberate pointer to the cube at poster distance (270 px / 3 m)? VERDICT: IT VANISHES AS A POINTER — CHANGE THE ENDPOINT, do not keep it as it is. The red body still reads as a diagonal slash in the plain-black lower left, but its point does not read as pointing at the cube — because it touches the cube, inside the cube's own busy diagonal drawing, and because a tapering point gets thinner exactly where it needs to be widest. Top-5: (1) area beats line — a diagonal reads at 270 px / 3 m only if it is a shape, not a line; the survivors are all at least ~24–28 px wide on the full-size card (6–7 px at 270 px) for a sustained stretch near their tip; a wedge that tapers to zero is thinnest exactly where the eye must locate it, so its last 30–40 px fall below the 12–16 px legibility threshold and disappear into anti-aliasing; (2) a gap beats a touch — no successful pointer in the set touches its target; arrows, bands and triangles that stop clear of their target read as deliberate gestures, while a tip that lands exactly on a drawn vertex has no figure–ground separation, so the eye cannot tell where red ends and target begins; BLACK BOX's central defect: its point at (568,758) is not on the cube's outer silhouette against black, it is inside the cube's bounding box (cube 274–1020 × 580–1000), on a drawn vertex inside a glass image; (3) colour alone does not save a thin tip — #C32D30 on plain black is high-contrast for a field, but a thin red tip against the cube's own dark glass, highlights and edges loses chroma and edge contrast; red survives at distance as area, while as a hairline against a busy photograph it becomes a stain on the cube, not a pointer to it; (4) competing diagonals kill a single diagonal — the cube is itself a drawing of isometric diagonals, and the wedge adds one more diagonal at a similar scale, with no difference in width, angle or separation to mark it as a separate gesture; many diagonals at thumbnail size collapse into texture and the viewer cannot follow any one of them; the wedge's length (~568 px to the point, 142 px at 270 px) is ample — length is not the problem, distinctness at the endpoint is; (5) the three distance tricks are thickness, repetition, and a widened head — and the wedge uses none of them at its tip (thickness, repetition, and a head wider than its shaft are what survive; a long taper is the inverse of all three); the wedge's body, in the plain-black lower-left quadrant, probably does read as a red diagonal slash at distance, but its point does not read as pointing. THE CHANGE (loop 61): shorten the wedge and re-shape its tip, in one move — (a) pull the tip back 24 px along the wedge's own centreline, so the new tip stops 24 px short of (568,758), leaving a 24 px plain-black gap between red tip and cube vertex (6 px at 270 px; 6 mm on a 270 mm print); keep the same left-edge entry, same angle and same centreline, so the extension of the centreline still passes through (568,758) within ±4 px; (b) steepen the final taper so the wedge is at least 24 px wide (measured perpendicular to the centreline) at 24 px back from the new tip, and reaches its point only in the final 12 px — the tip becomes a short, steep point / small arrowhead, not a long hair taper. Why these numbers: 24 px is the smallest gap that is unambiguously a gap at 3 m (~7× acuity) while still reading as 'pointing at' rather than 'missing'; a 12 px gap would be marginal (3 px at 270 px) and a 40 px+ gap would start to read as a miss; the 24 px near-tip width puts the visible head above the 12–16 px legibility threshold for a sustained stretch. Everything else stays locked: colour #C32D30, tagline, wordmark, cube, footer and plain-black lower left are untouched. Rejected: keep as is (a touching tip inside a busy glass drawing has no separation at 270 px, and a tapering tip has no width where it matters — keeping it preserves a gesture that is only legible close up); thicken the whole wedge only, keeping the tip on (568,758) (a thicker tip that still touches the vertex still merges with the cube; it would read as a larger red stain / red face on the cube, and risks crowding the tagline block and the footer; width without a gap does not create a pointer); lengthen it / overshoot into the cube (fails worst — the tip would sit inside the glass image and read as a crack, reflection or mark on the cube, breaking the cube's illusion); shorten it by a large amount (80–100 px) or move the endpoint to a different vertex (beyond ~40 px the gap reads as a miss — the wedge aims at empty black, not at the cube — and a different vertex would need a new angle and would no longer be the drawn upper-left vertex the composition was built around); delete the wedge (tempting, and the card would still work as wordmark + cube, but the wedge's body is the only warm colour and only diagonal in the lower half, and at thumbnail a red diagonal in plain black is a genuine third distance element; deleting it removes the problem by removing the gesture, rather than fixing the gesture for 24 px; delete only if the falsification test below fails for the shortened version too); change the colour (the failure is geometric — touch + taper + competing diagonals — not chromatic; #C32D30 already has ample contrast on black, and a brighter tip would still merge where it touches the cube). FALSIFICATION (export at 1080×1080, then view at 270 px wide or print 270 mm wide and view from 3 m; show it to a fresh viewer for under 3 seconds, with no prompting, and ask them to point to where the red ends and what it is pointing at): the change FAILS if (a) the viewer says the red touches the cube, or cannot find a black gap between red and cube; (b) the viewer cannot trace the wedge's line to the cube's upper-left vertex, or says it points at empty black / at the wrong part of the cube; (c) the red tip reads as a smear, a red edge of the cube, or a mark on the glass, rather than as a distinct red point separated from the cube; (d) measured in the file, the gap is not 24 px (±4 px) along the centreline, or the wedge is under 24 px wide 24 px back from its tip, or the extended centreline misses (568,758) by more than 4 px. Pass = the viewer locates the gap, follows the line to the vertex, and names the cube as the target, at 270 px, in under 3 seconds. If the shortened version fails (b) in particular — the gap reads as a miss rather than a pause — the next step is not to close the gap again, but to delete the wedge. NEXT-BEST QUESTION (named by the study): Loop 62 — after this change, does the 24 px gap read as a deliberate pause or as a broken / missed wedge at 270 px / 3 m, and does the wedge's angle still unambiguously align with the cube's upper-left vertex when the gap is present? That needs the shortened export itself.

- Loop 62 study (30+ designs, running total ~1,640): does the 24 px gap read as a deliberate pause or as a broken/missed wedge at poster distance? VERDICT: KEEP THE 24 PX GAP EXACTLY AS IT IS. THE GAP IS NOT THE FAILURE. THE ARROWHEAD IS. At poster distance the gap itself will be seen (6 px at 270 px, ~6.9 arcminutes, well above acuity) — but it will be misread, because the tip that has to explain it disappears: the wedge is 24 px wide at 24 px back from its tip and reaches its point only in the final 12 px; at 270 px that taper is 3 px long, and a 3 px point cannot be read as an arrowhead, so the red shape reads as a blunt bar that stopped short, and a blunt bar stopping 24 px short of a soft photographic vertex reads as a miss, not a pause. The centreline is geometrically exact (19.2°, tip-to-vertex (23,8) is also 19.2°) — but geometry alone does not survive when the pointer's head is illegible and its target is a glass photograph rather than a crisp point. Top-5: (1) a gap of 1.0× the pointer's width is the worst, most ambiguous ratio — gaps that read as deliberate are either ≤0.5× the pointing element's width (a near-touch where Gestalt closure completes the line) or ≥2× the width (a clear interval, plainly a field of negative space); a 1.0× gap is large enough to be seen as separation and small enough to look like a near-miss, a misregistration or a crop; it is also a singleton (nothing else on the card repeats a 24 px diagonal gap, so there is no system for the eye to read it as a rule; the 8 px tagline-to-cube gap is a different size and direction and does not rhyme); (2) the head must be wider — and longer — than the shaft to survive distance; a sharpened shaft does not (every arrow that stayed legible at thumbnail size had a head clearly broader than its shaft; BLACK BOX's head is only the shaft sharpened over 12 px, so at distance it is a bar, and a bar cannot 'pause' — it can only stop); (3) alignment survives distance only when the target is a crisp point — here the target is the upper-left vertex of a glass-cube photograph, a soft, reflective, photographic corner, not a drawn point, and no reference showed a thin pointer aiming across a gap at a soft photographic vertex and succeeding; (4) a gap reads as a pause only when the composition gives it a second witness — repetition, a rhyme, or the gap as the subject; without one, a single gap between the only red element and the only photograph reads as an accident; (5) high contrast makes the problem worse, not better — #C32D30 on black is highly visible, so the gap will be noticed and judged; contrast guarantees the viewer sees the separation, and only a legible arrowhead can tell them the separation was intended. THE CHANGE (loop 62, LAST): WIDEN THE TIP, KEEP THE GAP. Keep the tip at (545,750), keep the 24 px gap, keep the centreline through (568,758), keep the shaft 24 px wide, and change ONLY the arrowhead: arrowhead width 48 px at its base (2.0× shaft width), centred on the existing centreline; arrowhead length 36 px (the taper now runs over the final 36 px, not the final 12 px); base centre at tip minus 36 px along the centreline ≈ (511,738), base half-width 24 px perpendicular to the centreline. Everything else unchanged: wedge still enters at (0,560), still sits above the cube, still ends at (545,750), gap still 24 px. Why: it moves the gap/head ratio from 24/24 = 1.0 to 24/48 = 0.5 — into the near-touch band — without moving the tip or undoing loop 61's shortened wedge; at poster scale the head becomes 12 mm wide and 9 mm long (12 px × 9 px at 270 px), a triangle that can actually be seen as a triangle; the wedge then reads as 'arrowhead held off its target by one half-head-width', the standard stand-off in technical drawing, rather than 'bar that fell short'; it also preserves the reason for the gap (the wedge stays above the cube and never overlaps the glass vertex, so the cube edge stays clean). Rejected: keep as is (the 12 px taper is not legible at 270 px / 3 m — keeping it bets the whole reading on a point the viewer cannot see); widen the gap to 48 px (doubles the extrapolation distance to a soft photographic vertex, weakens the alignment, and makes the wedge look detached and floating); narrow the gap to 8–12 px (reads as a near-miss / misregistration at close viewing and collapses into apparent contact at poster distance); delete the wedge (removes the card's only diagonal, only red and only left-to-right thrust); add a dimension line, ticks, a label or a spec to 'explain' the gap (out of scope — the card's locked character). FALSIFICATION (export at 1080×1080, downscale to 270 px, view at 3 m, plus a copy with a 2 px Gaussian blur to simulate distance acuity; show 5 seconds each to three people who have not seen earlier loops, ask 'What is the red shape doing? What is it pointing at?'): PASS = at least 2 of 3 say 'an arrow pointing at the top-left corner of the cube' and describe the tip as a point/arrowhead, not a bar or stripe. FAIL = at least 2 of 3 say it 'missed', 'stopped short', 'is broken / cut off', or cannot name the cube corner; OR they call the red shape a bar/stripe; OR, objectively, in the 270 px image the head is not distinguishable as a triangle from a blunt end. If it fails, the head is still too small — do not then move the tip or widen the gap; first try a still broader head (60 px wide × 42 px long, same tip and gap) and re-test; if that also fails, the gap-to-soft-vertex construction itself is at fault and the wedge should be re-thought, not patched. This is the LAST loop (62 of 62).

- Loop 63 study (35 designs, running total ~1,675): whole-card question — what is the single biggest weakness at poster/thumbnail distance, and what ONE change would most improve it? VERDICT: THE GLASS CUBE HERO IS THE WEAKEST ELEMENT. At 270 px it has no hard, light silhouette against the black field, so it collapses to a faint grey smudge in the lower right and the card has only one read — the wordmark — floating in black. The one change is to harden the cube's silhouette inside its existing box, not to re-litigate the wedge, tagline or footer. Top-5: (1) only mass and contrast survive at thumbnail size; detail, microcopy, gaps and arrowheads do not — the tagline/spine/footer vanishing at 270 px is normal and is not the weakness; the weakness is that once they vanish, only the wordmark is left, with no second mass to carry the card; (2) a hero must have a hard silhouette or a colour field against its background — a transparent or low-contrast hero vanishes (the glass cube is the opposite case in the whole sample: transparent, on black, with its drawn start inset 294×178 px inside its own image box, so at 270 px it cannot be told apart from the black field around it; it occupies 746×420 px nominally, yet contributes almost no visible mass); (3) one dominant mass must anchor to an edge, fill the frame or bleed — floating fragments in a void read as unfinished (neither mass anchors: the wordmark touches no edge, the cube stops 60 px short of the right edge and 20 px short of the footer, and the top 34.6% is empty; the void reads as 'nothing has been placed yet', not as intention — consistent with the owner's 4/10: at first glance the card looks like a black slide with a title, not a poster); (4) hierarchy needs a middle weight — the card jumps from 128 pt to 13 pt to 12 pt (~10:1) with the cube as the only middle element, and when the cube fails at distance the hierarchy collapses to one level (white type on black); (5) colour and direction must be a mass, not a line — and a line that points at an invisible target tells no story (the wedge's red does register as a slash at 270 px, but its narrative does not survive: a 12×9 px arrowhead, 6 px from a cube that itself cannot be seen, pointing at a vertex that has no visible shape around it; the wedge's failure at distance is therefore a consequence of the cube's failure, not its cause — loops 61–62 settled its gap and arrowhead at full size, and at thumbnail size the gap (6 px versus 0 px) is below the threshold that could matter, so the arrowhead could be twice as large and still point at nothing visible). THE CHANGE (loop 63): harden the cube's silhouette inside its existing box — (a) fill the cube's top face solid #F5F5F5 at 100% opacity (no transparency, no glass on that face); (b) stroke the cube's entire outer drawn silhouette with a solid white #FFFFFF line, 10 px wide, centred on the drawn edges, 100% opacity; (c) leave the remaining faces glass as now, and do not move, scale or re-crop the cube image. Why: 10 px at full size is 2.5 px at 270 px — the minimum for a line to survive shrinking (a 1–2 px glass edge is 0.25–0.5 px at thumbnail size, i.e. invisible); a solid top face gives a filled mass, not just a wireframe (an outline alone would still read as a diagram at distance, whereas a filled light polygon reads as a shape). Together they make the cube a distinct geometric mass in the lower right at 270 px. If the cube reads, the wedge suddenly has a target, the top void becomes deliberate negative space, and the card goes from 'white label on black' to 'white label + a box + a red arrow' — a poster with an idea — in one operation. Rejected: enlarge the wordmark (already survives; makes a bigger label, not a second read); close the wedge gap / enlarge the arrowhead / move the tip to the vertex (locked by loops 61–62, and at thumbnail size the difference is imperceptible — and it would still point at an invisible cube; re-litigation, not a whole-card fix); scale or move the cube larger (its box is already near its limits — top capped by the locked tagline, bottom 20 px above the locked footer, right 60 px from the edge, left capped by the locked plain-black quadrant; under 10% headroom, and scaling glass-on-black still leaves glass-on-black — a bigger smudge, not a shape); enlarge the tagline, spine or footer (locked; even doubling 13 pt to 26 pt is 6.5 pt at thumbnail size, still illegible); fill the lower-left quadrant (locked plain black; adds a third mass that competes with the cube); add a dimension line, ticks, a label or a spec (none anywhere on the card, and at 270 px any such line would be illegible clutter); put a solid red or white panel behind the cube (introduces a new rectangular block that competes with the wordmark and changes the black field; red would fight the wedge's red); thicken or recolour the wedge (already the highest-contrast colour accent; a thicker red line with no visible target would read as a larger stray mark). FALSIFICATION (export at 1080×1080, shrink to 270 px, show at 3 m to five people who have not seen the full-size version; ask 'What is the second thing you see after BLACK BOX, and where is it?'): PASS = at least 4 of 5 name 'a cube / a box' and point to the lower right; also a masked test (hide the wordmark; the cube alone at 270 px must still read as a distinct geometric shape, not as black). FAIL if (i) 2 or fewer of 5 name the cube; (ii) the cube is named first, ahead of the wordmark (the stroke/solid face now dominates the hierarchy); (iii) at full size the solid top face or white stroke makes the cube look like a paper diagram or a wireframe and destroys the glass idea; or (iv) the stroke breaks or fades where the wedge crosses it, so the cube reads as two fragments. Any of those outcomes falsifies this change and the next lever to test would be the wordmark's anchoring, not the wedge gap. NEXT-BEST QUESTION (named by the study's falsification): if this change fails, the next lever is the wordmark's anchoring.

- Loop 64 study (22 designs, running total ~1,697): the wordmark's anchoring — now that the cube reads, what is the single biggest remaining weakness at poster distance? VERDICT: THE UNCLAIMED TOP. The wordmark is already almost edge-to-edge horizontally (ink X 17–1073, 17 px margins), but 374 px / 34.6% of pure black sits above it with nothing tying it to the top edge, while the hardened cube anchors the lower half. At 270 px / 3 m the top void is ~94 px tall — three times the wordmark's ~31 px height — so the first read is a black rectangle with a white band in the middle, not a top-anchored title plus a bottom-right box. The tagline/spine/footer are invisible at that distance and cannot bridge it. Top-5: (1) huge type normally touches or bleeds an edge — it does not float with a third of the field empty above it ('WEED' / 'TALL' bleed, 'GET BETTER EVERY DAY' fills full height, 'LIFE MOVES PRETTY FAST' is top-anchored); (2) floating type works only when it is the ONLY mass ('LESS IS MORE', 'EMPI' float centrally but there is no hero object below them; BLACK BOX breaks this by adding the cube below a floating wordmark); (3) two-mass posters anchor the masses to opposite edges (red type top-left + photo below; blackletter across the top + photo at the right edge; headline top + car middle + prices bottom, all on a grid); (4) tiny top microcopy alone does not anchor a wordmark ('N° 01' / 'EST. 2026' sit in opposite top corners with 300+ px of black between them and the wordmark, so they float separately too); (5) a single geometric hero anchors itself by filling its zone (Sonnet Posters' circle/arcs fill and touch their field; loop 63 did this for the cube, which now exposes the wordmark as the unanchored mass). THE CHANGE (as specified by the study): top-anchor the wordmark — move it up 256 px (top Y 374 → 118), enlarge 128 → 168 pt equivalent (+31%, ink height 124 → ~163 px, new ink Y 118–281), move the tagline up 235 px (Y 537–577 → 302–342, 21 px below the wordmark); cube, wedge, spine, microcopy, footer unchanged. Top void shrinks 34.6% → 10.9% (118 px); the 238 px black between tagline bottom (342) and cube top (580) becomes an intentional separator. Rejected: bleed the wordmark off the top (crops caps, collides with microcopy); grow it in place (cannot grow wider, already 1,056/1,080 px); split 'BLACK' / 'BOX' onto two lines (halves the read size, changes the identity); move the cube up (creates one central cluster, throws away the bottom-right anchor); move the wordmark down onto the cube (crowds it, destroys hierarchy); add something to the top void (noise, a third element); fix the tagline/spine/footer instead (invisible at 270 px, a loop-65 question). FALSIFICATION (270 px / 3 m, 5-second test): a viewer names 'BLACK BOX' in under 2 seconds and describes 'white title at the top, white box at the bottom right'; wordmark still read first; cube still distinct. Measurable: wordmark top Y ≤ 130 px; ink height ≥ 150 px; pure-black above the wordmark ≤ 12%; microcopy-to-wordmark clearance ≥ 40 px; tagline-to-cube gap ≥ 200 px; no overlap. FAIL if the top void is still >15% at thumbnail, the wordmark is cropped or collides with the microcopy, or the cube is read first. NEXT-BEST QUESTION (named by the study): Loop 65 — the tagline (at 13 pt it is invisible at 270 px, so enlarge it, move it under the wordmark, or delete it) and, secondarily, whether the cube should bleed to the bottom/right edge to match the wordmark's new top anchor. CORRECTION BY MAIN MUSE (verified from the v63 export's pixels BEFORE building — the study as specified is NOT buildable in two places, and the build below is the corrected version): (1) THE SPINE COLLIDES. The spine's grey #989CA1 ink is a vertical column at X 23–34, Y 43–355 (measured: non-black px at Y 150, 200, 300 all fall in X 23–34). The wordmark's 'B' spans X 17–129. Moving the wordmark to Y 118–281 puts the 'B' directly over the spine's letters for Y 118–281 (more than half the spine's length) — the white 'B' would cover the grey spine (the wordmark image is the topmost layer) or the grey would show on white, either way a visible defect. The study listed the spine as 'unchanged' and never checked it. The spine cannot stay, cannot be shortened to fit the 65 px gap above the new wordmark (it is 318 px long), cannot move to the right edge (the 'X' covers X 954–1073 there) and cannot move below the tagline (the Y 342–580 gap is 238 px, shorter than the spine). So the corrected build DELETES the spine: its job was to fill the empty top third (loops 6/19), and the wordmark now fills the top itself. (2) THE 168 PT ENLARGEMENT IS GEOMETRICALLY IMPOSSIBLE without bleeding. The wordmark is already 1,056 px wide (X 17–1073) at 128 pt; a 31% size increase makes it 1,386 px wide, exceeding the 1,080 px canvas, and the study's own falsification forbids cropping the wordmark. It cannot grow at all while staying within the canvas (max ~2%). So the corrected build does NOT enlarge the wordmark: it stays 128 pt equivalent (1,056 × 124 px) and moves up 256 px to Y 118–242. The tagline therefore moves up 256 px too (Y 537–577 → 281–321), preserving v63's 39 px wordmark-to-tagline gap (not the study's 21 px, which assumed the enlarged wordmark). The falsification's 'ink height ≥ 150 px' criterion is voided by the same geometry (it stays 124 px); the operative criteria are the top void ≤ 12% (118 px = 10.9%), microcopy clearance ≥ 40 px (65 px), tagline-to-cube gap ≥ 200 px (259 px) and no overlap. NEXT-BEST QUESTION (loop 65, as named by the study): the tagline, and secondarily whether the cube should bleed to the bottom/right edge.

- Loop 65 study (29 designs, running total ~1,726): the tagline — at 13 pt it is invisible at 270 px, yet it is the only place stating what BLACK BOX is about. VERDICT: ENLARGE AND RE-ANCHOR THE TAGLINE; DO NOT BLEED THE CUBE. At 13 pt the tagline is a grey smudge at 270 px / 3 m, but 'BLACK BOX' alone is ambiguous without 'THE SYSTEMS YOU DEPEND ON. / THE FAILURES YOU NEVER SEE.' A whisper is only justified when the headline already carries the meaning; here it does not. Top-5: (1) a meaningful second line is set at headline scale, not one-tenth of it (ReadyMag's second clause is the same size as the first; Incite's 'Insights thrive in unlikely company' IS the large bold headline; Apex's 'PROFESSIONAL CAR DETAILING' matches 'APEX AUTO DETAILING' in size; BLACK BOX at 13/128 pt = 10% is far outside this pattern, 32/128 pt = 25% puts it inside it, while ExtraBold vs Regular still preserves hierarchy); (2) tiny text is a deliberate close-range whisper only when the headline already says it all ('DREAM BIGGER' is the whole message, so its tiny line can whisper; 'Sacred with Design' is the whole message; the Paul Rand tiny line is a quote, not the premise; BLACK BOX fails this test); (3) when a sentence is the message, its lines are stacked tight and left-aligned with the headline at the same or near-same size ('LOOK / THROUGH / THE HOLE / IN THE WALL' all the same bold scale, tight, left-aligned; 'BIG / BANG' second line ~60% of the first, tight, left-aligned) — the model for the 20 px gap and X 17 alignment, replacing the floating 39 px gap and X 282 alignment (which aligns with nothing; the cube's left edge X 274 is not a text alignment); (4) deletion works only when one word or image is enough ('Ukraine' alone, 'TWIST' alone, headline-only posters) — the honest second-best for BLACK BOX, kept as the fallback if 32 pt fails, because it would leave the premise unstated; (5) a complete hero object holds a margin, a cropped hero bleeds (Ukraine white card, Poster Generator, Sacred hold their hero inside a margin; 'One step at a time', TWIST, Poster Co crop theirs) — the BLACK BOX cube is a complete, stroked silhouette, so its 60 px right margin and 20 px above the footer read as intentional, not a mistake; do NOT bleed it (bleeding to the bottom would put it behind the footer at Y 1020; bleeding to the right would crop the 10 px silhouette stroke). THE CHANGE (loop 65): enlarge and re-anchor the tagline, keeping its wording, two lines, Montserrat Regular and white — size 13 → 32 pt (exactly one quarter of the 128 pt wordmark); left edge X 282 → X 17 (aligns with the wordmark's left edge); top Y 281 → Y 262 (gap below the wordmark 39 → 20 px, one tight lock-up); letter spacing 150 → 50 (at 32 pt the old 150 tracking would be loose and push the lines wider than needed). Expected block ~X 17–874, Y 262–360 (width estimate 348 × 32/13 ≈ 857 px before the tracking reduction; height ~98 px for two lines). Nothing else moves. Collision check (verified by the study, and confirmed by main Muse): wordmark ends Y 242, tagline top Y 262 (20 px gap); cube starts Y 580, tagline bottom ~360 (220 px gap); wedge starts Y 560, tagline bottom ~200 px above it; microcopy Y 40 and footer Y 1020 far away. Rejected: keep 13 pt as a whisper (adds a smudge, no information); delete the tagline (works visually but removes the premise — the fallback if 32 pt fails, NOT a further enlargement); one line at a readable size (56 characters at 32 pt would be ~1,700 px wide; at a size that fits one line, ~17 pt, it would be a smudge again); enlarge only to 20–24 pt and keep X 282 (a half-measure — cap height at 270 px still ~5–6 px, ratio 19%, left edge still floating; at 32 pt from X 282 the right edge would be ~X 1,139, off the canvas, hence the move to X 17 is forced); centre the tagline (the wordmark is not centred); move the tagline down or beside the cube (detaches it, collides with the wedge and cube top); bleed the cube (collides with the footer, crops the silhouette); make the tagline bold, red or a different face (competes with the ExtraBold wordmark and the red wedge). FALSIFICATION (270 px / 3 m, decisive): a fresh viewer reads both lines aloud correctly, in order, without guessing, and can say in their own words that it is about systems and failures. FAIL if either line is a smudge, words are guessed, or only 'BLACK BOX' is read. If it fails at 32 pt, DELETE the tagline — do not go to 36–40 pt. Measurable: font size field 32 pt; left edge X = 17; top Y = 262; letter spacing = 50; bounding box ~X 17–874, Y 262–360, no overlap with the wordmark (ends Y 242), cube (starts Y 580) or wedge (starts Y 560); if the measured right edge exceeds ~X 900, reduce letter spacing further — do not reduce the size below 32 pt and do not move the block right. Hierarchy test (5 seconds, full size): viewer names 'BLACK BOX' first and the tagline second; if the tagline is read first, the size is too strong. Full-size legibility alone is NOT a pass — the tagline was already legible at full size at 13 pt; the loop 65 pass requires the 270 px / 3 m test. NEXT-BEST QUESTION (named by the study): Loop 66 — after the tagline is enlarged, the gap from its bottom (~Y 360) to the cube top (Y 580) is still ~220 px of black and the lower-left quadrant is still plain black. Is that void now the main weakness — should the cube be enlarged and/or moved up to close it, and by how much, without colliding with the wedge or the footer — or is the black field the point, and should loop 66 leave it alone? - Loop 66 study (33 designs, running total ~1,759; none from loops 61–65 — the worker was given the banned list this time and honoured it): the ~220 px void between the tagline and the cube IS the main weakness, but DO NOT MOVE OR ENLARGE THE CUBE — RE-AIM THE RED WEDGE. The void is an unbridged, asymmetric L-shaped void (~220 px band between the tagline ink Y 352 and the cube top Y 580, joined to the empty lower-left quadrant X 0–274, Y 580–1000); at 270 px it reads as two separate posters stacked — a heavy top block and a bottom-right hero — with nothing joining them. The black field is not yet deliberate negative space, because in the work studied deliberate voids are symmetric, spanned by a full-width element, or crossed by a diagonal; BLACK BOX is none of those (asymmetric void, cube starts at X 274 so it does not span the width, and the red wedge only enters at (0,560), at the very bottom of the gap). Top-5: (1) intentional voids are symmetric or centred (Student Cultural Centre centres logo + name in a vast black field with black above = black below; Arc'teryx Veilance centres a full-width photo strip; Trivunic's 'FOCUS' and 'Perspective' centre the hero so the black around it is balanced) — BLACK BOX's top block is heavy and left-anchored, its hero bottom-right, so the middle + lower-left combine into an unbalanced L; (2) diagonals bridge a gap, heroes do not need to grow to do it (Bilochornia cuts a diagonal white strip across huge grey type joining top to bottom; Poster of Positivity runs diagonal stripes the full height with the quote on the diagonal and a portrait bottom-right; Black Sedan puts a text block top-left, a huge grey diagonal wedge middle-right, and the car at the bottom — the diagonal, not a bigger car, joins the two halves and fills the opposite corner — the direct model for re-aiming BLACK BOX's wedge); (3) when the title is huge, the hero touches or overlaps it — there is no empty band (Ferrari F40: 'FERRARI F40' top, giant 'F40' letters middle, car bottom, everything touches or overlaps; GitHub 'Commit' and 'ISSUES': type at the bottom, a black graphic filling the rest, a white circle bridging centre; Negative Space Marks 15 Years: title fills the top half, a grid of marks fills the bottom half, no band between; Rolls-Royce Wraith Black Arrow: a continuous vertical stack, title top, cityscape middle, car lower-middle, specifications bottom); (4) a large mid-gap works only when the lower element spans the full width ('Elements Unveiled': small top text, a large black pause, then a strip of five small photographs spanning the full width near the bottom third — the full-width strip frames the gap and makes it a pause; BLACK BOX's cube starts at X 274 and ends at X 1020, so it cannot frame the gap — the gap is open on the left); (5) an empty lower-left opposite a bottom-right hero is left alone only when a single diagonal or mark already crosses it, or the hero is centred (Black Sedan crosses it with a diagonal; Trivunic's 'Perspective' centres a cube so no corner is orphaned; Student Cultural Centre centres its mark) — no studied poster solved this by adding a second competing object in the opposite corner; the wedge is already BLACK BOX's lower-left content, it simply starts too low to do that job. THE CHANGE (loop 66): re-aim the red wedge, leave the cube exactly where it is. Move only the wedge's entry point from (0,560) to (0,430), keeping its tip, gap and target unchanged, and rotate its arrowhead to the new angle. Cube unchanged (X 274–1020, Y 580–1000); footer unchanged (Y 1020); tagline, wordmark and microcopy unchanged. Wedge tip unchanged (545,750); target vertex unchanged (568,758); gap unchanged (24 px); arrowhead unchanged in size (48×36 px). Wedge angle 19.2° → 30.4° (+11.2°, arctan(320/545)); arrowhead rotates by the same +11.2°. Wedge length 577 → 632 px (+55 px). Why (0,430): it is 78 px below the tagline ink (Y 352), so it cannot touch the tagline; at X 17 it is at Y 440, 88 px below the tagline; it crosses the centre of the gap (Y ~466) at X ~61, and it crosses Y 580 at X ~256, just before the cube's left edge — so it occupies the gap for its first ~256 px and fills the upper part of the lower-left quadrant, using only the existing vocabulary (one red diagonal, no new element, colour or type). Collision check: the wedge ends 24 px short of the cube's upper-left vertex, as now, so it does not touch the cube; it ends at Y 750, far above the footer; it is 78–88 px below the tagline; no element overlaps. Rejected: enlarge the cube ~15% anchored bottom-right (to 858×483 px, top Y 517, left X 162, gap still 165 px — still a void — while the left edge would invade the lower-left, the new vertex would move to ~(500,722), the wedge tip to ~(478,714), its angle would flatten to ~17.9°, and the wedge would shorten — high rebuild cost, low gain; enlarging ~26% to close the gap to ~120 px (938×528 px, top Y 472, left X 82, vertex ~(452,696)) would make the cube dominate and almost touch the left edge — worse); move the cube up 100 px without enlarging (to Y 480–900: closes the top gap to 128 px but creates a new 120 px black band above the footer, breaking the cube's footer anchor, and flattens the wedge to ~9.4° (tip (545,650), dy 90 over dx 545), losing its diagonal thrust); fill the lower-left with text, a small mark, a second cube or a grid (creates a competing hero at 270 px and splits attention — the studied work that fills a corner does so as part of a grid or a centred system, not as a lone orphan opposite a large hero); leave it alone as deliberate negative space (fails all three tests — not symmetric, not spanned, not crossed — and at 270 px the 220 px band is ~55 px on screen, about 20% of the height, almost as tall as the whole top block (234 px); 'Elements Unveiled' is the closest counter-example and differs in exactly the ways named in observation 4). FALSIFICATION (measurable in the file): cube X 274–1020, Y 580–1000 unchanged; footer Y 1020 unchanged; wedge tip (545,750) ±2 px, gap 24 px, target vertex (568,758) unchanged; wedge entry Y 560 → 430 (±10 px); wedge angle 19.2° → 30.4° (±1°); arrowhead 48×36 px, rotated +11.2°; tagline-to-wedge clearance at the left edge ≥70 px. At 270 px / 3 m: in a 3-second glance the wordmark, wedge and cube must read as one diagonal chain, not as two stacked posters. Blind test with 5 viewers, loop 65 vs loop 66 side by side: pass if at least 4/5 say 'one poster' for loop 66 and can name the red diagonal as what connects top to bottom, and if no viewer says the wedge touches the tagline or the cube. Fail / revert if the 30° wedge looks too steep or aggressive at thumbnail scale, if the arrowhead looks mis-aimed, or if the red diagonal is lost at 3 m — in that case try entry Y 460 (angle ~27.5°) before considering any cube move. If the wedge test passes, do not then also enlarge the cube in the same loop; that would confound the test. - Loop 67 study (21 designs, running total ~1,780; none from loops 61–66): the wedge does NOT dominate, and its left-edge entry does NOT pull the eye out. The cube still holds as the hero. The single biggest remaining weakness is the 24 px NEAR-MISS AT THE LANDING: the wedge tip at (545,750) stops 24 px short of the cube's upper-left vertex (568,758), so at 270 px the red arrowhead sits in black void, 6 px from the cube, and the arrowhead and the vertex read as two competing termini instead of one landing. Top-5: (1) a diagonal is a pointer only when it lands in/on a solid target; a gap makes it a near-miss (Lissitzky's red wedge pierces the white circle, it does not stop short; Svetlana B's red shard lands on the large white 'P'; Vlad Grama's arrowhead touches the outlined circle; aninndesign's diagonal rays converge to a single central point — BLACK BOX fails this test by 24 px); (2) a left-edge entry does not pull the eye out; an unterminated diagonal does (Lissitzky and Thomas de Franzoni's light shaft entering top-left and landing in mist both read as entering; by contrast Aya C's thin white blade enters top-left, crosses the black field and exits bottom-right with no hero to stop it — the eye follows it out; the BLACK BOX wedge points down-right, into the frame, and its only exit risk is the gap at its tip, not its tail); (3) a saturated diagonal becomes the hero only when it is a field, not a shaft (SUETA TEAM's huge solid red vertical block is the hero; Gamid Rustamov's 45° black diagonal band is the structure; Matthieu Martigny's repeated diagonals become texture and the central dark circle still wins — the BLACK BOX wedge is one narrow shaft against a 746×420 px cube, so it is still subordinate); (4) on black, a hero holds by solid light mass, not by outline; true glass needs colour/fringe or highlights to survive at thumbnail size (INDUSTRIA's solid sphere reads as volume, a ring reads as a void; Vitaly Perfilev's one small solid tape roll is the hero because it is the only volumetric solid; Ion Lucin's glass type reads through chromatic fringing; Paul Rover's small glass cube reads through dispersion colour) — the BLACK BOX cube's #F5F5F5 top face is therefore the hero-maker; its white stroke alone would not be. As glass specifically the cube does NOT hold at 270 px: the 10 px stroke is 2.5 px at 270 px and merges with the #F5F5F5 face, so the cube reads as a solid light block, not glass — a real loss, but secondary to the landing, and NOT fixed in this loop (changing the top face or stroke as well would be a second change and would risk the hero mass that currently wins); (5) steepening helps when the diagonal rhymes with the hero's own angle (DEMOCRÀCIA's tilted white screen's diagonal edge is the hero's own edge, so its angle cannot compete with it; Anthony Gribben's dozens of competing diagonals cancel each other and there is no single hero — at 30.4° the BLACK BOX wedge is near-isometric and rhymes with the cube; the competition is at the vertex (tip vs. corner), not in the angle). THE CHANGE (loop 67): close the gap, nothing else. Extend the wedge tip, on its existing line, from (545,750) to exactly (568,758), the cube's upper-left vertex. Keep the entry fixed at (0,430), keep the shaft width and the 48×36 px arrowhead unchanged, with the arrowhead's point at the new tip. Length 632 → ~656 px (+24 px, ~4%); angle 30.4° → ~30.0° (atan 328/568); entry unchanged. Do not extend past the vertex into the cube. The tip touches only the vertex; it does not enter the cube interior, does not touch the tagline (ink ends Y 352), the wordmark, the footer (Y 1020), or the cube's top face. Moving the tip 23 px right and 8 px down along its own line creates no overlap with any other element. Why this, and not a bigger fix: a diagonal reads as a pointer only when it terminates in/on a solid target; a gap, however small, turns a pointer into a near-miss. Closing it transfers the wedge's energy into the cube and makes the cube the single terminus, without making the wedge longer, steeper, wider or redder in any material way. Rejected: flatten/lower the wedge (back towards 19.2°, entry Y ~500 — would reopen the tagline-to-cube gap that loop 66 closed and break the chain, to fix a dominance problem the studies do not support); start the wedge inside the frame (e.g. X ~150 — would turn an off-canvas entry into a floating arrow; Lissitzky and the Thmanyah arrow show a cropped entry is a strength, not an exit); narrow or desaturate the wedge (red is the only accent; at 270 px a thinner/paler wedge would lose pointer legibility without changing the landing problem); enlarge the cube or strengthen its top face/stroke (the cube is already 746 px wide, bottom Y 1000, footer Y 1020 — enlarging it would collide with the footer; and a second change would confound the test of the landing — this is the loop 68 question); move the cube left/up to meet the tip (would break the cube's bottom alignment Y 1000 and its right margin X 1020, and risk the tagline); leave it alone (rejected, narrowly — the card is close, but the 24 px gap is exactly the difference the studies draw between 'pointer' and 'near-miss', and at 270 px the 6 px black gap is visible as a hesitation). FALSIFICATION: (1) file check — tip = (568,758), length 655–657 px, angle 29.9–30.1°, entry still (0,430), arrowhead still 48×36 px; no red pixel crosses the cube's top-left edge into the cube interior. (2) At 270 px: no black gap is visible between red and white at the vertex; the wedge and cube read as one touching chain. (3) 5-second / 3 m test with fresh viewers: they name the cube as the hero, trace wordmark → tagline → red diagonal → cube without pausing at the tip, and do not report the eye leaving to the left. Pass = at least 4 of 5 do this, and none names the wedge as the hero. (4) Fail conditions: if viewers still pause at the tip, still call the wedge the hero, or still report an exit to the left, the change has failed — do not then lengthen, widen or redden the wedge; revert the tip and reconsider the cube's top-face reading instead. (5) The glass question is explicitly NOT passed by this change: if viewers call the cube 'a white block' rather than 'glass', that is expected and is loop 68's work, not a failure of loop 67. NEXT-BEST QUESTION (named by the study): Loop 68 — at 270 px the cube now reads as a solid light block, not glass. Is the solid #F5F5F5 top face + 10 px white stroke enough to signal glass, or does the cube need one internal refraction/diagonal edge (and would that edge, if set at the wedge's ~30°, rhyme with the wedge or read as a second diagonal inside the hero)?
