- Loop 77 study (36 designs, running total ~2,076; none from loops 61–76): VERDICT — REMOVE THE TOP-FACE FRINGE ENTIRELY. The single biggest remaining weakness is that fringe: a 33 px long, ~2 px wide, ~30% opacity chromatic mark at (655,754)–(688,758), inside the solid #F5F5F5 top face. It is now both redundant and unreadable, and the brighter seam core has removed the reason it was added. THE ONE CHANGE (loop 77): delete the top fringe only — revert that strip to solid #F5F5F5, exactly as in the v72 cube top. No other change: leave the seam (saturated blue #1D4ED8, ~20 px total, with its 2 px #DBEAFE core, L* ~92, (697,767)–(647,903)), the right-face fringe (~4 px, ~18 px east of the fold), the white 10 px silhouette, the wedge and its tip at (568,758), the wordmark, tagline, microcopy and footer exactly as they are. Do not darken the top face, do not touch the seam or the right-face fringe, and do not add any red inside the cube. WHY: (1) The top face is already the brightest plane (mean L* ~96.5, against ~76 front-left and ~36.5 right, ΔL* ~40 across the fold). That tonal step alone explains 'lit glass' — the fringe adds no new information about plane orientation or light direction, which the seam already supplies. (2) The fringe is structurally orphaned: short, eastern-portion only, parallel to the lower edge of the top face but not touching it. In the work studied, refraction that reads is edge-anchored/contiguous with a fold; an isolated interior line reads as a smudge or compression artefact. (3) It fails at both viewing distances for different reasons: at 270 px it is ~0.5 px and invisible, so it contributes nothing to the thumbnail; at full size it is visible only on close inspection, where its shortness, faintness and isolation make it look accidental rather than deliberate — loop 74 had already judged it the least coherent of the three signals, and the new L* ~92 seam core has since made it the faintest signal on the brightest plane, which inverts expectation (faint signals belong in shadow, where the right-face fringe works). The premise for adding it in loop 73 — that the top would otherwise read as a 'lid' — no longer holds: the seam core now provides the light event that explains the top's brightness. COLLISION CHECK: removal creates no collision. Top stays brightest (L* ~96.5 > front-left ~76), the ΔL* ~40 step is unchanged, seam and right-face fringe are untouched, the wedge tip at (568,758) is untouched, the silhouette is untouched, and no red element is introduced inside the cube. The only risk, a 'lid' reading, is contradicted by the evidence below. Top-5: (1) a flat, bright top needs no fringe (Novelo's 'Refraction studies', Dribbble — a pale faceted cube/sphere whose top face is flat and pale, with refraction only on the side faces; it reads unmistakably as glass, the top explained by being the brightest plane bounded by clear edges); (2) solid flat tops are the norm in glass cubes (Xu's '3d Glass Cube with Spline', Dribbble — four small cubes whose top faces are solid flat colour (white, yellow, pink, blue-grey) with no refraction marks at all; refraction lives in the side faces and gradients; the tops read as glass tops by tonal step and boundary alone); (3) one strong signal explains the light; an empty interior does not hurt (Wise's 'Light Prism', Dribbble — black ground, white triangle outline, a single rainbow spectrum exiting to the right; the triangle interior is empty black, with no faint mark inside, yet it reads unmistakably as a prism; the strong external/edge signal does all the explanatory work); (4) refraction that reads is edge-anchored; isolated faint marks drown (Coyle's 'Prism', Dribbble, and Pixelbuddha's 'Abstract Prism Textures' / 'Radiance Prism Photo Effect', Dribbble — in Coyle the strong blue/purple refraction sits at the fold/edge and the rest of the glass is flat; in Pixelbuddha the beams are large, saturated and contiguous; a faint, short, isolated chromatic trace next to such a signal does not register as a second cue — it collapses into texture/noise); (5) minimal black work is one dominant signal plus silence; faintness only reads when it is long, repeated or the main signal on its own object (Weber's 'Refractions.', Dribbble — one strong chromatic-aberration wordmark on black, no faint second mark; Ayman's 'Portfolio 2026', Behance — huge black 'Portfolio', one white mark, silence elsewhere; Naumann's 'WWP°264 "traces"' and 'HOLO 4/5', Dribbble — faint chromatic traces read only because they are long, repeated and structured across the whole field, a single 33 px trace does not meet that threshold; Up-Brands' 'LUMI & VOID', Dribbble — faint dichroic signals earn their place when each is the main signal on a separate object/plane, not a third, weaker echo on the same object beside a dominant one). Rejected: keep at 30% (no build) (the 'completes the light system' hypothesis, but the system is now complete without it — seam (dominant) + right-face fringe (second) already give a strict two-step hierarchy, and the top's brightness is already explained by the seam core; keeping it preserves a mark that is invisible at 270 px and looks accidental at full size); strengthen it (e.g. to 50–60%, wider or longer) (would destroy the hierarchy by making the third signal compete with the seam, add visible noise on the brightest plane at 270 px, and still leave it an interior line unanchored to an edge; strengthening to match the seam was expressly ruled out, and any lesser strengthening does not fix the structural problem of isolation/shortness); move it to the edge / lengthen it along the whole lower edge of the top face (would put a chromatic band directly on the fold the seam already occupies in visual terms, risk blurring the top/front-left boundary, and turn a whisper into a second seam competing with the C–B fold); replace it with a subtler tonal gradient on the top face (would darken part of the brightest plane and risk dropping the top below the front-left face or weakening the tonal step; the evidence (Novelo, Xu) shows a flat top works, so no replacement is needed). FALSIFICATION: at 270 px / 3 m — no viewer should be able to tell which version is which; in both, the cube must still show two distinct side faces, an unmistakable fold, the top as the brightest plane, and the wedge tip as the first landing after the wordmark; if removal changes the thumbnail reading at all, the verdict is wrong — but the fringe is ~0.5 px there, so a thumbnail difference would itself falsify the claim that it was invisible. At full size — viewers asked 'what is the top face made of — glass or a lid?' must score v77 equal to or better than v76, must name the seam as the light event and the right-face fringe as the second signal, and must not report a smudge/artefact on the top face in v77; if v77 is reported as a 'lid'/opaque/flat more often than v76, or viewers report something missing from the top, the removal has failed and the fringe should be reconsidered (not strengthened to match the seam). Measurable check in the file: in v77 the strip (655,754)–(688,758) must sample as solid #F5F5F5 (mean L* ~96.5); the top face must remain the brightest plane (L* ~96.5 > front-left ~76); ΔL* front-left to right must remain ≥35 (target ~40); seam core #DBEAFE L* ~92, right-face fringe, 10 px white silhouette and wedge tip (568,758) must be pixel-identical to v76; the file diff must show change only in that 33 × ~2 px strip. NEXT-BEST QUESTION (named by the study): Loop 78 — now that the hierarchy is seam (dominant) + right-face fringe only, does the right-face fringe (~4 px, ~18 px east of the fold) still earn its place, or does the seam core alone carry the cube? Test removing the right-face fringe against keeping it: does it still read as a refraction line in the dark face, or does it now read as a second seam competing with the fold?

- Loop 78 study (40 NEW designs, running total ~2,116; none from loops 61–77 except the recounts noted below): VERDICT — REMOVE THE RIGHT-FACE FRINGE ENTIRELY. The single biggest remaining weakness is that the fringe is a second, parallel chromatic line ~18 px east of the one fold that matters: at full size it competes with the seam and reads as a second fold / false bevel, and at 270 px / 3 m it is ~1 px and effectively invisible, so it earns its place at neither distance. THE ONE CHANGE (loop 78): delete the whole right-face fringe — the faint ~4 px-wide chromatic line, cyan west / pale core / magenta east, running approximately (707,792)–(671,890), ~18 px east of the C–B fold centreline — and leave the underlying right face as flat (46,90,120). No replacement, no widening of the seam, no lightening of the right face, no repositioning, no other change. The seam, its 2 px #DBEAFE core, all three faces, the silhouette, wedge, wordmark, tagline, microcopy and footer are untouched. WHY: in every geometric glass cube studied, dispersion sits ON a fold or edge, never as a second parallel line inside a face. Faces are carried by a flat tonal step, not by an interior line. A parallel line offset from a fold is therefore read as structure — another fold, bevel or face — not as texture. The one exception proves the rule: in abstract, geometry-free refraction work (e.g. DISPERSION by Alexey Grigoriev; Light Prism Series by Danny Ivan) many parallel streaks work because there is no fold for them to compete with; in a cube, there is. And the dark face does not need the fringe: dark, flat faces read as glass in This is Cube, Luminal Orbit and GEOMETRY OF ICE through tonal step + edge colour + silhouette alone. At 270 px the fringe contributes nothing, so removing it cannot weaken the 3 m read; at full size it removes the only competing signal. COLLISION CHECK: seam untouched (blue #1D4ED8, ~20 px total, plus 2 px pale core #DBEAFE L* ~92 on the centreline, (697,767)–(647,903), remains the sole chromatic line in the cube; the fringe lay east of it and its deletion cannot touch it); core untouched, still on the fold centreline, with no second pale line to confuse it with after removal; right face reveals the existing flat dark face (46,90,120), L* ~36.5, with no hole, gap, inpainting or re-render needed, boundaries unchanged, cube still 746×420 at (274,580); front-left face untouched, pale glass ~(199,201,189), L* ~76–80, tonal step ΔL* ~40–44 across the fold, now cleaner — one fold, one step, one line; top face untouched, plain solid #F5F5F5 (loop 77's removal stands); silhouette untouched, 10 px white stroke; red wedge untouched, centreline (0,430)→(568,758) at 30.0°, #C32D30, tip touching (568,758), nearest fringe point ~(707,792) ~140 px away; wordmark, tagline, microcopy and footer all far from the fringe (Y 792–890, X ~665–715) and unchanged; canvas geometry unchanged, only pixels inside the fringe's bounding box (approx. X 665–715, Y 785–895) change. Top-5: (1) dispersion sits ON a fold, never beside it (This is Cube — Vitalii Novoseltsev, Behance — on black, a tilted glass cube carries all its colour exactly on its fold edges, a thin rainbow line on each edge centreline, while its large dark faces are flat tonal planes with no parallel interior line; a dark face reads as glass by tonal step + edge colour + silhouette, and the fold line alone is the refraction signal); (2) the discipline of keeping colour on the fold (Glass Dispersion Logo Design & 3D Animation — Paul Rover, Behance — a small glass cube on black above the wordmark CATEGORY: dispersion is confined to the cube's edges/folds, faces are flat dark / pale blue, and the separate rainbow strip sits at the bottom of the poster, outside the cube, never inside a face parallel to a fold); (3) a dark face without an interior line is not dead, it is quiet (Luminal Orbit — Glass Cube Motion Study — negi design, Dribbble — small blue glass cubes in a ring on near-black, no interior fringe at all, cubes read through silhouette, highlight and tonal faces; directly answers the 'flat dead space' worry); (4) the physical logic — refraction colour belongs on the fold, not beside it (GEOMETRY OF ICE (Part 3) — Jan Erik Waider, Behance — real ice facets: colour and brightness sit on the fold/edge itself, each facet a flat tonal plane, no chromatic line offset from a fold); (5) if extra refraction is wanted, it should be a wash or an edge, not a hard offset line (Prism Crystal Suncatcher - 2D Animation — Yeonwoo Lee, Behance — refraction is a soft wash across the whole crystal and glow at its edges, never a hard second line parallel to an edge inside a face). Rejected: keep the fringe as-is (adds nothing at 270 px; at full size a second signal in the same colours (cyan/magenta) as the seam, parallel to it and 18 px away — the geometry of a second fold); move the fringe closer to the fold / merge it into the seam (thickens and blurs the dominant signal, risks swallowing the 2 px #DBEAFE core, changes the seam, which is not the weak element); move it further east, or make it thinner/fainter (distance does not change its reading — a fainter parallel line is still a parallel line, and a fainter one is even less visible at 270 px); replace it with a soft tonal gradient or glow on the right face (the flat dark face already works per Top-5 nos. 1, 3, 4; a gradient would soften the ΔL* ~40–44 step that defines the fold and would be a second, different change); keep the fringe and remove the seam core instead (the core is the dominant, on-fold signal; the fringe is the subordinate, off-fold one — removing the strong signal to save the weak one inverts the hierarchy); add a matching fringe to the top face for symmetry (loop 77 removed the top-face fringe for the same competition reason; symmetry of a fault is not a fix). FALSIFICATION: 270 px / 3 m blind-read test — show v77 and v78 side by side at 270 px, viewed from 3 m, 2 seconds each, to 10 viewers who have not seen the card; ask 'How many faces does the cube have, and how many coloured lines are in it?'; PASS for v78 if it scores at least as well as v77 on '3 faces, 1 line' and no viewer fails to see the cube in v78; FAIL if v78 loses cube/face recognition to v77, or viewers report the cube as flatter/deader in v78. - Loop 79 study (35 NEW designs, running total ~2,151; none from loops 61–78 except the recount noted below): VERDICT — WIDEN THE BLUE SEAM FEATHER ONLY; do NOT widen the core. The single biggest remaining weakness: at 270 px / 3 m the fold does not fail because the core is 2 px — it fails, if it fails at all, because its only surviving carrier, the saturated blue seam, is only ~20 px wide in full size, i.e. a ~5 px blue mark at 270 px. The 2 px #DBEAFE core is already 0.5 px at 270 px and is therefore effectively invisible at thumbnail, whatever its full-size width. Widening it cannot rescue the thumbnail, and at full size it risks becoming a white stripe. THE ONE CHANGE (loop 79): widen the blue seam feather only; do NOT widen the core. Core UNCHANGED — 2 px, #DBEAFE, L* ~92, centred exactly on the existing centreline (697,767)–(647,903), length ~145 px; no change to colour, length, endpoints or position. Seam total width 20 px → 26 px, i.e. ±13 px either side of that centreline instead of ±10 px. Colour at centre unchanged: saturated #1D4ED8 at full strength adjacent to the core, falling softly to the face colour at ±13 px, with no hard edge. Use a soft linear feather so that at the old ±10 px boundary the blue is still ~30–40% opacity, not 0%. The extra 3 px each side is feather only. At 270 px this makes the blue mark 26 × 0.25 = 6.5 px instead of 5.0 px (+30%), while the core remains 0.5 px. At full size the seam is 26 px, 3.5% of the 746 px cube width — still a refraction glow, not a band. Nothing else changes: no face, wedge, type, silhouette, colour or position change. WHY: in every relevant design, what survives at small size is a broad saturated colour area or a large tonal step, never a 1–3 px pale line. Thin pale lines vanish in thumbnails and at distance, while the object still reads through its face planes. The BLACK BOX fold already has the strongest possible tonal carrier — ΔL* ~44 across the C–B fold (pale front-left ~(199,201,189), L* ~76–80, against dark right (46,90,120), L* ~36.5) — so the cube will still read as a two-face cube at 270 px even with the core lost. What is at risk at distance is not the cube shape but its glass-ness: the single blue refraction mark. The studies show that mark must be broad enough to survive as colour, not as a hairline: Prism Forge and NEON Portraits survive as broad saturated streaks/bands tens of pixels wide; the Suncatcher survives as broad pastel washes plus point sparkles; Sol Gomez Villasuso's cube survives with no highlight line at all, through large red/teal blocks. Conversely, Zosia Biela's thin pale glass edges disappear entirely at thumbnail size, and the cube still reads — proving a 2→3 px change (0.5→0.75 px at 270 px, still sub-pixel, still blended into the blue by any downsampler) cannot be the thumbnail fix. At full size, a 3 px pale line 145 px long, L* ~92 against a dark face L* ~36.5 (ΔL* ~55), would read as a deliberate white stripe, not a glint — the point-sparkle and broad-glow examples, not long thin white lines, are what read as glints. Widening the soft blue feather by 30% therefore buys the only real thumbnail gain available, at the lowest full-size risk: a soft edge cannot become a stripe. COLLISION CHECK: centreline (697,767)–(647,903) unchanged; endpoints unchanged; length ~145 px unchanged; core stays 2 px #DBEAFE on the centreline, so the seam + core remains the ONLY chromatic line in the cube, no new line, no second colour; faces unchanged in colour and L* (the extra feather is semi-transparent blue at low opacity at ±10–13 px; the hard tonal step ΔL* ~44 at the fold is preserved — the blue sits on the fold, it does not recolour either face as a whole); top face #F5F5F5 unchanged (the seam's top endpoint (697,767) is well below the top face, and widening is perpendicular to the fold, not along it, so it cannot reach the top face); silhouette untouched (the fold is interior; at its midpoint (672,835) the widened seam spans roughly X 660–684, Y 830–840, hundreds of pixels from the outer silhouette); wedge tip untouched (seam top endpoint (697,767) is ~129 px to the right of the tip (568,758); a 3 px widening each side cannot reach it; blue #1D4ED8 and red remain separated by >100 px of pale face; no merging at thumbnail, the gap is still ~32 px at 270 px); wordmark (Y 118–242), tagline (Y 262–364), microcopy (Y 40) and footer (Y 1020) all far from the seam (Y 767–903); canvas 1080×1080, cube (274,580) 746×420, the widened seam stays entirely inside the cube; one-red rule preserved. BUILD NOTE BY MAIN MUSE: the study's "Gaussian (sigma ~6.5 px)" and its "26 px ±1 px at 5% of peak" do not agree with each other — a Gaussian with sigma 6.5 px falls to 5% at ±15.9 px, i.e. ~32 px total, not 26. A LINEAR feather from the flat region to the face colour at ±13 px satisfies both of the study's measurable checks (30–40% blue at ±10 px, 5% at ~±12.6 px → ~25 px total, inside 26 ±1), so the build uses a linear feather, as in loop 75. The build repaints the whole feather zone (not a patch on top of the old feather), because the old feather already reaches the face colour at ±10 px — patching would put a hard step there. Top-5: (1) a thin pale core is not load-bearing for the fold ('Glass cube and spherical light' — Sol Gomez Villasuso, Behance — a glass cube on black/grey, its vertical fold a hard edge between a red left face and a teal sphere/right face, with no highlight line at all; the cube reads at full size and in the search thumbnail through large colour/tonal blocks alone); (2) 2→3 px cannot rescue thumbnail legibility ('Glass Cube 3d Animation' — Zosia Biela, Behance — an open glass cube on blue, its edges thin pale lines ~1–2 px; in the full project the edges are barely visible, in thumbnails they disappear entirely, yet the cube still reads as an open box through its face planes, blue ground and spheres); (3) the surviving refraction signal should be broad and saturated, with white as a point, not a stripe ('PRISM FORGE: Dynamic & Geometric Logo Design' — Moo AI, Behance — a faceted grey 'P' on black; facets read through large tonal planes, the refraction that survives is broad saturated streaks (cyan, magenta, yellow, tens of pixels wide) and a white-hot point/glow at the centre, not a long thin white line); (4) broad colour, not a hairline, carries refraction at distance ('NEON PORTRAITS with PRISMATIC GLASS' — NKXD°, Behance — prismatic light on faces survives the thumbnail as broad colour bands/washes across the face, tens of pixels wide; the thin glass rims and hairline reflections vanish at small size); (5) a glint should be a point/soft glow inside colour ('Prism Crystal Suncatcher - 2D Animation' — Yeonwoo Lee, Behance — a crystal/moon suncatcher on orange: the crystal reads through broad pastel washes and facet planes, and its glints are four-point point sparkles, not long pale lines; widening a long pale line is the wrong way to make a glint). Rejected: widen core 2 px → 3 px (at 270 px 0.75 px, still sub-pixel and blended into the blue by downsampling — no measurable thumbnail gain; at full size 50% wider, 145 px long, L* ~92 against L* ~36.5, would read as a white stripe / chalk line, breaking the 'only chromatic line' rule in spirit and competing with the 10 px silhouette); widen core to 4 px or more (same reasons, more strongly — unambiguously a stripe at full size); remove the core / reduce to 1 px (the core is the full-size glint; removing it would leave only a soft blue band with no hot centre, and Prism Forge / Suncatcher show a hot centre is what makes refraction read as light, not paint); widen the seam to 32 px or more, or make the blue hard-edged / 100% opaque to ±13 px (at full size a blue band, not a refraction glow; at 270 px, 8 px, it would start to compete with the red wedge as a second coloured bar; 26 px is the smallest widening that gives a +30% thumbnail gain); increase blue saturation/opacity without widening, or darken the right face further to raise ΔL* (saturation is already #1D4ED8 at full strength on the centreline, ΔL* ~44 is already very large; neither addresses the width threshold at 270 px, and darkening the face would change the verified face tones); move the seam, add a second seam/line, or lengthen the seam (would move the fold, create a second chromatic line, or touch the wedge tip / top face, and none is needed — the fold position is verified); change nothing (the 5 px thumbnail blue mark is at the threshold where compression and distance can wash a soft feather out, leaving only the tonal step; the studied broad-colour examples show a modest widening is the conservative insurance for that mark). FALSIFICATION: 270 px / 3 m blind-read test — build the 26 px version and a 20 px control, both at 270 px, shuffled, no labels; PASS if, in 5 viewers who have not seen the full-size card, at least 4/5 in each version name the object as a cube / two-faced glass cube without prompting, AND at least 4/5 in the 26 px version (vs at most 2/5 in the control) report a blue line/mark on the fold without being told it is there; FAIL if the 26 px version does not beat the control on the blue-mark question, or if any viewer calls the mark a second wedge / blue stripe; also at 270 px, measure the seam in the exported file — the blue mark must be 6–7 px wide (26 × 0.25, ±0.5 px tolerance) and the core must not be separately visible as a white pixel row. Full-size blind-read test (1080 px, normal viewing distance, then 3 m): PASS if at least 4/5 viewers call the centre 'a glint / refraction / light on the fold' and none calls it 'a white stripe / white line / chalk line'; and at least 4/5 still call the cube glass (not a flat two-tone shape); FAIL if 2 or more call it a white stripe, or if the seam is called a blue band rather than a refraction line; at 3 m, PASS if at least 4/5 still locate the fold (point to the C–B fold) within 5 seconds; FAIL if the fold is located only by the tonal step with no blue reported. Measurable file checks (on the exported 1080×1080 file): across the fold at its midpoint (672,835), perpendicular to the centreline: core exactly 2 px wide, centre pixel(s) #DBEAFE (±3 per channel), L* 90–94; blue peak #1D4ED8 within ±3 px of the centreline; total seam width, defined as where blue saturation falls below 5% of peak, 26 px ±1 px (was 20 px ±1 px); no hard step at ±10 px (opacity there 30–40%, not 0%); faces sampled 20 px either side of the fold at mid-height: left ~(199,201,189), L* 76–80; right (46,90,120), L* 35–38; ΔL* ≥42; no other pixel in the cube may be #DBEAFE except the 2 px core, and no red except #C32D30; endpoints, wordmark (Y 118–242), tagline (Y 262–364), wedge tip (568,758) and footer (Y 1020) pixel positions unchanged from v78 within ±1 px. COUNT CORRECTION BY MAIN MUSE: the worker claimed 36 new designs, but 1 is a recount — Yeonwoo Lee 'Prism Crystal Suncatcher - 2D Animation', studied in loop 77 and again in loop 78, now a third time (the banned entry 'Prism Crystal Suncatcher' did not match the suffixed title). True new count is 35, running total ~2,151 (not ~2,152). TITLE-VARIANT LESSON: the same work under a suffixed/expanded title ('- 2D Animation', 'Logo Design & 3D Animation') counts as banned too — future briefs must say so explicitly, and the banned file should carry the base title as the match key. - Loop 80 study (34 NEW designs, running total ~2,185; none from loops 61–79): VERDICT — 26 px is already too wide. At both distances it reads as a blue band / second coloured bar, not as one glass refraction line, and it competes with the red wedge and with the top face. THE ONE CHANGE (loop 80): narrow the seam, and remove its pale core as part of that same seam change; change nothing else. Replace the present 26 px seam + 2 px pale core with ONE single seam, 12 px wide in total on the 1080 px poster, centred on the unchanged centreline (697,767)–(647,903), colour #1D4ED8 throughout. Construction: 8 px solid #1D4ED8 at the centre, feathering linearly to transparent over 2 px on each side (8 + 2 + 2 = 12 px total). No #DBEAFE core anywhere; no other colour, position, length or angle change. Length stays ~145 px (centreline length 144.9 px); width/length falls from 17.9% (26/145) to 8.3% (12/145). At 270 px the seam becomes 3.0 px wide × 36 px long (solid ~2 px), instead of 6.5 px wide. Chromatic seam area falls from ~3,770 px² (26 × 145) to ~1,740 px² (12 × 145), a 54% reduction. WHY: in every successful glass/prism work studied, saturated colour is either (a) a whole face/volume, with thin pale edges, or (b) a thin fringe/line at an edge — never a mid-width saturated strip stranded down the middle of a fold. The 26 px seam is neither a face nor a line: 26 px is 3.5% of the cube's 746 px width and 17.9% of its own 145 px length, so at 270 px it is 6.5 px wide against a 36 px length — the proportions of a bar, not a line. A bar of saturated #1D4ED8 is the only other saturated shape besides the red wedge, so the eye reads two coloured bars: red (wedge, arrowhead 48 px) and blue (seam), 129 px apart, instead of one red accent + one glass line. The top face #F5F5F5 is still the brightest plane by luminance (L* ~96, against blue L* ~35 and red #C32D30 L* ~35–40), but luminance does not win at thumbnail: chroma area does. Halving the blue area restores the intended hierarchy — white wordmark/top face first by luminance and area, red wedge first by chroma, blue seam subordinate. Evidence: 'Refracted' (Hup Studio) keeps the glass itself almost colourless — colour lives in the flower behind it, refraction is distortion, not a coloured stripe; 'Micro refractions' (Farid Ghanbari) uses broad, feathered, multi-hue caustic washes, never a single hard saturated bar; 'Prism light motion' (Gleb Kuznetsov) puts colour as a broad pale wash across the whole top face, with only thin pale edge lines; 'MICROSOFT • Fluid Framework' (Wes Cockx / Microsoft Design) makes blue whole faces/volumes with thin pale edges; 'Cube refraction c4d' (Artur Mineev) and '717C Glass 3D' (andbro.co) use colour only as thin rainbow fringes at glass edges, distorting what is behind the glass; 'REFRACTION CUBE 3D' (Denis Kuzminyh) is the closest black-ground analogue: its top face stays flat black, and saturated magenta/blue appear only as a thin rim along the top edge; 'Neon Circle wave line Animation on Black Background' (Easin arafat) shows saturated blue on black reading as a line only because its rings are thin strokes; on black posters, 'Do Something First' (Syed designs) and 'Fight Brutalism' (Riley @ Studio.909) likewise keep to one dominant accent/type and otherwise black/white — no second mid-width coloured bar. COLLISION CHECK: centreline (697,767)–(647,903) unchanged to ±1 px; length, angle and endpoints unchanged; only half-width changes from 13 px to 6 px each side of the centreline; pale core #DBEAFE deleted — it was invisible at 270 px and, at full size, split the seam into two parallel blue strips with a pale gap, increasing the perceived width; deleting it is part of this one seam change, not a second change; front-left face ~(199,201,189), L* ~76–80: seam now extends 6 px onto it instead of 13 px; blue-on-pale contrast remains high, so the line is still legible along its full length from that side; right face (46,90,120), L* ~36.5: seam extends 6 px onto it instead of 13 px; #1D4ED8 (29,78,216) against (46,90,120) is lower-contrast on this side (mainly the B-channel difference, 216 vs 120), so the right half is fainter — accepted: the left half carries the line at thumbnail, and the full 12 px is still measurable at full size; the tonal step ΔL* ~44 across the C–B fold is unchanged; the seam no longer masks it with a 26 px band; top face #F5F5F5 untouched, still the brightest, flattest plane; seam top end (697,767) is far below the top face (cube top ~Y 580) and does not touch it or its 10 px white silhouette stroke; no fringe is reintroduced on either face; red wedge #C32D30 unchanged — centreline (0,430)→(568,758) at 30.0°, tip still touching the cube's upper-left vertex (568,758), arrowhead still 48 × 36 px; gap from wedge tip to seam top end stays ~129 px (dx 129, dy 9), but that gap is now 10.8× the seam width (129/12) instead of 5.0× (129/26), so the two no longer read as a matched pair of bars; at 270 px the gap is ~32 px, the wedge arrowhead ~12 px wide, the seam ~3 px — wedge dominant, seam subordinate; wordmark (ink X 16–1077, Y 118–242), tagline (box X 17, Y 262, W 972.6, H 102; ink Y 272–352), microcopy 'N° 01' / 'EST. 2026' (Y 40), footer '@BLACKBOXSYSTEMSLAB' / 'VOL. 01' (Y 1020) all untouched and clear of the seam (seam Y 767–903; footer is 117 px below the seam's lower end, Y 903→1020); canvas geometry: the whole 12 px seam lies inside the cube image (X 274–1020, Y 580–1000) and inside the 1080 × 1080 canvas; the fold is interior, so a 6 px half-width cannot cross any cube edge or the canvas edge; no element moves, so no new overlap is created. BUILD NOTE BY MAIN MUSE: the build must RESTORE the face in the annulus the old feather occupied (24.1 < |d| ≤ 52.3 file) — simply drawing the narrower seam on top would leave the old feather's outer part still blue and the seam would stay 26 px wide. East side restores to flat (46,90,120); west side restores to the face colour sampled per-s at d=−56 (pure face in v79, since both feathers ended at ±52.3) — the render is smooth across d there, so the sampled colour is a good approximation of the hidden face, verified after building by checking for a step at |d|=40 and |d|=52.3. Top-5: (1) even saturated colour on a black cube must be a rim/line, not a bar down a fold, and the flat top plane stays uncontested ('REFRACTION CUBE 3D Concept of a Multimedia Art Object' — Denis Kuzminyh, Behance — on a black ground its cube's top face stays flat black while saturated magenta/blue appear only as a thin rim along the top edge); (2) refraction reads as a face wash plus a thin edge — a hard saturated stripe down a fold is not how this language works ('Prism light motion' — Gleb Kuznetsov, Dribbble — the cube's top face is a broad pale iridescent wash (palette includes #F5F5F3, close to the card's #F5F5F5); its edges are thin pale lines); (3) a blue of this hue works as a fringe of a few pixels; made solid and 26 px wide it becomes a separate object ('Cube refraction c4d' — Artur Mineev, Dribbble — black ground, white type; the cube's colour is thin rainbow fringes along its edges, including a blue fringe close to #084DB2); (4) the binary: colour is either a face (large, graded) or a line (thin); a 26 px strip in the middle of a fold is neither, so it reads as a foreign bar ('MICROSOFT • Fluid Framework' — Wes Cockx / Microsoft Design, Behance — blue is whole faces/volumes, graded across large planes, with thin pale edges); (5) the brightest, flattest plane should carry the read; a wide saturated line inside the glass steals that read ('717C Glass 3D' — andbro.co, Dribbble — the glass is near-white/clear, the white '717C' lettering is distorted by refraction, and colour appears only as thin fringes at the glass edges). Rejected: keep 26 px / widen further (width/length 17.9% is a bar at both distances; widening only increases chromatic area and the wedge competition); return to 20 px (loop 78 width) (20/145 = 13.8%, 5 px at 270 px — still bar-like, and it is a revert, not a tested fix); narrow to 6–8 px total (at 270 px that is 1.5–2 px, at risk of aliasing out against the dark right face (46,90,120) and of disappearing at 3 m; 12 px (3 px at thumbnail, 2 px solid) is the smallest width that stays reliably visible); desaturate/lighten the blue (e.g. to a pale #93C5FD) (it would vanish against the pale front-left face (199,201,189), lose the refraction identity, and introduce a third blue tint; the problem is width, not hue); shorten the seam to the upper half of the fold only (a shorter 26 px bar has a worse width/length ratio, reads even more as a bar, and looks unfinished/broken at full size); move the seam off the C–B fold (the fold is where refraction physically occurs; moving it breaks the glass logic); brighten the top face to pure #FFFFFF or enlarge it (#F5F5F5 is already L* ~96; the gain is imperceptible and does not fix the band ratio — the seam would still compete); thin the wedge or move its tip away from (568,758) (the wedge is the single intended chromatic accent; the competition is caused by the seam's width, and moving the tip would break the verified tip-to-vertex touch). FALSIFICATION: 270 px / 3 m blind-read test — export the card at 270 × 270 px, show it for 3 seconds at 3 m to 5 viewers who have not seen v79/v80, ask 'What do you see first? What is the blue mark? What is the brightest/flattest part?'; PASS if ≥4/5 say 'one glass cube' and describe the blue as 'a (thin) line / edge / seam / refraction' (not 'a bar / stripe / band / second bar'), name the white top face (or the white wordmark) as the brightest/flattest thing before the blue, and do not name the blue before the red wedge; FAIL if ≥2/5 say 'blue bar / stripe / band' or name the blue first. Full-size blind-read test: same 5 viewers, full 1080 px at normal viewing distance, no time limit, ask the same questions plus 'Where is the blue, and what is it doing?'; PASS if ≥4/5 call it 'a line / seam on the fold' and locate it on the C–B fold (697,767)–(647,903), and say the top face is the brightest, flattest plane; FAIL if ≥2/5 call it 'a band / stripe / bar' or say it competes with / is a second wedge. Measurable file checks (on the built v80 file, before any blind test): (a) on a cross-section perpendicular to the centreline at its midpoint (672,835), saturated #1D4ED8 pixels span 12 px total ±2 px (10–14 px including feather); (b) zero pixels of #DBEAFE in the seam; (c) centreline endpoints (697,767) and (647,903) within ±1 px of v79; (d) top-face centre sample still #F5F5F5; (e) wedge tip still (568,758) ±1 px and wedge colour still only #C32D30; (f) at a 270 px export, the seam measures 3 px ±1 px wide. Any of (a)–(f) failing means the change was not built as specified. - Loop 81 study (35 NEW designs, running total ~2,220; none from loops 61–80): VERDICT — pull the wedge tip back 10.0 px along its 30.0° centreline. Weakness: the red wedge tip kisses the cube's upper-left vertex (568,758) exactly. At that point three things meet — white top face #F5F5F5, pale front-left face ~(199,201,189), and the black field — and the 48×36 px red arrowhead collapses onto them. At 270 px / 3 m that is a 3–4 px red/pale/white muddle, not a readable strike; at full size it reads as a collision / rendering smudge on the cube's cleanest corner, not as pointing. Narrowing the seam to 12 px in loop 80 did not fix this: it removed a competitor inside the cube, but the tip–vertex kiss is a separate junction fault, on the outside of the cube. THE ONE CHANGE (loop 81): pull the wedge tip back 10.0 px along its 30.0° centreline, shortening the wedge from the tip end only. Old tip (568,758); new tip (559.3,753.0) — shift vector (−8.7,−5.0) px, i.e. 10.0 × (cos 30°, sin 30°) = 10.0 × (0.866, 0.500). Gap created: exactly 10.0 px of pure black #000000, measured along the centreline, between the new red tip and the vertex (568,758). Everything else frozen: centreline origin (0,430) and angle 30.0° unchanged; new centreline length (0,430)→(559.3,753.0) = 645.9 px (was 655.9 px); arrowhead unchanged at 48 px wide × 36 px long, now with its base centre at (528.1,735.0); wedge colour still the sole red #C32D30; seam, faces, silhouette, wordmark, tagline, microcopy and footer unchanged. Do NOT translate the whole wedge PNG: that would move the left-edge entry from (0,430) to (0,425). Shorten/trim the tip end only, keeping the entry, angle and arrowhead geometry. Why 10 px, not 6 or 12: at 270 px (×0.25) 10 px = 2.5 px of black — the smallest gap that survives downscaling as a clean sliver; 6 px = 1.5 px at thumbnail, below the ~2 px survival threshold, and would re-collapse into a kiss. At full size 10 px = 0.93% of the 1080 width, 1.34% of the 746 px cube width, 27.8% of the 36 px arrowhead length — the same order as the existing 10 px white silhouette stroke, so it reads as a deliberate system measure, not an error. 12 px (= the seam width) would echo the seam and is halfway back to the 24 px gap rejected in loops 61–66. WHY: in every relevant full project opened, an arrow/line either stops clearly short in empty field, or crosses decisively through an object — none parks its tip exactly on a vertex or edge. Arrow Posters and Electric Boogie show red arrows carrying their meaning in clear space, with no contact at all. Stray Arrow and PAARD PUSH FORWARD show tips kept in white/black void beyond the object they point at. RED GIANT shows thin lines that either run clean through circles or stop in open cream — never a tangent kiss. MIRROR HOUSE shows a glass cuboid whose vertices read precisely because nothing touches them. Mirror | Eyes shows prismatic bands legible because they cross open skin and never coincide with a feature corner. The seam change supports the pull-back, not keep-as-is: with the seam now a single clean 12 px blue line (3 px saturated blue at 270 px), the cube interior is quiet, so the only remaining noise at the junction is the red tip itself — removing it from the vertex lets both the seam and the vertex be read cleanly. The centreline still passes exactly through (568,758), so the eye completes the last 10 px; pointing is preserved, impact is replaced by aim. COLLISION CHECK: wedge tip new (559.3,753.0), red #C32D30, 10.0 px from vertex along 30.0°; no red pixel touches the cube; vertex (568,758) clean and untouched; top face, front-left face and silhouette meet there with no red overpaint; arrowhead (48×36) wholly in black void; nearest point is the tip, 10 px from the vertex; its side corners are ~52 px from the vertex; its base centre (528.1,735.0) is ~46 px from the vertex along the centreline; no part overlaps the cube silhouette; seam unchanged, 12 px, centreline (697,767)–(647,903); nearest seam point to the new tip is (697,767), 138.4 px away — no interaction, no second red/blue junction; faces untouched (front-left pale ~(199,201,189), L* ~76–80, right face (46,90,120), L* ~36.5; tonal step ΔL* ~44 across the C–B fold preserved); silhouette 10 px white stroke on the top face untouched; no red crosses it; wordmark (Y 118–242), tagline (Y 262–352, box X 17), microcopy (Y 40), footer (Y 1020) all ≥200 px from the tip area; unaffected; canvas geometry: tip (559.3,753.0) is inside the 1080×1080 canvas, 520.7 px from the right edge, 327.0 px from the bottom; gap 10 px = 2.5 px at 270 px; arrowhead at thumbnail = 12.0×9.0 px, still a readable arrowhead; the wedge still enters at (0,430) on the left edge; colour discipline: still one red only, #C32D30 (wedge, glows, halos); no new colour, line, star, spine or hairline introduced. BUILD NOTE BY MAIN MUSE: the wedge is a separate full-bleed PNG (`slash-wedge-point-746-gap0-head48-steep30.png`), not the cube — the build edits that file surgically (erase the old arrowhead + tip end, redraw the arrowhead translated by (−8.66,−5.0) and a short shaft bridge at the measured local width), never a whole-PNG translate and never a from-scratch rebuild, so the shaft outside the tip region stays byte-identical. Top-5: (1) a red arrow reads as pointing — more cleanly — when it stops short in empty space ('Electric boogie | Identity' — Anna Cheboksarova, Behance — on the black posters the red diagonal loop's arrowhead is a small open V floating in black void, and the small red arrows sit in the gaps between letters, never touching a letterform); (2) direction is carried by shaft, head and chevrons, not by contact with a target ('Arrow Posters' — Roshan Sam, Behance — the thin red arrow under "ARROW" sits in a clear beige field, its tip ending well short of any letter or edge, with three red chevrons at the tail); (3) even a "hit" arrow keeps its tip legible by ending in empty field, not on an edge ('Stray Arrow' — Yu Osawa, Behance — the horizontal arrow pierces the samurai head, but its tip is kept clear in white space beyond the red disc behind it); (4) arrows used as direction, not as spears striking a target ('PAARD PUSH FORWARD' — Studio Lennarts & De Bruijn, Behance — large yellow arrowheads stop inside their own colour blocks and never pierce the next block, circle or type); (5) the ambiguous middle — a 0 px kiss on an edge — is the one relationship competent minimal posters avoid; clear separation or decisive overlap are the only clean options, and separation is the one that preserves BLACK BOX's clean vertex ('RED GIANT - Minimalist poster design' — Vlad Grama, Dribbble — thin vertical lines either run cleanly through the red/orange circles or stop in open cream; none parks tangentially on a circle's edge). Rejected: keep as-is (tip touching 568,758) (the seam narrowing removed an internal competitor, not the external kiss; at 270 px the tip + vertex + arrowhead still collapse into a red/pale/white blob, and at full size red over a three-way corner reads as collision, not strike); pull back 6 px, new tip (562.8,755.0) (1.5 px at 270 px, below the ~2 px survival threshold — anti-aliasing would re-merge tip and vertex; also smaller than the 10 px silhouette stroke, so it would look accidental); pull back 12 px, new tip (557.6,752.0) (works at thumbnail (3 px) but at full size equals the seam width, creating a second 12 px measure, and is halfway back to the rejected 24 px gap — it starts to read as a miss); pull back 24 px (loops 61–66 gap), new tip (547.2,746.0) (already tried and rejected; at 6 px at thumbnail the arrow visibly misses the cube and the strike/aim is lost); push the tip INTO the cube (overlap by 10–20 px) (red would overpaint the pale face and white silhouette, break the clean vertex, and at thumbnail merge with the blue seam area; it turns pointing into impaling); remove or shrink the arrowhead (a second change, and the arrowhead is the direction cue that survives at 270 px (12×9 px); removing it would weaken the read the gap is meant to protect); rotate the wedge to aim at the cube centre or another vertex (changes the 30.0° centreline and the (0,430) entry — a different design, not a junction fix); widen the seam again to compete with / distract from the tip (reverses loop 80 and reintroduces the problem the seam narrowing solved). FALSIFICATION: 270 px / 3 m blind-read test — show the v81 export at 270 px wide (or printed at 270 px, viewed from 3 m) to ≥5 viewers who have not seen the brief, with no prompt beyond "what do you see?"; PASS if ≥4/5 say the red arrow points at the cube's corner and there is a small black gap, and ≤1 says "touching / colliding / muddle"; FAIL if ≥2 say touching, colliding, or cannot separate the tip from the cube, or if ≥2 say the arrow missed the cube. Full-size blind-read test: same viewers at full size (1080 px); PASS if ≥4/5 say the arrow "points at, but does not touch, the corner" and the gap "looks intentional"; FAIL if any say "it missed / fell short" or "it is touching / crashing into the cube". Measurable file checks (v81 export, before any other change): (a) tip pixel at (559,753) is red #C32D30; (b) 3×3 sample centred at the gap midpoint (563.6,755.5) is pure black #000000 in all 9 pixels; (c) pixel at the vertex (568,758) is NOT #C32D30; (d) tip-to-vertex distance = 10.0 ± 0.5 px, centreline angle = 30.0° ± 0.5°, entry still (0,430); (e) arrowhead still 48×36 px, seam still 12 px total with 3 px saturated blue at 270 px, wedge colour still #C32D30 only; (f) at 270 px the black gap between red tip and pale face measures 2.5 ± 0.5 px; (g) no pixel outside the wedge tip region differs from v80. Any (a)–(f) failure falsifies the build; (g) failure means a second change crept in. Solid-head arrows cluster at shaft:head 1.3–2.0 (WeRoad 1.4–2.0; Ivanovsky ~1.5–2; EarthWurx ~1.3; Abstract X ~1.5; OppositeDay 1:1). The only thin shafts that work are open chevrons or line arrows whose head is the same stroke as the shaft (La Corriols del Vallès) — a logic that cannot transfer to BLACK BOX, whose head is a solid 72 × 60 px triangle (2,160 px²). The systematic benchmark, HTML Arrows (Dixon & Moe, Awwwards), shows every Unicode arrow (U+2190–U+219F), including the north-east arrow U+2197 in exactly the BLACK BOX direction, with a small narrow head, head length at least equal to its width and an apex of roughly 30–45°. Eight Arrows (vishal-hotwani, Awwwards) has a head about 1.37 times as long as wide with an apex of about 40°, on a thin shaft — and it still reads as sharp at small size. La Filmoteca d'estiu (DEMOCRÀCIA®, Behance) makes its point as one long tapered white wedge, apex about 20–25°, length far greater than width, whose tip touches/overlaps the figures below it — no floating gap, no short triangle. Catch — Wayfinding System Concept (Aleksei Slepov, Behance) does not use a wide filled triangle at all: its point is a sharp shaft corner/minimal chevron, proving direction is carried by the shaft and the head must only terminate it sharply, not become a separate blunt block. Ligne 18 — Find your line (L4nc, Dribbble) treats the line/trajectory as the point, at the official 18 m indoor archery distance, and deliberately moves away from red-and-black target language — at distance a short head plus a visible gap reads as a miss, not as intention. Fieldhouse (Muhammad Ibrahim, Dribbble) likewise carries direction with a long red diagonal bar and no triangle head, its end flush with its target. Together these say: lengthen the point, do not widen it; a 6 px gap then reads as a hairline separation, while a 10 px gap behind a 60 px head reads as a miss. Top-5: (1) HTML Arrows — Dixon & Moe (Awwwards): a complete chart of Unicode arrows U+2190–U+219F; every head is narrow, length ≥ width, apex roughly 30–45°; the north-east arrow U+2197 is the BLACK BOX direction. Proves 61.9° / width > length is outside the normal arrowhead range. (2) Eight Arrows — vishal-hotwani (Awwwards): blue arrow measured at about 1.37 length/width and about 40° apex on a thin shaft, still sharp at small size. Proves a longer-than-wide head is the working proportion, and gives the 40–46° target band for the new 46.4° apex. (3) La Filmoteca d'estiu — DEMOCRÀCIA® design (Behance): a long, acute white tapered wedge (apex about 20–25°) whose tip touches/overlaps its target. Proves points read by length and taper, not by width, and that a floating gap is not how a pointed poster element meets its target. (4) Catch — Wayfinding System Concept — Aleksei Slepov (Behance): the arrow's point is a sharp shaft corner/minimal chevron, with no wide filled triangle. Proves a wide 72 × 60 px triangle is not needed to point, and that a blunt filled head becomes a separate block rather than a termination. (5) Ligne 18 — Find your line — L4nc (Dribbble): archery identity built on the line/trajectory at 18 m, deliberately avoiding red-and-black target language. Proves that at distance the trajectory and the gap are judged together — a short head plus a relatively large gap reads as a miss, which is why the head must be lengthened as the gap is closed to 6 px. Rejected: close the gap to 6–8 px only, keeping 72 × 60 px / 61.9° (the head would still be wider than long and blunt at full size, and at 270 px still 18 × 15 px; the gap would be smaller but the point would still not look sharp. The evidence condemns the proportion, not only the gap); keep exactly as-is (61.9° is outside the 30–50° band in every studied arrow, the 0.83 length/width ratio is the reverse of the studied ratio, and 10 px is 16.7% of head length, which is why the thumbnail reads as a miss); narrow the head to 56 px wide × 60 px long (apex 50.0°) (it would shrink the head's presence (14 px wide at 270 px) and weaken the loop-82 enlargement, whereas lengthening to 84 px preserves the 72 px width and makes the head 21 px long at thumbnail); lengthen further to 96 px (apex 41.1°) (the head would become spear-like (length/shaft 3:1), the base would retreat to s = 554, and the gain over 84 px / 46.4° is not supported by the evidence; 46.4° already sits in the studied 40–50° band); close the gap to 0 px / touch the vertex (it would break the loop-81 intent (a gap of pure black, vertex clean white), risk red anti-aliasing onto the white vertex at full size, and read as touching/merging at 270 px); replace the filled head with an open chevron (as in Catch) (it would be a second, larger change to the wedge's identity and would lose the solid red mass that loop 82 built; lengthening the existing filled head is the smaller, buildable fix). WHY, grounded in the designs studied: the arrows that read as one mass at small size do it by making the shaft carry the head — thick shaft, step small relative to the shaft — not by shrinking the head. BLACK BOX's head is long (84 px, length/width 1.17) and its back is a straight base with no notch, so the shaft alone must anchor it; at 44.4% anchorage it is below the ~50–60% anchorage seen in the successful examples. Widening the shaft to 36 px crosses the 50% / 2.00:1 threshold with the smallest possible intervention, preserves the head's 18 px thumbnail presence and its 46.4° apex, and leaves an 18 px step at full size — still unmistakably a deliberate shoulder, not a merge. Top-5: (i) ART WEEK 21 | Dynamic Minimalist Poster Design, Nazli Aydin (Dribbble): magenta arrows with constant-width shafts bleed off the right edge at full width while their 3D cube heads sit inside the frame; the bleed reads as continuation precisely because width at the edge equals width everywhere (ratio 1.0) — BLACK BOX at 0.44 is the inverse of this. (ii) Art exhibition in a museum, Aurélie Gasser (Behance): the CALATRAVA poster crops letters hundreds of pixels tall, cutting off about a third of the letterforms — a crop reads as deliberate only when the cut element is large and the cut is substantial; a 16 px / 4 px sliver is the opposite case. (iii) FRAME — Poster Series & Exhibition Identity, Marta Wasilewska (Behance): a thin blue arrow loops fully inside the frame and never touches an edge, reading as a drawn mark, not an entry — touching the edge at thin width is the worst of both readings, it claims entry while drawing like an interior mark. Top-5: UP Logo exploration, Arrow logo — Zikospace (Dribbble): a white negative-space arrow whose head is about 2.8–3.4× its shaft, on a short shaft — proves a head at 2.0× is below the range in which a head dominates a thick shaft; ~2.7–3.0× is the working minimum. Sun, arrow - Logo Explorations — Victor Murea (Dribbble): a broad, shallow chevron head about 4× its shaft is the whole width of the mark — proves that with a thick shaft, dominance comes from head width, not head length alone. Arrow Logo Mark — Ahmed (Dribbble): a large diagonal triangular head about 3.7× its bar, occupying about half the mark — proves a long, thick shaft still reads as accelerating when the head is several times the shaft. Growth | Typographical Poster — Karl Bembridge (Behance): the 't' is a thin teal growth-chart arrow; its modest head works only because the shaft is thin — proves the ratio, not the absolute head size, is what matters, and that the BLACK BOX's thick shaft therefore needs a larger head. P Logo Design | Direction & Business Growth logo — Anik Khandaker / Riya Moni (Behance): a black P with a wide white chevron head against a narrow white shaft — proves, in negative space, that the step from shaft to head must be large and legible at small size, as the new 30.3 px step (7.6 px at 270 px) is. Rejected: keep the head exactly as-is (72 × 84) — ratio 2.00:1 at the base, 18 px vs 9 px at 270 px, step 4.5 px per side at thumbnail — the evidence band starts at ~2.7:1, and the head reads as a cap on a fat bar at both distances. Re-grade the shaft thinner, e.g. 24→28 px (taper ~0.40°/side, 26.8 px at s = 380, ratio 72/28 = 2.57) — it restores the ratio arithmetically but undoes loops 86–87, thins the shaft to 6.7 px at 270 px, makes the taper almost invisible, and leaves the head still only 18 px at thumbnail — the climax stays small in absolute terms; the studied marks keep thick shafts and enlarge the head. Widen the head only, e.g. 96 × 84 (apex ~59.7°, length/width 0.88) — it blunts the apex and undoes the loop-84 sharpening; the head becomes a squat flat triangle, not a piercing wedge. Lengthen the head only, e.g. 72 × 112 (apex ~35.6°, length/width 1.56) — width and ratio stay 2.00:1, so the thumbnail problem is unsolved; it makes a needle, not a dominant head. Grow the head more, e.g. 108 × 126 (×1.5, ratio ~3.05 at the base, area +125%) — it overshoots the evidenced band, risks the head reading as a separate red triangle detached from the shaft, and gives the red mass more weight than the cube's left edge needs. Add a second chevron, a double head, or a stronger glow/halo — it adds a new element and breaks the single-red / only-chromatic-line discipline without fixing the geometric ratio. By area it cannot outweigh the cube. Its perceived weight is chroma plus halo: a halo spreads tinted black well beyond the solid edge, more than doubling the effective red footprint, and at thumbnail it merges head and shaft into a red smear that stops the eye. The 30.3 px shoulder step, by contrast, is a clean 2.71:1 head/shaft ratio with straight head edges and a 46.4° apex — a normal arrowhead break, not a notch. 'Where Minimalism Comes From: Russian Constructivism' — Grigorii Lapin for The Designest (Dribbble): the huge red 'M' stops the eye; the black CONSTRUCTIVISM wedge, a sharp taper with no shoulder step, points straight through — proves taper without a step reads as through-line, block does not. 'LIVE SESSION — Constructivist Poster Design' — Gamid Rustamov (Dribbble): 45° diagonal, red kept thin, flat and unglowed (thin lines, small triangles, one flat red triangle); the black diagonal carries the reading — proves a diagonal vector works when red has no halo. 'RED BOMB™ — Structural Packaging & Preserves Identity' — Harrynson Ramirez / Trento Studio (Behance): a red label is deliberately the hero on heavy black stock — proves that red-as-hero is a real, intentional effect, and the one to avoid when red is meant only to point to the cube. Keep everything exactly as-is — the glow is the unmeasured multiplier, it more than doubles the effective red area and, at thumbnail, merges head and shaft into a smear; keeping it leaves the loop-89 question unanswered. Darken/desaturate the red (e.g. away from #C32D30) — it changes the single brand red, weakens thumbnail contrast, and is unnecessary; the glow, not the hue, is the lever. 'Plakat festiwalu Jazz nad Odrą' — Monika Waryszak (Behance): thin gold lines on a near-black poster survive only because ~100 wavy lines repeat across the whole field — the seam, with no repetition, cannot borrow that survival mechanism; width is its only available mechanism. - Loop 92 study (21 NEW designs — the worker claimed 21, verified by main Muse, no recounts — running total ~2,533): VERDICT — the single biggest remaining weakness is the gap itself at full size: at 14 px it is 14.6% of the 96 px arrowhead width and 39.8% of the 35.2 px shaft width at the head base, large enough, on a 1080 px poster, for the eye to read the wedge as stopping short of — hesitating before — the cube's upper-left vertex, rather than as confidently aimed at it. At 270 px the cost of closing it is negligible (3.5 px → 3.0 px of dark, still a clear deliberate break), while at full size the gain is real. The aim is carried by the 556 px shaft and by exact alignment, not by the size of the break, so the break should be as small as thumbnail legibility allows. THE ONE CHANGE: narrow the gap from 14 px to 12 px, by moving the whole wedge forward 2.0 px along its own centreline, at 30.0°, with nothing else changed. New tip (557.6, 752.0); new head base centre (460.6, 696.0); new head base corners (436.6, 737.6) and (484.6, 654.4); head base station s = 532 (was s = 530). Gap ratios after the change: 12 px = 12.5% of head width 96 px (was 14.6%); 10.7% of head length 112 px; 1.6% of cube width 746 px (was 1.9%); 34.1% of shaft width at the head base, 35.2 px (was 39.8%). At 270 px: gap 3.0 px of dark (was 3.5 px); head width 24 px, so the gap is still 12.5% of head width at thumbnail. Unchanged: angle 30.0°, entry centre (0, 430), entry width 24.0 px, top edge (0, 416.1), bottom edge (0, 443.9); head 96 × 112 px, apex 46.4°, head/shaft ratio 2.72:1, shaft taper 0.61° per side, shaft 32.1 px at s = 380 and 35.2 px at the head base, vertex (568, 758), cube, seam, wordmark, tagline and footer all unchanged. Top-5: 'Target' — Mujahid Robiul (a short, off-axis projectile reads as a miss, while contact reads as a hit — the difference is axis plus proximity, not gap alone; the strongest warning against a larger gap). 'arrow+target' — Rob Eagle (aim at a point is conventionally shown by contact; any gap is a deliberate statement, so it should be minimal). 'Free Minimalist Arrow Logo' — logodrop.co (a white chevron head detached from its shaft by a wide negative-space gap still reads unambiguously as one arrow because the axis is exact — a 12 px gap cannot break the arrow if the 30.0° alignment is exact). 'Pointer' — Alex Lookdesign (stopped-short can read as pointing, but only for a containing target, so a point vertex needs a tighter gap than a circle does). 'The Space Between Us' — Thomas de Franzoni ('what connects us is not what we share, but the space we leave for one another' — the 12 px break is that space, not a failure to reach). At full size a 46.4° wedge is 10.3 px wide 12 px back from its tip, so it looks like a broad wedge about to dock with the white vertex; at 270 px its 96 px head is 24 px wide and squeezes the 3.0 px black channel between two large masses, so the black reads as a hairline / anti-aliasing fringe, not a deliberate pause. 12 px is the thumbnail floor for distance, but only if the tip is sharpened. THE CHANGE: HOLD the gap at exactly 12 px and SHARPEN the apex from 46.4° to 36.0°, keeping head length at 112 px. Tip stays frozen at (557.6, 752.0); base centre stays frozen at (460.6, 696.0); head width falls from 96 px to 72.8 px. New base corners: (442.4, 727.5) and (478.8, 664.5). - **Loop 101 — FREEZE THE HARD EDGE: BUILD NOTHING ON THE SEAM (study 16 NEW — worker claimed 18, 2 recounts — total ~2,795; banned file now 802 unique titles covering loops 61–101):** VERDICT — the single biggest remaining weakness is the full-size pale-face edge of the seam: a hard 1 px step from solid #1D4ED8 to the pale face ~(199,201,189) on a flat face, which is the one place a first-time viewer could momentarily parse the blue as a painted sticker. The evidence says that risk does not materialise, and the posed fix would make it worse. THE ONE CHANGE: build nothing on the seam. Freeze v100 exactly — seam centreline (697,767)–(647,903), length ~144.9 px, solid #1D4ED8, 0 px feather, no pale core, maximum width 20.0 px at the midpoint (672,835) only, width profile s=0: 0; s=18: 8.8; s=36: 15.0; s=54: 18.7; s=72.5: 20.0; s=91: 18.7; s=109: 15.0; s=127: 8.8; s=144.9 (B): 0, both long edges hard 1 px transitions, true points at C (697,767) and B (647,903), dark edge hard. WHY: painted/sticker readings occur where flat colour sits on a uniform substrate with no geometry underneath it (a flat blue bar on black reads as paper/paint precisely because nothing changes beneath it; hard edges read as torn paper, a material, not light). Our seam fails that test for a sticker: its centreline coincides with the C–B fold, both its points sit on the fold, and it is symmetric about the fold, so it straddles two faces whose tones already step ΔL* ~44 (pale L* ~76–80 against dark L* ~36.5). A sticker sits on one face; this seam is visibly one object crossing a fold, and its two edges accordingly have different contrasts — a high lightness step on the pale side, a hue-only step on the dark side — which is the signature of light on a fold, not of a flat graphic. Second, the vesica shape itself is anti-sticker: its edges narrow continuously to points and are never parallel, so there is no run of "sticker edge" anywhere. Third, in every light example studied, hard edges are the norm and softness lives inside the light form or in the surrounding field, not in a 2 px edge ramp. A 2 px ramp is below the threshold of an optical effect and at the threshold of a print artefact: at 270 px it is 0.5 px and invisible, so it cannot change the distance reading, and at full size it would read as a pale-blue fringe — a printed gradient edge — rather than as light. WHY: in 'Flat vs Gradient Colors' (Aqeela Musharraff) the same crystal is drawn twice side by side: on the left every facet is a single flat colour with hard points and no internal gradient, and it still reads unmistakably as a crystal — a light-refracting solid — because the facets meet at points and differ in tone; on the right the gradient version, with internal diagonal streaks and bright spots, reads as a glossy render, a different register altogether. Adding a #3B82F6 core would move BLACK BOX toward that right-hand register. In 'THE END' (IO Rosemary) a flat, near-white, hard-edged vertical sword-blade streak on black reads unambiguously as light/steel with no internal gradient at all, because it is anchored — hilt above, body below, black field around it. The BLACK BOX seam is anchored far more tightly: it sits exactly on the C–B fold, its two points are the fold's own vertices, and the faces either side step by ΔL* ~44. A painted mark would be a uniform-width stripe, or a shape crossing the fold indifferently; no painted mark tapers continuously from 20.0 px to true points at exactly the two fold vertices. That width profile is itself the light evidence. Conversely, 'Light Portal Core' (Lucid mk2) shows what a genuine bright core actually looks like: a soft, diffuse, symmetrical glow, brightest at the centre and fading outward with mottled texture — not a hard 4 px step. A hard step would not replicate that; it would be a third device, a pinstripe. And a 4 px core cannot even be built cleanly inside this vesica: scaled to the vesica it would be 4.0 px at the midpoint, 3.7 px at s=54/91, 3.0 px at s=36/109 and only 1.8 px at s=18/127, vanishing and aliasing near the points; kept at a constant 4 px it would end in flat 4 px stubs at C and B and destroy the true points. Either way it damages the one thing that settles the reading. It would also break the card's one-blue discipline and re-open loop 80, which deleted the pale core for the same reason. At 270 px the core would be 1.0 px and invisible, so it buys nothing at distance and risks a stripe at full size. - **Loop 103 LEARNING STEP (YouTube, 2026-11-07 ~21:45–21:57):** "5 Poster Design Tips to Make Your Work Stand Out" — Collect & Contrast (Austin Dingess), https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WZsawVesxY0, 8:15, published 24 Feb 2025, 249,620 views, ~10k likes. Watched in full, in order, no skipping; no subtitle track existed ("Subtitles/closed captions unavailable"), so the worker listened to the audio properly in ~60-second segments and watched the frame at each segment. Chapters: Intro 0:00, Tip 1 0:33, Tip 2 3:07, Tip 3 4:05, Tip 4 5:00, Tip 5 6:16. THE FIVE TIPS: (1) Use the Camera Raw filter — finish by merging all layers into one Smart Object and grading the whole design as one colour system (exposure, then hue first in the Color Mixer, then saturation and luminance); hard warning: "if your design is bad, this tip is not going to save it" — it takes a great design "from a 9 to a 10" and no further. (2) Design in black and white — greyscale first (black background, white text, grey box where an image goes) so you focus on layout and composition only; if the layout is exciting in black and white, colour only makes it better; it does not work the other way around. (3) Break the grid — find one thing that is not part of the grid (a snake slithering off the page; one part of a photo poking out of its square container); one deliberate break, not several. (4) Push ideas to their absolute limit — take really big type and move it off the page so the bottoms of the letters are cut off, or blow up / stretch photography, or stretch type to see how tall the letterforms can be; push it as far as it can go, then take exactly one step back (especially with typography, which must stay legible). (5) Remix the finished design as one layer — merge the whole project into one layer at the end, then blow it up, move it around, chop it up, layer copies over each other, mask the typography back in so it stays readable; the same finished design, explored in different options. BIGGEST LESSON FOR THIS CARD: push ONE element to its absolute limit, then take one step back — the wordmark or the cube. The wordmark is already full-width (ink X 16–1077) but fully contained — nothing is cropped, nothing touches an edge. Scale it far past 128 pt until its letters are actually cropped by the poster's edges (or scale the 746×420 cube until it bleeds off the bottom-right corner), keep pushing until it feels too loud and slightly uncomfortable, then reduce it by exactly one step so the words remain readable. Do not push the 32 pt tagline or the 12 pt footer — they must stay legible. If no element touches, crosses or is cropped by an edge, it has not been pushed far enough, and the card will stay 2/10 no matter how the colours are graded. APPLICATIONS TO THIS CARD (from the worker): Tip 1 — limited and dangerous if misused (the card has no photography, and it is rated 2/10, not 9/10, so a finishing colour pass cannot rescue it; the 40 loops of small refinements were, in effect, Tip 1 thinking applied to a weak layout); the transferable principle is only to judge the card as one whole colour system at the very end. Tip 2 — a devastating diagnostic: strip the blue seam and red wedge to grey and ask if the layout is exciting; the answer is no (a neat, polite stack with no tension and no path for the eye), so colour is not the fix, and the next loop should be judged in greyscale first. Tip 3 — directly applicable: the card currently violates it in every element (wordmark block, tagline block, cube rectangle and footer are all grid-aligned rectangles, nothing breaks out); the most honest candidate is the red wedge, whose tip stops 16 px short of the cube's vertex — letting it touch, pierce or cross the cube edge would be the one grid-break. Tip 5 — the lowest-risk way to attempt the loud version: duplicate the whole 1080×1080 poster as one flattened layer, blow it up 150–200%, move it off-centre, chop it, layer a smaller copy peeking through at the side, mask the wordmark back in — a bolder variant to judge in minutes without disturbing the frozen card. Do NOT apply the five tips one at a time, politely, as five more small refinements — that would repeat loops 63–102. Combine them in one variant: one element pushed to its limit, one grid-break, judged in black and white first, then a final unified colour pass. (close second, foundational, less about standing out); Wave Index "How I Made This INSANE Brutalism Poster!" - **Loop 104 LEARNING STEP (Instagram Reel, 2026-11-07 ~22:16–22:26):** "Graphic Design Tip — Master Visual Hierarchy" — thecampuscreative / The Campus Creative, https://www.instagram.com/reels/DfOIXbXOZDO/. Watched through several full loops with the sound on, well over 3 minutes of playback. Instagram's desktop player shows no duration, so none is recorded. Instagram labels the Reel "AI content" — the presenter footage is an AI-generated presentation of the lesson, not a live studio recording; the design principle and the worked example are still coherent. The Reel has no on-screen text, captions/subtitles or numbered steps; its teaching is carried by the spoken voiceover (Hinglish/Urdu, repeated on the loop), the worked poster example in Photoshop, and the full written caption (read in full). The audio transcription was garbled, but the repeated sentence was consistently audible as: headline prominent, subtext as subtext, details small, highlight the date. THE LESSON: visual hierarchy means making one headline dominate by size, keeping all supporting text visibly secondary, and using colour contrast to pull the eye to the key detail, so a viewer scans a poster in a clear order instead of having every element compete. Caption rules: (1) make the main headline stand out through size; (2) keep supporting information visually secondary; (3) use colour contrast to draw attention to important details; (4) arrange content so viewers can scan the poster quickly. Practical takeaway (caption, final line): "Establish one clear focal point before styling the remaining text." The example poster's 3-level order (Photoshop frames, in order): headline "SCHOOL SCIENCE DAY" large bold blue capitals top; subtext "EXPLORE THE WORLD OF SCIENCE" smaller black capitals beneath; details "DATE: 15 DECEMBER 2026 / TIME: 10:00 AM / VENUE: SCHOOL AUDITORIUM" small black lower, with the DATE line highlighted in yellow in the final close-up (the Reel's only literal highlight — it marks the date, not just bolds it); bottom blue band "DISCOVER • EXPERIMENT • LEARN" in white. The reading order and the weight order are the same, top to bottom. BIGGEST LESSON FOR THIS CARD: establish ONE clear focal point before styling anything else — and on this card that means deciding, explicitly, whether the cropped wordmark is the focal point or the cube/wedge is, and then making every other element visibly secondary to it in size, weight and colour contrast, in reading order. If the wordmark stays cropped and full-width, it must be given a clean exit downwards (a tagline unambiguously second in weight, then a wedge that leads the eye from the tagline to the cube, then a seam given a real highlight lift so it can be the final stop); if that cannot be done without the pale cube and red wedge out-pulling the tagline, then the focal point has to change — the wordmark must be un-cropped and given breathing room, or the cube/wedge must be demoted — because a poster with three focal points has no eye-path, only a stack. APPLICATIONS TO THIS CARD (from the worker): DIRECT HIT — the card has at least three high-contrast competitors for first attention (cropped white wordmark full-width ExtraBold; pale cube top face #F5F5F5, the brightest large area, 746×420; red wedge #C32D30, the only warm colour, a large diagonal) plus the blue seam #1D4ED8 as a fourth, smaller magnet; nothing has been demoted enough to let one win cleanly. The text hierarchy is clean (tagline 32 pt Regular vs wordmark ExtraBold; microcopy/footer 12 pt grey) but the NON-TEXT elements were never made secondary the same way. Colour contrast cuts against the intended path: the only colours are the red wedge and blue seam, so by the Reel's own rule those two are the contrast magnets regardless of where they sit in the intended wordmark → tagline → wedge → cube → seam order; the wedge will out-pull the tagline, the pale cube top will out-pull both by brightness, and the seam (20.0 px max, no pale core) is too small to be a reliable fifth stop unless the eye is already on the cube. The intended 5-step path is NOT in weight order and NOT top-to-bottom — the wedge and cube interleave, and the seam is INSIDE the cube, so the last step requires the eye to re-enter an element it has already passed; the Reel's example never asks the eye to re-enter an element. The card has no highlighted key detail: the element it wants the eye to end on (the blue seam, the "about to strike" moment at the wedge tip 16 px short of the vertex) has no highlight treatment at all. ANSWER TO THE LOOP'S QUESTION: the eye will very likely still read "BLACK BOX" first (size + white-on-black earn that) but will NOT reliably travel wordmark → tagline → wedge → cube → seam in 3 seconds.
