- **Loop 105 LEARNING STEP (website article, 2026-11-07 ~22:37–22:40):** "Typography Hierarchy Poster: A Practical Reading Path" — Linh Nguyen, Graphic Designer, inkydesignworks.com, https://www.inkydesignworks.com/posts/typography-hierarchy-poster, 28 Sep 2026. Read in full, in text form, every section, table, example and warning; no login wall or paywall. THE LESSON: build a poster's reading path — primary, secondary, tertiary — by deciding the message order first, then making scale, weight, placement, colour and whitespace all agree on that order, and stress-testing the result at thumbnail/distance/blur and in five seconds. KEY POINTS (in the article's order): (1) Opening thesis — the problem is rarely that the headline is not large enough; it is that every element is asking for attention at the same time. (2) Three-second rule — in three seconds a viewer should understand the main event, the central idea, and the action to take. (3) Hierarchy is the delivery mechanism, not a finishing touch — posters are read across a room, while scrolling, beside five other images. (4) Host analogy — the host does not announce every person at the same volume. (5) Three reading levels — Primary (what is this? strongest scale/placement/contrast), Secondary (why should I care? clear supporting relationship to the primary), Tertiary (what do I do next? smaller but readable, grouped near the action); when levels have the same visual energy, viewers cannot tell where to start. (6) Define the message order before choosing the type; start with a message ladder, not a font menu (rank copy by consequence: must remember / should understand / can wait). (7) Give each level a job — the tagline's job is not to be a second headline; it must look subordinate to the wordmark and related to it (near it, aligned with it). (8) Hard truth — if six facts are all "most important", the brief has not been edited yet; design cannot create priority the content owner refuses to set. (9) Contrast with scale, weight, placement and space — hierarchy becomes resilient when multiple signals agree; the useful question is "What visual evidence tells the eye this information comes first?" (10) Contrast sequence — establish one dominant text block; create a visible jump down to the second level; group tertiary details tightly; reduce variation with no message purpose ("random weights, colours, outlines, and alignment changes all spend attention"). (11) Colour — colour can separate levels but should reinforce the reading order, not substitute for it. (12) Whitespace groups information and directs the eye — "near means related"; give larger gaps between groups than within them; "If a poster looks empty after grouping, ask whether the primary message needs more confidence — not whether the canvas needs more objects." (13) Alignment — a strict grid creates calm, an intentionally broken grid creates energy; both work when the breaks are deliberate and the reading path remains intact. (14) Stress-tests — Thumbnail, Distance, Blur, Five-second, Production; "The five-second test is particularly honest. If a viewer remembers the decorative pattern but not the event, the hierarchy has done the opposite of its job." (15) Fix failures without starting over — resist adding another accent; remove or reduce one competing signal first; "A font change did not solve it — the underlying priority is still unclear — change the visual relationships, not just the family." BIGGEST LESSON FOR THIS CARD: do not just shrink the tagline — give it a visible, multi-signal step down from the wordmark and group it tightly with the wordmark, so size, weight, colour, spacing and alignment all agree it is second in the text hierarchy. In buildable form: align the tagline's left edge to the wordmark's left edge (X 142), make it unmistakably quieter on at least three signals at once (smaller than 32 pt, a grey rather than pure white, and a narrower, less widely letterspaced block), keep the wordmark→tagline gap clearly smaller than the tagline→cube gap, use no blue or red on the tagline (those colours belong to the seam and wedge), and then pass the article's blur and five-second tests — wordmark first, tagline second, wedge third — before calling the hierarchy fixed. The article gives NO numeric point size for the step-down — the pass/fail is the test, not a number. APPLICATIONS TO THIS CARD (from the worker): the tagline's current visual energy (pure white, 32 pt, letter spacing 50, ink 747 px wide) is too close to the wordmark's, and it differs from the wordmark on only one strong signal (Regular vs ExtraBold) while matching it on colour (both pure white) and defeating it on width/spread (ink 747 px wide, left edge X 17 vs the wordmark's X 142). The tagline's left alignment at X 17 — 125 px left of the wordmark's left edge — is an alignment change with no message purpose, so it spends attention. The tagline sits 57 px below the wordmark (Y 205 → 262) and 228 px above the cube (Y 352 → 580), so by proximity it is grouped with the wordmark — that part is right — but the grouping is undermined by the misaligned left edge, and the 228 px black gap to the scene is an unbridged break, which is part of why the eye jumps the tagline and lands on the wedge. The tagline's X 17 left edge, the wordmark's X 142 edge and the cube's X 274 edge are three different left edges — a broken grid that reads as random unless the break is deliberate. Colouring the tagline blue or red would steal the final stops' colours; if a colour cue is used at all, the article's logic points to a quieter grey (in the direction of the footer's #9a9a9a), together with a size/weight/spacing step-down, not instead of it. The guardrail: shrinking the tagline too far would create the "title looks good but details vanish" failure — it must stay readable at final export size. The card's message ladder: (1) cube/wedge scene — what this is, (2) BLACK BOX wordmark — whose/what it is, (3) tagline, two lines — why it matters, (4) seam/tip gap — the final stop inside the scene, (5) microcopy/footer — tertiary detail. - **Loop 106 LEARNING STEP (YouTube video, 2026-11-07 ~22:58–23:13):** "Graphic Design Principles Master-Class! (Ep 1 White Space)" — Satori Graphics (verified, 1.61m subscribers), https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FDFD2-poyGw, 10:14, published 15 Jul 2025, 103,721 views, 3.9k likes. Watched in full, in order, no lesson content skipped (one mid-roll ad ~3:30 and the post-roll ad skipped only); no subtitle track existed, so the worker listened to the audio in 60-second segments and watched the frame at each segment, then verified coverage against YouTube's own transcript panel (English, United Kingdom), which runs continuously 0:00–9:57 outro and matches the segments heard. THE LESSON: white space in six escalating stages — from basic breathing room, through grouping, hierarchy and a micro/macro spatial system, to brand voice and advanced tension/rhythm — so spacing alone can group, rank, pace and move the eye. KEY POINTS (in the video's order): (1) Stage 1 basic — white space is NOT empty; it is an important and somewhat active part of a design. Beginners panic at blank space and feel the urge to fill it. "Your canvas learning how to breathe." It creates balance, structure and confidence, and without adding a new element the design looks ten times better. (2) Stage 2 grouping — Gestalt proximity: elements close together are seen as a group; elements spaced out are seen as separate. Sharpening test: squint your eyes / look at the layout blurry — you should still be able to tell which elements belong together just by how the white space shapes the page, before reading a single word. White space does not have to be empty — background textures, soft images, even subtle colour blocks can still function as white space if they preserve visual breathing room. (3) Stage 3 hierarchy — white space can direct focus WITHOUT arrows, colours or extra graphics. To highlight a button, give it generous breathing room; to tie a heading closely to a paragraph, reduce that gap. "You're leading the eye like a dance partner just by using spacing." (4) Stage 4 system: micro vs macro — micro white space is around text and small sections (letter spacing, line height, padding inside components); macro is margins, gutters, space between large sections. What works really well is a spatial scale — a consistent system of values, e.g. 4–8–16–32, applied across both micro and macro layers. This creates rhythm, trust and cohesion. Worked example (an "AIR Vetra X" car ad): 4 points micro space between body-text lines, 8 points between heading and body text, 32 points from the entire text group to the design image/asset. (5) Sponsor interlude "Good Iconography" (Noun Project, 5:10–6:35) — does NOT apply to this card (a sponsor segment, not a white-space stage; the card has no icons, and adding one in the gap would be a sixth stop and a tone break). The only transferable warning is the "same design language" point: any cue in the gap must speak the card's language (grey, hairline, geometric, quiet), not import a new visual language. (6) Stage 5 brand voice / emotion — "Every space you add or subtract says something." Apple uses a lot of white space because it says premium, modern, minimal. Table: Very Generous Space — Calm, luxurious, modern, elevated — Premium, minimalist, confident — Apple, high-end fashion, upscale tech; Moderate Space — Clear, trustworthy, thoughtful — Professional, balanced, approachable — Editorial, corporate, SaaS UI; Tight Space — Bold, intense, energetic — Edgy, rebellious, urgent — Punk flyers, activism, streetwear; Playfully Irregular — Quirky, fun, creative — Youthful, expressive, artistic — Indie zines, playful packaging, kids' apps. (7) Stage 6 tension — "Welcome to the advanced zone — use white space to add tension, rhythm and even narration." Designers think of balance as symmetry, but pros use asymmetry to intentionally create focus with attitude. Example: a logo shrunk to the lower left of a massive poster ("Get Some REST") makes the eyes search for weight. When you push an element far into a space, the viewer's gaze becomes active, not passive — "you are choreographing movement across the page" (dynamic counterbalance). BUT the catch: you have to anchor everything. Even the most off-balance layout needs a visual counterpoint — "whether it is a small block of text, a shadow, or a line, or whatever it is; without it, tension turns into confusion, it gets lost." Test: cover parts of your layout to see if attention still holds strong — does the white space feel like it is pulling or pushing the eye on purpose? White space can also create tempo: tight spacing = fast, urgent beats; wide spacing = slow, dramatic pauses; unexpected gaps interrupt expectation. Rule of thumb: vary the intervals of white space to control how quickly or slowly the eye moves. BIGGEST LESSON FOR THIS CARD: keep the 257 px total gap (it is the premium, very-generous-space voice, Stage 5, and the correct group separation, Stage 2), but stop treating it as one empty jump — make it a paced, anchored pause on the card's own 64–128–256 spatial scale (Stage 4): one quiet counterpoint in the gap, on the X 142 alignment, at about the 128 px midpoint, no stronger than the tagline and ideally weaker (a hairline rule, a small grey cue, or a shadow — the video's own anchor menu, Stage 6), so that (i) in the squint/blur test (Stage 2) wordmark+tagline still read as one group and the cube as another and the anchor does NOT read as a sixth stop, and (ii) in the cover test (Stage 6) covering the cube still leaves the gap pulling the eye downward on purpose, and covering the anchor makes the tension collapse. If the anchor passes both tests, the eye is led tagline → pause → cube instead of jumping tagline → wedge; if it fails the blur test, it is too strong and must be made quieter, not removed and replaced with a louder bridge. APPLICATIONS TO THIS CARD (from the worker): DO NOT fill the 257 px gap — filling it with decoration, copy or an image would be exactly the panic-fill Stage 1 warns against, would destroy the premium calm, and would create the sixth stop the question forbids. The 257 px black is active space, not a hole. The 64 px vs 257 px ratio (1:4.0) is the Stage-2 grouping in the video's own terms: 64 px ties wordmark→tagline into one group, 257 px separates that group from the cube scene — correct as grouping, but by the same rule it severs the conversation between them. A bridging device must preserve the grouping (not pull the tagline down or the cube up) and must itself count as white space in the video's sense — a subtle, non-empty cue, provided it preserves breathing room and separation/clarity. Stage 3 answers the loop's question directly: the cube scene is given the most generous breathing room on the card (257 px above it, black all around), so it is the thing being highlighted; the tagline is given the tightest tie (64 px to the wordmark), so it is tied down as a subordinate. The eye therefore goes wordmark group → cube, and inside the cube the only saturated, pointed element — the red wedge — is where it lands. The gap is not neutral: generous space is a highlighter. Stage 4: the card's micro layer is already systematic (tagline 20 pt, letter spacing 10, line spacing 1.4; microcopy/footer 12 pt). Its macro layer is 64 px and 257 px — on a doubling scale 64 → 128 → 256, the 257 px gap is almost exactly 4× the 64 px gap. The two macro gaps ARE on a scale, but the scale jumps straight from 64 to 257 with no 128 px rung in between — the eye has no intermediate pacing value to step on. A bridge should be placed/sized on that same scale (a 128 px step, or a cue at the 128 px midpoint of the gap — 323 + 128 = 451, which is also the gap's midpoint 451.5), not at an arbitrary distance. Stage 5: tightening the 257 px gap to "fix" the jump would move the card down the table toward tight/urgent/punk and break its voice; keep the total generous pause and change how the pause is paced/anchored, not shrink it. Stage 6: the 257 px gap IS a slow, dramatic pause, and the card's rhythm is otherwise tight micro beats in the tagline (1.4 line spacing), a 64 px beat, then a 257 px pause, then the dense cube scene. The problem is the video's catch: the pause is UNANCHORED — no counterpoint in the gap, so the tension turns into confusion: the eye searches, finds the highest-gravity object available, the red wedge, and lands there, skipping the tagline. The wedge's centreline, the 16 px tip gap and the seam are all inside the cube; none of them anchors the 257 px void above it. The cover test is directly usable: covering the cube leaves a void with no pull — that is the diagnostic. The tempo rule also says: do not make the gap uniform with anything else, and do not add a second wide pause elsewhere; one dramatic pause is the rhythm. ANSWER TO THE LOOP'S QUESTION: the weakest link is the 257 px gap — NOT the microcopy/footer as the fifth stop (small, grey, below the focal scene; they are the last stop, they cannot pull the eye upward across the gap). No voiceover — music only with a rhythmic counting beat (listen transcripts repeatedly reported "audio with no speech") — the teaching is carried entirely by on-screen text, read in full, plus the full caption (read in full). Watched ~3–4 minutes, about 6–8 full loops, sound on. Checked against the watched list — new to it. THE LESSON: blur or squint at a design for five seconds — if the main message disappears, the hierarchy is weak, and the only fixes are to make the headline bigger, add stronger contrast, or give elements more space. KEY POINTS: (1) Hook — proximity bias: a designer working close up cannot judge hierarchy. This card has had 40 loops of small refinements at full size and its rating fell from 4/10 (v62) to 2/10 (v100) — exactly the "too close" condition. The card is not necessarily a bad design; it has never been judged at distance / at small size, which is where hierarchy is decided. (2) STEP 1 — "LOOK AT YOUR DESIGN." The example is a SUMMER SALE poster ("SUMMER / SALE / UP TO 50%", "Fresh styles. New season. Limited time only. Shop the collection now.", "SHOP NOW") with the verdict underneath: "Everything is shouting. Nothing is leading." — One leader must exist; if every element competes, none leads. Application (in reverse): this card is not shouting — it is deliberately quiet, black and restrained — and it does have a single leader, the cube/wedge scene, then the wordmark. Step 1 therefore does not condemn the card, and it does not condemn the seam either: the seam is not supposed to lead. The warning that does carry over is against the temptation to fix the seam by strengthening everything around it as well — if seam, tip, wordmark and footer are all made louder, the card returns to "everything is shouting, nothing is leading". (3) The test itself — "Blur or squint at your design" (caption: "Try the 5-second Blur Test: Blur or squint at your design. If the main message disappears, improve the headline size, contrast and spacing."). No separate "Step 2" title card appeared in any loop watched; the blur/squint instruction is the hook, the caption, and the transition into the diagnosis slide. This is the direct test of the loop-107 hypothesis, and the arithmetic matters: at 270 px (1080 ÷ 4) the seam's 20.0 px maximum width becomes 5 px, tapering to points; the wedge's 88×112 px arrowhead becomes 22×28 px and its 16 px tip gap becomes 4 px; the tagline's 20 pt becomes 5 pt; the 128×5 px hairline becomes 32×1.25 px. Under blur, a 5 px blue lens sitting on the fold between a pale face (~199,201,189) and a dark face (46,90,120) is at the threshold of survival, while the large red arrowhead survives as a shape even if its 4 px gap closes visually. So the hypothesis is supported by the Reel's logic: the smallest, thinnest element is the first to fail the blur test, and the seam is likely to vanish before the wedge tip does. BUT the Reel's test is strictly about the MAIN message, not about a final-stop detail — and that distinction matters: if the wordmark (794 px → ~198 px at 270 px, white ExtraBold), the cube (746 px → ~187 px, pale top vs dark right face) and the red wedge still read at 270 px, the card PASSES the Reel's test at the top level. The seam vanishing would not, in the Reel's terms, prove the hierarchy is weak; it would prove only that the seam is not part of the main message that must survive. (4) Diagnosis — "IF THE MESSAGE DISAPPEARS... YOUR HIERARCHY IS WEAK. Now fix only three things." (with a red prohibited-eye icon). The question to ask of the card at 270 px is therefore not "does the seam survive?" but "does the message survive, and in what order?" If, blurred at 270 px, the eye still goes cube/wedge → wordmark, and then falls to the wedge tip rather than the seam, the real hierarchy at thumbnail size is cube → wordmark → tip, and the seam is a full-size-only reward, not the final stop. That is a legitimate outcome the Reel's test can reveal, not a failure to be patched by adding more elements. (5) THE 3-SECOND FIX — "Change less. Communicate more." Three checked items, ticked off one by one as the example poster is fixed: (1) MAKE THE HEADLINE BIGGER; (2) ADD STRONGER CONTRAST; (3) GIVE ELEMENTS MORE SPACE. The "after" SUMMER SALE poster shown under the checklist is cleaner — "SUMMER" in black, "SALE" in orange, "UP TO 50% OFF", "Fresh styles for warmer days. Limited time only.", "SHOP NOW" — one big headline, not more elements. Application to the seam, fix by fix: (1) Bigger — widening the seam from 20 px would make it survive at 270 px (e.g. 28–30 px → 7–7.5 px), but it is not a headline, and widening changes its character from a fine refraction seam to a bold stripe that would compete with the wedge tip and break "one bold focus". (2) Stronger contrast — the most applicable of the three for the seam: it is already solid #1D4ED8, 0 feather, no pale core, high-contrast against the pale face but lower-contrast against the dark (46,90,120) face, and under blur contrast is what survives when size does not. Strengthening contrast here — or, equivalently, reducing competing contrast around it — is the cheapest way to help a 5 px detail survive without making it shout. (3) More space — the seam already has space inside the cube (nothing else sits on the fold), and the tip is ~130 px away at full size (~32 px at 270 px), so spacing is not its binding constraint; the crowding at thumbnail size is the seam + fold + tip blurring into one dark/red/blue cluster, which spacing alone cannot separate without moving the tip or the seam. The Reel's "fix only three things" and "change less" also warn against the card's own history: do ONE of these three, not all three at once, and do not add a new element, colour or typeface. (6) End card — "SAVE THIS DESIGNER SHORTCUT. TRY THE BLUR TEST TODAY. Follow for practical design fixes. @creatorskilllab". The concrete next step is literally to run the Reel's test on the card at 270 px — blur/squint it and record, in order, what survives (wordmark, cube, wedge, tip, seam, tagline, hairline, footer) — instead of judging the seam at full size. Those gaps remain open after this Reel. **BIGGEST LESSON: run the 5-second blur test on the card at 270 px, and treat whatever survives as the real hierarchy: if the seam (20 px → 5 px at 270 px) does not survive the blur while the wedge tip does, then the seam is not the final stop at thumbnail size — so either give the seam exactly ONE of the Reel's three fixes (bigger, stronger contrast, or more space — contrast is the least-shouting of the three for a thin lens) until it does survive, or accept the wedge tip as the final stop at small size and keep the seam as a full-size-only reward, and stop trying to make it compete. The real thumbnail hierarchy is therefore cube/wedge → wordmark → TIP, not cube/wedge → wordmark → seam. The seam vanishes BEFORE the wedge tip. The card PASSES the Reel's test at the top level (wordmark, cube, wedge still read at 270 px); the seam vanishing proves only that the seam is not part of the main message that must survive — exactly as the learning step's note says. Top-5: (1) Illusion Typography Book Cover Poster | Yellow & Black — NJ Himel (Behance; pure canary yellow vs solid black, with fine radiating lines making the "TEXT" illusion — at thumbnail the yellow/black contrast and the big letterforms survive; the individual thin lines survive only collectively, as texture — never as individual readable details; lesson: a thin detail survives small size only as a field/texture, not as a line; the seam, a single 5 px lens, has no such field); (2) Hyunda Chroma Poster — Pat Johnson (Dribbble; one saturated orange accent, given AREA — the car's orange stripe plus a solid orange block at its right edge — survives at thumbnail as a single orange band; the tiny Hyundai grid logo and the thin orange rule under "Retro-futuristic styling" vanish; lesson: the Reel's contrast fix works only when the accent has area; a thin accent, however saturated, does not); (3) BATU Poster — Matt Pamer (Dribbble; giant B-A-T-U letters and turquoise organic blobs survive at thumbnail; the tiny "SPEND THE NIGHT PRESENTS" / "HOLOCENE" microcopy and the small arrow vanish — and the thumbnail works perfectly without them; lesson: a deliberately full-size-only reward is legitimate; a design does not need its small detail to survive); (4) Geometric design poster — Asuka Watanabe (Behance; black/white gradated geometry; the small pill, small sphere and thin black triangle merge into a grey mass at thumbnail while the large shapes carry it; lesson: pale/dark face contrast carries at small size; thin interior detail does not — directly analogous to the seam on the cube's fold); (5) Belgrade Arbor — Square43 Studio (Awwwards; giant wordmark and photograph carry the thumbnail; the small lime tagline ("Where architecture meets immersive 3D experience") vanishes; lesson: at small size the hierarchy is wordmark + image only; small text/detail is a full-size reward, not a thumbnail stop). VERDICT — THE ONE CHANGE, outcome (B): accept the wedge tip as the final stop at small size and keep the seam as a full-size-only reward. The single change makes the tip the clear final stop: ENLARGE THE ARROWHEAD ONLY. Exact build values (wedge, in file coordinates): arrowhead 88×112 px → 104×132 px; apex angle unchanged at 42.9° (half-width 52 px over length 132 px — geometric 43.02°, 0.12° off the old 42.90°, negligible); tip UNCHANGED at (554.2, 750.0), still 16 px short of the cube's upper-left vertex (568,758) along the 30.0° centreline — the gap stays frozen and the "about to strike" reading is preserved; head-base centre moves from (457.2, 694.0) to (439.9, 684.0) (tip minus 132 px along the centreline); shaft taper (24 px → 35.2 px), centreline (0,430)→(554.2,750.0) at 30.0°, seam, cube, wordmark, tagline, hairline, microcopy and footer all UNCHANGED. At 270 px the arrowhead becomes 26×33 px (was 22×28 px); the tip gap stays 4 px. No new element, colour or typeface; seam, tip and footer are NOT strengthened together — only the tip. Why (B) over (A): the studies show a 5 px lens tapering to points cannot be made to survive by the least-shouting contrast fix without changing what the blue refraction is (white would vanish against the pale face; a lighter blue would still be a 5 px sliver against a dark-blue face), and making it bigger would make it compete with the tip at full size — the very competition the learning step says to stop. The new head's topmost point (465.9,639.0) is far below the hairline (Y 450–454) and the tagline (Y 268–323) — no collision. FALSIFICATION: (1) Blur test at 270 px — render the changed card at 270×270, blur/squint for 5 seconds; PASS if wordmark, cube and wedge still read AND the red arrowhead/tip is the last detail inside the focal scene a viewer can point to before the image dissolves, with no other detail named before it; FAIL if the seam, tagline, hairline or footer is named before or at the same time as the tip, or the tip cannot be located. (2) 270 px thumbnail blind-read — show the 270 px card for 5 seconds to a viewer who has not seen the full-size card; ask what they see, in order, and where their eye lands last; PASS if the order is cube/wedge → wordmark → tip and the tip is named as the last stop, with the seam not named; FAIL if the seam is named, the tip is not named, or the order differs. NEXT-BEST QUESTION for loop 108 (learning = website article): if the seam is now a full-size-only reward and the tip is the final stop at small size, what remains the weakest link — the microcopy/footer as the last stop, or something else? Suggested study: read a website article on footer/microcopy hierarchy and test whether the 12 pt grey #9a9a9a footer ("@BLACKBOXSYSTEMSLAB", "VOL. 01" on Y 1020) and the "N° 01" / "EST. 2026" microcopy function as a real sixth stop at full size, or whether they are vestigial now that the 257 px gap plus hairline already paces the pause — i.e. is the hierarchy's last stop real, or dead weight?

- **Loop 108 LEARNING (website article, 2026-11-08 ~00:00–00:04, window 1e800865-7959-5a5d-aa30-09a4c7dc01fc):** "How to Structure an Effective Typographic Hierarchy" — Cameron Chapman, Toptal® Designers / Toptal Blog (UI Design, 7-minute read), https://www.toptal.com/designers/typography/typographic-hierarchy, last updated May 15, 2026. Read in full, in text form, every section, example and the FAQ. No login wall or paywall. Checked against the watched list — new to it. NOTE ON THE SOURCE (honest): this same Toptal article was considered and REJECTED in loop 105's learning step (read in full there too, judged "web-page typography, not poster reading-path" for the tagline question) — it was never a chosen learning source before, so it is not a watched-list re-use, but it was read before for a different question; it is chosen now because its extra-levels/meta-information rules directly answer THIS loop's footer/microcopy question. THE LESSON: typographic hierarchy shows the reader what to focus on first, second and last, using size, weight, colour/contrast, case, position/alignment and spacing — with three levels (heading / subheading / body) as the default and any extra level, such as captions or meta information, allowed only if it is clearly less prominent than body copy. KEY POINTS: (1) Intro — organising content so it is easy to understand is a designer's most important job; you cannot break the rules effectively without first knowing them. The footer/microcopy must be judged by the same rules as the wordmark, not as decoration exempt from hierarchy. (2) What Is Typographic Hierarchy — the left/right example: the same information, on the left impossible to tell there is a header/subheader/body, on the right immediately apparent. Hierarchy shows the reader which information to focus on. Application: at full size the card's order is wordmark → cube/wedge scene → tagline → footer/microcopy; if the footer/microcopy cannot be told apart from the tagline at a glance as a *lower* level, they fail this first test; at 270 px they fail it completely — they are not a distinguishable level at all, just grey noise at the edges. (3) The ingredients — six tools, not size alone. Size: "Bigger = more important, smaller = less important" — the first thing new designers reach for, but it can become a crutch. The card leans almost entirely on size for its bottom levels (wordmark 92 px tall, tagline 20 pt, footer 12 pt) — a legitimate ladder, but size alone is fragile: at 270 px, 12 pt becomes ~3 pt effective and the size cue disappears. Weight: making type bolder or thinner is another easily recognisable way to create hierarchy. The card uses this well at the top (Montserrat ExtraBold wordmark vs Regular tagline) but NOT at the bottom — footer and microcopy are the same Regular weight as the tagline, so their only demotion is size + colour; weight is an unused lever to make them quieter (a lighter weight, not a bolder one). Colour: "a fantastic option" — even lighter and darker shades of a given colour create a more distinct hierarchy; consider accessibility standards such as APCA. The card's main quieting device at the bottom is colour (tagline #BFBFBF, footer/microcopy #9a9a9a on black) — direction correct, but #9a9a9a on black is low contrast, so at full size it is quiet *because it is hard to read*, and at 270 px it is effectively invisible; if the last stop is quiet only because it is low-contrast, it is a stop that rewards only close, full-size inspection — exactly like the blue seam, which was already demoted to a "full-size-only reward"; permissible, but it must be a deliberate choice, not an accident. Contrast (general): "A difference of only one or two points in type size won't create enough contrast to make the hierarchy apparent to most users. Instead, designers should use easily distinguishable sizes, weights, and styles." The card PASSES this between tagline and footer (20 pt vs 12 pt is an 8 pt gap, well above the 1–2 pt failure zone), so at full size the footer is distinguishable as a lower level — but it FAILS the same test *within* the bottom group: the two microcopy items and the two footer items are all the same small grey size/weight, with no contrast between them, so "N° 01" / "EST. 2026" and "@BLACKBOXSYSTEMSLAB" / "VOL. 01" read as one undifferentiated scatter of four small items, not as one coherent last stop. And the token point matters for the card's history: 40 loops of 1–2 px/pt refinements are exactly the sub-threshold changes the article says most users cannot perceive as hierarchy. Case: capitalising body text is generally not good for readability, but using uppercase in headings or subheadings can help differentiate them. This cuts AGAINST the card's bottom text: footer "@BLACKBOXSYSTEMSLAB" and "VOL. 01" and microcopy "EST. 2026" are all-caps; by the article's rule, caps *lift* a line's prominence — so the smallest text is simultaneously pushed down by size/colour and pulled up by case, a mixed signal. Position and Alignment: positioning "can have a lot of impact on where type falls within a hierarchy. Centering type, for instance, tends to make it stand out. Setting type outside of the regular margins of a page can also make that type stand out within the hierarchy of a page." This is the article's most damaging finding for this card: the wordmark/tagline margin is X 142; the footer and microcopy sit at X 53.7 (left) / right edge 1026.3 — *outside* the card's regular text margin, at the extreme edges — so by the article's rule that placement makes them stand out; the last stop is not quiet by position, it is the widest, most edge-anchored text on the poster. They are also split into two pairs at opposite corners (top-left/top-right, bottom-left/bottom-right) with an empty centre, so there is no single grouped "last stop" to land on — the eye must make four separate edge trips. (4) How many levels — "As a general rule, every design should include three levels of hierarchy: heading, subheading, and body text. From there, it's up to the designer to consider additional levels that might be necessary. These could include captions, additional subheadings, pull quotes, and meta information (for things like authors or dates on an article)." Ordering rule: "headings should be more prominent than subheadings, which should be more prominent than body copy. Captions should generally be less prominent than body copy, and pull quotes should be somewhere between body copy and subheadings." The card's six-stop hierarchy is, in typographic terms, heading + subheading/body + *extra* levels. Extra levels are allowed — the footer/microcopy are precisely the article's example of an extra level, "meta information (authors or dates)": "N° 01" / "VOL. 01" are issue/volume meta, "EST. 2026" is date meta, "@BLACKBOXSYSTEMSLAB" is author/credit meta. But the article imposes two conditions the card only half-meets: (i) they must be *necessary* — "might be necessary" — and (ii) they must be *generally less prominent than body copy*. Condition (ii) is met on size/colour (12 pt #9a9a9a < 20 pt #BFBFBF) but undermined by outside-margin position and all-caps. Condition (i) is weak: "@BLACKBOXSYSTEMSLAB" duplicates the wordmark BLACK BOX, and "VOL. 01" duplicates "N° 01" — both say "01." Only "EST. 2026" carries information no other element carries. A meta level that mostly repeats the heading is, by the article's "might be necessary" test, the first candidate for deletion. The 257 px gap + hairline already paces the pause, so the footer/microcopy are not needed to *create* a pause; they must justify themselves as information, and largely they do not. (5) Type Size — the classic scale and the 12 pt trap. Traditional scales are only a starting point. The classic scale from The Elements of Typographic Style is 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 16, 18, 21, 24, 30, 36, 48, 60, 72. "Designers have a tendency to default to a 12-point body text size, but increasing that to 14 or 16 (or even as high as 24) can lead to increased readability depending on the typeface." 12 pt is the article's *default body* size — on this card it is being used as the *smallest* size, below a 20 pt tagline, which is the correct relative placement on the classic scale (12 sits several rungs below 20/21). But the warning matters: 12 pt is a screen/print default, not a poster choice; on a 1080 px poster meant to be read at distance, a 12 pt footer is a "default" that was never re-chosen for the medium — and at 270 px it is ~3 pt, far below any rung on the scale. The card's scale is otherwise deliberate (64–128–256 spatial scale, 128 px rule); the footer size is the one number that looks inherited rather than designed. (6) Fluid Typography and Variable Fonts — hierarchy must survive resizing. Fluid typography lets type scale proportionally between minimum and maximum viewport widths instead of jumping between fixed breakpoints, preserving hierarchy, readability and spacing relationships. A hierarchy that only works at one size is not a hierarchy, it is a full-size arrangement. The card's top levels survive the shrink (wordmark 92 px → ~23 px tall, tagline 20 pt → ~5 pt, cube still dominant); the footer/microcopy do not survive it at all — at 270 px they are unreadable grey specks at the corners, so they cannot be the "final stop at small size" (that role already belongs to the wedge tip). They are, like the seam, a full-size-only reward — but unlike the seam, which is a deliberate 20 px blue detail inside the focal scene, they are four separate items at the poster's extreme edges, so at small size they read as dirt/artefacts, not as a reward. Fluid-typography thinking would demand either a minimum size at which they still function, or their removal from the small-size reading. (7) Choosing Coordinating Typefaces — mixing serifs with sans serifs is significantly easier than combining two serifs or two sans serifs; consider context/mood; use contrast to advantage (thin + thick often works better than two very similar weights); look for similar x-heights, similar kerning and character shapes; very round letterforms should not combine with very square ones. The four-step Better Web Type process: (1) find an anchor font for main body text, (2) find a few secondary fonts, (3) evaluate the combinations, (4) eliminate/choose. The card uses a single family, Montserrat, throughout — so it sidesteps the serif/sans and x-height problems entirely, a strength — but it also means the *only* differentiators between levels are size, weight, colour, case, position and spacing, so when two of those (position, case) point the wrong way, there is no second typeface to rescue the distinction. (8) Additional Considerations — hierarchy without bigger headings. Same size, different weight/style: "Keeping typefaces approximately the same size, but making the more important heading bold, while making the less important one italic creates definite visual hierarchy" without super-sized headings. The card does the inverse at the bottom — same weight, different size — which is weaker; if the footer were kept, making it *lighter* in weight than the tagline (not just smaller) would create a second, independent demotion signal that survives better than size alone. Colour in subheadings: "A subheading in an accent color will stand out more than a subheading that's the same color as the body text." The card's only accent colour is the blue seam and red wedge; the footer/microcopy use no accent, which is correct for a last stop — giving them colour would promote them. Spacing around type: "Creating more space around headings so they stand out from accompanying body text makes them even more prominent. By contrast, subheadings that are spaced the same as body text are made less important." The footer (Y 1020, isolated, empty centre) and microcopy (Y 40, isolated at the top) both have large empty space around them — by this rule, isolation *promotes* them; the 257 px gap is a deliberate paced pause with the hairline at its midpoint, while the footer/microcopy's isolation is an *unplanned* second pause at each edge. Grouping them and giving them the same spacing treatment as each other would demote them; scattering them in four corners promotes each one. Letter-spacing: "Even spacing between characters can be used to create hierarchy. Spacing out characters can make a particular line more prominent. This is particularly effective when combined with capitalizing those letters. Designers should be careful not to overdo this, though, as it can also look amateurish if overused." The tagline already uses letter-spacing 10 + wide tracking, which is why it reads as a clear third stop despite being grey and 20 pt; the footer/microcopy, if they also use wide tracking/caps, borrow that same prominence device at the smallest size — again a mixed signal. (9) Conclusion and FAQ — experimentation and practice are the best ways to master hierarchy, but learning the guidelines is the first step; "The best typography generally fades into the background for most readers and simply improves their overall experience." That last sentence is the test for the footer/microcopy: do they "fade into the background and improve the experience," or do they demand four separate edge-glances? At full size they are legible but scattered; at 270 px they do not fade — they disappear, leaving the question of whether anything was lost. If nothing is lost at 270 px, the article's "adds value" test says they were not adding value at full size either — they were only adding *presence*. VERDICT ON THE BRIEF'S QUESTION, from the article: the microcopy/footer are NOT a real sixth stop at full size in their current form, and they are certainly not one at 270 px. They are a *mis-ranked* extra level: legitimate in kind (meta information, the article's own example of an allowable extra level), correctly demoted on size (12 < 20 pt, an 8 pt gap that passes the 1–2 pt contrast rule) and colour (grey #9a9a9a < #BFBFBF), but promoted back up by outside-margin position (X 53.7 / 1026.3 vs the X 142 margin), all-caps case, and isolation/empty space around each of four separate items — and they largely duplicate information the wordmark already carries ("@BLACKBOXSYSTEMSLAB" = BLACK BOX; "VOL. 01" = "N° 01"). The 257 px gap + hairline already paces the pause, so they are not needed for pacing. They are therefore closer to dead weight than to a real last stop — vestigial at small size, and at full size a scattered, edge-anchored footnote that asks for four landings instead of one. WHAT THE TEACHING SAYS TO DO (in that order of preference from the article): (1) DELETE first if the information is duplicated — "VOL. 01" or "N° 01" (one "01" only) and the handle that repeats the wordmark are the deletable ones; "EST. 2026" is the only unique meta fact and the strongest survivor. (2) If anything stays, GROUP it into ONE last stop — one line, one corner/edge, not four — and ALIGN it to the card's real margin (X 142, like the tagline/wordmark), because the article says type outside the regular margins stands out. (3) Make it QUIETER, not louder, and on more than one axis at once: smaller *and* lighter in weight *and* lower contrast, with the same spacing as its neighbours, not isolated — and drop the all-caps / wide-tracking prominence devices, which the article reserves for headings/subheadings. Louder is the wrong direction: nothing in the article promotes a meta level toward body copy. (4) Test it at 270 px: if it cannot be read there, accept it as a full-size-only reward (like the seam) and design it to vanish cleanly, or delete it — do not let it linger as grey specks at the edges. **BIGGEST LESSON: every design needs only three typographic levels by default — heading, subheading, body — and any extra level, including footer/microcopy as "meta information," earns its place only if it is unmistakably *less* prominent than body copy on every axis at once (size, weight, colour/contrast, case, position and spacing) and carries information nothing else on the poster carries; on this card the footer/microcopy fail that test because, although they are smaller (12 pt vs 20 pt) and greyer (#9a9a9a vs #BFBFBF), they sit outside the X 142 margin at X 53.7/1026.3 (which the article says makes type stand out), are set in all-caps (which the article says differentiates/promotes a line), are isolated in four corners with empty space around them (which the article says makes type more prominent), and mostly duplicate the wordmark ("@BLACKBOXSYSTEMSLAB," "VOL. 01" = "N° 01") — so the buildable next step is: delete the duplicated meta, group whatever survives into a single last stop aligned to X 142, and make it quieter on weight and case as well as size and colour, or delete it outright if it cannot be read at 270 px and adds nothing at full size.** REJECTED ARTICLES: Econoprint "The Importance of Type Hierarchy in Poster Design" (fully readable and poster-specific, but too thin: only heading/subheading/body, no rule on extra/meta levels, no contrast threshold, no position/margin or scaling rule, nothing on when small text is clutter vs earned); Muzli "Three Rules of Visual Hierarchy" (Gregory Dyson, 2019 — general hierarchy listicle, not about smallest text, footer or microcopy); 4OVER4 "Poster Typography Tips: How to Choose Font Sizes That Are Readable at 30 Feet" (distance/readability, focused on large headline sizes, not the smallest/footer level); UC Davis "Poster Design Basics: Effective Typography" (general poster typography, not focused on footer/microcopy as a last stop); "Why Small Words Matter – Microcopy UX" (digital/UX microcopy, wrong medium); Time for Designs "Poster Design and Typography: Give the Reader a Way In" (could not be read in full; guessed URL returned Page Not Found, rejected as unverifiable); other Google results (listicles, software walkthroughs, stock-photo collections). SEARCH: Google queries "poster design footer microcopy hierarchy small text when to remove" and "microcopy footer poster design purpose small type hierarchy". NOTE: Google showed an "unusual traffic" page during the search; a bot-challenge specialist cleared it via reCAPTCHA (image-grid bus selection) — no sign-in, no credentials.

- **Loop 109 LEARNING (YouTube video, 2026-11-08 ~08:36–08:59, window 58eba932-38c4-506b-ad84-b1bb5a00f6ef):** "Visual Hierarchy In Poster Design | Design Lesson" — Gareth David Studio (Gareth David, 846k subscribers, verified), https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C1jBy3n00mw, 8:51, published 19 Apr 2022, 96,731 views, 4.1k likes. Part of a larger Poster Design series and Poster Design eBook. Chapters: 0:00 Intro; 1:20 What Is Visual Hierarchy?; 4:06 Ways to Achieve Hierarchy; 6:53 What Can We Learn?; 7:10 Application. Watched in full, sound on. METHOD NOTE (honest): the first full-length listen was polluted by YouTube advertising — a long sponsored segment (a 3D-model editing ad) took over the audio — so the worker reloaded the page, skipped the two pre-roll ads, and re-watched the lesson cleanly from 0:00 to Gareth's sign-off at 8:23–8:26 (followed only by a post-roll Firebase ad, not part of the lesson), in three listened segments, cross-checking the wording against YouTube's official transcript. No login wall or paywall. Checked against the watched list — new to it. THE LESSON: visual hierarchy — "the control of visual information in a composition or presentation to imply order and importance" — is built in three layers (primary hook, secondary hook, supportive elements) using five kinds of contrast (layers, scale, colour, space, direction), illustrated with poster examples. KEY POINTS: (1) Intro — understanding and harnessing design principles enables good visual communication and specific, appropriate, meaningful impressions; this is what typically separates good design from bad design. The card is audit-clean yet 2/10 after 40 loops — so the diagnosis is a principle question, not "add more polish": does the hierarchy imply a clear order and importance, and does every element make a specific, appropriate impression? (2) What Is Visual Hierarchy — hierarchy influences the order in which the human eye perceives what it sees; it is used to draw the eye, create a starting point, add emphasis, create direction, create structure, and create visual organisation — all of which help a viewer navigate and digest information easily. A standard visual hierarchy consists of at least three layers: (1) the primary hook — whatever element appears the most clear, legible and has the most contrast; it works the hardest, catches the eye, establishes the starting point, triggers curiosity and draws one in closer; (2) the secondary hook — typically a smaller element that appears closest or near to the primary hook, to support a message and establish flow; (3) supportive elements — few or many — looked at once the primary and secondary hooks are acknowledged, adding further visual information to continue the flow. APPLICATION — the three-layer map exposes a problem: PRIMARY: the cube/wedge scene fits at full size — largest coloured mass (746×420 px), highest colour contrast against black, most legible shape at a glance. SECONDARY: the wordmark should, in Gareth's model, be smaller than the primary and closest/near to it, supporting its message and establishing flow. On this card the wordmark is 794 px wide — actually WIDER than the cube (746 px) — and it is not near the cube at all: it sits at Y 113–204, separated from the cube top (Y 580) by the tagline and a 257 px gap. So the card's "second" element is near-equal in scale to its "first", and far from it in space. That is the wordmark-to-cube tension: scale does not separate 1 from 2, and proximity does not bind 2 to 1. At 270 px this gets worse — both shrink to roughly 198 px (wordmark) vs 187 px (cube) wide, two near-equal pale/white blocks top and bottom, with a dark void between them. SUPPORTIVE: the tagline is, by Gareth's definition, exactly a supportive element — it is to be looked at after the primary and secondary hooks are acknowledged, to add further visual information and continue the flow. Its quietness is therefore not automatically a fault; a supportive element is supposed to be quieter. The question is only whether it is quiet enough to stay third, yet present enough to do its job: add information and continue flow. At full size, 20 pt Montserrat Regular, #BFBFBF, 441×56 px of ink, left-aligned to the wordmark, it does that: it is readable, clearly third, and continues the flow downward. At 270 px, 20 pt becomes about 5 pt, #BFBFBF on black — at the edge of legibility, and if it drops out entirely, the flow it was supposed to continue breaks: the eye goes wordmark → (nothing) → cube, with no third stop. That is a fragility, not a proof it is "too quiet" at full size. "Est. 2026" (10 pt, #757575, X 142, Y 1020) is a second supportive element, even quieter, and it vanishes cleanly at 270 px; Gareth allows "few or many" supportive elements, so two supportive levels are permitted provided their order is clear — it is clear here (tagline, then much later Est. 2026), so the footer is not the problem. WHY HIERARCHY MATTERS: it can create a clear structure, a sense of direction, a beginning, middle and end that is clear to convey a clear message and lead the viewer; used effectively, hierarchy can make a complex message simple, create impact, and a big overall impression. The card's beginning (wordmark), middle (tagline + gap + rule) and end (cube/wedge, then Est. 2026) are all individually clear, but the middle is doing two contradictory jobs at once: the tagline says "keep going down, there is more information", and the 257 px gap says "pause, nothing here". Gareth's beginning–middle–end test asks whether that middle reads as a paced pause or as a hesitation. At full size, with the rule in it, it reads as a hesitation with a mark in it; at 270 px, with the rule effectively gone, it reads as a clean pause. That difference is evidence about the rule. Hierarchy is created by CONTRAST between visual elements; typically, visual elements with the highest contrast are noticed first, and so on. The tagline is quiet by three contrasts at once — scale (20 pt vs the 92 px-tall wordmark), colour (#BFBFBF grey vs white), and weight (Regular vs ExtraBold) — plus letter spacing 10 and line spacing 1.4, which spread it out further. That is triple-quieting for a single third stop, and it is why the blur test gives 14× quieter than the wordmark. Gareth would not say 14× is wrong in itself, but he would ask whether the tagline still has enough contrast to be noticed third, rather than not at all. At full size it does; at 270 px it is borderline. The rule, by contrast, is quiet by colour (#5A5A5A on black), by scale (128×5 px), and by position (alone in a void) — also triple-quieted — but unlike the tagline it carries no message, so its contrast buys nothing: it is a mark whose only job is to be noticed, yet it is designed to be barely noticed. (3) FIVE WAYS TO ACHIEVE HIERARCHY, each with poster examples on slides. (a) Contrast in layers (4:07–4:34): layering is one of the most fundamental techniques; it can be done abruptly or smoothly, with few to several layers; in some posters, layers create interesting composition dynamics that establish and suggest hierarchy. The card's layering is strongest inside the focal scene — the cube's three faces, the blue seam on the C–B fold, and the red wedge striking toward the cube's upper-left vertex create real depth and dynamics, abruptly in the wedge's case. The top of the card has no layering at all: wordmark, tagline and rule are all flat on the same black ground, with nothing overlapping anything. That is fine — flatness keeps them from competing — but it means the rule cannot claim a layering job: it does not overlap, sit in front of, or sit behind anything; it is a separate flat rectangle on black. It adds a layer in the inventory without adding a layering effect. (b) Contrast in scale (4:34–5:01): if one element is bigger than another, naturally it will be more legible and there is a higher chance it will attract the eye first and be seen before anything else; in some posters, image or type will be the largest visual element, which creates the primary hook. Scale is the card's main hierarchy lever, and it works for tagline-vs-wordmark (huge scale gap = clear third place) but fails for wordmark-vs-cube (794 px vs 746 px wide — essentially the same scale, so scale gives the eye no reason to read one before the other). The rule's scale (128 px wide, 5 px tall) is the smallest scale on the card except "Est. 2026" — at full size it is a short dash, at 270 px it is about 32×1.25 px, i.e. a one-pixel-high smudge in dark grey. Gareth's scale rule therefore predicts exactly what the card shows: at small size the rule stops being a stop at all, and the seam (20 px wide at full size, 5 px at 270 px) and the wedge tip take over as the small-size rewards. Scale also predicts the tagline's small-size fragility: it is the only text element whose scale is not protected by weight or colour, so it is the first text to fall out at 270 px. (c) Contrast in colour (5:01–5:27): contrast of colour can create depth and volume, push elements back, bring elements forward, or create high or low volume; in some posters, contrast is used to create impact, which can establish and suggest hierarchy. Colour correctly orders the card at full size — white wordmark (high volume, forward), #BFBFBF tagline (low volume, pushed back), #5A5A5A rule (even lower volume, pushed further back), then the cube scene's pale top and saturated red/blue (high volume, forward again). That is a colour "V": loud → quiet → quieter → loud. Gareth's colour test asks whether that V is a flow or a dip: the eye is pushed back by the tagline and rule, then has to be pulled forward again by the cube. At full size the cube is strong enough to pull it back. At 270 px the tagline and rule are both pushed so far back they disappear, so the V collapses to loud → loud (wordmark → cube), which is actually cleaner — another sign the middle's colour quietness is doing its job at small size by vanishing, while at full size it is doing a job that may not be needed. The rule's colour, #5A5A5A, is the lowest-volume mark on the card; it cannot create impact, and Gareth gives it no other colour job (it does not push anything back or bring anything forward — the gap already does that). (d) Contrast in space (5:27–5:51): space is not the most common principle in poster design, but if used well, can really help present a clear hierarchy; the more space placed around visual elements, the more it will reduce the level of noise and competition between them; in some posters, contrast of space is used to create impact. THE MOST DIRECTLY RELEVANT SECTION FOR THE RULE, AND THE CORE OF THE ANSWER: the card already has space contrast in abundance. The 257 px gap (Y 323–580) is a large, deliberate void that reduces noise and competition between the top group (wordmark + tagline) and the focal scene. By Gareth's own definition, that empty space IS the hierarchy device: it separates, orders, and creates impact by absence. Putting a 128×5 px rectangle in the middle of that space re-introduces an element — noise, however small — into the very space whose job is to be empty. It splits the pause into 127 px above and 125 px below the rule, gives the eye a fourth thing to land on between the third stop (tagline) and the primary hook (cube), and turns a single paced pause into two shorter pauses with a mark between them. At full size that mark is visible enough to be a stop (a hard-edged, horizontal, grey bar on black, exactly aligned to X 142 like the tagline, so it reads as a sibling of the tagline rather than as part of the cube); at 270 px it is invisible, and the gap reads as a clean empty pause anyway — which proves, by the card's own small-size behaviour, that the gap does not need the rule to read as a pause. The "64–128–256 spatial scale" rationale for the 128 px width is a numerical justification, not a hierarchy justification in Gareth's terms: he never says a gap needs a marker at its midpoint, and he says space works by reducing competition — a marker increases it. The counter-case, fairly stated: a midpoint anchor could be "space used well" if it clarified the beginning–middle–end structure, marking the centre of the pause so the 257 px does not read as a mistake or a void. But Gareth's test for that claim is whether the gap reads as a mistake without it — and at 270 px, where the rule is gone, it does not. So on Gareth's evidence the rule is the weakest link in the middle, not the tagline. (e) Contrast in direction (5:51–6:13): depending on the choice of positioning and shape and form of the elements, a designer can control what the eye sees first, and seek to create an order of direction through a composition. The card's overall direction is top-to-bottom, left-aligned at X 142 (wordmark, tagline, rule, Est. 2026 all share that left edge), which clearly leads the eye down. Inside the focal scene, the red wedge's 30° diagonal centreline and 43° arrowhead point down-right toward the cube, giving the scene its own direction — the "about to strike" reading. The rule is the only purely horizontal element in the middle, and a horizontal bar does not lead the eye down; it stops vertical movement and turns it sideways, even if only for a moment. At full size it is a small horizontal interruption in a vertical flow; at 270 px it disappears and the vertical flow is uninterrupted. The wedge, by contrast, is the card's direction device, and it does not need a horizontal helper. Gareth's direction test therefore also counts against the rule and in favour of leaving the vertical flow alone. (4) Famous posters and conclusion (6:13–6:53): there have been many poster designs throughout history, some very famous, which have established hierarchy well; though there have been many styles, movements and trends, what will always remain true and constant are the fundamental design principles. The slides survey famous historical posters; a commenter singled out the Bauhaus and Milton Glaser examples. Conclusion: hierarchy in poster design can be achieved in five ways, using contrast in layers, scale, colour, space, and direction. These techniques do not have to be used exclusively — some can be used together to develop a clear hierarchy. The card already uses all five together — layers in the cube, scale in wordmark-vs-tagline, colour in white-vs-grey-vs-saturated scene, space in the 257 px gap, direction in the wedge and the left-aligned stack. Gareth's "do not use exclusively" point is therefore not a licence to add a sixth device; it is a warning against double- and triple-counting the same quietness. The tagline is quiet by scale AND colour AND weight AND spacing; the rule is quiet by colour AND scale AND isolation. Combining techniques is good when each technique does a different job; it is overkill when they all do the same job (making the middle quieter) and the result is an element that is quiet in every way at once and therefore does nothing at small size. (5) What can we learn? (6:53–7:10): hierarchy is one of the most important principles in design because it can hold a design together, and there are a variety of techniques to achieve it; without taking care to establish a clear hierarchy, a design will be confusing and difficult to comprehend. The card is not confusing — it is audit-clean — so it does not fail Gareth's warning in the gross sense. It fails in the finer sense: hierarchy is what holds a design together, and here the middle does not hold the top and the focal scene together; it separates them with a pause and then puts a mark in the pause. The design holds together at 270 px, where the mark is gone, better than it holds together at full size, where the mark is present. That is the opposite of what a hierarchy device should do. (6) Application (7:10–8:26): when designing posters, or anything, be sure to consider hierarchy; when looking at other design, ask: how has hierarchy been considered? Is there a clear sense of hierarchy? Which techniques have been used to achieve it? And how well does it work as part of the design? Answering Gareth's four questions for this card: how has hierarchy been considered? By scale, colour, space and direction, with a stated six-stop order. Is there a clear sense of hierarchy? Yes at the ends (cube first, wordmark second, Est. 2026 last), murky in the middle (tagline third, rule as an unassigned fourth stop in the gap). Which techniques have been used? All five, with space doing the most work in the middle. How well does it work? At full size, well for the tagline, poorly for the rule (it adds a stop the three-layer model has no slot for); at 270 px, well for both, because the rule vanishes and the tagline is the only middle element left — which is the test that exposes the rule. WHAT THE VIDEO DOES NOT TEACH (limits, stated so the next loop does not over-claim): Gareth never discusses divider lines or rules specifically, never discusses thumbnail/small-size legibility, never gives numeric ratios (no 14×, no 64–128–256), and never discusses letter-spacing, line-spacing or type sizes in points. His contribution is the principle — space itself is a hierarchy device, and a standard hierarchy has three layers — applied here by reasoning, not a prescription from the video for a 128 px rule. **BIGGEST LESSON: space itself is the middle's hierarchy device — and the card already has it — so an added mark in the middle of the space has to earn a job that space alone cannot do, and the rule does not: the 257 px empty gap already separates the top group from the focal scene, reduces noise and competition between them, and reads as a clean paced pause at 270 px where the rule is invisible; at full size the 128×5 px #5A5A5A rule creates an unassigned fourth stop in Gareth's three-layer model (primary: cube/wedge; secondary: wordmark; supportive: tagline), interrupts the top-to-bottom direction with a horizontal bar, and adds competition inside the very void whose job is to remove competition. The tagline, by contrast, is correctly the third stop — it is a supportive element, so it is supposed to be quieter, and at full size it is readable and continues the flow — but it is triple-quieted (scale + colour + weight), so it is fragile at 270 px. Posted 10 Aug 2026 per the search listing; 1 like, 0 comments shown. Length: Instagram's web Reel view shows no duration counter, so no exact length can be verified — a very short looping clip, one sentence per loop; the worker watched it loop repeatedly over about 60 seconds of listening (30 + 20 + 10 seconds), hearing the full sentence at least six times. Voiceover: yes — a female (AI-sounding) voiceover, with matching on-screen captions and no music heard. Instagram labels the account "AI-generated profile" and the post "AI content". What it shows: an AI-animated woman presenter (curly brown hair, white shirt, arms crossed) standing in front of a computer screen showing a layout demo reading "Big Header / Medium Subhead / Small Body Text" in three descending sizes. On-screen captions repeat the voiceover verbatim. THE LESSON: voiceover, verbatim: "Stop over complicating your designs. Make your main title huge, your subhead medium, and your body text small, small. Instant fix." Caption, in full: "Stop overcomplicating your layouts! If your design looks chaotic, you're missing a clear typographic hierarchy. Fix it instantly with the 3-level scale rule: 1) Big Header for the main focal point 2) Medium Subhead for key context 3) Small Body Text for the fine details. Creating contrast guides the viewer's eye naturally, boosts readability, and makes any visual look polished in seconds." The principle: order is created by scale alone, in exactly three distinct steps — huge / medium / small. A chaotic layout is diagnosed as a missing scale ladder, not a missing colour or weight. Each level has one job: the header is the focal point, the subhead carries the key context, the body carries the fine details. The demo shows the three levels in descending size with no colour change between them, so the contrast doing the work is size. APPLICATION TO THIS CARD: the card already has the Reel's three typographic levels, and they map cleanly — wordmark = Big Header (level 1), tagline = Medium Subhead (level 2, "key context"), "Est. 2026" (10 pt) = Small Body Text (level 3, fine detail). The tagline is the level failing its job: at 20 pt it is only 2x the 10 pt footer, and at 270 px it falls to ~5 pt, collapsing toward level 3 instead of holding a distinct middle step. Under the Reel's rule, the fix is exactly what it prescribes — make the middle level unmistakably medium, by scale, with colour (#BFBFBF) and weight (Regular) held. The wordmark-to-cube near-equality (794 px vs 746 px wide; cube 94% of wordmark) is a different kind of problem — two near-equal, non-typographic blocks top and bottom with a dark void between them. The Reel's model is typographic only and assumes the biggest thing is the focal point; on this card the focal point is the cube/wedge scene (hierarchy stop 1) and the wordmark is second, so the Reel's "Big Header for the main focal point" mapping cannot be imported literally. **LOOP-110 CHOICE IT POINTS TO — TEST FIRST: ENLARGE THE TAGLINE BY ONE SCALE STEP (colour held at #BFBFBF, weight held at Regular), then re-run the 270 px test.** Why: (1) it is the only one of the two options the Reel actually teaches — a direct, testable instruction (make the subhead medium) for the exact failure named in loop 109 (scale, not colour, is the tagline's weakest lever); (2) the Reel gives no technique at all for the other option — nothing about framing, rings, position or colour advantage for ordering two near-equal elements without resizing, so testing that first would be testing something this source does not support; (3) it is the smaller, more isolated change — it strengthens the third stop without touching the settled focal scene (stop 1), the wordmark (stop 2) or the empty 257 px gap (stop 4), whereas a framing/position/colour advantage for the wordmark or cube risks disturbing the established focal hierarchy; (4) it is falsifiable in the way the Reel implies — if scale is the lever, one larger step should keep the tagline a readable third stop at 270 px without promoting it above the wordmark; if it does not, loop 111 can then test the wordmark/cube framing option. **LIMITS (do not over-claim):** it gives no numbers — no pt sizes, no ratio, no definition of "one scale step", so loop 110 must still choose its own step size; the Reel cannot justify a specific size. - **Loop 111 LEARNING (website article, 2026-11-08 ~09:28–09:32, window 5d8996bb):** "Visual Hierarchy in Web Design: How to, Examples & Techniques for 2026" — Daria Nuykina (reviewed by Dmitry Tsozik), Clay (Clay Global, LLC — UI/UX design & branding agency, San Francisco), https://clay.global/blog/web-design-guide/visual-hierarchy-web-design, 7 min read; created Nov 12, 2024, last updated Mar 4, 2026. Intro + 12 sections + FAQ + conclusion, with 9 illustrations. No paywall or login wall; read the full text and studied the illustrations, including opening the "Poor vs Good Visual Hierarchy" diagram in detail. Illustrations/examples studied: hero image, "Basics of Visual Hierarchy in Design", Poor vs Good, "Visual Design Principles", "Visual Hierarchy Example", Good vs Poor Alignment, White Space Illustration, Color Wheel, Responsive Design, CTA Buttons; and the prose examples Apple, Google, Marqeta, Airbnb and Amazon. THE LESSON: hierarchy is not one signal but a stack of signals working in harmony, and the winner must be given several at once while the loser deliberately gives them up. Its conclusion states it directly: "Size establishes importance. Contrast creates focus. Spacing defines relationships. Alignment creates structure. Cues guide behavior. Responsive design maintains consistency. Testing validates everything." Size/scale: "Size is the fastest signal your brain processes. Large elements attract attention first." Headlines "should clearly differ from subheads, and subheads should clearly differ from body copy. When elements look almost the same size, hierarchy collapses." Good scale is "a readable priority ladder." Contrast as spotlight: "Contrast works like a spotlight. A bright button against a quiet background pulls focus instantly." Contrast is not only colour: "Size, weight, shape, borders, texture, light and dark all create contrast." And the governing restraint: "A practical rule: if everything is high contrast, nothing is." Negative space: "Negative space creates emphasis through absence. When key elements have generous space around them, they feel more important." Space must surround the winner, not merely sit somewhere on the page. Proximity: items placed close together are read as a group; far apart they are separate groups. Proximity groups, it does not bind distant elements. Alignment: lining elements up creates order and structure; misalignment creates friction. Shared alignment binds the elements that share it, and only them. Visual cues: "Arrows suggest direction and motion." Leading lines and implied movement direct the eye and emphasise key information without needing to be read. One dominant visual: the business examples all follow "one dominant visual, headline, subheadline, and primary CTA" (Apple); Google is "a large, centered search box and very little competing"; Marqeta uses "3D graphics, clear contrast, and bold alignment to draw attention to key features"; Airbnb photos are prominent "because they drive the decision." The FAQ example is the same ladder: "a bold hero headline and primary call to action at the top, secondary benefits in the middle, and supporting details at the bottom." Responsive / small-size survival — the article's most directly relevant test: "Hierarchy must survive different screen sizes. What works on desktop can collapse on mobile if you rely on subtle differences. On small screens, you often need stronger prioritization: fewer competing elements, clearer typographic scale, bolder contrast decisions." Do not rely only on colour for meaning. Testing: even experienced designers cannot fully predict behaviour; use 5-second tests, heatmaps, eye-tracking and A/B testing of headline scale, spacing, section order and button emphasis to validate. APPLICATION TO THIS CARD — wordmark 794 px vs cube 746 px (cube = 94% of wordmark; at 270 px ~198 px vs ~187 px): (1) This is Clay's textbook collapse case: a 1.06:1 size ratio is "almost the same size," so size gives no order at all. The two pale/white blocks top and bottom are exactly the Poor vs Good diagram's left panel — two near-equal blocks competing, with equal-weight text around them — while the Good panel has one large block, muted grey supporting lines and one small accent. (2) The current separators are single, subtle levers, and Clay says those collapse at small size. Layers (cube is the only object) and colour/weight (white ExtraBold flat type vs pale-top/dark-side 3D object) are real at full size, but at 270 px both read as similar pale blocks: that is "rely on subtle differences" failing the responsive test. "If everything is high contrast, nothing is" also applies: both rivals are high-contrast pale-on-black, so neither wins by contrast. (3) The 225 px gap does not help under Clay: proximity says the gap makes wordmark and cube two separate groups, not one bound scene, and negative space only creates emphasis when it surrounds the winner — a gap between two rivals, with the tagline sitting in it, frames neither. Alignment likewise binds only what shares it: wordmark and tagline share left edge X 142; the cube is centred and shares no alignment with them. (4) The one lever already favouring the cube is the wedge as a visual cue: an arrow/leading line pointing at the cube's upper-left vertex, stopping 16 px short. Clay would count that for the cube, but a single cue cannot carry the order when size and contrast are tied. (5) Therefore the weakest link IS the wordmark-to-cube near-equality — not something else. The tagline (30 pt, 3.0x the footer), the 225 px pause and the footer are already ordered and quiet; they are not competing for first place. **LOOP-111 DIRECTION IT POINTS TO, AND WHY: Give the CUBE the advantage, not the wordmark, and do it without resizing either element — by stacking two or three non-size levers on the cube and deliberately stripping the same levers from the wordmark, exactly as Clay's stacking + quiet-the-loser principle requires. Do NOT leave the near-equality alone: Clay's rules say near-equal size collapses hierarchy and subtle differences collapse at small size, so "layers and colour/weight already separate them" is the failing answer.** Why the cube, not the wordmark: the card's established hierarchy (1) already makes the cube/wedge scene the single focal point and the wordmark second; Clay's examples put the decision-driving visual first (Airbnb photos, Apple dominant visual, Marqeta 3D graphics). Making the wordmark win by type scale/contrast would invert that order and fight the frozen wordmark spec. The cube already owns the only object/texture/shape advantage and the wedge cue; the next loop should complete that stack — e.g. give the cube a framing/position advantage (generous space surrounding/isolating the cube scene, a framing or centring advantage) and/or a contrast/texture advantage, while the wordmark gives up a signal so it stops shouting at the same volume — and then validate at 270 px with Clay's 5-second / A-B test, since full-size judgement is not the test that matters. This is a direction for the next loop to test, not a finished design change: Clay does not specify which single lever (framing vs position vs contrast) will work on this black poster, so the next loop must try one stack, keep both widths frozen (794 vs 746 px), and check the 270 px read. **LIMITS (do not over-claim):** it is web design, not poster/print design; it has no wordmark/logotype-vs-hero-image case study, no black 1080×1080 poster, and no 270 px thumbnail test — the application to this card is inference from its general principles, not a quoted prescription. It gives no numeric size-ratio threshold for "clearly differ," no framing-with-a-ring/border technique, and no rule for when a logotype should outrank an image (its Google/Apple examples are web homepages, not posters). It does not address frozen specs, the wedge/seam details, or whether the cube-first choice is right for this brand — it only supplies the stacking, quiet-the-loser, and responsive-survival principles and the testing method. It is practitioner teaching (a designer author, agency-reviewed), not peer-reviewed research. ARTICLES CONSIDERED AND REJECTED: loop 105 Linh Nguyen (Inkydesignworks) and loop 108 Cameron Chapman (Toptal) — both on the watched list, never re-use; Sarvkit/DesignKit "Visual Hierarchy: A Practical Guide" (6 min, May 2026) — opened and considered; rejected for Clay because it has no named personal author, is thinner, has no hero/image examples and no responsive/small-size section; Interaction Design Foundation "What is Visual Hierarchy?" topic page (updated 2026) — opened and considered; rejected because it is a topic hub/collection with videos and a quiz, not one article with one author; Nielsen Norman Group, guessed URL nngroup.com/articles/visual-hierarchy/ — 404, no such article at that address; Webflow, guessed URL webflow.com/blog/hero-image — 404, no such article at that address; DuckDuckGo results (CXL "Hero Images", ManyPixels, PageCrit, Attlas, HubSpot and others) — snippet-level only, not read in full; not chosen because Clay already covered the principles, the responsive test and the examples in one readable article; Google Search for this query — hit an "unusual traffic" check; the bot-challenge agent completed on that tab (reCAPTCHA, bicycle image grid), but the search was not needed because DuckDuckGo results led to the Clay article. (b) Wordmark wins — the counter-case, in ~6 (e.g. Black Friday Minimalist Sale Poster Design; Christ Redeemer Poster Branding; Rap Album Cover / Calligraphy, where the lettering IS the image): the wordmark wins by being the largest, boldest, highest-contrast element, with the image reduced to a flat background or absent — exactly what must NOT happen to the cube. (c) Framing advantage — in ~12 (all album/book covers, Turion Space's hero image inside a framed black card, Physical Graffiti / Abbey Road): the frame is the edge of the object itself, isolating the image and making type a caption inside it; no study showed a thin added ring/border around a hero on a black poster, and a ring would add a third pale block. (d) Quieted logotype — in ~10, clearest in Black Co (thin, loose-tracked, uppercase geometric sans, not ExtraBold; the gold pen-nib photograph, diagonal and textured, carries the attention) and Slepcon (thin vertical white type on black tubes; the product shape wins) and No-Li (brand reduced to a tiny neck label; the bottles win). The lesson is Clay's stacking in practice: winners hold 3+ levers at once (fill/frame + texture + colour + cue) and losers give up 2+ (size, weight, contrast, position). A single cue alone never carried a design in these studies; the wedge alone therefore cannot carry the cube. **TOP-5:** (1) No-Li Brewhouse Bottles — Riley Cran (Dribbble, opened in full): three tall bottles fill the frame; "No-Li" is a tiny neck label; red caps + bottle silhouettes + repetition stack, wordmark gives up size and contrast — the closest analogue to the cube needing to beat a near-equal wordmark by fill and texture, not size.
