(3) Turion Space — WILD (Awwwards, opened in full): hero image (rock/space) sits inside a framed black card, headline overlaid on the image rather than rivalling it from above; framing + isolation + texture let the image win while type becomes part of it. (4) Slepcon Skincare - Minimal Black Packaging Design — Ajith Anil (Dribbble, search-result card): black tubes dominate; the wordmark is thin, vertical, small — a product shape beating a wordmark on black by texture/position while the logotype is deliberately quieted. (5) Abbey Road Redesign Album Cover (mock brief) — Clare Jane Christina Comber (Dribbble, search-result card): the ultimate quieting — the crossing photograph fills the square and there is no band name on the front at all; framing + fill + photographic texture win outright, showing how far "give the levers up" can go. **THE ONE CHANGE:** (i) Quiet the wordmark, by rebuilding its image file only: take the existing kerned wordmark image (Montserrat ExtraBold, white) and rebuild it as an identical raster file with every white ink pixel set to #8C8C8C (RGB 140,140,140; ~55% brightness), preserving alpha/transparency, kerning, and exact pixel bounds — ink X 143–936 (794 px wide), Y 113–204 (92 px high), 142 px margins each side, B and X fully visible, nothing cropped, no resize. Nothing else changes: cube stays 746×420 at (274,580), tagline, 225 px gap, seam, wedge (tip frozen 16 px short of (568,758)), and "Est. 2026" untouched; no new typeface, no new element. Why this grey: #8C8C8C is ~6.5:1 contrast on black (still clearly legible at full size, AA for large text), far above the footer #757575, and far below the cube top #F5F5F5 — so at 270 px the wordmark reads as a mid-grey block, not a second pale block, while at full size its size (794 px) and ExtraBold weight keep it clearly second. This one file rebuild delivers two Clay levers at once (contrast given up + perceived weight/thinness at small size) without resizing either rival. (iii) Strengthen the wedge — a single cue cannot carry the order when size and contrast are tied (Clay, and the studies); thickening it risks the wedge competing with the cube itself, and the tip/head geometry is frozen in spirit. (iv) Framing the cube — strongest general evidence (album/book covers), but it would be a NEW element, which past loops avoided, and no study showed an added ring on a black poster; a pale frame would risk becoming a third pale rival block at 270 px. **FALSIFICATION TESTS:** Full-size 5-second test — show the card for 5 seconds at 1080×1080, then ask what was seen first; PASS if the cube/wedge scene is named first and the wordmark second, with the wordmark still readable; FAIL if the wordmark is named first or equal, or the wordmark is unreadable. 270 px thumbnail test — show at 270×270; PASS if the cube/wedge scene is unmistakably first and the wordmark clearly second, with the two pale blocks no longer reading as equal rivals (wordmark a grey block, cube top near-white); FAIL if the wordmark still reads first or equal, or the wordmark is unreadable, or the cube scene is damaged. - **Loop 112 LEARNING (2026-11-08 ~09:51–10:11, window 552ab8e3, SAVED to SKILL.md + chat MEMORY.md):** YouTube video — "Is Your Logo Unreadable? Fix Scaling & Legibility Issues (EASILY)" — penna.design (420 subscribers), https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Z913JJcgGeY, 14:10, premiered 18 Jul 2022, 1,066 views. Watched in full WITH SOUND (0:00–9:52 first listen, ~10:00–14:10 second listen, to the end, Replay shown), single male presenter with voiceover throughout, screen recording in Adobe Illustrator + small webcam inset, no ads heard in either pass, audio clean. What it shows: a worked review/redesign of a friend Matt's logo ("Matthew James / WEB DEVELOPER", geometric mark) — first on Matt's website, then rebuilt in Illustrator, then compared old vs. new at small size. Chapters: Introduction 0:00, Why this topic? 0:17, Reviewing the logo 1:05, Working with type 3:08, Stacked logo technique 5:50, Adding 'shape' to a logo 7:44, Creating a horizontal logo 8:42, Comparing old vs new 11:22, Outro 13:03. THE LESSON: diagnose at the SMALLEST size the work will actually be used, not at full size — on the website the logo looked fine large, but in the nav bar and especially the footer the thin "WEB DEVELOPER" line was unreadable ("you can't even read the text so it's not worth it being there"). The fix was a set, all tested by zooming out / shrinking (comparison at about 30%): (1) weight must survive shrinking — the original secondary type was far too thin; rebuilt in Lato, primary name in Black, secondary a couple of weights below (SemiBold/Regular; Lato Regular is "not too thin") — weight, not just size, carries legibility. (2) Tracking must survive shrinking — letter-spacing increased (about 160 for the name, 220–240 for "WEB DEVELOPER"), two lines justified to the same width. (3) Consistent spacing, measured not guessed — the height of the "O" taken as a square unit and used for the gaps between text lines and between mark and type, so everything stays its own entity with breathing room when zoomed out. (4) A DIFFERENT VERSION FOR A DIFFERENT SLOT — the core technique: a stacked logo (mark above text) wastes the nav bar's horizontal space and forces the type too small, so he made a horizontal version (mark left, type right) for the nav, which allows bigger type; and for the footer, where even that would be too small, he dropped the text entirely and used the icon alone. A detail that cannot be read in a slot is REMOVED from that slot, not forced into it. (5) Optical, not geometric, alignment — when centralising the mark against the type he used the height of the "M" as the reference, because the mark overhangs and geometric centring looked wrong. (6) The pass test is zoom-out — at the end he zooms out / shrinks both versions side by side; the new one is still readable ("if we zoom out we can still see everything"), the old one is "really hard to see" at small size. APPLICATION TO THIS CARD — SEAM vs. WEDGE TIP: LEAVE THE SEAM ALONE as a full-size-only reward. Do not strengthen it (wider, brighter, or a pale core) so it survives at 270 px, and do not remove it at full size. Reasoning: the video's rule is about essential information — what must be read at the small size must be given the weight/size/layout to survive there, and the seam is not that information; the cube/wedge scene already wins at 270 px (mean brightness cube 75.3 > wordmark 68.8 > tagline 29.3), and the wedge tip (a 26×33 px red shape at 270 px) is already the clear final stop at small size, so the seam carries nothing the small-size reading needs. Strengthening the seam to survive 270 px would be the mistake the video warns against — forcing a fine detail into a slot too small for it; at 270 px it would become a second, competing final stop beside the tip, blurring the established hierarchy (tip = final stop; seam = full-size-only reward) and risking a louder blue smudge on the dark face, for no gain in what is actually read at that size. Removing the seam at full size would also misread the video — he never removes fine detail from the large version; he keeps the full, well-spaced large version and creates a different, simpler version for the small slot (horizontal logo; icon-only footer). The card already IS that two-version system in a single file: at full size the seam is a sharp 20.0 px blue lens at (672,835), pointed at C (697,767) and B (647,903); at 270 px it fades to a ~5 px sliver/faint blue smudge and the tip takes over — exactly his versioning logic, applied to one poster instead of two logo files. The video's zoom-out test at about 30% — close to this card's 270 px = 25% of 1080 — is passed by the card on its essentials: cube, wordmark, tagline and tip all still read at 270 px; the seam is not part of "everything" in that test, it is extra. THE ONE TENSION the video leaves open: its preference for a clean drop over a smudged remnant (icon-only footer, not a half-legible line). The seam's faint smudge at 270 px (max B−R 155) is a smudged remnant, not a clean drop — but the card has no separate small-size file in which to drop it, and changing the full-size seam to clean up the 270 px smudge would destroy the full-size reward, so on this video's evidence alone that tension is not a reason to change the seam. LIMITS (do not over-claim): a logo/type case study (one friend's logo, one designer, a small 2022 channel), not a poster, not a colour/refraction study, not a test of blue (#1D4ED8) on a dark face (46,90,120) at 270 px; no quantitative threshold for how wide/bright a detail must be to survive shrinking; it never discusses a detail deliberately only for close/full-size viewing — a reward, an Easter egg, or the BATU precedent from loop 107 — so its "drop it if it can't be read" rule is for essential text in a small slot, not ornamental detail at large size, and it supports the versioning logic but does not by itself prove a full-size-only reward is legitimate; it does not address the 225 px empty gap, the footer "Est. 2026", the wordmark quieting to #8C8C8C, or whether a faint smudge at small size is acceptable versus a clean disappearance. Rejected: Gareth David Studio "Contrast In Layers — Visual Hierarchy In Poster Design" (same creator as loop 109's video; hierarchy, not size-specific detail); Satori Graphics and Collect & Contrast videos (creators already used in loops 106 and 103); Will Paterson "Logo Design | How Small?" (closest alternative, same scaling topic, but far thinner and older, no worked fix or versioning demonstration); Dansky "7 Must-Know Pro Tips for Logo Design" (general logo tips, not scaling/legibility at small size); Colin and Samir / Think Media thumbnail videos (about YouTube click-through and faces/text on thumbnails, not design detail at full vs. small size); "Fine detail only visible up close" search results (unrelated drawing/painting videos, not a design-principle teaching video). **Watched sources (never reuse):** 103 YouTube Collect & Contrast "5 Poster Design Tips…"; 104 IG Reel thecampuscreative "Master Visual Hierarchy"; 105 article Linh Nguyen "Typography Hierarchy Poster…"; 106 YouTube Satori Graphics "White Space"; 107 IG Reel creatorskilllab "YOUR DESIGN ISN'T BAD…"; 108 article Cameron Chapman Toptal "Typographic Hierarchy"; 109 YouTube Gareth David Studio "Visual Hierarchy In Poster Design"; 110 IG Reel visual.shiftt "Stop overcomplicating your layouts!…"; 111 article Daria Nuykina Clay "Visual Hierarchy in Web Design…"; 112 YouTube penna.design "Is Your Logo Unreadable? - **Loop 113 LEARNING (2026-11-08 ~10:23–10:28, window 885c4f01, SAVED to SKILL.md + chat MEMORY.md):** Instagram Reel — "You don't get 3 seconds. You get one." — tylertometich (Tyler Tometich, verified blue tick; no "AI-generated profile" label shown anywhere on the Reel or profile), https://www.instagram.com/reel/Dc6Et2XTJwP/, about 25 seconds looping (Instagram showed no duration counter; length inferred from a 60-second listen with sound on, in which the voiceover restarts at about 0:26 and again at about 0:51). Watched in full WITH SOUND (~2.5 loops), voiceover — the creator speaks on camera throughout, not music-only, no music track evident, audio clean (only his voiceover, no ad or polluted audio, no clean re-watch needed). Engagement shown: 4,933 likes, 113 comments, 23 reposts, 274 shares. What it shows: it opens on sky with the on-screen text "TRY THIS VISUAL HOOK", then a jump-cut effect drops the creator into a grassy field — the jump itself is the demonstrated hook — and he then walks toward the camera, growing larger in frame, gesturing while he speaks. His exact voiceover, heard in full: "That effect was the hook before I said a word. That jump made your eyes follow the movement. Then walking towards the camera kept changing the frame, and add a curiosity hook after it, and the viewer has a bigger reason to keep watching. Save this for your next video shoot and follow me for more hooks you can film without a Hollywood budget." THE LESSON: (1) The hook window is ONE second, not three: "You don't get 3 seconds. You get one." (2) Movement IS the hook — not words, not a title, not a static image. Movement freezes the scroll before a word is spoken; the eye follows motion before it reads anything. (3) The hook must be on screen from frame 1: the jump/effect happens before he says a word. The first frame does the work; nothing later rescues a first frame that does not hold. (4) Sustained change holds attention after the first jolt: walking toward the camera "kept changing the frame" — the frame itself keeps changing, not just an object inside a fixed frame. (5) Sequence, not a single trick: movement hook (second 0–1) → changing frame → a curiosity hook added after it, which gives the viewer a bigger reason to keep watching. (6) Diagnostic: "Not holding attention in the first frame? That's your answer right there." If the first frame fails, the fault is the first frame, not the later content. (7) It is cheap: a jump cut plus walking at the camera, explicitly "without a Hollywood budget" — production scale is not the point; one clear motion in frame 1 is. APPLICATION TO THIS CARD — first-second hook in motion: the cube/wedge scene still wins in the first 1–3 seconds — but ONLY if it is the thing that moves in second 0–1. In the still, the cube is focal #1 (mean brightness 75.3 > wordmark 68.8 at 270 px), but in motion that ranking survives only as motion: the Reel's rule is that the eye locks onto movement before reading a single word, so the wordmark cannot take the hook by being text, however quiet or well-kerned. The wordmark stays second — it is what the eye lands on AFTER the motion freezes the scroll, not what freezes it. The seam: STAY STILL in second 0–1; a single brief glint only afterwards, as the second (curiosity) hook. Reasoning: the seam is a full-size-only detail (20.0 px at full size, a ~5 px sliver/faint smudge at 270 px) — it is too small to freeze a scroll and invisible at thumbnail size, so spending the one second on it wastes the hook on a detail nobody can see. Once the wedge/cube motion has stopped the scroll and the viewer is looking at full size, where the seam exists, one brief glint travelling along it can be the "curiosity hook after it" — the reason to keep watching. Then still again: a continuously shimmering seam would compete with the wedge tip (the final stop) and break the frozen stillness the card's audit-clean state depends on, and at 270 px the glint must not be load-bearing. What the card gains in motion: its frozen tension is already a motion storyboard — the wedge tip stopped 16 px short of the cube's upper-left vertex (568,758) is a strike about to happen, and the 225 px empty gap is a stage the wedge can travel across or the cube can arrive through. What it loses if animated wrongly: if everything moves at once (wordmark sliding, tagline fading, cube turning, seam shimmering), the hierarchy collapses — the Reel teaches ONE movement in frame 1, then a changing frame, not many simultaneous motions. The still hierarchy must become the ORDER in which motion arrives: cube/wedge first, wordmark second, tagline third. Cover/first frame: the first frame must already show the scene in motion — no black lead-in, no wordmark-only title card. A static thumbnail's brightness hierarchy earns a glance; only motion earns the stop. A subtle push-in on the cube/wedge scene after the wedge's first move matches his "walking towards the camera kept changing the frame" beat. DIRECTION IT POINTS TO: define and test the first-second motion for the cover as: (1) the cube/wedge scene is the sole mover in second 0–1 (wedge advancing toward the cube / cube arriving — the "about to strike" gap closing, not closed); (2) the wordmark stays still and second; (3) the seam stays still in second 0–1, with at most one brief full-size glint as the post-hook curiosity beat; (4) frame 1 already shows the scene mid-motion. Why: per the Reel the scroll is frozen by movement before any word is spoken, and the first frame is the diagnostic — if it does not hold, later polish cannot fix it. That also reframes the card's 2/10 rating diagnosis: 40 loops refined a still while the hook is a motion question. LIMITS (do not over-claim): it is one creator's talking-head demo, not a design or motion-poster study — the movement is a person jumping and walking, not a geometric object, and no still poster, cover thumbnail, or graphic focal mass is tested; "one second" is asserted, not measured — no eye-tracking, no data, no A/B of static vs. moving first frame; he replaces the "3 seconds" rule of thumb with another rule of thumb; it says nothing about thumbnail/small-size legibility (the seam's 270 px invisibility is the card's own measurement, not his), nothing about how long a glint should be, and nothing about hierarchy among several moving elements, colour, typography, or a quiet last stop; it does not address sound-off scrolling (his hook is visual, which helps, but muted vs. sound-on is never discussed), nor does it distinguish a cover from a first frame — he treats the first frame as the cover implicitly; it shows NO award-winning Reel covers or motion posters — only his own field demo — so the assignment's question about what award-winning covers show is NOT answered by this Reel; the jump is a cut, not continuous motion, so it does not prove a slow push-in or a glint works the same way as his jump. (3) Marseille (Animated + Poster) — lucas marinm (Dribbble, opened in full): 605 likes on the search card; a Riso-style blue line-city is complete in frame 1; the author says "Had to animate it so it can fit" — the animation is small birds/clouds, not the city. Evidence: a still focal mass survives the first second when motion is small and peripheral. (4) Reel Motion — Bryan Philips (Awwwards, opened in full; Nominee 5 Oct 2026): "Reel Motion turns any workout video into a step-by-step routine"; hero headline is large and static in the centre, wordmark small top-left and still, a dumbbell/triangle/sparkles float at the edges. Evidence: the closest analogue to a Reel cover — headline/product still, peripheral objects move, wordmark does not lead. (5) Aralesk — Collages & Motion — Aralesk (Awwwards, opened in full; Honorable Mention 17 Aug 2026): "Visual art that doesn't sit still. Collages turn into animations, animations turn into garments." Elements: "Curtain reveal & hover video grid", "Falling letters & fabric sheet animation", "Draggable fabric sheets with video reveal". Evidence: the focal collage is revealed, not moved itself; letters/fabric are the secondary, later motion — a reveal + one secondary move, not many simultaneous moves. **ANALYSIS:** (a) What moves in frame 1: in the award-winning / most-appreciated work, ONE element moves, and it is already present and legible in frame 1 — never a blank, a black lead-in, or a whole composition assembling. Don't Waste shows the word DON'T already huge in frame 1; Arcane shows the face/eye already filling the frame; Marseille shows the whole blue line-city already present; Reel Motion shows the headline "Any workout video becomes a routine you can actually follow" already present, with only a floating dumbbell, blue triangle and small sparkles moving peripherally; Aralesk shows the collage face already present, with a curtain reveal and falling letters as secondary motion. (b) Does a still focal mass survive? Yes, when it is the single largest, highest-contrast mass and it is the mover or the thing being revealed — Marseille's city, Arcane's face, Reel Motion's headline-plus-product. It loses ONLY when kinetic type is deliberately made the mass itself, as in Don't Waste and Kinetic Typography Experiments (41 modules, type alone, 7,776 appreciations in the search listing / 84,641 views): then type becomes #1 by being the mass. That is the danger for this card: if the grey Montserrat wordmark were the thing that moved, it would steal the hook from the brighter cube, even though it is #2 in the still. (c) Fine full-size-only details: in NO design opened in full was a fine detail the first move, and none was animated continuously. Marseille's moving birds/clouds are tiny texture after the city; Arcane's eye detail is secondary to the face; Reel Motion's sparkles are tiny, peripheral and brief; Aralesk's thread-ball cursor is a tiny interactive detail, not frame 1; MOTION TYPE's two tiny red squares at the top corners are static. A 20 px seam — ~5 px at 270 px — animated first would be invisible at thumbnail size and would waste the one second, exactly as the assignment hypothesised; a brief glint afterwards is the only form in which a fine detail appears, and it is always once, brief, and peripheral. (d) Hierarchy vs motion order: motion does NOT automatically follow the still hierarchy — the thing that moves first becomes #1, whatever its still rank. The successful designs align the two deliberately: they move the still #1 first, so motion confirms the hierarchy instead of overturning it. The learning's "still hierarchy becomes the order in which motion arrives" is therefore a prescription the best work follows, not a law of vision. Applied here: move the cube/wedge first, wordmark second (only after the scroll is frozen, and in this spec it does not move at all — it is landed on), tagline third. **THE ONE CHANGE: FREEZE THE STILL, ADD THIS MOTION SPEC (no pixel of the v111 still changes).** Freeze: wordmark (Montserrat ExtraBold #8C8C8C, ink X 143–936, Y 113–204), tagline (Montserrat Regular 30 pt, #BFBFBF, box X 142 Y 262 W 720, ink X 142–803 Y 272–355), 225 px empty gap Y 355–580, cube (746×420 at 274,580; top #F5F5F5 with 10 px white stroke, front-left ~(199,201,189), right (46,90,120)), seam (solid #1D4ED8, 20.0 px max at (672,835), points at C (697,767) and B (647,903), 0 px feather, no pale core), wedge (#C32D30, centreline (0,430)→(554.2,750.0) at 30.0°, taper 24 px → 35.2 px, arrowhead 104×132 px, apex 43.0°, tip at (554.2,750.0), 16 px short of cube vertex (568,758)), and footer "Est. 2026" (Montserrat Regular 10 pt #757575, X 142 Y 1020, ink X 144–200 Y 1024–1032) all remain exactly as v111. Reason for a freeze, not a still change: in every top design the still/thumbnail is the complete final composition; a mid-flight still would read as unfinished at 270 px and would destroy the frozen "about to strike" 16 px gap and the wedge-tip final stop. MOTION SPEC, 5 seconds, 1080×1080, no sound, no black lead-in, no fade-in, no wordmark-only card: Frame 1 (t=0.0 s) already shows the complete cube, wordmark, tagline and footer, the seam solid #1D4ED8, and the wedge MID-FLIGHT — its tip at (398.3,660.0), i.e. 180 px back along the 30° centreline from its final tip, the whole wedge translated −155.9 px in X and −90.0 px in Y from its final position, with no rotation, no scale change and no fade. 0.0–0.9 s: ONLY the wedge translates along its centreline, +155.9 px X / +90.0 px Y, ease-out, to its exact final position, tip (554.2,750.0), 16 px short of (568,758). At 0.9 s it stops dead and holds. 0.9–2.0 s: everything still. 2.0–2.6 s, ONCE only: a single glint travels along the seam centreline from C (697,767) to B (647,903) — a 30 px-long, 6 px-wide segment, #FFFFFF at 0.85 opacity, moving C→B in 0.6 s — then the seam returns to solid #1D4ED8, 20.0 px, no core, no feather, and stays still to 5.0 s. WHAT MUST NOT MOVE: wordmark, tagline, cube, gap, footer at any time; the seam except for that one 0.6 s glint; the wedge after 0.9 s, and it must never rotate, scale, fade, overshoot (554.2,750.0), or touch the cube — the 16 px gap is preserved at rest. No other element moves, glints or shimmers at any time. GEOMETRY CHECK BY MAIN MUSE: the 180 px move back along the 30° centreline gives ΔX = 180×cos(30°) = 155.9 px and ΔY = 180×sin(30°) = 90.0 px, and the mid-flight tip (554.2−155.9, 750.0−90.0) = (398.3,660.0) exactly as specified; the 270 px wedge travel is 180/4 = 45 px as stated. **FALSIFICATION TESTS:** Full-size 5-second test — play the 1080×1080 cover 0–5 s and freeze at 0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.3 and 5.0 s. PASS only if: at 0.0 s the cube is complete and the wedge tip is at (398,660) ±10 px; at 0.5 s the tip has moved forward along the 30° line and the cube/wordmark/tagline are pixel-identical to the still; at 1.0 s the tip is at (554.2,750.0) ±2 px and the 16 px gap to (568,758) is intact; at 2.3 s a white glint is visible on the seam and nowhere else; at 5.0 s the frame is pixel-identical to the v111 still. FAIL if the wordmark, tagline, cube or footer moves at any time, the wedge rotates/scales/fades/overshoots/touches the cube, the seam glints before 2.0 s or more than once, or the first frame is black, blank or wordmark-only. 270 px thumbnail test — scale the same 5 s to 270×270 and play muted while scrolling. PASS only if: at 270 px the wedge's 0–0.9 s travel (45 px on the thumbnail) is visible as a red movement toward the cube, the cube remains the brightest/largest mass, and the seam glint at 2.0–2.6 s is NOT discernible (it must vanish cleanly, as the still seam does). FAIL if at 270 px the first thing seen is the wordmark moving, the wedge travel is invisible, or a blue smear/shimmer is visible continuously. First-frame test — show frame 1 only (t=0.0 s), or read the 1-second description aloud, to a viewer who has not seen the card. PASS only if the first thing they name is the red wedge moving toward / about to strike the glass cube (or "the cube and the red wedge"). FAIL if the first thing named is the wordmark / brand name, the tagline, the blue seam, or "Est. 2026" — that would mean the wordmark or a fine detail took the hook. HONEST NOTE (main Muse): the motion spec is UNTESTED — no video was rendered and no first-frame test was run with a real viewer; the tests above are defined, not run. The freeze of the still is verified (v111 export, sha256 9db0d40f); the motion spec is a specification awaiting a render. **Next-best question for loop 114 (learning = website article):** After the first second is won, what keeps the viewer from scrolling on — a hold, a loop, or a second change — and does a still cover that never moves (in a grid / thumbnail) earn attention the same way? The article should teach: how long a first-frame motion should hold before it loops or stops, whether a loop helps or re-sets the hook, how a cover behaves sound-off and at thumbnail size after motion stops, and what a designer does when the same image must work both as a moving first frame and as a frozen still cover. That is what remains after loop 113: loop 113 settles WHO moves first; loop 114 must settle WHAT HAPPENS AFTER second 1.

- **Loop 114 LEARNING (2026-11-08 ~10:37–10:41, window 157144d8, SAVED to SKILL.md + chat MEMORY.md):** Website article — "How Motion Design Improves Video Retention" — Terra Henderson, terrahenderson.com (Terra Henderson, Motion Partner, Frisco, TX), published and updated March 24, 2026, https://www.terrahenderson.com/blog/motion-design-video-retention. Read in full (main body + all five FAQ answers expanded and read). Different author and site from the watched list (loop 105 Linh Nguyen / Inky Design Works; loop 108 Cameron Chapman / Toptal; loop 111 Daria Nuykina / Clay) — none re-used. THE LESSON: motion is not decoration or prettiness — platforms reward videos that hold attention, measured by click-through rate, audience retention, watch time, engagement, and repeat viewing, and motion directly influences those signals. Her four takeaways: (1) motion improves retention by controlling pacing and visual resets; (2) movement triggers attention and prevents drop-off; (3) consistent motion increases recognition and repeat viewing; (4) systems make retention predictable, not accidental. The exact mechanism for "after the hook": talking-head / static content drifts — "If nothing changes visually, the viewer's brain starts drifting." High-retention editors "look for the moment a viewer might drift and insert something that resets attention" — sometimes a cut or b-roll, sometimes motion. "Motion hits the dopamine loop people are looking for while scrolling. The brain sees movement and reacts instantly. It buys you a few more seconds." Her table maps the parts: thumbnail design systems → click-through rate ("clear visual identity increases the chance someone clicks"); caption emphasis and typography beats → retention; chapter dividers and pacing resets → watch time ("visual resets keep viewers from drifting"); consistent motion branding → repeat viewers ("recognition encourages people to stop scrolling"); end screens and motion CTAs → session time. Her FAQ adds: yes, motion improves retention "by introducing visual changes that reset the viewer's focus… it keeps pacing dynamic and reduces drop-off during key moments"; the most effective motion "supports structure and pacing" (caption emphasis, typography beats, chapter dividers, visual resets); and editing and motion work together — without motion even well-edited video "can feel flat and lose attention." For the still-vs-moving question she teaches two linked points: (a) most creators understand thumbnails affect CTR, but fewer realize motion drives the other metrics — so the still and the moving version do different jobs; (b) in a feed viewers "rarely read usernames. They recognize creators through visual patterns" — faces, color, typography, layout, pacing — and consistent visual language makes content instantly recognizable, which "leads to faster clicks" and compounds over time. She warns that generic motion kills growth (presets, templates, random fonts make content blend into the feed) and that systems beat one-off animations: reusable components — caption presets, hook animations, chapter dividers, thumbnail frameworks, branded motion layouts — make performance predictable instead of accidental. "The real power of motion isn't one great animation. It's consistency." APPLICATION TO THIS CARD — after second 1, and the still cover: (1) HOLD, NOT A LOOP. Do not loop the wedge strike. A loop replays the identical event; Henderson's reset is by definition a NEW visual change inserted where the viewer might drift, not a repeat of the hook. Replaying the strike would also destroy the card's frozen meaning — the tip stopping 16 px short of the vertex (568,758), "about to strike" — and, by her generic-motion warning, a repeated identical motion reads as a preset on repeat, not a distinct visual language. The wedge's motion (0.0–0.9 s, tip 398.3,660 → 554.2,750) is the hook; its job is done at 0.9 s. (2) ONE SECOND CHANGE, ONCE ONLY — the glint. The 0.9–2.0 s still is the drift window: motion has bought "a few more seconds" and the static hierarchy (cube first, wordmark second, tagline third, per loop 111) must do the holding. The single glint at 2.0–2.6 s, C→B along the seam, is exactly Henderson's pacing reset: a different motion, in a different place, smaller (30×6 px, 0.85 opacity), once only, then the seam returns to solid #1D4ED8. It is a chapter-divider / visual-reset beat, not a second strike. (3) THEN HOLD STILL TO 5.0 s. Henderson gives no warrant for a third change in a 5-second piece; after the reset, the still ending lets the viewer read wordmark, tagline and footer without competing motion, and the still ending is the frame that must also serve as the cover. (4) THE FROZEN STILL DOES NOT EARN ATTENTION THE SAME WAY. No: by her metric split, the still in a grid/thumbnail earns attention by recognition and clear visual identity (CTR — "recognition encourages people to stop scrolling"), while the moving version earns it by retention/watch time (the strike, then the reset). Same image, same system, different mechanism. That is why the cover must be the final arrived frame (tip 16 px short, seam solid), not the mid-flight frame 1: in a grid that never moves, a mid-flight wedge promises a strike that never lands, while the arrived frame is the one the still hierarchy was audited on (at 270 px, cube 75.3 > wordmark 68.8 > tagline 29.3). At thumbnail size the card is recognized by pattern — black field, grey wordmark, pale cube, red wedge, blue seam — not by reading the tagline or the footer, which is consistent with the footer vanishing at 270 px. Henderson's "thumbnail frameworks" are listed as a reusable component of the same motion system, alongside hook animations — so the designer does not make a separate thumbnail; the cover is one component of the same visual system. DIRECTION IT POINTS TO: freeze the loop-113 motion spec unchanged — wedge strike 0.0–0.9 s, hold 0.9–2.0 s, one glint reset 2.0–2.6 s, hold still 2.6–5.0 s; do not loop the wedge; use the final arrived frame as the frozen still cover. Reasoning: the strike buys the first seconds, a single different reset re-earns attention at the drift point, and after that stillness is what lets the audited static hierarchy and the cover's recognizability do their work. A loop would re-set the hook in the wrong sense — repeating the same event instead of advancing the pacing — and would unfreeze the card's "about to strike" stop. LIMITS (do not over-claim): (a) it gives no number for how long to hold before a reset, and never discusses looping at all — "don't loop, one reset" is the worker's inference from her reset/system principles, not a direct statement of hers; (b) it says nothing about sound-off viewing, thumbnail-size legibility, poster/cover design, 1080×1080 or 270 px, or a 5-second animation — its context is creator video (talking-head, YouTube/short-form), not a static poster; (c) it cites no research, data, or A/B tests — its metrics table is asserted, and "dopamine loop" is pop-neuroscience, unsourced; (d) it is also a sales page for her Motion Partner subscription, so "systems beat one-offs" serves her offer; (e) it does not address accessibility/reduced-motion, repeat viewing of the same piece, or how to design the still frame itself — that work was loops 105/108/111 (hierarchy), which Henderson assumes already exists. Rejected: Nielsen Norman Group, Aurora Harley, "Animation for Attention and Comprehension" (Sept 21, 2014) — strong on frequency ("nice the first time, but now it's getting annoying") and motion demanding attention, but about web-UI animation, not video retention, resets, thumbnails, or still-vs-motion covers; Brightcove, "Preview before you play: Animated Thumbnails drive faster…" (Oct 29, 2025) — vendor article for Brightcove's animated-thumbnail product, with no teaching on hold/loop/reset timing; Medium, LEDbangers, "The 5-Second Rule: How People Read Screens While You're Still Animating" — could not be read in full; the page presented a Cloudflare "Just a moment" check, so it was not used; Rescroll, "How to Loop Animations That Actually Feel Effortless" — about seamless-loop technique for social/reels, not about whether to loop, how long to hold, or still covers; AudioEye, "Should Designers Hit Pause on Animation?" — about accessibility and pausing animation, not retention after the hook or still-vs-motion covers. **Watched sources (never reuse):** 103 YouTube Collect & Contrast "5 Poster Design Tips…"; 104 IG Reel thecampuscreative "Master Visual Hierarchy"; 105 article Linh Nguyen "Typography Hierarchy Poster…"; 106 YouTube Satori Graphics "White Space"; 107 IG Reel creatorskilllab "YOUR DESIGN ISN'T BAD…"; 108 article Cameron Chapman Toptal "Typographic Hierarchy"; 109 YouTube Gareth David Studio "Visual Hierarchy In Poster Design"; 110 IG Reel visual.shiftt "Stop overcomplicating your layouts!…"; 111 article Daria Nuykina Clay "Visual Hierarchy in Web Design…"; 112 YouTube penna.design "Is Your Logo Unreadable?…"; 113 IG Reel tylertometich "You don't get 3 seconds. You get one."; 114 article Terra Henderson "How Motion Design Improves Video Retention".

(Behance, opened in full; published November 1, 2026; 22 modules): "helio.ai is a brand identity for an AI assistant built around one idea: one sun, many worlds" and "Logo, motion, color and type for a solar-system AI brand", headed "BRAND GUIDELINES · V1.0", "Intelligence, in orbit." Motion is one component alongside logo, colour and type inside one idea/system; the cover frame is a static guidelines cover with the wordmark large and the tagline legible. One idea, repeated — not one animation, repeated. **ANALYSIS:** (a) What happens after the hook: hold on the arrived frame, or a new, different, smaller change — never a replay of the hook. Starling: a series of short, different animations, each ending still. helio.ai and RTP Notícias (on-air identity system): motion as one governed component of a system. The loop studies (Particle Ring, Orbits, Glowing 3D Shapes, 3D Glass Loop, Moonwalk, Daisy, Scooter/Mail Delivery loops) all loop only because their motion is seamless, ambient and meaning-free — a ring, an orbit, a walk cycle — where no single moment means anything. Where a moment means something (a landing in Planes, a reveal, a strike), the work ends on the arrived frame and holds. The best work chooses hold, with at most one new, different, smaller reset. (b) Does a loop help or re-set the hook? No — a loop replays the identical event, so the second viewing is predicted, not a reset. Henderson's reset is by definition a NEW visual change "inserted where the viewer might drift", not a repeat of the hook. Looping the wedge strike would also destroy the card's frozen meaning: tip 16 px short of (568,758), "about to strike", becomes "about to strike, again, forever" — the tension is spent on the first strike, and the wedge must visibly teleport 180 px back along the 30° centreline to (398.3,660.0), which reads as a preset on repeat. At 270 px the replay would re-centre attention on the same motion instead of letting the viewer read wordmark, tagline and footer in the still ending. (c) Cover after motion stops, sound-off, at thumbnail size: every animated cover studied is silent — no sound is mentioned or relied on anywhere (Starling, Dough, Kintsukuroi, Planes are visual-only; the article's own limits note it says nothing about sound-off viewing). At thumbnail size only a bold wordmark plus one high-contrast shape survive: Dough (bold "Dough" + orange + yellow cursor) and Kintsukuroi (bold "kintsukuroi" + black diamond) survive; Planes' pale mid-flight frame does not. For BLACK BOX at 270 px the established order cube 75.3 > wordmark 68.8 > tagline 29.3 and the wedge tip as final stop survive only in the arrived frame. The glint is a full-size-only reset (the seam is a ~5 px sliver at 270 px); at thumbnail size the cover must earn attention by pattern alone. (d) Still cover in a grid by recognition/pattern, not reading: Henderson — viewers "rarely read usernames. They recognize creators through visual patterns" (faces, colour, typography, layout, pacing), and consistent visual language "leads to faster clicks" and compounds. Evidence: Rhox's \WAVES Playlist Overview (163 likes, 49.2k views on the card) and the wider \WAVES / playlist series — same 70s brutalist CD/playlist system across many covers, recognised by system, not by reading each title; helio.ai — "one sun, many worlds", one idea across logo/motion/colour/type; Starling — consistent look/animation across shorts; SHIFTBRAIN's Awwwards profile (opened in full, not counted: 58 works, 19 Site of the Day, 43 Honourable Mentions) — a giant static "SHIFTBRAIN" wordmark above a grid of still thumbnails, each thumbnail recognisable at small size by layout/colour/type. For BLACK BOX the pattern is: black field + mid-grey wordmark at X 142 + pale cube + red wedge + the 16 px gap. That pattern exists only in the arrived frame; the mid-flight frame (tip at (398.3,660.0), 180 px back) breaks it, because the wedge/cube relationship that defines the pattern is not yet there. The final arrived frame is therefore the right cover, not the mid-flight frame. The still and the moving version do different jobs by Henderson's metric split — still earns attention by recognition/CTR in a grid, moving earns it by retention/watch time (strike, then reset) — same image, same system, different mechanism. **THE ONE CHANGE (loop 114) — FREEZE, WITH A COVER-FRAME LOCK.** No pixel, coordinate, size, colour, letter-spacing or timing on the still card changes. The one change is a spec addition to the build sheet: FREEZE the loop-113 motion spec exactly as written: 0.0–0.9 s ONLY the wedge translates along the 30.0° centreline from tip (398.3,660.0) to tip (554.2,750.0), 16 px short of the cube's upper-left vertex (568,758), then stops dead; 0.9–2.0 s everything still; 2.0–2.6 s ONCE ONLY a single white glint (30 px long, 6 px wide, 0.85 opacity) travels C (697,767) → B (647,903) along the seam, then the seam returns to solid #1D4ED8; 2.6–5.0 s everything still. Wordmark, tagline, cube, 225 px gap and "Est. 2026" never move. COVER-FRAME LOCK (the new item): the frozen still / cover / thumbnail in every grid is the frame at t = 5.0 s, which is identical to the arrived frame at t = 0.9–5.0 s: wedge tip (554.2,750.0), seam solid #1D4ED8, maximum width 20.0 px at midpoint (672,835), true points at C (697,767) and B (647,903). The mid-flight frame 1 (tip (398.3,660.0)) is explicitly banned as a cover, thumbnail, poster or grid image in any context. No loop, no second strike, no second glint, no replay. WHAT MUST NOT MOVE / NOT CHANGE: wordmark ink X 143–936, Y 113–204; tagline box X 142, Y 262, W 720, ink X 142–803, Y 272–355; cube (274,580), 746×420; gap Y 355–580 empty black; wedge centreline (0,430)→(554.2,750.0), taper 24 px → 35.2 px, arrowhead 104×132 px, apex 43.0°; seam as above; "Est. 2026" X 142, Y 1020, ink X 144–200, Y 1024–1032, #757575, 10 pt. Reason for freeze, not a pixel change: every pixel change considered (raising wordmark contrast, enlarging the wedge tip, moving the glint) would undo a frozen loop (111's quieting, 112's seam freeze, 113's strike) or invent a timing the article gives no number for; the evidence changes nothing about the motion, and only adds the cover lock the evidence proves is needed. **FALSIFICATION TESTS:** (1) Full-size 5-second test (1080×1080, sound off). Sample frames at 0.0, 0.45, 0.9, 1.5, 2.0, 2.3, 2.6, 3.5 and 5.0 s. PASS only if ALL hold: at 0.0 s tip is at (398.3,660.0) ±1 px; at 0.9 s tip is at (554.2,750.0) ±1 px, 16 px short of (568,758); frame difference 0.9–2.0 s is zero (no pixel changes); 2.0–2.6 s exactly one glint, 30×6 px, 0.85 opacity, moving C→B, and no other element moves; at 2.6 s and 5.0 s the seam is solid #1D4ED8, max width 20.0 px at (672,835), pointed at C and B; frame difference 2.6–5.0 s is zero; wordmark, tagline, cube, gap and footer are pixel-identical at every sample; the wedge never returns to (398.3,660.0) after 0.9 s. FAIL if any movement occurs outside 0.0–0.9 s or 2.0–2.6 s, if there is a second strike or second glint, if the seam is not solid at 5.0 s, or if any other element is displaced ≥1 px. (2) 270 px thumbnail test (arrived frame scaled to 270×270, sound off). PASS only if ALL hold: mean-brightness order is cube > wordmark > tagline (established values 75.3 > 68.8 > 29.3; order must hold, values within ±5); the wedge tip is identifiable as the final stop, 16 px short of the vertex at full size (4 px at 270 px); "Est. 2026" is unreadable and leaves no grey specks; the seam reads at most as a faint blue smudge (max B−R ≤155 at 270 px); the card is recognisable as the same card as the full-size version by pattern (black field, grey wordmark, pale cube, red wedge) without reading the tagline. FAIL if the order inverts, if the tip cannot be told apart from the vertex or from the mid-flight position, if footer specks appear, or if the seam dominates the thumbnail. (3) First-frame test (cover only, in a grid). Show only the t = 5.0 s arrived-frame cover, sound off, for 3 seconds, in a grid of at least 9 covers including other black posters. PASS only if ALL hold: a viewer who has seen the moving version identifies this cover as the same card without reading the tagline, by pattern alone; the reading order in the cover is cube/wedge scene first, wordmark second, tagline third; and the viewer can state the wedge is at its final position (16 px short of the vertex), not mid-flight. FAIL if the viewer reads the tagline first, cannot tell the arrived frame from the mid-flight frame, or confuses this cover with another cover in the grid. A mid-flight-frame cover shown as a control must fail this test. **LIMITS NOTED:** no retention numbers, A/B tests or loop data were found in the designs themselves — Dribbble/Behance/Awwwards show what was made and how it was framed, not measured retention; the verdict therefore rests on the pattern across 45 designs plus the five full opens, not on a metric. The article's own limits (no hold duration, no discussion of looping, no sound-off/thumbnail/poster data, no cited research, sales-page context) stand as stated in the learning and were not cured by this study. **LOOPS 103–114 COMPLETE (2026-11-08).** Final card = v111 (export sha256 9db0d40f, 159,372 bytes) + loop-113 motion spec + loop-114 cover-frame lock. Design-study total ~3,312 (loops 61–114 banned file now 1,319 titles). Loops 103–110 built, 111 built, 112 freeze, 113 freeze-the-still + motion spec, 114 freeze + cover-frame lock. Final delivery to Kind: the v111 PNG + the all-114-lessons summary document.

(2) MICRO-GAP TANGENT (thumbnail failure): the 16 px wedge-tip standoff collapses to ~3–4 px at 270 px and reads as a rendering error, clipping bug, or accidental collision — not tension. (3) INVERTED TYPOGRAPHY HIERARCHY: the tagline (#BFBFBF) is brighter than the wordmark (#8C8C8C), so the eye hits the secondary text first, violating the reading hierarchy. - **Loop 115 LEARNING (2026-11-08 ~11:12–11:48, window cc412941, SAVED to SKILL.md + chat MEMORY.md):** YouTube video — "The Principles of Design | FREE COURSE" — Envato (presenter Laura Kiong, graphic designer with 15+ years' experience), 21:46, 1.9m views, 4 years ago, 58k likes, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9EPTM91TBDU. Watched in full WITH SOUND (0:00–21:46 across three listening sessions; pre-roll/mid-roll ads skipped, all lesson content heard). Different creator from the watched list (103 Collect & Contrast, 106 Satori Graphics, 109 Gareth David Studio, 112 penna.design) — none re-used. THE LESSON: eleven principles as the foundation of a composition, each with two worked examples (mostly Envato Elements templates): balance, unity, contrast, emphasis, repetition, pattern, rhythm, movement, proportion, harmony, variety. Balance: every element carries visual weight through scale, shape, colour and texture; a lack of balance makes a poster feel as if it is falling to one side (symmetrical book cover; "Summer Party" flyer — a slightly off-centre pineapple counterbalanced by a large title on the left). Unity: the harmony produced by all elements creating a relationship "as organically as possible"; a lack of unity makes a design feel disorganised and cluttered (What New Design Museum poster — big numbers, vertically rotated months, captions beside each picture relating naturally; "back to school" flyer unified by one palette and one illustration style). Contrast: the level of difference between elements, creating visual hierarchy so the viewer knows what to look at first, through colour, shape and typeface (yellow-and-purple poster; magazine cover where the largest all-caps text reads as the title). Emphasis: attention to one specific element through colour, lines and positive/negative relationships — contrast produces emphasis (book cover breaking the repetition of heads and changing one head's colour; pineapple flyer with multiple leading lines pointing to the centre). Repetition: repeating one element for consistency (leaf-like shape four times in different colours; yellow wavy shape across a branding set). Pattern: repetition of multiple elements (wave pattern poster with a single white text box for the date; elephant-pattern business card). Rhythm: visual tempo from elements used repeatedly with variation — organised movement (coloured rectangles, yellow blocks larger than red; concert flyer with triangles in different sizes and colours, where a single central triangle alone would be heavy and static). Movement: the path the eye takes through a composition; a dynamic composition should lead the viewer to the most important element (motorcycle poster occupying two-thirds of the page, its energy and wheel leading the eye to a child on the opposite side, counterbalanced by simple text at the top; flyer where organic branches add movement in the middle while information in a capsule or underlined at the bottom grounds the poster). Proportion: a sense of unity when elements relate well — main information big and clear, supporting information smaller (poster with a large central name and smaller supporting elements; magazine spread with a large "HERO" title worked over the image). Harmony: cohesiveness — elements need not be identical but related through the same palette, similar typefaces or similar styles; related elements should be "cousins, not siblings" (book cover with large all-caps background text, yellow close to white, handwritten details and organic scribbles, all handmade and therefore related; CD cover with pastel colours in harmony, geometric shapes contrasting with an organic image, diagonal strokes going downward enhancing the shapes). Variety: contrast and tension that intrigue, as long as they enhance the theme (strict rigid grid broken by handwriting and a dynamic angled image, text blocks top-left and bottom-right, heavy blue-green background; compartments mixing colours, typefaces, text, illustration and image, with enough repetition to belong together). Conclusion: the principles are a foundation for a strong structure, a way to decode other designs, and an editing process — if something is missing, add or remove an element; every element should have a function and carry the message cleanly and clearly. APPLICATION TO GEMINI'S THREE POINTS: (1) The rift — the lesson's diagnosis matches Gemini's: the card has two unconnected weights (light-grey text hard-left at the top, heavy cube anchored right and bottom) with no shared axis, counterweight or leading line, so the eye bounces between quadrants. Direction: (a) give the two groups a shared tether — align the cube's left edge or upper structural vertex to the structural left margin at X 142, or extend a shared horizontal/vertical axis through wordmark, tagline and cube; (b) use the wedge as a leading line in the lesson's sense — the pineapple lines and the motorcycle wheel both point the eye to the focal element, whereas the card's wedge enters from the extreme top-left edge and stops 16 px short of the cube, reading as a floating vector; make its centreline originate from a logical boundary (the text block, the left margin, or a container edge) and pass through or align with the tagline/wordmark edge, creating one intentional diagonal flow from text to cube; (c) use balance as counterweight — as in the pineapple flyer, a large element on one side is balanced by a strong element on the other, so either the text system must gain visual weight or the cube must move closer to it / shrink, otherwise the 225 px black gap stays a severance rather than a pause; (d) use harmony/repetition to tie the groups — repeat a colour, angle or shape across both groups ("cousins, not siblings"), e.g. the wedge's 30° angle or the seam's blue echoed in a small repeated cue in the text zone, rather than adding unrelated decoration. The gap itself is NOT condemned by the lesson — empty space can ground a design (capsule/underlined information grounding the branch flyer) — but only if the elements on either side are tethered by axis, weight or a leading line; un-tethered, it severs. (2) The 16 px gap — the lesson never discusses near-misses, tangents or minimum clearances, but its logic points the same way as Gemini: every element must have a legible function, and emphasis/movement only work if the cue survives reading; a 16 px stop collapsing to ~3–4 px at 270 px cannot function as "tension" — it reads as an accident. Variety says tension is only good when it enhances the concept and is clearly deliberate; an ambiguous middle distance is neither a clear stop nor a collision. Direction: widen the stop to at least the 36–48 px Gemini proposes, or close/overlap the tip — do not keep an in-between distance that only reads at one size. (3) The inverted hierarchy — the lesson's strongest direct support, through contrast, emphasis and proportion: contrast creates hierarchy and a focal point; without it the viewer does not know what to read first; proportion requires the main information big and clear and supporting information smaller. The tagline (#BFBFBF) brighter than the wordmark (#8C8C8C) is exactly the inversion the lesson warns against. Direction: flip the tonal weight — wordmark brightest/crispest, tagline dropped to a darker receded grey (e.g. #757575 or lower). ONE CAUTION: the footer is already #757575 at 10 pt, so dropping the tagline to the same tone would merge two levels; the rebuild must keep the three text levels distinct by size/weight/position as well as tone (wordmark largest and brightest, tagline middle, footer smallest and quietest), not by tone alone. DIRECTION FOR THE REBUILD: tie text to cube with one shared left margin (X 142) or one shared diagonal axis; make the wedge a genuine leading line from a logical boundary to the cube rather than an off-canvas vector; close or clearly widen the wedge-tip gap; restore the tonal order wordmark > tagline > footer. LIMITS: no alignment system (never teaches grids, margins, axes, baselines — the very mechanism Gemini's fix (1) needs; its "balance" is judged by eye, not by measurement); no diagonal composition section (no diagonal flow, diagonal grids, or using a diagonal element to tether text to image; the leading-line and movement examples are the closest it gets, and they are brief); no empty-space/white-space principle (white space is not one of the eleven, so it never distinguishes a unifying pause from a severing dead zone, and never discusses a 225 px gap); no small-size, scaling or legibility guidance (nothing on how a gap, seam or tonal difference survives downscaling to 270 px, nothing on tangents or near-miss collisions); no tonal hierarchy in monochrome (contrast examples are colourful — yellow/purple, pastels, blue-green — and type-size based; it does not address a black poster where hierarchy must be carried by grey values alone); no motion, no seam, no blue/red accent logic (the 5-second motion spec, the cover-frame lock and the "kill or commit to the blue seam" question are all outside it; nothing about a detail that is a full-size-only reward); thin and template-bound in places (each principle gets only two quick examples, many of them Envato Elements templates rather than minimal black posters; the repetition/pattern/rhythm sections are the least relevant); the course is also an Envato Elements showcase in framing, with repeated prompts to use its templates and assets. CONFLICTS WITH THE CARD'S FROZEN ELEMENTS: its celebration of loud, busy unity, of pattern/repetition and of variety (handwriting breaking a rigid grid, mixed compartments) points towards adding elements, whereas the card's frozen minimalism (one cube, one wedge, one seam, black field) forbids that — its advice must be applied by alignment, weight and leading lines, not by adding pattern, colour or decoration. Likewise its contrast advice cannot simply be applied by brightening the wordmark or enlarging the tagline, since the wordmark's size, colour (#8C8C8C) and position, the tagline's 30 pt size and spacing, the 225 px gap, the cube's position and size, the wedge geometry and 16 px stop, the seam and the footer are all frozen by loops 112–114; any change to them is a decision for the rebuild, not something this learning step authorises. Rejected: Envato "Rules of Composition | FREE COURSE" (33 min — strong generally, but longer and framed around photography/art rules rather than unifying a text block with a graphic object in a poster); Kittl "Understanding Unity: The Principles Of Graphic Design" (3:49 — too short and thin for the rift, gap and hierarchy questions together); GCFLearnFree.org "Beginning Graphic Design: Layout & Composition" (5:15 — introductory overview, too basic and too brief); 4 The Creatives "Alignment in Graphic Design" (6:36 — alignment only, no unity, visual flow, weight or hierarchy); Gareth David Studio "Poster Grids YOU MUST USE For Professional Results!" (14:00 — grids only, and the creator is on the never-re-use list, loop 109); Satori Graphics "The FULL 2026 Guide To Layout & Composition" (creator on the never-re-use list, loop 106); Collect & Contrast, penna.design and the other loop 103/112 sources (never-re-use list). **Watched sources (never reuse):** 103 YouTube Collect & Contrast "5 Poster Design Tips…"; 104 IG Reel thecampuscreative "Master Visual Hierarchy"; 105 article Linh Nguyen "Typography Hierarchy Poster…"; 106 YouTube Satori Graphics "White Space"; 107 IG Reel creatorskilllab "YOUR DESIGN ISN'T BAD…"; 108 article Cameron Chapman Toptal "Typographic Hierarchy"; 109 YouTube Gareth David Studio "Visual Hierarchy In Poster Design"; 110 IG Reel visual.shiftt "Stop overcomplicating your layouts!…"; 111 article Daria Nuykina Clay "Visual Hierarchy in Web Design…"; 112 YouTube penna.design "Is Your Logo Unreadable?…"; 113 IG Reel tylertometich "You don't get 3 seconds. You get one."; 114 article Terra Henderson "How Motion Design Improves Video Retention"; 115 YouTube Envato (Laura Kiong) "The Principles of Design | FREE COURSE".

All other counted designs were search-result cards only, stated plainly. **VERDICT ON GEMINI'S THREE POINTS (plus the seam): (1) THE RIFT — SUPPORTED. (2) THE GAP — SUPPORTED. (3) THE INVERTED HIERARCHY — SUPPORTED, strongly. (d) THE SEAM ("kill or commit") — QUALIFIED: widen, do not remove.** TOP-5 (counted items only): (1) Poster for theatrical performance — Irina Yaremenko (Behance, opened in full, published 26 Mar 2018): the black version — giant white type fills the field edge to edge; the small secondary text sits in a column sharing the poster's left edge; one thin white diagonal line cuts down through the type block itself — a leading line inside the group, not decoration. The white version inverts to black type on white. Hierarchy is by size at full contrast (white on black / black on white); the primary is never dimmed; there is no gap anywhere — the type IS the image, contact throughout. (2) KAIJU/ROLL — Visual Identity & Branding Concept — Daria Vasileva (Behance, opened in full, published 17 Apr 2026, 130 comments): the wordmark is printed on every box face at the same diagonal angle as the box edges (the isometric diagonals, ~30°) — type and object share one diagonal system; the black monster silhouette is the counterweight; the wordmark is repeated on every face ("cousins, not siblings"). No standoff anywhere: the text sits ON the object. (3) Rose Island — También with Maël Ruffini (Awwwards, opened in full, SOTD 15 Nov 2022, 7.6/10): a ONE-colour palette, #EA5600. The black wordmark is the largest and highest-contrast element and leads; the orange image block sits directly below it with no gap (stacked contact); wordmark and image share one left edge. (4) Studio Silex — Darío™ (Behance, opened in full, published 12 Jun 2019, 268 appreciations): the first poster is only the word "SPARK" in white at top-left on an otherwise entirely empty black field. The control case: a huge empty black void works when there is only ONE group — nothing on the other side needs tethering. With two groups, an untethered void severs. (5) Brand Breeder — Six Socks Studio (Awwwards, opened in full, SOTD 7.4/10, 22 Nov 2022, palette of exactly two colours, #F2D556 and #E4E1DB): the huge black wordmark and the black image block below it share the same left and right margins. (STRUCK top-5 item, recount: Experimental poster — Shahnaz (Dribbble, opened in full): red type "LET ME SHOW YOU WHERE WE CAN" overlaps the black-and-white photograph (contact, not a standoff); three red vertical bars at the left run from the type down the full height of the photograph, sharing the type's left edge — a repeated-colour leading line tethering type to image; type and photo share the same left edge and the same width; the type is the brightest and most saturated element and leads; the photograph's greys recede. A black surround frames the whole poster. Evidence real, but already studied — not new.) ANALYSIS: (a) THE RIFT — four tethering mechanisms, in order of frequency across the 44: (i) A SHARED LEFT MARGIN / SHARED EDGE — the dominant mechanism, measured in the full opens: Shahnaz (struck, recount), the theatrical poster (type block and secondary column share the poster's left edge), Brand Breeder (wordmark and image block share the same left and right margins), Rose Island (wordmark and orange block share one left edge). (ii) OVERLAP / CONTACT — Shahnaz's type overlaps the photograph (struck); KAIJU/ROLL's wordmark printed on the boxes; the theatrical poster's type fills the field. (iii) A SHARED DIAGONAL — KAIJU/ROLL's isometric diagonals; the theatrical poster's thin diagonal through the type. (iv) COUNTERWEIGHT AND REPETITION — KAIJU/ROLL's repeated wordmark and monster silhouette; Random Posters NO. I repeats "No Doubt" as the tie. NOT ONE of the 44 designs leaves two groups separated by an empty band with no shared edge, no overlap and no diagonal. The card has all three absences at once (text left edge X 142, cube left edge X 274 — a 132 px offset — and a wedge entering from the canvas edge). Gemini point (1) is SUPPORTED; the shared margin is the primary fix, the diagonal is the secondary one. (b) THE GAP — no ambiguous small standoff was found anywhere in the 44. What exists is contact/overlap (the majority), or a large clear void (Studio Silex "SPARK": ~85% of the poster empty; Brand Breeder: wordmark and image block stacked with zero gap). No design points a sharp element at a target and stops a few pixels short; pointed elements either touch/overlap or are far away. At 270 px the card's 16 px gap is ~4 px; Gemini's 36–48 px is 9–12 px at 270 px, which is the smallest distance that still reads as a deliberate gap in the sample's thumbnails (e.g. the clear black between Shahnaz's red bars and the photograph edge at card size, ~8–10 px — struck evidence, but the measurement stands as a sample observation). Gemini point (2) is SUPPORTED; 36 px is the minimum, 42 px is the value specified (inside Gemini's 36–48 px band with margin at both ends). (c) THE INVERTED HIERARCHY — in all 44 designs the primary wordmark/title is the brightest and the largest element. Monochrome hierarchy is carried by three things: full contrast for the primary (white on black — the theatrical poster, Studio Silex; black on white/cream — Rose Island, Brand Breeder); size (the primary is roughly 3–10x the secondary); and position (primary top-left, read first). Secondary text is smaller and the same tone or dimmer — NEVER brighter than the primary. The Awwwards palettes prove the point by restraint: Brand Breeder uses two colours, Rose Island one. The card's #BFBFBF tagline over a #8C8C8C wordmark is the only inversion in the sample. Gemini point (3) is SUPPORTED, strongly. Consequence, stated plainly: fixing it revises the loop-111 hierarchy — the wordmark becomes first and the cube second at both sizes. That is the intended trade, not an accident: the sample's unified posters almost all lead with the title. (d) THE SEAM — fine details in the sample are either LONG and HIGH-CONTRAST (the theatrical poster's diagonal: full poster height, white, only ~2–3 px wide but ~800 px long — visible at any size because of length and contrast) or CHUNKY (KAIJU/ROLL's monster eye, Shahnaz's red bars, ~10 px at card size — struck). No design carries a short, 20 px, low-contrast coloured lens as a meaningful element. Small text in the theatrical poster IS unreadable at card size and simply vanishes — and the poster still works, because it is non-load-bearing. The seam is non-load-bearing (the wedge tip is the final stop at small size), so keeping it is defensible — but at 20 px it is below the sample's survival threshold. Gemini's preliminary point is QUALIFIED: widen, do not remove. 36 px (9 px at 270 px) is the supported minimum for it to read as deliberate at full size and as a visible sliver at thumbnail size. **THE ONE CHANGE FOR LOOP 115 — "TETHER, WIDEN, FLIP"** — one coherent rebuild (all coordinates 1080×1080): (A) TETHER THE CUBE TO THE TEXT MARGIN. - **Loop 116 GEMINI CRITIQUE (2026-11-08 ~12:18–12:20, SAME dedicated chat, SAVED to SKILL.md + chat MEMORY.md):** full v115 context sent FIRST, then the v115 PNG uploaded. **GEMINI'S RATING: 4.6/10 — essentially unchanged from loop 115's 4.5/10 (up 0.1).** Its opening verdict: "Looking at v115 as an actual poster — stripping away all the coordinate tables and pixel counts — it fails the core test of a high-end editorial or documentary cover. It feels like an academic UI wireframe that someone pasted a generic 3D asset into. At full size, it looks clinical and uninspired; at a tiny YouTube grid thumbnail size, the entire middle of the poster collapses into a black void with a random red stick floating in it." **IMPROVEMENTS, IN ORDER OF IMPACT:** (1) **THE DEAD VOID & THE "FLOATING GRAPHIC" SYNDROME** (single biggest weakness): "The poster is bifurcated. You have a typographic block jammed at the top, a massive dead ocean of pure black stretching across the center, and a small, isolated 3D box stranded at the bottom. The red wedge cutting diagonally across this emptiness doesn't feel like an aggressive kinetic strike; it feels like a stray line tool error. Because the background is an absolute, flat #000000 void with zero environmental texture, depth, or gradient, the cube and wedge look like they are floating in space with no spatial relationship to anything, no gravity." Fix: "Kill the dead void. Introduce subtle, sophisticated atmospheric depth behind the cube — not wallpaper, but a faint, almost invisible smoked glass panel, a barely-there radial gradient, or a subtle depth haze — to give the cube something to sit in/on, to anchor it. Or radically close the gap: move the cube up until it shares an edge/overlaps with the typography block, making one solid compositional unit rather than two disconnected islands." (2) **MATERIAL FAKE-OUT (THE PLASTIC TOY CUBE):** "For a channel called BLACK BOX focused on heavy systems and engineering failures, this cube looks like a low-poly plastic toy from a cheap mobile game, or a matte cardboard box. The top face is a flat opaque white sheet of paper, the pale grey-green face is a flat pastel (no internal reflection or refraction), and the dark blue side is a flat navy square, with no internal depth, lighting gradient, or material behaviour to suggest dense glass, steel, or a black box recorder. The only thing that reads as 'glass' is the thin blue seam, which reads like a decorative crack rather than a refraction." Fix: "Rebuild the shader logic entirely. The top face needs to stop looking like a solid white sheet — it needs a translucent glassy top, internal reflections, internal depth, and light travelling through it. Add a subtle directional light gradient across the faces, internal bevels, and caustic highlights. If you cannot make the glass believable, pivot the material completely — make it a solid brutalist black metal/steel monolith (heavy, dangerous, industrial). The current halfway material is the worst of both worlds." (3) **SAFE, PREDICTABLE GRID ALIGNMENT:** "Everything is rigidly pinned to the exact same vertical invisible wall on the left. While logically clean, visually it is the safest, most predictable choice. At thumbnail, the alignment is invisible; the viewer only sees a stack of boxes — text block, black block, cube block — aligned like form fields or a UI mockup, not a poster with hierarchy and movement." Fix: "Introduce calculated visual weight shifts. Let the focal graphic or the kinetic wedge break the alignment intentionally — let the wedge extend beyond the left edge, or let the cube shift off-axis to create deliberate visual tension. Or make the cube massive, cropping it at the edge of the frame, to create scale drama. Right now every element politely fits inside the margins, nothing feels bold, aggressive, or like it is breaking out / sliding off the edges." **DID IT CHANGE ITS MIND FROM LOOP 115? Partly, and in a pointed way.** It did NOT retract loop 115's three fixes — it credits the X:142 cube move with fixing the structural anchor/split-screen floating, and the wordmark-brightness correction with fixing the typography hierarchy. But it now treats the cure as a new disease: the rigid X:142 alignment itself is fault #3 ("predictable, mechanical grid"), and the 225 px gap it previously called a "clean empty pause" is now fault #1, a "dead void" — it explicitly suggests closing that gap or overlapping the cube with the typography, which contradicts the v115 hierarchy point (4). The widened 42 px wedge gap and 36 px seam get NO credit in the image reply; the seam is dismissed as a "decorative crack" and the wedge as a "stray line tool error" / "random red stick" at thumbnail size. Its new direction is therefore: add atmospheric depth or close the gap, rebuild the cube's material (real glass or brutalist metal — not the current halfway material), and break the grid with deliberate asymmetry or scale. **PRELIMINARY REPLY (to the context message alone, before the image was uploaded): 4.8/10**, same three faults in the same order — (1) Dead Zone and Passive Composition (225 px gap still dead, lower half "heavy, clunky isometric geometry drifting in an empty void"; fix by integrating the wedge with the typography or adding subtle gradients/grain/grid whispers); (2) Toy-Like Aesthetic of the Cube ("flat vector polygons", 10 px white stroke "like a thick cardboard cutout edge", "low-poly asset from a 2015 tech demo"; fix with real glass shading, surface gradients, internal reflections, optical falloff); (3) Predictable, Mechanical Grid Predictability ("total predictability breeds boredom"; fix by letting something break the 142 px wall, e.g. the wedge extending out of bounds, or bolder cube scale contrast — "Stop designing for the guidelines, start designing for instant visceral stopping power"). It said the loop 115 fixes left "a hyper-rational, sterile vector exercise… an architectural diagram… the soul has been mathematically engineered out of it." The image-based 4.6/10 is the authoritative loop-116 result; the preliminary 4.8/10 is recorded for completeness. **HONEST NOTES (main Muse):** Gemini's fault #1 directly contradicts its own loop-115 position (the gap was a "clean empty pause" then, a "dead void" now) and the v115 hierarchy point (4) — the study must test it against real designs rather than accept it. Fault #2 is new and substantive: no loop has ever questioned the cube's MATERIAL — the cube file has been refined for 100 loops as a flat-shaded glass render, and Gemini is the first eye to call it a plastic toy. Fault #3 attacks the loop-115 cure itself (the shared X:142 margin) — the study must test whether breaking the grid helps or whether the shared margin is what holds the composition together. The 0.1 rise means the loop-115 rebuild bought almost nothing in Gemini's eyes — the next study has to decide which of these three faults is real and which is Gemini moving the goalposts.

- **Loop 116 LEARNING (2026-11-08 ~12:21–12:38, window 9257c6e4, SAVED to SKILL.md + chat MEMORY.md):** Instagram Reel — "How to create this nice glass effect in Photoshop?" — easyeditpro (New York), https://www.instagram.com/reel/C0gwKpGNsxz/, about 29 seconds (Instagram shows no duration; the voiceover restarts at about 0:29), 67K likes, 158 comments, 14 reposts, 570 shares, 6 December 2023. Watched in full WITH SOUND twice (plus an initial partial play). English voiceover (synthetic-sounding; the live transcript garbles some words) over a screen-recorded Photoshop demonstration, with the full recipe also written in the caption. THE LESSON: glass is not a flat fill — it is a distortion of what lies behind it, driven by a texture you build yourself: (1) "Select area and add black and white gradient with opacity, set gradient angle 180." (2) "Duplicate and rotate your gradient shapes." (3) "Select all layers, convert them to a smart object and add Gaussian blur with radius 1." (4) "Save the texture on your computer." (5) "Open photo you want edit, select the area, copy and paste." (6) "Convert to a Smart Object." (7) "Go to the filter gallery, set Glass Distortion." (8) "Add your saved texture, and do some experiments for a different result." (9) "To add blur to your text convert it to a smart object, go to the blur gallery and choose Iris blur." On screen: the Filter Gallery Glass settings used were Distortion 16, Smoothness 2, Texture: Texture 2, Scaling 64%, Invert off. The finished frame shows a photograph and text seen through a wavy, rippled glass — highlights broken up, edges bent — rather than a tinted rectangle laid over it. APPLICATION: Fault (2) MATERIAL FAKE-OUT — the direct hit and the strongest lesson. The card's cube faces are uniform fills (top #F5F5F5, pale face ~(199,201,189), dark face (46,90,120)), exactly the "flat opaque white sheet / flat pastel / flat navy square" Gemini attacked. The Reel's answer: build a black-and-white gradient displacement map (angle 180, duplicated and rotated so the distortion is non-uniform, blurred at radius 1 so it is smooth, not noisy), save it, and drive Glass Distortion through it as a Smart Object filter. Applied to the 746×420 cube at (142,580), each face would keep its base tone but gain internal variation — light apparently travelling and bending across the face — instead of a new colour or a decorative overlay. The 36 px blue seam is the most direct application: rather than a solid #1D4ED8 pointed lens (540,835, narrowing to points at C (565,767) and B (515,903)), treat the C–B fold as a refraction zone — distortion plus a directional gradient — so it reads as light bending at the fold, not as "a decorative crack". The Iris-blur step is a second, smaller lesson: selective blur is a depth cue, so different focal planes (wedge vs cube vs tagline) could be separated by blur rather than by spacing alone. Fault (1) THE DEAD VOID — only partial. The Reel does not teach smoked-glass panels, radial gradients, depth haze or grain on a black field; its glass sits over a photograph, not over black. What it does point to is a direction: make the black field itself a barely-there distorting/textured medium rather than a flat void — e.g. a very low-opacity, large-scale version of the same gradient texture/haze behind the cube, in the 225 px gap (tagline ink bottom Y 354 to cube top Y 580), so the cube sits in something without the background becoming wallpaper. At the Reel's full strength the effect reads as water/rippled glass and would destroy the card's frozen minimalism; the transferable version is low-strength and large-scale, and that restraint is an INFERENCE, not something the Reel demonstrates. Fault (3) SAFE, PREDICTABLE GRID — not taught. The Reel's own demonstration is a single centred texture; it says nothing about asymmetry, off-axis placement, cropping a massive focal object, or when breaking a grid helps vs destroys a composition. The shared X 142 margin, the 42 px wedge gap, and any off-axis shift of the cube get no guidance from this source. DIRECTION FOR THE REBUILD: rebuild the cube faces as glass-distortion surfaces (gradient displacement map, Smart Object, Glass filter, experimenting with Distortion/Smoothness/Scaling around the Reel's 16/2/64%), keeping the existing base tones; rework the seam as a refraction zone rather than a solid lens; add a faint textured haze behind the cube in the gap at very low opacity; use Iris blur sparingly for plane separation. Do not copy the Reel's wavy "Ocean Ripple"-style look at full strength. LIMITS: Photoshop-only 2D filter, not true 3D glass: no true refraction, caustics, internal reflection, bevels or directional light gradient, and no guidance on the brutalist black-metal pivot Gemini offered as an alternative. No black-field atmosphere, no grain, no grid-breaking. Only ~29 seconds long, so "in depth" means a complete reproducible recipe, not a principles lecture. The voiceover is short and synthetic-sounding and its live transcript is unreliable on numbers (one play transcribed the Gaussian blur as "radius 4"; the caption's radius 1 is the reliable figure). The effect is demonstrated on a photograph and text, not on a geometric cube, so transferring it to flat-shaded faces is an inference to be tested, not a demonstrated result. It also never discusses when distortion tips over into noise or wallpaper — the exact risk for the 225 px gap. Rejected: George Designer "Create Realistic Glassmorphism & Textured Glass Effects in Photoshop" (instagram.com/reel/Detnbf5xeCF/) — same Glass-filter idea but thinner: preset only (Distortion 18, Smoothness 8, Scaling 57%), no custom texture recipe, garbled/mixed-language voiceover, low engagement. Noor (noor.creative.design) "How to create cinematic posters with glass effect" (instagram.com/reel/DbGZHA0Mtdm/) — music-only (Billie Eilish, "Armani White"), no voiceover or on-screen steps. Aayush (aayushh.exe) "Create a Realistic Glass Effect in Photoshop!" (instagram.com/reel/DezD--buoYq/) — music-only (Tame Impala, "Dracula"), no voiceover and no written recipe. Diana Trish, spotlight effect Reel (instagram.com/reel/DZ9w2BKIcZe/) — a single gradient-and-blur spotlight trick for depth; no glass material and no grid teaching. Mariana (mariana.rar), split-object floating product poster (instagram.com/reel/DaAgIEGttgx/) — music-only (Harry Styles, "Watermelon Sugar"); teaches layering/shadow depth only, no glass material or grid principle. SB (sb.graphicdesign) "How to use grid systems" (instagram.com/reel/DbvMPwCoWJ-/) — music-only, static 2×2 poster collage with the lesson in the caption; teaches using grids, not breaking them. Shaurya Soni "Glassmorphism in Adobe Illustrator" (instagram.com/reel/DXeWfLJieJM/) — UI-focused soft blur/transparency only, no refraction or depth. GraphiVox fluid-gradient poster Reel — colourful liquid gradient; atmosphere only, no glass/material/grid, and its colour would fight the black card. Chrome/metallic text-effect Reels — metallic text, not object material, and no depth or grid teaching.
